b-j-habibie: Bacharuddin Jusuf Habibie was born on 25 June 1936 in Parepare, South Sulawesi, the son of Alwi Abdul Jalil Habibie, an agriculturist of Bugis-Gorontalese descent, and R. A. Tuti Marini Puspowardojo, a Javanese noblewoman from Yogyakarta. He began to study aviation at Delft in the Netherlands but, because of the dispute between the two countries over West New Guinea, moved to the Technische Hochschule Aachen in Germany, where he took an engineer's degree in 1960 and a doctorate in aerospace engineering in 1965. In 1962 he married Hasri Ainun Besari, a medical doctor.

He joined Messerschmitt-Bölkow-Blohm in Hamburg, where he worked on the Airbus A-300B and reached a middle management post in 1974. That year President Suharto recruited him to return as part of a drive to industrialise Indonesia. Two years later he became head of the new state aircraft maker, known as IPTN, which built Puma helicopters and CASA planes and in 1995 produced a small passenger aircraft, the N-250, a commercial failure.

From 1978 he was state minister of research and technology. By 1991 he oversaw ten state-owned industries, among them shipbuilding, steel, arms and energy; an estimate of 1993 put their cost at nearly 2 billion dollars a year in state funds. In 1990 he was elected the first chair of the Indonesian Association of Muslim Intellectuals, a modernist organisation that gave him a political base. When Suharto signalled in January 1998, during the Asian financial crisis, that he wanted him as vice-president, the rupiah fell.

As president he also forbade the official use of the terms pribumi and non-pribumi, lifted restrictions on the teaching of Mandarin Chinese and passed laws giving autonomy to regencies and cities. He had opposed independence for East Timor and offered special autonomy; the armed forces' leaders were not consulted on his decision to hold a referendum. After the vote of 30 August 1999 pro-Indonesian militias killed and displaced large numbers of people, and on 12 September he accepted a peacekeeping force mandated by the United Nations.

A leaked telephone call with his attorney general raised doubts about the investigation of Suharto. The Bank Bali scandal of 1999, in which bank funds reached members of his re-election team, damaged him further. In October 1999 the assembly known as the MPR rejected his accountability speech by 355 votes to 322, and he withdrew his candidacy; Abdurrahman Wahid succeeded him. He died in the Gatot Soebroto Army Hospital on 11 September 2019 and was buried at the Kalibata Heroes' Cemetery beside his wife.
baal: Baal is a title meaning owner or lord in the Northwest Semitic languages of the ancient Levant. It was used of people before it was applied to gods. By the third millennium BCE the name appears as a proper name in a list of deities at Abu Salabikh. Most scholars hold that this Baal was the storm and fertility god Hadad, whose true name may have come to be thought too holy to speak, as Bel was used for Marduk among the Babylonians. By the 1st millennium BCE the two were distinct: Aramaeans worshipped Hadad and Phoenicians and other Canaanites Baal.

The Ugaritic texts show Baal as a weather god with power over lightning, wind, rain and fertility, called rider of the clouds and Victorious Baal. The dry summers were explained as his time in the underworld, and his return in autumn brought the storms. In Canaan he eventually supplanted El as leader of the gods and patron of kingship. The Baal Cycle is one of the longest surviving epics of the ancient Near East. In it Baal defeats Yammu, the sea, and Mot, the death god. Worship spread to Egypt by the Middle Kingdom and across the Mediterranean with Phoenician colonisation. At Carthage Baal Hammon was the supreme god, with Tanit as consort.

The name occurs about 90 times in the Hebrew Bible. In 1 Kings 18 the prophet Elijah contests the priests of Baal before Jezebel, and the story ends in rain. Many scholars think Jezebel's Baal was Melqart of Tyre; John Day argues it was Baal Shamem. Some scholars hold that the early Hebrews also used the title for Yahweh, though others say this is uncertain. In later tradition names with Baal were changed, so that one Israelite name became Ish-bosheth, bosheth meaning shame.

Baal Zebub, the god of Ekron, became in Christian tradition Beelzebub, whom the New Testament writers identified with Satan. Classical writers rendered the various Baals as Belus. The Quran presents Baal as a false god opposed by Elijah. In modern Hebrew, baal is the commonest word for husband.
baalbek: Baalbek lies east of the Litani River in Lebanon's Beqaa Valley, about 67 km northeast of Beirut. The hilltop of Tell Baalbek shows signs of almost continual habitation over the last eight to nine thousand years. It was well watered by a stream from the Rās al-ʿAyn spring and, in spring, by meltwater from the Anti-Lebanon. Its position in a fertile valley, on a major watershed and along the route from Tyre to Palmyra should have made it wealthy early, yet it is never mentioned in any known Assyrian or Egyptian record, unless under another name.

In the Canaanite period the local temples were devoted chiefly to the Heliopolitan Triad: a male god, Baʿal, his consort Astarte and their son Adon. The site of the present Temple of Jupiter was probably the focus of earlier worship. After Alexander the Great's conquest in the 330s BCE the city, as Heliopolis, formed part of the Diadochi kingdoms of Egypt and Syria. The Romans annexed it, and the settlers of the colony Colonia Julia Augusta Felix Heliopolitana were probably veterans of the 5th and 8th Legions under Augustus. Coins of nearly every emperor from Nerva to Gallienus were struck there.

Muslim forces occupied Baalbek in 634, 636 or 637, according to different accounts, either peacefully or after a defence. The ruined temple complex was fortified as al-Qala', "The Fortress", but the Umayyad caliph Marwan II sacked it with great violence in 748, dismantling it and largely depopulating the town. Fatimid Egypt conquered it in 942. The Byzantines under John I sacked and razed it in 974. The Ottomans took it in 1516 and gave the sanjak of Homs and local tax concessions to the Harfush family, prominent among the Shiites of the valley. Its decline in the eighteenth century is ascribed to several causes, among them the growing attraction of Zahlé.

Emperor Wilhelm II of Germany passed through Baalbek on 1 November 1898 on his way to Jerusalem and noted both the splendour of the Roman remains and the poor state of the modern settlement. An archaeological team he sent began work within a month, and Otto Puchstein and his colleagues worked until 1904, producing a carefully researched and fully illustrated series of volumes. They found nothing datable before the Roman occupation, although later excavation under the flagstones of the Great Court found three skeletons and a fragment of Persian pottery of the 6th to 4th centuries BCE.

The temples have suffered from earthquakes, from iconoclasm and from the reuse of their stone. The Temple of Jupiter still had 27 of its original 58 columns standing in the sixteenth century, nine before the earthquakes of 1759, and six now. The ruins were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984.
baath-party: The party was founded on 7 April 1947 in Damascus as the Arab Ba'ath Party, by the merger of the Arab Ba'ath Movement of Michel Aflaq and Salah al-Din al-Bitar with followers of Zaki al-Arsuzi. Aflaq was an Antiochian Orthodox Christian, al-Bitar a Sunni Muslim and al-Arsuzi an Alawite who later became an atheist. Baath means resurrection. Its ideology mixed Arab nationalist, pan-Arab, socialist and anti-imperialist interests and called for the unification of the Arab world into a single state, under the motto Unity, Freedom, Socialism. In 1953 the party merged with Akram al-Hourani's Arab Socialist Movement, becoming the Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party.

Branches were founded in Iraq, Jordan, Lebanon and other Arab countries, though the party would hold power only in Iraq and Syria. In the Syrian election of 1954 it won 15 of 142 seats and became the second-largest party in parliament. The United Arab Republic of Egypt and Syria was formed in 1958 and dissolved after the 1961 coup. During the union, military activists formed a Military Committee that took control of the party from civilians.

In Iraq the Ba'ath took power in the Ramadan Revolution of 1963 but lost it a couple of months later. In Syria the Military Committee, with Aflaq's consent, seized power in 1963. A struggle followed between the civilian faction of Aflaq and al-Bitar and the Military Committee of Salah Jadid and Hafez al-Assad. The 6th National Congress of October 1963 moved the party toward Soviet-style socialism, and the Military Committee's coup of 1966 ousted the National Command and split the party into Iraqi-dominated and Syrian-dominated parts.

Its structure was set at the 2nd National Congress in 1954. A National Command, headed by a Secretary-General, ruled between National Congresses, and each Arab state was a region, a term meant to deny these countries the status of separate nation-states. Members were forbidden to make contact between groups of the same level, so all contact passed through a higher command. There were three kinds of member: supporter, apprentice and active member. The party has held no government since the fall of the Syrian regime on 8 December 2024.
babrak-karmal: Babrak Karmal was born Sultan Hussein on 6 January 1929 in Kamari, a village in Kabul. His father, Muhammad Hussein, was a general in the Royal Afghan Army, and the family was among the wealthier ones of Kabul. His ethnic background was disputed, as he variously claimed to be a Pashtun or a Tajik.

He was imprisoned from 1953 to 1956 for activities the government judged too radical, and there a fellow prisoner, Mir Akbar Khyber, introduced him to Marxism. He took the name Babrak Karmal, which means Comrade of the Workers in Pashto, to distance himself from his bourgeois background. When the 1964 constitution legalised new parties, the People's Democratic Party of Afghanistan (PDPA) was founded in January 1965 in the home of Nur Muhammad Taraki. It soon split into the Khalq, led by Taraki and Hafizullah Amin, and the Parcham, led by Karmal.

Karmal was one of four PDPA members elected to the lower house in 1965 and sat until 1969. The Parchamites took part in Mohammad Daoud Khan's overthrow of the monarchy in 1973, but from the mid-1970s Daoud purged them. Karmal became Deputy Chairman of the Revolutionary Council after the Saur Revolution of 1978. The Khalqists then pushed the Parchamites aside. After a failed Parchamite coup Amin began a purge, and Karmal was sent into exile in Prague.

In December 1979 Soviet troops intervened in Afghanistan, assassinated Amin and installed Karmal as Chairman of the Revolutionary Council and Chairman of the Council of Ministers. He served as general secretary of the PDPA from 1979 to 1986. His government released 2,600 of 2,700 prisoners under a general amnesty, issued the Fundamental Principles of the Democratic Republic of Afghanistan and replaced the red Khalqist flag with one of black, red and green. Many Afghans nonetheless saw him as a Soviet puppet.

Soviet leaders came to blame Karmal for the failure to consolidate the government. Mikhail Gorbachev removed him in 1986 and put Mohammad Najibullah in his place, and Karmal went into exile in Moscow. Najibullah allowed him to return to Kabul on 20 June 1991. After Najibullah's government fell on 16 April 1992, Karmal was based at Hairatan and was associated with Abdul Rashid Dostum.

He later called the Saur Revolution a great crime, since the country had not been ready for revolution. He died of liver cancer in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital in early December 1996, on either 1 or 3 December according to different sources.
babur: Babur was born on 14 February 1483 in Andijan, in the Fergana Valley, the eldest son of Umar Shaikh Mirza II, ruler of Fergana, and of Qutlugh Nigar Khanum, daughter of Yunus Khan, the ruler of Moghulistan and a descendant of Genghis Khan. He came from the Turkic Barlas tribe, which was of Mongol origin and had embraced the Turco-Persian tradition. His first language was Chagatai, and he was equally fluent in Classical Persian. The nickname Babur, from the Persian word for tiger or panther, may have been easier for his Turco-Mongol army to pronounce than Zahir ud-Din Muhammad.

His father died, by one account, in a dovecote that toppled into a ravine, and in 1494 Babur became the Timurid ruler of Fergana as a boy. Two uncles and nobles who preferred his brother Jahangir threatened his succession, and he secured his throne mainly with help from his maternal grandmother. He lost Samarkand three times, the last to the Uzbek ruler Muhammad Shaybani.

In 1504 Babur conquered Kabul. After losing Samarkand for the third time he turned to India, reaching the Chenab River in Punjab in 1519. The Delhi Sultanate under Ibrahim Lodi was crumbling, and Babur received invitations from Daulat Khan Lodi, the governor of Punjab, and from Ibrahim's uncle Ala-ud-Din. In 1526 he defeated and killed Ibrahim at the First Battle of Panipat and founded the Mughal Empire. He then defeated a coalition of Rajput and Afghan warlords under Rana Sanga of Mewar at the Battle of Khanwa, through skilful troop positioning and the use of gunpowder.

After Panipat his main difficulty was holding the territory, since many Central Asian followers found Hindustan hot and alien and wanted to return to Kabul. He gave away the captured treasure generously. From Ottoman commanders he adopted the use of matchlocks and cannons in the field, not only in sieges. According to the Baburnama, his campaign in northwest India targeted Hindus and Sikhs as well as non-Sunni sects of Islam.

Babur died in Agra and was succeeded by his son Humayun. He was first buried in Agra and, as he had wished, reburied in Kabul between 1539 and 1544. He wrote the Baburnama, a memoir in Chagatai Turkic that was translated into Persian under his grandson Akbar. A passionate maker of gardens, he introduced the symmetrical four-part charbagh to the plains of northern India, where it became a trademark of Mughal architecture.
babylonia: Babylonia was an Akkadian-speaking state and cultural area based on the city of Babylon in central-southern Mesopotamia. It emerged as an Akkadian-populated but Amorite-ruled state about 1894 BCE. Mesopotamia had a long history before then: Sumerian civilisation emerged there about 5400 BCE, and the Akkadian speakers who went on to form Akkad, Assyria and Babylonia appeared somewhere between the 35th and 30th centuries BCE. In the 3rd millennium BCE Sumerian and Akkadian speakers lived in close cultural symbiosis, with widespread bilingualism, and Akkadian gradually replaced Sumerian as the spoken language around the turn of the third and second millennia, though the timing is debated.

The Akkadian Empire (2334-2154 BCE) united Akkadians and Sumerians under one rule, and later disintegrated through economic decline, climate change and civil war, followed by attacks from the Gutians. Sumer rose again with the Third Dynasty of Ur. Under Hammurabi, who flourished about 1792-1752 BCE on the middle chronology, Babylonia briefly became the major power in the region and created a short-lived empire. It fell apart rapidly after his death and reverted to a small kingdom centred on Babylon. Babylon replaced Nippur, where the god Enlil was supreme, as the major religious centre of Mesopotamia in his reign.

Like Assyria, with which it was often in rivalry, Babylonia kept written Akkadian for official use despite its Amorite founders and Kassite successors. It kept Sumerian in sacred texts although Sumerian was no longer spoken. Because Babylonia had abundant clay and little stone, its temples were massive structures of mudbrick supported by buttresses, which led to the early development of the pilaster and column, frescoes and enamelled tiles. Walls were brilliantly coloured and sometimes plated with zinc or gold. The scarcity of stone made every pebble precious and led to high perfection in gem-cutting.

Babylonian astronomers recorded centuries of observations in the cuneiform series Enūma Anu Enlil. Its Tablet 63, the Venus tablet of Ammi-Saduqa, lists the first and last visible risings of Venus over about 21 years and is the earliest evidence that a planet's phenomena were recognised as periodic. The oldest rectangular astrolabe dates to Babylonia about 1100 BCE, and the MUL.APIN contains catalogues of stars and constellations.

The Assyro-Babylonian culture of the Bronze Age and early Iron Age remained an important cultural centre even under long periods of outside rule. Babylonia, and its capital in particular, has long had a place in the Abrahamic religions as a symbol of excess and dissolute power. The Hanging Gardens of Babylon are seen as a symbol of luxurious power, and the Tower of Babel as a symbol of arrogant power.
babylonian-captivity: In the late 7th century BCE the Kingdom of Judah was a client state of the Assyrian empire. Assyria was overthrown by Babylon, and Josiah, king of Judah, was killed fighting the Egyptians at the Battle of Megiddo in 609 BCE. After Babylon defeated Pharaoh Necho at Carchemish in 605 BCE, King Jehoiakim began paying tribute to Nebuchadnezzar II. The court at Jerusalem split between a party favouring Egypt and one favouring Babylon, and Judah revolted after Egypt defeated Nebuchadnezzar in battle in 601 BCE.

Nebuchadnezzar besieged Jerusalem from late 598 BCE. Jehoiakim died during the siege and was succeeded by his son Jehoiachin, also called Jeconiah. The city fell in 597 BCE, a capture also recorded in the Babylonian Chronicles, and the king, his court and other prominent citizens, among them the prophet Ezekiel, were taken to Babylon; about 7,000 people were exiled in this first wave. Zedekiah was set on the throne.

Zedekiah later revolted and allied himself with Pharaoh Hophra. Nebuchadnezzar returned, and in 587 BCE he destroyed the city wall, the Temple and the houses of the leading citizens. Zedekiah's sons were executed before his eyes, and he was blinded and taken to Babylon. Judah became a Babylonian province. Archaeology shows widespread destruction in Judah's towns, and the population fell from roughly 110,000 to between 15,000 and 40,000, through deportation, war deaths, famine and flight. The governor Gedaliah was assassinated, and many refugees fled to Egypt.

The exiles were settled in agricultural communities, one of them Tel-Abib near Nippur. Tablets found in Babylon record rations for Jehoiachin, called king of the land of Yahudu. Without the Temple, worship moved largely into private homes, with circumcision, Sabbath observance and reading of the Psalms and Law kept up. After the Persian conquest, the Cyrus Cylinder speaks of restoring temples and returning exiled peoples but does not mention Judah; Lester Grabbe holds that the return was a trickle over decades rather than a single event. Part of the community stayed in Mesopotamia, and Jewish communities also existed in Egypt.

The period produced much Hebrew literature, including the Book of Lamentations, and many scholars place the redaction of the Torah in or after it. The Aramaic-based alphabet came into use. The philosopher Yehezkel Kaufmann wrote that with the exile the religion of Israel comes to an end and Judaism begins.
bacolod: Bacolod lies on the north-western coast of Negros, bounded on the west by the Guimaras Strait, which separates it from Western Visayas, and by the city of Talisay to the north, the town of Murcia to the east and the city of Bago to the south. Its name comes from the Hiligaynon word bakólod, meaning a hill, mound or small rise, since the resettlement was founded on a stony, hilly area, now the barangay of Granada. The climate is tropical monsoon, with a wet season from May to December and a dry season from January to the last week of April.

Church accounts describe the early town as a small riverside settlement called Magsungay, a dependency of the neighbouring Bago when Bago became a small town in 1575. The missionaries placed it under the protection of Saint Sebastian in the middle of the 18th century, after the magistrate Luis Fernando de Luna donated a relic of the saint, and it came to be called San Sebastián de Magsungay.

A battle was fought at the Matab-ang River in 1897. On 5 November 1898 the Negrense Revolutionary Army, armed with knives, bolos, spears and rifle-like nipa palm stems, captured the convent, now the Bishop's Palace, where Colonel Isidro de Castro y Cisneros and his Spanish troops surrendered. The success was attributed to the low morale of the Spanish detachment after its defeats in Panay and Luzon and to the psychological warfare of Generals Aniceto Lacson and Juan Araneta. The Cantonal Republic of Negros became a United States territory on 30 April 1901, and Bacolod again became capital of Occidental Negros.

Japanese forces occupied the city on 21 May 1942 and used the house of the sugar planter Generoso Villanueva as their headquarters for the Central Visayas. Joint Philippine and American forces liberated it on 29 May 1945. It was classified as a highly urbanized city on 27 September 1984.

Bacolod is the capital of the province of Negros Occidental and the largest city in the Negros Island Region, with 624,787 people at the 2024 census, though it governs itself independently of the province. It is divided into 61 barangays. The city is known for the MassKara Festival, held in October, in which dancers wear masks, and the Panaad Festival each April. The San Sebastian Cathedral stands on the public plaza, and the Negros Museum occupies a building put up in 1925 as the provincial agriculture building.
bactria: The Bactrian plain lay between the Amu Darya, the ancient Oxus, to the north and the Hindu Kush to the south and east. Rivers such as the Balkh, Kunduz and Sari Pul have been used for irrigation for millennia, and the land was noted for its fertility. Several trade routes from India and China, including the Silk Road, passed through Bactria, which allowed the accumulation of great wealth as early as the Bronze Age. The Bronze Age Bactria–Margiana Archaeological Complex, also called the Oxus civilization, is dated to about 2200 to 1700 BCE.

Cyrus the Great annexed Bactria in the sixth century BCE, and with Margiana it formed the twelfth satrapy of Persia. After Darius III's defeat, the satrap Bessus tried to organise resistance but was captured by other warlords and handed to Alexander the Great, who conquered the region by force and diplomacy and married Roxana, daughter of the satrap Oxyartes. After Alexander's death Bactria passed to the Seleucid Empire. About 245 BCE the satrap Diodotus I declared independence and founded the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom. Euthydemus I and his son Demetrius I crossed the Hindu Kush and began conquering the Indus valley, while the general Eucratides made himself king of Bactria.

Nomads overran the Greco-Bactrians in the 2nd century BCE, beginning with the Sakas in 160 BCE and then the Yuezhi, who held Bactria by the time of the Chinese envoy Zhang Qian, about 127 BCE. Greek political power ended, but Greek cultural influence continued for centuries, and the Bactrian language adopted the Greek alphabet. Zhang Qian described the country, which the Chinese called Daxia, as an affluent urban civilisation of about one million people living in walled cities. The Yuezhi prince Kujula Kadphises united the region in the early 1st century and laid the foundations of the Kushan Empire. In 663 the Umayyad Caliphate attacked the Buddhist Shahi dynasty in Tokharistan and captured the area round Balkh.

In the Zoroastrian tradition Bactria is one of the sixteen perfect Iranian lands created by Ahura Mazda, and the Avesta calls it beautiful Bactria, crowned with flags. It was one of the early centres of Zoroastrianism. Its capital Bactra, modern Balkh, was the centre of an Iranian Renaissance in the 8th and 9th centuries, and New Persian first emerged there as an independent literary language. The Samanid Empire was founded by descendants of Saman Khuda, a Persian from Bactria, and the spread of Persian led to the decline of Bactrian. The Bactrian camel is named for the region.
bad-arolsen: Bad Arolsen is a small town in northern Hesse, in the district of Waldeck-Frankenberg, roughly 45 kilometres west of Kassel. Until 1997 it was called simply Arolsen, Bad being the German word for spa. The oak in its civic coat of arms stands for the surrounding woods and indirectly for the fresh air for which the town is known as a climatic spa. It lies on the railway line from Kassel to Korbach.

The earliest documents naming the place date to 1131, when an Augustinian nunnery was founded there under the name Aroldessen. The nunnery was secularised in 1526, and the counts, later princes, of Waldeck converted it into a stately home. It was torn down in 1710 and replaced by a Baroque palace, built between 1713 and 1728 for Friedrich Anton Ulrich, Prince of Waldeck and Pyrmont. The town beside it was laid out on a Baroque chequered grid. A mirror-image layout planned for the east of the palace was never built, because the money ran out after the western part was done.

From 1918 to 1929 Arolsen was the capital of the Free State of Waldeck-Pyrmont, called the Free State of Waldeck after 1922, which was then incorporated into Prussia. From 1943 to 1945 the Nazis ran a subcamp of the Buchenwald concentration camp there, which held 185 prisoners in all. After the war the town lay in the American occupation zone and became part of West Germany.

Since 1946 Bad Arolsen has been the headquarters of the International Tracing Service, which searches for civilians lost to their families through war or political unrest during the Second World War. Its archives hold vast numbers of documents on Nazi persecution, and its records were opened to the public in November 2007. The Baroque palace survives, with ceiling paintings by Carlo Ludovici Castelli, and so does the Grosse Allee, a broad avenue about a mile long lined with some 880 oaks, laid out in 1676. The sculptor Christian Daniel Rauch, born in 1777, was a native of the town.
bad-ems: Bad Ems lies on both banks of the River Lahn, the natural border between the Taunus and the Westerwald, two parts of the Rhenish Slate Mountains, within the Nassau Nature Reserve. It is the administrative seat of the Rhein-Lahn district and stands on a cluster of mineral hot springs. The waters are high in sodium bicarbonate and range in temperature from 27 to 57 °C. Natural Ems salt is produced from them and is sold for drinking and inhalation.

In Roman times a castrum was built at Bad Ems as part of the Upper Germanic Limes, and distinct traces of the border remain in the woods around the town. Bad Ems was first mentioned in official documents in 880 and received its town charter in 1324. The Counts of Nassau and Katzenelnbogen rebuilt the bath. In the 17th and 18th centuries it was considered one of Germany's best-known bathing resorts, and in the 19th century it welcomed visitors from all over the world and became the summer residence of European monarchs and artists, among them Kaiser Wilhelm I, Tsars Nicholas I and Alexander II of Russia, Richard Wagner and Fyodor Dostoevsky.

Metal ores, mainly lead, silver, zinc and copper, were mined here from Roman times, with underground mining first mentioned in 1158 and continuing, with long interruptions, until 1945. In 1870 the town, then part of Prussian Hesse-Nassau, became known as the place where the Ems Dispatch originated, instigating the Franco-Prussian War. In 1876 Alexander II signed the Ems Edict, banning the use of the Ukrainian language, in the Haus Vier Türme.

Bad Ems has around 9,000 inhabitants. In 2021 it became part of the transnational UNESCO World Heritage Site Great Spa Towns of Europe, because of its hot springs and its 18th to 20th century architecture. Its former mine, known as Mercur, has been a museum since 1996.
bad-homburg-vor-der-hohe: Bad Homburg lies on the southern slope of the Taunus mountains and is the district town of the Hochtaunuskreis in Hesse. It belongs to the Frankfurt Rhein-Main urban area. Its official name, Bad Homburg v.d.Höhe, distinguishes it from other places called Homburg; the name derives from the Hohenberg Castle, and the suffix vor der Höhe was probably first recorded in a document of 1399. The prefix Bad, meaning bath, was conferred in 1912.

Local tradition places the first documented mention in 782, as the Villa Tidenheim of the Lorsch codex. The local historian Rüdiger Kurth questioned this, and University of Frankfurt excavations begun in 2002 found no settlement between the start of the Christian era and the 13th century. The first solid evidence is the Eberbach chronicles, which name Wortwin von Hohenberch as founder about 1180. Homburg acquired market rights about 1330. In 1622 it became the capital of the Landgraviate of Hesse-Homburg, whose first landgrave was Friedrich I; the landgraviate passed to the Kingdom of Prussia in 1866 after the Austro-Prussian War.

The spa industry began with the discovery of the Elisabethenbrunnen in 1834. The brothers François and Louis Blanc built the first spa building and casino in 1841–1842, and the town was linked to Frankfurt by railway in 1860. Russian nobility favoured it, and Edward VII of the United Kingdom took fasting cures there 32 times. In 1888 Kaiser Wilhelm II made the castle his imperial summer residence. A Jewish community, permanent from the early 16th century, had a Judengasse from 1703 and a Hebrew printing house in the early 18th century; of the 74 Jews who remained on 17 May 1939, 42 were deported in 1942 and 1943 and did not return.

After the two world wars the spa trade declined, and the town became the seat of financial and administrative bodies: in 1947 the Bizone Economic Council placed its Special Money and Credit Centre there, managed by Ludwig Erhard, and several federal debt and equalization offices stayed after the founding of West Germany. The Bad Homburger Golf Club is Germany's oldest golf club, and the Russian Chapel, laid down in 1896, and a garden pavilion sent by King Chulalongkorn of Siam in thanks for a cure, erected in 1914, recall the town's international guests. Among those born there are the physician Paul Ehrlich and the writer Shmuel Yosef Agnon.
bad-kreuznach: Bad Kreuznach lies between the Hunsrück, Rhenish Hesse and the North Palatine Uplands, at the mouth of the Ellerbach where it empties into the lower Nahe, about 14 kilometres south-southwest of Bingen am Rhein. It stands in the Nahe wine region, known for Riesling, Silvaner and Müller-Thurgau wines. The town is the seat of its district and acts as the administrative, cultural and economic centre of a region with more than 150,000 inhabitants. Its best-known landmark is the Alte Nahebrücke, a medieval bridge from around 1300 that carries houses built between 1582 and 1612.

There is evidence of a Celtic settlement here as early as the 5th century BCE. About 58 BCE the area became part of the Roman Empire and a Roman vicus arose on the road between Mainz and Trier, named according to legend after a Celt called Cruciniac. About 250 CE a very large luxurious villa-style palace was built, and in 370 Emperor Valentinian I had an auxiliary castrum built to help defend the frontier against Alemannic raids. After Rome's fall, Kreuznach became a royal estate in the Frankish realm around the year 500, and Louis the Pious stayed at its royal palace in 819 and 839.

In the 11th century the settlement passed to the High Foundation of Speyer and shortly after 1105 to the Counts of Sponheim. They built the castle Kauzenburg between 1206 and 1230, and a New Town grew up on the Nahe's north bank. Kreuznach received town rights, market rights and tolling rights in 1235 and 1270, and withstood a siege by Archbishop-Elector Baldwin of Trier in 1320. In 1375 the townsfolk rose against the town council, and Count Walram I of Sponheim had four leaders beheaded. The Reformation was introduced in 1557. Karl Marx married Jenny von Westphalen in the Pauluskirche on 19 June 1843.

Bad Kreuznach is a spa town, advertised as the world's oldest radon-brine spa, and a centre for the care of rheumatic illness. Its baths contain the noble gas radon, and graduation towers stand in the Salinental. Winegrowing is also important: its 777 hectares of vineyard make it the largest winegrowing centre in the Nahe region. Its economy rests mainly on small and medium businesses, with chemical, optical and machine-building industries.
bad-mergentheim: Mergentheim is mentioned in chronicles as early as 1058, as the residence of the family of the counts of Hohenlohe. In 1219 the brothers Andreas, Heinrich and Friedrich von Hohenlohe joined the Teutonic Order and gave it their two castles near Mergentheim. One was abandoned and the other became the seat of the Order's local commander. Mergentheim received town privileges in 1340 and rapidly became the most important of the Order's eleven commanderies.

Around the time the Deutschmeister moved there, Grand Master Albrecht von Zollern-Brandenburg resigned, left the Order, introduced the Reformation and, supported by the King of Poland, turned the Order's eastern territories into a secular duchy. The Order's rulers in Germany, now styling themselves Hoch- und Deutschmeister, made Mergentheim the new headquarters and expanded the castle into a palatial residence.

For the next centuries the town served as the centre of the Order's southern German lands, much like the residence of a ruling prince. Maximilian Franz, a son of Maria Theresa, loved the place, and for the general chapter of 1791 he brought the orchestra of the Archbishopric of Cologne, in which Ludwig van Beethoven played viola. Napoleon dissolved the Order in the states of the Rheinbund in 1809.

Mergentheim's fortunes declined after 1809, but they revived in 1826, when a shepherd, Franz Gehring, discovered rich mineral springs nearby. The water proved to be the strongest sodium-sulfate water in Europe and was reported to help in treating digestive disorders. The town became an officially recognised spa in 1926 and took the name Bad Mergentheim. Its best-known building is the Mergentheim Palace, the Teutonic Order's former home, a complex built over eight hundred years, which now houses the museum of the Order. The inventor of the Linotype, Ottmar Mergenthaler, was born in the village of Hachtel, now part of the town.
bad-pyrmont: Bad Pyrmont stands on the river Emmer, about 10 km west of the Weser, in the district of Hamelin-Pyrmont in Lower Saxony, Germany. It has a population close to 19,000. It gained its reputation as a fashionable place for princely holidays in the 17th and 18th centuries, and it is the centre of the Religious Society of Friends, the Quakers, in Germany. Its economy is geared largely to tourism, and Bad Pyrmonter mineral water is bottled in the town.

The town was formerly called simply Pyrmont and was the seat of a small county for much of the Middle Ages. The county gained its independence from the County of Schwalenberg in 1194 and kept it until the comital line died out in 1494. It then passed by inheritance to Spiegelberg, in 1557 to Lippe and in 1583 to the County of Gleichen.

In 1625 it became part of the much larger County of Waldeck, also by inheritance. In 1668 the Imperial Chamber Court rejected the claim of the Bishopric of Paderborn that Pyrmont had been pledged as security for a loan, and confirmed the rights of the Count of Waldeck, who gave the Amt of Lügde, until then the county's capital, to the bishopric in compensation. In January 1712 Emperor Charles VI raised the Count of Waldeck and Pyrmont, who had combined the two titles the previous year, to hereditary prince.

From 1805 to 1812 Pyrmont was again a separate principality, after the death of the previous prince. The two parts were reunited in 1812, and Waldeck-Pyrmont kept its status after the Congress of Vienna in 1815 and joined the German Confederation. The people of Pyrmont protested in 1813 at their lack of autonomy, and until a formal union in 1849 the two territories remained constitutionally separate.

From 1868 Prussia administered the principality, under a ten-year contract that was repeatedly renewed, and in 1871 it became a state of the German Empire. The prince abdicated during the German Revolution at the end of World War I, and after a local plebiscite the town and district of Pyrmont were detached and incorporated into the Prussian Province of Hanover.

The spa has a large Kurpark with an outdoor palm garden. The Baroque castle, built in 1706–10, is part of a substantial complex of fortifications dating from the 16th century and now houses the Museum of Municipal and Spa History. The physicist Max Born, a Nobel Prize winner, spent his last years in the town.
bad-reichenhall: Bad Reichenhall is the administrative centre of the Berchtesgadener Land district in Upper Bavaria, Germany. It lies near Salzburg in a basin ringed by the Chiemgau Alps, among them Mount Staufen (1,771 m) and Mount Zwiesel (1,781 m). It is a traditional centre of salt production, in which water saturated with salt from brine ponds is evaporated.

The earliest known inhabitants belonged to the Glockenbecher culture, a Bronze Age culture, from about 2000 BCE. In the La Tène period, about 450 BCE, organised salt production began using the local brine pools, and a Celtic place of worship stood at the Langacker. From 15 BCE to 480 CE the area was part of the Roman province of Noricum. A monastery of St Zeno was founded in 1136.

Between 1617 and 1619 a wooden pipeline 31 km long, with a fall of more than 200 m, was built to carry brine to Traunstein. In 1834 a major fire destroyed two thirds of the town's buildings. Tourism began in the early 19th century, and Reichenhall became a health resort; from 1890 it was called Bad Reichenhall. The Predigtstuhl Cable Car, an aerial tramway up the Predigtstuhl mountain, opened in 1928.

Allied bombing on 25 April 1945 killed 200 people and nearly destroyed the town centre, with its hospitals and railway station, while the barracks were undamaged. The area was under American military governance from 1945 to 1948, and the Americans set up a displaced persons camp where Holocaust survivors lived for several years before emigrating. David Ben-Gurion visited it in 1947 and saw the artworks of Samuel Bak, one of the survivors there.

The town was named Alpine Town of the Year in 2001 and later joined the Alpine Pearls. It remains a spa town and a traditional centre of salt production, and the nearest airport is Salzburg Airport, 12 km to the north-east.
badajoz: Badajoz is the capital of the province of Badajoz in the autonomous community of Extremadura, Spain. It stands on the left bank of the river Guadiana, close to the Portuguese border, 61 kilometres from Mérida and 227 kilometres east of Lisbon. Its municipal territory of 1,470 square kilometres, one of the largest in Spain, includes the main city and about 26 secondary settlements. Archaeological finds in the area date to the Bronze Age, megalithic tombs to as far back as 4000 BCE, and excavations have revealed remnants from the Lower Paleolithic. Artifacts also come from the Roman town of Colonia Civitas Pacensis in the area.

The Muladi nobleman Ibn Marwan founded Badajoz, known to its Muslim rulers as Batalyaws, around 875, after he had been expelled from Mérida, and it was the seat of an autonomous rebel state until the 10th century. In 1021, or possibly 1031, it became the capital of the small Taifa of Badajoz, with some 25,000 inhabitants, noted for high cultural production under the Aftasids despite military and political instability. Alfonso VI of León invaded it in 1086, the Almoravids in 1092 and the Almohads in 1147. The Kingdom of León conquered it in 1230, and it became a royal demesne and the seat of an opulent diocese.

The city endured spells of calamity from civil wars and conflicts with Portugal; the Portuguese attacked in 1660, and the Peace Treaty of Badajoz between Spain and Portugal was signed on 6 June 1801. In 1812 Arthur Wellesley, Earl of Wellington, besieged the French garrison of about 5,000 men from 16 March. The assault of 6 April on the breaches cost some 5,000 of 15,000 British soldiers and failed, but an attack on the castle and an undamaged wall took the town. The victorious troops then sacked it, killing and raping civilians; some 200 to 300 civilians were probably killed or injured, and it took three days to restore order. Wellington wrote that he hoped never again to put his troops to such a test.

In the Spanish Civil War the Nationalists took Badajoz. After the battle several thousand inhabitants were taken to the bullring, and on 14 August 1936 hundreds of Republicans were shot there. It is estimated that over 4,000 people were murdered by the Nationalists afterwards. Their commander, Juan Yagüe, later became Minister of Aviation and was popularly known as the Butcher of Badajoz.

Badajoz is the most populated city of Extremadura, with 150,376 inhabitants in 2010, and a major commercial centre in southwestern Spain and a bridge for trade and cultural relations with Portugal. A heavy flood on 6 November 1997 devastated several neighbourhoods and killed 21 people. The Badajoz-Elvas-Campo Maior eurocity initiative seeks closer cross-border cooperation with Elvas and Campo Maior.
baden-wurttemberg: Baden-Württemberg is a landlocked state east of the Rhine, which forms the southern part of Germany's western border with France. It also borders Switzerland, Rhineland-Palatinate, Hesse and Bavaria. Baden runs along the flat right bank of the Rhine from the north-west to Lake Constance, while Württemberg and Hohenzollern lie further inland among hillier country such as the Swabian Jura. The Black Forest formed part of the border between Baden and Württemberg, and most of the major cities stand along the Neckar, which flows past Tübingen, Stuttgart, Heilbronn, Heidelberg and Mannheim.

Around 100 CE the Roman Empire occupied Württemberg and built a limes along its northern border. In the third century the Alemanni forced the Romans back beyond the Rhine and Danube, and in 496 the Alemanni were defeated by a Frankish invasion led by Clovis I. The region later formed part of the Holy Roman Empire and stayed largely Catholic after the Reformation, though northern and central Württemberg has been Protestant since 1534, with its centre at the Tübinger Stift.

At the start of the 20th century the area consisted of the Grand Duchy of Baden, the Kingdom of Württemberg and the Prussian province of Hohenzollern, all part of the German Empire since 1871. In the revolution of 1918 their monarchs were deposed, and after 1933 their democratic institutions were abolished. After the Second World War the Allies created South Baden, Württemberg-Baden and Württemberg-Hohenzollern, and in April 1952 these merged to form Baden-Württemberg as a state of West Germany.

Baden-Württemberg has more than 11 million inhabitants. Stuttgart is the capital and largest city, followed by Mannheim and Karlsruhe, where Germany's supreme constitutional court sits. The state is divided into four administrative districts: Freiburg, Karlsruhe, Stuttgart and Tübingen. Heidelberg, founded in 1386, is the oldest university within the territory of modern Germany, and Freiburg and Tübingen followed in 1457 and 1477. Alemannic and Franconian dialects are spoken, and the Black Forest and Lake Constance are popular destinations.
baghdad: Baghdad stands on a vast, almost entirely flat and low-lying plain bisected by the Tigris, formed by the periodic flooding of the river. The river divides the city into an eastern half, Risafa, and a western half, Karkh. The Diyala river, a tributary of the Tigris, flows south-east of the city and borders its eastern suburbs.

After the fall of the Umayyads the victorious Abbasids sought a new capital. On 30 July 762 the Caliph al-Mansur commissioned the construction of Baghdad, guided by the Iranian Barmakids, believing the site ideal for ruling the Islamic Empire. He hired two designers, Naubakht, a Zoroastrian, and Mashallah, a Jew from Khorasan, who chose an auspicious founding date under the sign of Leo. The historian al-Tabari recorded a prophecy of Christian monks about a leader named Miklas who would build a great city there, and al-Mansur, once called Miklas, saw it as a good omen.

Baghdad became the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and an intellectual and cultural centre, with institutions such as the House of Wisdom and a multi-ethnic, multi-religious population. For much of the Abbasid era, the Islamic Golden Age, it was one of the largest cities in the world, and its population peaked at more than a million. The Round City, its original core, ceased to exist as a result of the Mongol siege. The Mongol Empire largely destroyed Baghdad in 1258, and a long decline followed, marked by frequent plagues and shifts of power between successive empires.

Later Baghdad was the administrative centre of Ottoman Iraq, with authority over the provinces of Basra, Mosul and Shahrizor. During the First World War it was made the capital of Mandatory Iraq. After Iraq was recognised as an independent monarchy in 1932 the city gradually regained some of its prominence as a centre of Arab culture. It suffered severe damage in the Iraq War, which began with the invasion of 2003, and lost much cultural heritage and many historical artifacts.

Baghdad is the capital and largest city of Iraq and its seat of government, on the banks of the Tigris. Its estimated population is 8 million. Historic mosques, churches, mandis and synagogues reflect its diversity, and the Masjid al-Kadhimayn, the Buratha Mosque, the Shrine of Abdul-Qadir Gilani and the Abu Hanifa Mosque are visited by millions each year. The University of Baghdad is the largest university in Iraq, and the city joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network as a City of Literature in December 2015.
bahadur-shah-ii: Bahadur Shah Zafar, born on 24 October 1775, was the second son of Akbar II and succeeded him in 1837. By then the Mughal Empire had been reduced to the city of Delhi and the territory around it as far as Palam. The East India Company was the dominant power in India, provided the emperor with a pension, and collected taxes in Delhi and maintained a military force there. Zafar had no interest in statecraft or imperial ambition.

He was a noted Urdu poet and wrote many ghazals. His court was home to Mirza Ghalib, Daagh Dehlvi, Momin Khan Momin and Mohammad Ibrahim Zauq, who was also his mentor. He was a devout Sufi, and in one of his verses he stated that Hinduism and Islam share the same essence.

When sepoys of the rebellion reached Delhi in May 1857, Zafar asked why they had come, since he had no means to maintain them. He yielded to their demands when told that they could not defeat the Company without him. On 16 May sepoys and palace servants killed fifty-two Europeans held prisoner in the palace, despite his protests. It was later believed that he was not directly responsible but might have prevented the killings.

As the siege of Delhi turned against the rebels, Zafar took refuge at Humayun's Tomb. Company forces under Major William Hodson captured him on 20 September 1857. The next day Hodson shot his sons Mirza Mughal and Mirza Khizr Sultan and his grandson Mirza Abu Bakht.

Zafar's trial in the Red Fort in 1858 lasted 21 days. He was charged with aiding the mutinies, encouraging war against the British Government, assuming the sovereignty of Hindostan, and being accessory to the murder of Christians. In his defence he stated that he was helpless before the will of the sepoys. Because of Hodson's guarantee on his surrender, he was exiled to Rangoon rather than sentenced to death.

He died on 7 November 1862 at the age of 87 and was buried that afternoon near the Shwedagon Pagoda. His exile ended the nearly 500-year Timurid line, and he is seen as a hero of the rebellion of 1857.
bahadur-shah-of-gujarat: Born Bahadur Khan into the Muzaffarid dynasty, he was the son of Prince Khalil Khan, who became sultan in 1511 as Muzaffar Shah II, and of Rani Lakshmi Bai, daughter of a Gohel Rajput. His grandfather, Sultan Mahmud Begada, kept him at court. When his elder brother Sikandar Shah was named heir, Bahadur Khan feared for his life and fled, first to Chittor and then to Ibrahim Lodi; he was present at the Battle of Panipat without taking part in the fighting.

Muzaffar Shah II died in 1526. Sikandar Shah was murdered after a few weeks on the instructions of his slave Imad-ul-Mulk Khush Kadam, who put an infant brother on the throne as Mahmud Shah II. Bahadur Khan returned, the nobles joined him, and he marched on Champaner, executed Imad-ul-Mulk and had the child poisoned.

Bahadur Shah campaigned in the Deccan in 1528 and 1529, taking the fort of Ahmednagar and forcing the rulers of Ahmadnagar and Berar to sign a humiliating treaty. The fortress of Mandu fell on 28 March 1531, when Sultan Mahmud Shah II of Malwa and his seven sons were captured; they were later put to death by their guards during a rescue attempt. In 1532 he raised a siege of Chittor in return for an enormous ransom. Until his defeat by Humayun the power of Gujarat was at its height, with the rulers of Ahmednagar and Burhanpur acknowledging him as overlord.

The quarrel with Humayun began because Bahadur Shah had sheltered the Mughal prince Muhammad Zaman Mirza. The rout near Mandasur is usually explained by the treachery of Rumi Khan, the Turkish head of the Gujarat artillery. Bahadur Shah fled to Mandu, Champaner and finally Diu. When Humayun left to face the revolt of Sher Shah Suri, the country rose, and Bahadur Shah defeated the Mughals at Kanij and expelled them from Gujarat.

The Treaty of Bassein was signed on 23 December 1534 aboard the galleon St. Mattheus. Having recovered his kingdom, Bahadur Shah regretted the alliance. In February 1537 he visited the Portuguese viceroy's ship off Diu and was attacked and killed on his way back, on 13 February; his body was thrown into the sea. According to the Mirat-i-Sikandari, the viceroy had intercepted his message inviting the Deccan sultans to ally against the Portuguese. He left no son, and after his chosen heir, his nephew Miran Muhammad Shah of Khandesh, died on the way to Gujarat, the nobles chose Mahmud Shah III, son of his brother Latif Khan.
bahrain: Bahrain is a generally flat and arid archipelago in the Persian Gulf, lying between Qatar and the northeastern coast of Saudi Arabia. A low desert plain rises gently to a low central escarpment, whose highest point is the 134 metre Mountain of Smoke (Jabal ad Dukhan). About 92 per cent of the country is desert, with periodic droughts and dust storms. Land reclamation has enlarged the area from 665 to 780 square kilometres, and by August 2008 the number of islands and island groups had risen from 33 to 84.

The name Bahrain is the dual form of the Arabic word bahr, 'sea', so al-Bahrayn originally means 'the two seas'. Which two seas is disputed: the bay east and west of the island, the seas north and south of it, and the salt and fresh water above and below the ground have all been proposed. The term appears five times in the Quran but does not refer to the modern island, which the Arabs originally called Awal. Until the late Middle Ages 'Bahrain' meant a region of Eastern Arabia stretching from Basra in Iraq to the Strait of Hormuz.

Bahrain was home to Dilmun, a Bronze Age trade centre linking Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley, and was later ruled by the Sumerians and Babylonians. From the 6th to the 3rd century BCE it was part of the Achaemenid Empire. By about 250 BCE Parthia had brought the Persian Gulf under its control, and it established garrisons along the southern coast of the Gulf to control trade routes.

The ancient Greeks called the island Tylos and knew it as a centre of pearl trading. The admiral Nearchus, serving under Alexander the Great, is believed to have been the first of Alexander's commanders to visit it. He recorded large plantations of cotton trees on Tylos, from which cloth called sindones was made. Bahrain became part of the Hellenised world: the language of the upper classes was Greek, with Aramaic in everyday use, and local coinage shows a seated Zeus, who may have been worshipped there as a form of the Arabian sun-god Shams.

Bahrain is a kingdom, a semi-constitutional monarchy since 2002, with a bicameral National Assembly. Its capital and largest city is Manama. The King Fahd Causeway, completed in December 1986, links it with the Saudi Arabian mainland. It has been ruled by the Al Khalifa family since 1783 and became independent from the United Kingdom in 1971.
baikonur-cosmodrome: The cosmodrome lies on the Kazakh Steppe about 90 metres above sea level, 200 kilometres east of the Aral Sea and 33 kilometres north of the Syr Darya, close to Töretam, a station on the Trans-Aral Railway. It is the largest operational space launch facility in terms of area. The site was chosen by a commission led by General Vasily Voznyuk, influenced by Sergey Korolyov, chief designer of the R-7 missile. It had to be surrounded by plains, because the rocket's radio control system needed uninterrupted signals from ground stations hundreds of kilometres away, and the trajectory had to lie away from populated areas. A site nearer the equator is also an advantage. The commission chose Tyuratam, a village in the heart of the steppe.

The Soviet government issued the decree for Scientific Research Test Range No. 5 on 12 February 1955, and the range was founded on 2 June 1955 as a test centre for the R-7 Semyorka, the first intercontinental ballistic missile. It was soon expanded with launch facilities for space flights. The cost of the launch facilities and of several hundred kilometres of new road and railway made it one of the most costly infrastructure projects of the Soviet Union. A supporting town was built for the workers and became the city of Leninsk in 1966.

An American U-2 reconnaissance plane first photographed the range on 5 August 1957. Until 1991 its primary purpose was to test liquid-fuelled ballistic missiles, and it remained under the control of the Ministry of Defense until the second half of the 1990s.

Many historic flights began here: Sputnik 1 on 4 October 1957, Luna 1, the first spacecraft to pass close to the Moon, on 2 January 1959, Yuri Gagarin's flight on 12 April 1961 and Valentina Tereshkova's in 1963. In 1960 a prototype R-16 missile exploded before launch and killed over 100 people.

Most sources say the name Baikonur was chosen about 1961 to mislead the Western Bloc towards a mining town some 320 kilometres to the northeast; NASA's history says it was the name of the Tyuratam region. Leninsk was renamed Baikonur on 20 December 1995.

Russia has retained control of the facility since the Soviet Union ended, first through the Commonwealth of Independent States, and in 2005 ratified an agreement with Kazakhstan to lease it until 2050. All Russian crewed spaceflights are launched from Baikonur, which has supported the Soyuz, Proton, Tsyklon, Dnepr, Zenit and Buran rockets. Its internal railway, of 1,520 mm gauge, is the largest industrial railway in the world. A museum beside the cottages once used by Korolyov and Gagarin holds space artefacts, and a test article of the Buran programme stands at its entrance.
bakhchysarai: Bakhchysarai lies in a narrow valley of the Çürük Suv river, about 30 kilometres south-west of Simferopol. The name comes from the Persian bāghche-sarāy, "Garden Palace"; in Crimean Tatar bağça means garden and saray palace. The earliest known man-made objects in the valley date from the Mesolithic period, and settlements have existed there since Late Antiquity. The fortress of Qırq Yer, now Çufut Qale, Salaçıq and Eski Yurt were built before the town itself and have since been absorbed into its urban area.

Bakhchysarai first appears in documents in 1502. In 1532 Sahib I Giray, Khan of Crimea from 1532 to 1551, established his residence there, and from then it was the capital of the Crimean Khanate and the centre of the political and cultural life of the Crimean Tatars. Cossacks sacked the town in 1675 during Ivan Sirko's Crimean campaign, and it was burned in 1736 during the Russo-Turkish War of 1735 to 1739. After the Russian Empire annexed the Khanate in 1783 it became an ordinary town without administrative importance, but it stayed a cultural centre of the Crimean Tatars for several decades, helped by Ismail Gaspirali, who founded the newspaper Terciman there in 1883.

During the Crimean War the town served as a hospital for wounded Russian soldiers. The Battle of the Alma was fought not far away in 1854, but Turkish and allied forces never took the town, since their main objective was Sevastopol. In 1930 it had 10,450 inhabitants, 7,420 of them Crimean Tatars. On 18 May 1944 the Sürgün, the deportation of the Crimean Tatars, prompted by accusations of collaboration with the Axis occupiers, emptied the city of them. They could not return until 1989, when Soviet policies relaxed.

The main landmark is the Hansaray, or Khan's Palace, the only surviving palace of the Crimean khans, which is open as a museum. Other sites in or near the town include the Zincirli Madrasa, the Orta Cami and Tahtali-Jami mosques, the Cave Monastery, Chufut-Kale and Tepe-Kermen. Russian readers know the town from Alexander Pushkin's poem The Fountain of Bakhchysarai (1822), and Adam Mickiewicz devoted some of the best of his Crimean Sonnets (1825) to its landmarks.
bal-gangadhar-tilak: Tilak was born Keshav Gangadhar Tilak on 23 July 1856 in a Marathi Chitpavan Brahmin family in Ratnagiri; the family moved to Poona in 1867. His father, a schoolteacher and Sanskrit scholar, died when Tilak was sixteen. Tilak took a degree in mathematics at the Deccan College in 1877 and a law degree in 1879. In 1880 he co-founded the New English school, and in 1884 the Deccan Education Society, which set up Fergusson College in 1885, where he taught mathematics. He left the society in 1890 for more openly political work. He had started the weeklies Kesari, in Marathi, and Mahratta, in English, in 1880 to 1881.

Tilak joined the Indian National Congress in 1890 and opposed its moderate approach to self-rule. Measures against the plague in Pune in 1897 caused widespread resentment, and Tilak published inflammatory articles in Kesari and Mahratta. After two British officers were shot by the Chapekar brothers he was charged and sentenced to 18 months in prison. He took up the slogan Swaraj is my birthright and I shall have it. After the Partition of Bengal he promoted the Swadeshi and boycott movements. At the Surat session of 1907 Congress split into a radical faction led by Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal and Lala Lajpat Rai, and a moderate one.

In 1908 he was convicted of sedition over articles in Kesari and sentenced to six years in Mandalay, where he was held until 16 June 1914. He rejoined Congress at the Lucknow pact of 1916 and helped found the All India Home Rule League, whose membership grew from 1400 in April 1916 to about 32,000 in 1917. He also turned the household worship of Ganesha into a public festival in 1894 and began celebrations of Shivaji's birthday in 1895, though these celebrations also contributed to religious tensions. He died on 1 August 1920.

In prison at Mandalay he wrote the Gita Rahasya, interpreting the Bhagavad Gita as justifying activism, which he called karma-yoga, against the dominant renunciate readings. Tilak supported self-rule without a complete break with the British Empire. He opposed the age of consent bill and the first girls' high school in Pune, and he refused to sign a petition against untouchability in 1918. He also wrote The Arctic Home in the Vedas, arguing that the Vedas were composed in the Arctic.
baldwin-iv-of-jerusalem: Baldwin was born in mid-1161, probably at Ascalon, the son of Amalric, then count of Jaffa and Ascalon, and Agnes of Courtenay. His parents separated when he was two, after the High Court forced Amalric to annul the marriage on grounds of consanguinity as the price of being accepted as king in 1163. At nine he was sent to be educated by William of Tyre, who noticed early signs of leprosy, though the disease was diagnosed only after Baldwin became king.

After Amalric's death the High Court chose Baldwin unanimously, expecting that a husband would be found for his sister Sibylla to succeed him if he proved to be ill. He was crowned on 15 July 1174. Miles of Plancy and then Count Raymond III of Tripoli ruled as regent until Baldwin came of age at 15 in 1176. His planned attack on Egypt failed for lack of cooperation from his vassals.

In November 1177 Saladin invaded the kingdom while the Frankish army was in northern Syria. Baldwin and Raynald of Châtillon repelled him at Montgisard. Baldwin could not marry, and the question of succession dominated his reign. In 1180 Baldwin had Sibylla marry Guy of Lusignan, to forestall a coup by Raymond III and Bohemond III of Antioch, but Guy was opposed by much of the nobility. In 1182 Baldwin won the Battle of Le Forbelet.

From 1183 he could neither walk unsupported nor use his hands, and he went blind. He entrusted the government to Guy, but Guy's failure to lead and his insubordination led Baldwin to disinherit him, and to have Sibylla's young son crowned as Baldwin V. He was carried in a litter to lift Saladin's siege of Kerak, but failed to have Sibylla's marriage annulled.

In his last months Baldwin named Raymond regent for his nephew and died of a fever in 1185, no later than 16 May. He was buried in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, near his father. Baldwin V died the next year, Sibylla made Guy king, and Saladin destroyed the kingdom at the Battle of Hattin in 1187.

Historians have traced the instability to his reign, yet the kingdom lost no territory while he ruled. His chief contribution, in the view of historians, was his refusal to abdicate before finding a suitable successor, since only he could keep the nobles united. Pope Alexander III called his leprosy a just judgement of God.
balearic-islands: The archipelago lies in the western Mediterranean off the eastern coast of the Iberian Peninsula. It has two groups: the western Pityusic Islands, comprising Ibiza, Formentera and smaller islets, and the eastern Gymnesian Islands, principally Mallorca and Menorca. The Greeks called the islands Gymnesiai, and the Carthaginians and Romans used the name Baleares. Most ancient writers derived the name of the people from the Greek word for "to launch", from their skill as slingers. The earliest known habitation dates to about 2500 to 2300 BCE, by people associated with the Bell Beaker culture.

In ancient times the islanders of the Gymnesian Islands built talayots and were known for the sling. They served as mercenaries first under the Carthaginians and later under the Romans, each man carrying three slings of different lengths for stones of different sizes. Greek and Roman writers also told stories about their customs that the Romans found peculiar. The Phoenicians took possession of the islands early, and a trace survives in the town of Mago, now Mahón. Quintus Caecilius Metellus conquered the islands in 123 BCE, was given the surname Balearicus, settled 3,000 Roman and Hispanic colonists and founded Palma and Pollentia.

The Vandals under Genseric took them between 461 and 468, and Belisarius's troops restored Roman control in late 533 or early 534. In 707 the islands submitted to an Umayyad fleet, and in 903 Muslim forces captured them for the Emirate of Córdoba.

A crusade led by Pisa, with 420 ships, sacked Palma in 1115 and withdrew, and within a year the Berber Almoravids conquered the islands. King James I of Aragon captured Palma on the last day of 1229 after a three-month siege, took Menorca in 1232 and Ibiza in 1235. His will of 1276 created a Kingdom of Mallorca for his son James II, as a vassal of Aragon.

The kingdom ended when James III was killed at the Battle of Llucmajor in 1349 and the islands passed directly to the Crown of Aragon. Ottoman privateers raided them in the early 16th century, and in 1558 the corsair Turgut Reis ravaged them and 4,000 people were enslaved. Menorca was British for most of the 18th century after the Treaty of Utrecht of 1713, and returned to Spain by the Treaty of Amiens.

The islands form an autonomous community and province of Spain, with Palma as capital and largest city. They achieved self-government under a Statute of Autonomy in 1983, and Catalan and Spanish are co-official languages. They have 1,249,844 inhabitants and an area of 4,991.70 square kilometres. The four principal islands are major international tourist destinations.
balfour-declaration: Early British support for a larger Jewish presence in Palestine began in the early 1840s under Lord Palmerston and rested on geopolitical calculation, backed by evangelical sympathy for the restoration of the Jews, notably in Lord Shaftesbury. Zionism arose in the late nineteenth century in reaction to antisemitic and exclusionary nationalism in Europe. Around 1916 Jews were about 3 per cent of Palestine's population, which was mostly Muslim, with Christians second.

The British Cabinet first discussed Palestine on 9 November 1914. Within two months Herbert Samuel circulated a memorandum proposing support for Zionist ambitions to win Jewish support in the war. The first negotiations with the Zionists took place on 7 February 1917, and on 19 June Arthur Balfour asked Lord Rothschild and Chaim Weizmann to draft a public declaration. The War Cabinet decided to release it on 31 October 1917, after discussion that referred to the propaganda benefit among Jews worldwide. Palestine's Arab majority was not represented.

The text was a single sentence of 67 words, sent on 2 November 1917 from Balfour to Walter Rothschild for transmission to the Zionist Federation of Great Britain and Ireland. Two clauses promise support for a national home for the Jewish people in Palestine, and two safeguard clauses cover the civil and religious rights of existing non-Jewish communities there and the rights and political status of Jews in other countries. The term national home had no precedent in international law and was intentionally vague about whether a Jewish state was contemplated. Lord Milner's amendment replaced the draft's reconstituted with in Palestine. The text was published in the press on 9 November.

The declaration was the first public support for Zionism by a major political power and greatly raised support for it among Jewish communities. Christians and Muslims, almost 90 per cent of Palestine's population, strongly opposed it, and in the wider Arab world it was seen as a betrayal of the McMahon-Hussein correspondence with the Sharif of Mecca. Jerusalem surrendered to the British on 9 December 1917.

The declaration became a core part of the British Mandate for Palestine. The British government acknowledged in 1939 that the wishes and interests of the local population should have been taken into account, and in 2018 that the declaration should have called for protection of the Palestinian Arabs' political rights. It is considered a principal cause of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and indirectly led to the emergence of Israel.
bali: Bali is the westernmost of the Lesser Sunda Islands, 3.2 km east of Java across the Bali Strait and about 8 degrees south of the equator. It spans roughly 153 km from east to west and 112 km from north to south. Its fauna is Asian in character, since it lies just west of the Wallace Line. The name appears in ancient inscriptions in the compound Vāli-dvīpa, "island"; one of the earliest attestations is the Belanjong pillar inscription of King Sri Kesari Warmadewa, dated about 914 CE. The meaning of Vāli is uncertain, and one proposal derives it from Sanskrit bali, "offering".

Austronesian peoples, who migrated from Taiwan through maritime Southeast Asia, inhabited Bali around 2000 BCE, and stone tools of that time have been found near Cekik in the west. Ancient Bali had nine Hindu sects, each revering a particular deity. The first known European contact came in 1512, when a Portuguese expedition led by António Abreu and Francisco Serrão sighted the northern shores. Cornelis de Houtman, a Dutch merchant-explorer, arrived in 1597.

Dutch political and economic control began in the 1840s on the north coast, where the Dutch set competing Balinese realms against each other, and was extended in the late 1890s by exploiting struggles between the kingdoms of the south. British forces took the Japanese surrender in 1945 and handed the island to the Dutch in 1946, who made it one of the 13 districts of the State of East Indonesia. Bali became part of the Republic of the United States of Indonesia when the Netherlands recognised independence on 29 December 1949, and a province in 1958.

Bali is an Indonesian province whose capital, Denpasar, is the most populous city of the Lesser Sunda Islands; the upland town of Ubud is regarded as its cultural centre. About 86 per cent of its people follow Balinese Hinduism, which combines local beliefs with Hindu ones, and Balinese and Indonesian are the most widely spoken languages. Pre-modern society had four castes. Temples and homes are oriented between the mountain Gunung Agung (kaja) and the sea (kelod). The Subak irrigation system of the rice fields was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2012. Gamelan orchestras and dances such as legong, barong and kecak are central to its arts, and Nyepi, the Hindu New Year, is marked by a day of silence.
balikesir: Close to modern Balıkesir stood the Roman town of Hadrianutherae, which, as its name recalls, was founded by the emperor Hadrian. He came to the region in 124 CE and, after a successful bear hunt, established a city bearing his name. In the Byzantine period the neglected small town was known as Palaiokastron, Old Castle.

When the Turkomans came from Middle Asia into Mysia, they called the place Balukiser after the castle remains. Balıkesir, formerly called Karasi, was founded by Karasi Bey in the 13th century on the remains of the small town, and 1297 is taken as the date of its establishment, one of few cities founded by Turks in Anatolia. The Ottomans annexed it in 1345. An earthquake in 1898 destroyed much of it, leaving only 51 buildings undamaged. The Greek army occupied the city on 30 June 1919 and the Turkish army retook it on 6 September 1922.

Balıkesir lies in the Marmara region and is the seat of Balıkesir Province. The urban part had a population of 314,958 in 2022. A fire on 3 August 1950 destroyed the centre of the city, burning 498 shops, and it was rebuilt; it was the second biggest disaster in the city after the 1898 earthquake. The Yildirim Mosque, built in 1388, is the oldest surviving Ottoman work in the city, and of the Zaganos Pasha Mosque, built in 1461 and named after the grand vizier of Mehmet the Conqueror, only the mosque and baths remain.
balingen: Balingen is a town in Baden-Württemberg, capital of the district of Zollernalbkreis, near the Swabian Jura. It lies about 35 kilometres south of Tübingen and 70 kilometres south-southwest of Stuttgart. After Albstadt it is the second largest town in the district, and in 1973 it became the seat of the newly formed district of Zollernalb, which continued the old tradition of an official town. It is nicknamed Waagenstadt, the city of scales, and it is the home of the scale maker Bizerba.

Balingen is first mentioned in 863, and the earliest traces of settlement in the area are Alemannic terraced graves. According to historical records the town itself was established in 1255 by Count Friedrich von Zollern, and it was fortified before 1377. In 1403 the town, its castle and the Schalksburg estate were sold to the County of Württemberg, which made it the seat of an administrative district, Amt Balingen.

Fire repeatedly devastated the town. Chroniclers say it burned in 1286 during a feud between the Zollern and Hohenberg families, and further fires followed in 1546, 1607, 1672, 1724 and 1809. The last left only 55 of 445 buildings standing, and the rebuilding gave the town its classicist character. A civic foundation established a hospital in 1489 to care for the poor and the elderly. Balingen became part of the unified Germany in 1870. From 1939 to 1945 the town was the site of a subcamp of the Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp, which after the war became a French internment camp for former Nazi war criminals.

The castle, reconstructed in 1935, stands beside the old tanners' quarter, known as Little Venice. The Protestant church, finished in 1541, escaped the fire of 1809 and has a characteristic sundial in its apse. A publicly accessible sulphur spring, whose water has the smell of rotten eggs, is said to have healing powers. Among Balingen's natives are the Carthusian monk and humanist Gregor Reisch, who produced an encyclopedia of general knowledge.
balkan-league: After the Crimean War, Russia pursued indirect expansion in the Balkans by creating friendly states under its patronage, on the basis of the Panslavic movement. It helped establish an autonomous Bulgaria after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 and expanded Serbia. After its humiliation in the Bosnian Crisis, Russia pressed the two to compromise and ally against Austria-Hungary and the Ottomans. The Italo-Turkish War, which began in September 1911, exposed Ottoman weakness, and the Albanian Uprising of 1911 raised Serbian fears of an Albanian state closing its last direction of expansion. Serbia and Bulgaria signed an alliance on 13 March 1912; a secret chapter redirected it against the Ottoman Empire, and Serbia then allied with Montenegro and Bulgaria with Greece.

Their agreement stipulated that Bulgaria would receive all of Macedonia south of the Kriva Palanka–Ohrid line, while Serbia would expand to the north of it, including Kosovo, and westward to the Adriatic coast. Bulgaria refused to agree on any division of gains with Greece, as it expected its own army to occupy most of Macedonia and Thessaloniki first. Greece, led by Eleftherios Venizelos, was nevertheless essential, since alone of the four it had a major fleet that could prevent Ottoman reinforcements from crossing from Asia by sea. Montenegro, a small country and a close ally of Serbia, was regarded as a second-class partner with limited aims around Shkodër.

The Great Powers officially agreed on the territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire and warned the Balkan states, but their private signals differed, and the warning had no effect. Russia was the prime mover of the League, and France refused to support Russia in any conflict with Austria-Hungary caused by it. Montenegro declared war on 8 October 1912, and the other three states did so on 17 October, after an ultimatum on 13 October. The allied armies destroyed Ottoman power in Europe in a series of victories.

The old rivalries returned after victory, above all over the partition of Macedonia. The Great Powers insisted on an Albanian state and denied Serbia its gains on the Adriatic, so the Serbian share in Macedonia became more important. On 16 June 1913 Bulgaria attacked Serbia and Greece in the Second Balkan War. They repulsed it and invaded Bulgaria, and the Ottoman Empire and Romania also moved in. The peace left Bulgaria with some gains but cost it Eastern Thrace and most of Macedonia, and Bulgaria later entered the First World War on the side of the Central Powers. The Balkan Wars permanently broke the Russo-Bulgarian alliance and left Serbia and Montenegro as Russia's only allies in the region.
balkan-mountains: The range is conventionally taken to begin at the peak of Vrashka Chuka on the border between Bulgaria and Serbia. It runs more than 500 kilometres, first south-east along the border and then eastward across Bulgaria as a natural barrier between the northern and southern halves of the country, before reaching the Black Sea at Cape Emine. Botev Peak, at 2,376 metres, is the highest point. In the central and eastern sections the summit forms the watershed between the Black Sea and the Aegean. Bulgaria's longest river, the Iskar, cuts through the Iskar Gorge a few miles north of Sofia. The karst relief has produced many caves, among them Magura, with the most important European post-Palaeolithic cave paintings.

In antiquity and the Middle Ages the mountains were called Haemus, from a Thracian word for "mountain ridge". Greek myth explained the name either from haima, "blood", spilled when Zeus deflected the mountains Typhon hurled at him, or from King Haemus, who with his wife Rhodope was turned into a mountain for calling himself Zeus. The name Balkan is widely believed to have been brought by the Ottoman Turks and may derive from a Persian word for "high house". The Slavic name Stara Planina, "old mountain", is first attested at the beginning of the 16th century.

The range has had a special place in Bulgarian history since the founding of the state in 681, serving for centuries as a natural fortress and a barrier to Moesia, where most medieval capitals stood. Battles with the Byzantines took place at the Rishki Pass in 759, the Varbitsa Pass in 811, Tryavna in 1190 and Devina in 1279. At the Varbitsa Pass Khan Krum defeated a very large Byzantine army and killed Emperor Nikephoros I. Under Ottoman rule many haiduks found refuge there, and the poet Hristo Botev died in the western range near Vratsa in 1876. The Shipka Pass saw four battles in the Russo-Turkish War.

Twenty passes and two gorges cross the range. Central Balkan National Park protects ancient beech forests, listed in 2017 as part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Raysko Praskalo, the highest waterfall in the Balkans. Brown bears, wolves, chamois and deer live in the mountains, and edelweiss grows near Kozyata stena. The Belogradchik Rocks are the best-known rock formation. The range gave its name to the Balkans.
balkan-wars: The wars grew out of the incomplete emergence of nation-states on the European territory of the Ottoman Empire in the second half of the 19th century. Serbia gained territory in 1877 to 1878, Greece acquired Thessaly in 1881, and Bulgaria incorporated Eastern Rumelia in 1885. All three, with Montenegro, sought more land in Rumelia, which comprised Eastern Rumelia, Albania, Macedonia and Thrace. After the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 hopes of reform rose among the Balkan peoples, but after the failed counter-coup of 1909 the nationalist element dominated. Italy's victory in the Italo-Turkish War and revolts in Albania showed the empire's weakness, and in 1912 Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro formed the Balkan League.

The First Balkan War began on 8 October 1912, when the League attacked the Ottoman Empire. The Bulgarian army, the best trained, was expected to carry the main burden in Thrace and the Serbian army to act in Macedonia, while Greece was needed above all for its navy, which could cut Ottoman forces off from reinforcement by sea.
