The war ended with the Treaty of London on 30 May 1913.

The allies then quarrelled over Macedonia. Serbia and Greece revealed that they meant to keep the territory their forces held, although Serbia had promised Bulgaria most of Macedonia in the League's original agreement. Bulgaria attacked its former allies on 16 June 1913. Serbian and Greek forces repelled the offensive and invaded Bulgaria. Romania, whose armies were intact, invaded from the north, and the Ottoman Empire advanced in Thrace and regained Adrianople.

The Treaty of Bucharest, of 10 August 1913, partitioned Macedonia. Serbia gained north-east Macedonia and the eastern half of the Sanjak of Novi Pazar, doubling its size, while Montenegro took the western half. Greece more than doubled in size, gaining southern Epirus, most of southern Macedonia and the port of Kavala. Romania took the southern part of Dobruja, and Bulgaria kept western Thrace with the port of Alexandroupolis. The Great Powers had also secured an independent Albania.

The wars ended Ottoman rule over most of the Balkan Peninsula. They were marked by ethnic cleansing, and all parties were responsible for grave atrocities against civilians. In Turkey they are remembered as a major disaster. The enlargement of Serbia and the relative weakening of Austria-Hungary set the stage for the July crisis of 1914.
balkans: The Balkans take their name from the Balkan Mountains, which stretch across the whole of Bulgaria. The Balkan Peninsula is bordered by the Adriatic Sea in the northwest, the Ionian Sea in the southwest, the Aegean Sea in the south, the Turkish Straits in the east and the Black Sea in the northeast, and has an area of about 470,000 square kilometres.

Its northern border is variously defined, often as the Danube, Sava and Kupa rivers. Most of the area is covered by mountain ranges running from the northwest to the southeast, among them the Balkan Mountains, the Rila-Rhodope massif, the Dinaric Alps and the Pindus range. The highest point is Musala, at 2,925 metres, in the Rila range in Bulgaria.

The concept of the Balkan Peninsula was created by the German geographer August Zeune in 1808, who mistakenly considered the Balkan Mountains the dominant mountain system of south-eastern Europe. Geographers such as Carl Ritter objected, and in the 19th century the term was a synonym for Rumelia, the European provinces of the Ottoman Empire. Its definition is geopolitical rather than geographical, and the term has acquired a stigmatised, pejorative meaning related to Balkanization; the region may instead be called Southeast Europe.

The Balkans have been inhabited since the Paleolithic and were the route by which farming spread from the Middle East to Europe in the Neolithic, in the 7th millennium BCE. The first known Neolithic culture of Old Europe, the Kakanj culture, appeared in central Bosnia and covers the period from 6795 to 4900 BCE. The region of the Old Europe or Danube civilisation peaked between 5000 and 3500 BCE.

In the Early Middle Ages the Byzantine Empire was the dominant state in the region, militarily and culturally. In the second half of the 9th century the Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius spread the Byzantine variety of Christianity to the majority of the previously pagan inhabitants; it was adopted first by the Bulgarians and Serbs, with the Romanians joining a little later. In 1912 and 1913 Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro allied against the Ottoman Empire in the First Balkan War and partitioned almost all its remaining European territories, and events led to the creation of an independent Albanian state.

Bulgaria began the Second Balkan War by attacking its former allies, and collapsed when the Greek army invaded and Romania intervened; the Ottoman Empire used the chance to recapture Eastern Thrace, fixing its western borders that still stand today as part of modern Turkey.
balkars: The Balkars are a Turkic people of the North Caucasus and one of the titular populations of Kabardino-Balkaria. They call themselves Malqarlıla, Alanla or Tawlula, meaning mountaineers. They share their language with the Karachays, and the two peoples are sometimes treated as a single ethnicity. Their ethnogenesis has been described as one of the most difficult problems in Caucasian studies. Proposed contributions include ancient Caucasian peoples, the Bulgars and Khazars, the Iranian Alans and Kipchaks with their Cuman allies; one account points to the war between Timur and Tokhtamysh in 1395, which drove Kipchak soldiers into the mountains.
Most Balkars adopted Islam in the eighteenth century through contact with the Kumyks, Circassians, Nogais and Crimean Tatars, and the Sufi Qadiriya order has a strong presence in the region.

During the Caucasian War the Balkars and Karachays helped the Kabardians in their rebellions against Russia. In the battle on the Chegem river on 9 May 1804, Lieutenant General Glazenap reported that Kabardians, Balkars, Karachays and Ossetians fought from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. In 1828 General Emmanuel led an expedition of more than 3,000 men into Karachay, and the Karachays then gave hostages and accepted Russian terms. After the Caucasian War and the Circassian Genocide, about 10,000 to 15,756 Karachays and Balkars emigrated to the Ottoman Empire.

In 1944 the Soviet government forcibly deported almost the entire Balkar population to Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Omsk Oblast in Siberia. Starting on 8 March 1944 and finishing the next day, the NKVD loaded 37,713 Balkars onto 14 train echelons. By October 1946 deaths from malnutrition and disease had reduced their number to 32,817. The special settlement restrictions ended on 28 April 1956, but the Balkars could return to their mountain homeland only in 1957; during 1957 and 1958, 34,749 returned.

The Karachay-Balkar language belongs to the Kipchak group of Turkic languages. In the past Arabic was the written language for religious services and Turkish for business matters. From 1920 Balkar became the language of instruction in primary schools, with later instruction in Russian. Arabic letters were used to write Balkar until 1928, and Cyrillic after 1937. Ninety-six percent of the Balkars are bilingual in Balkar and Russian. The Balkars are considered deeply religious. The poet Kaisyn Kuliev wrote of his love for the Balkar land and its traditions.
balkh: Balkh lies about 24 km north-west of Mazar-i-Sharif and about 74 km south of the Amu Darya, at an elevation of about 365 m. French archaeologists found remains of a first settlement in the citadel, Bala Hissar, dating to the Early Iron Age, about 1500 to 1000 BCE. An earlier name, or the name of part of the city, was Zariaspa, which may come from the Zoroastrian fire temple Azar-i-Asp. The city's nickname is the mother of all cities.

The first historical reference is in the Mahabharata, which calls the place Valhika and says an important trade route passed through it. Balkh is the home town of Trapusa and Bahalika, the two merchants who, according to Buddhist scripture, became the Buddha's first disciples. Balkh was a refuge for Yazdegerd III when the Arabs conquered Persia in the 7th century; they attacked it in 645, compelled it to pay tribute in 653, and the Umayyad caliph Muawiya reconquered it in 663.

In 1220 Genghis Khan sacked Balkh, massacred its inhabitants and levelled the buildings that could be defended. Marco Polo, probably referring to its past, described it as a noble city and a great seat of learning, while Ibn Battuta, visiting about 1333, found it dilapidated and uninhabited. Timur captured it in 1389 and destroyed its citadel, which Shah Rukh rebuilt in 1407. Muhammad Shaybani's Uzbeks entered in 1506, and the Khanate of Bukhara ruled it apart from Safavid rule from 1598 to 1601. In 1850 Dost Muhammad Khan took it for the Emirate of Afghanistan.

Balkh is in northern Afghanistan, with Tajiks the majority of its people and Dari the main language. Much of the town consists of ruined buildings. Among its monuments are the Green Mosque, named for its green-tiled dome, and the Nine Domes Mosque, the earliest Islamic monument yet identified in Afghanistan. Buddhist structures have proved more durable than the Islamic buildings, among them Top-Rustam, a circular mound about 15 m high. Balkh had a major role in the development of Persian literature, and the poet Rumi was born there in the 13th century.
ballarat: Ballarat lies at the foothills of the Great Dividing Range in the Central Highlands of Victoria, on a gently undulating section of the midland volcanic plains, at an elevation of between 400 and 630 metres. The region was first populated by the Wadawurrung people. The first Europeans to sight the area were a party of six men in August 1837, who climbed Mount Buninyong.

Within months of Victoria separating from New South Wales in 1851, gold was discovered near Ballarat. Thomas Hiscock made the first publicised discovery at Buninyong on 2 August 1851, and on 19 August more gold was found at Poverty Point. A rush began within days, bringing thousands of prospectors to the Yarrowee Valley. Many immigrants, including many from Ireland and China, gathered in shanty towns around the creeks and hills, and the town became a boomtown that for a time rivalled Melbourne in wealth and cultural influence.

In 1854, after a period of civil disobedience over gold licences, local miners launched an armed uprising against government forces, known as the Eureka Rebellion. It led to the introduction of white male suffrage in Australia and is interpreted as the origin of Australian democracy. Its symbol, the Eureka Flag, has become a national symbol.

Ballarat was proclaimed a city on 9 September 1870. Unlike many gold boomtowns, its prosperity lasted until the late 19th century, because its fields sustained high yields for decades. Tents and timber buildings gave way to permanent buildings of stone and brick, built mainly from the wealth of early mining. As gold extraction slowed, Ballarat's importance relative to Melbourne faded rapidly, and growth all but stopped for decades.

Ballarat is a city in the Central Highlands of Victoria, Australia, and the commercial capital and largest city of the Central Highlands. It is known for its well-preserved colonial-era heritage and Victorian architecture. Her Majesty's Theatre, established in 1875, is the longest running lyric theatre building in Australia, and the Art Gallery of Ballarat is the oldest and largest regional gallery in the country. Federation University Australia traces its origin to the Ballarat School of Mines, founded in 1870.
baloch-people: The Baloch speak Balochi, a Western Iranian language of the Northwestern group that shares features with Parthian and Median. The origin of the name is unclear; Ernst Emil Herzfeld derived it from a Median term, brza-vačiya, meaning loud shouting. The linguistic connections of Balochi suggest that the original homeland lay east or southeast of the central Caspian region, and the Baloch began migrating eastward in the late Sasanian period, in movements that continued over several centuries for reasons unknown. Baloch lore holds instead that their ancestors came from Aleppo. A Middle Persian text on Sasanian geography names a mountain-dwelling people called the Baločān among the builders of 21 cities in Padishkhwārgar, a Sasanian province near Segistan.

Baloch tribes revolted against the Safavid government. Under the Afsharid ruler Nader Shah, Mohammad Khan Baloch became a military commander and governor of Fars, Kohgiluyeh and Khuzestan, and many Baloch were moved to Khorasan to guard the eastern border against Afghan invaders. The Khanate of Kalat, founded by Mir Altaz Sani Khan Qambrani, was a confederacy of Brahui tribes under a single ruler, the Khan; Mir Ahmad Khan I took Quetta, Mastung and Pishin from the Mughal governor at Kandahar.

The Talpur, a Baloch dynasty, rose to power in Sindh in the late 18th century and ruled until the British conquest of 1843. At the Battle of Miani, near Hyderabad, their last ruler, Amir Nasir Khan Talpur, was defeated by East India Company forces under Charles Napier.

The Baloch were traditionally nomadic pastoralists. About half live in the Pakistani province of Balochistan and 40 per cent in Sindh. They make up 3.6 per cent of Pakistan's population and 2 per cent of Iran's, and they are the largest non-Arab community in Oman. The great majority are Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school. Before Islam they followed Mazdakian and Manichean sects, and some tribes keep older customs such as the Nal oath, an ordeal of passing through fire to prove innocence.

Baloch ballads, kept in Balochi, tell of the wars of clans and the valour of chiefs, and of tragic love, as in the story of Hani and Sheh Mureed. Balochi rugs of wool, mirror-work and coin embroidery are widely known crafts.
balochi-language: Balochi, also rendered Baluchi, is a Northwestern Iranian language spoken by the Baloch people in the Balochistan region of Pakistan, Iran and Afghanistan. There are also speakers in Oman, the Arab states of the Persian Gulf, Turkmenistan and East Africa, and in diaspora communities elsewhere. Ethnologue gives 8.8 million speakers, and the varieties, which form a dialect continuum, have at least 10 million native speakers. It is an Indo-European language of the Indo-Iranian branch. Its original homeland is suggested to be around the central Caspian region.

The main varieties are Eastern (Soleimani), Southern (Makrani) and Western (Rakhshani). Koroshi, spoken in the Qashqai tribal confederation in the Fars province of Iran, is an isolated dialect distinct in grammar and lexicon. The Soleimani dialect, spoken in eastern Balochistan and parts of Punjab and Sindh, is often perceived as farther from the other two, probably because of influence from Brahvi, Pashto, Sindhi and Punjabi.

The normal word order is subject, object, verb, and the language has split ergativity: the subject is nominative except in past-tense constructions, where the subject of a transitive verb is marked as oblique and the verb agrees with the object. Like many Western Iranian languages it has lost the Old Iranian gender distinctions, and much of its number system is identical to Persian. The vowel system has at least eight vowels, five long and three short, and a rising tone marks questions without a question word.

Balochi was not a written language before the 19th century, and the Persian script was used where writing was necessary, although the language was still spoken in Baloch courts. British colonial officers first wrote it in the Latin script. After the creation of Pakistan, Baloch scholars adopted the Persian alphabet, and the first collection of poetry in Balochi, Gulbang by Mir Gul Khan Nasir, was published in 1951 in the Arabic script. Syed Zahoor Shah Hashemi later wrote a comprehensive guide to the usage of Arabic script and standardised it as the Balochi orthography in Pakistan and Iran, earning the title of father of Balochi. In Afghanistan it is still written in a modified Arabic script based on Persian.

Other scripts have also been tried. In 1933 the Soviet Union adopted a Latin-based alphabet for Balochi, used for children's books, newspapers and ideological works, but official use of the language was discontinued in 1938. A Cyrillic alphabet was finished in 1990, and school textbooks in it were printed from 1992 to 1993, but it fell out of use in the early 2000s. According to Brian Spooner, literacy for most Baloch-speakers is in Urdu in Pakistan and Persian in Afghanistan and Iran, rather than Balochi.
balochistan: Balochistan is a historical region in the far southeast of the Iranian plateau, bordering the Indian plate and the Arabian Sea. It is an arid region of desert and mountains, populated mainly by ethnic Baloch, and is split among three countries. It comprises the Pakistani province of Balochistan, the Iranian province of Sistan and Baluchestan with parts of Kerman, South Khorasan and Hormozgan, and the southern areas of Afghanistan. The Greeks of Alexander's time called the land Gedrosia. The Baloch are not mentioned in pre-Islamic sources and probably acquired their name only after arriving there.

Balochistan is among the earliest settled regions in the world. Its earliest settled villages, including Mehrgarh on the Kachi Plain, date to the ceramic Neolithic, c. 7000 to 6000 BCE, and by 2500 BCE Pakistani Balochistan was part of the cultural orbit of the Indus Valley civilisation. Alexander the Great conquered Gedrosia. From the 1st to the 3rd century CE the Pāratarājas, Indo-Scythian kings, ruled the region and are known mainly from their coins.

The region was fully Islamised by the 9th century and passed to the Saffarids of Zaranj, then the Ghaznavids and the Ghorids. The Baloch fought the Ghaznavid ruler Sebuktegin when he attacked Khuzdar in 994, and conflicts with the Buyids and Seljuqs drove waves of Baloch migration eastward from Kerman. Constant migration ruined much of their cattle breeding, so they combined settled agriculture with herding. The Khanate of Kalat, the first unified polity in the history of Balochistan, arose from a confederacy of Brahui tribes in 1666 under Mir Ahmad Khan I, who declared independence from Mughal suzerainty; the Ahmadzai dynasty ruled it until 1948.

The British took over Balochistan in 1839, mainly for military reasons, to station garrisons defending the frontiers of British India. A general insurrection against British rule began in 1840. The Mari tribe rose in revolt, and on 11 May 1840 a British contingent under Major Brown occupied Kahan Fort.

The largest part of the region lies in Pakistan, whose largest province by area is Balochistan. About 6.9 million of Pakistan's people are Baloch, and in Iran there are about two million. Nearly all Baloch belong to the Sunni sect of Islam, to which they converted after the Arab conquest of the seventh century.
baltic-sea: The Baltic Sea is an arm of the Atlantic Ocean stretching from 53°N to 66°N latitude and from 10°E to 30°E longitude. It is about 1,600 km long, an average of 193 km wide and an average of 55 metres deep, with a maximum depth of 459 metres on the Swedish side of the centre. It has about 8,000 km of coastline and occupies a basin formed by glacial erosion during the last few ice ages. It drains through the Danish Straits into the Kattegat, and includes the Gulf of Bothnia, the Gulf of Finland, the Gulf of Riga and the Bay of Gdańsk.

Before the Pleistocene a wide plain lay here around a great river that palaeontologists call the Eridanos, and several glacial episodes scooped out its bed into the sea basin. The later stages are named and dated, from the Baltic Ice Lake (16,000–11,700 years before the present) through the Yoldia Sea, the Ancylus Lake and the Littorina Sea to the Post-Littorina Sea of the last 4,000 years.

In the time of the Roman Empire the sea was known as the Mare Suebicum or Mare Sarmaticum. Tacitus, writing in 98 CE, described the Mare Suebicum, named for the Suebi, as a brackish sea in which ice broke apart in spring. The first to name it the Baltic Sea (Mare Balticum) was the eleventh-century German chronicler Adam of Bremen, who compared it to a belt stretching through the land; the precise origin of the name is unknown.

In the early Middle Ages Norse merchants built a trade empire all around the Baltic, later fighting the Wendish tribes of the southern shore for control of it. They also used the rivers of Russia as trade routes to the Black Sea. This is the Viking Age, and the Scandinavians have called the Baltic Austmarr, the Eastern Sea, since then. Historically the Kingdom of Denmark collected Sound Dues from ships at the entrances to the sea.

The Baltic is enclosed by Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Russia and Sweden, and is the world's largest brackish water basin. Artificial waterways join it to the White Sea by the White Sea–Baltic Canal and to the North Sea by the Kiel Canal. Its fauna mixes marine and freshwater species, and the common blue mussel makes up more than 90 per cent of its animal biomass.
baltic-way: The Soviet Union long denied that the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact had secret protocols and maintained that the Baltic states had joined the Union voluntarily. The Baltic states held that they had been incorporated by force and illegally. If the occupation could be tied to the pact, Soviet rule would have had no legal basis since 1940, and the independent states of the interwar period could be restored. The Estonian Rahvarinne, the Latvian Tautas fronte and the Lithuanian Sąjūdis planned the demonstration to show popular desire for independence and the solidarity of the three nations. It grew out of Black Ribbon Day protests held in Western cities from 1986.

The idea of a human chain appears to have been proposed at a meeting in Pärnu on 15 July 1989, and an agreement was reached on 12 August at Cēsis. Organisers assigned stretches of the route to towns and provided free buses, and Estonia declared a public holiday. The chain connected Vilnius, Riga and Tallinn. At 19:00 local time on 23 August the participants linked hands for 15 minutes. Elsewhere there were candles, masses and bell-ringing. The best Western estimates of participants range from one to two million, and aerial video showed an almost continuous line of people across the countryside.

On 18 August Alexander Yakovlev, head of a Soviet commission on the pact, admitted in Pravda that the secret protocols were genuine, though he denied that they affected the incorporation of the Baltic states. On 26 August the Central Committee of the Communist Party broadcast a stern warning against nationalist groups, but Moscow did not follow up on its threats. In December 1989 Mikhail Gorbachev signed the commission's report condemning the protocols. Free elections in February 1990 gave pro-independence candidates majorities in all three Baltic states, and on 11 March 1990 Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare independence.

The Baltic Way publicised the cause and made independence a moral question as well as a political one. It was one of the earliest and longest unbroken human chains in history, and in 2009 its documents were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register.
bamako: Bamako stands on the floodplain of the Niger River, near the rapids that divide the upper and middle Niger valleys, in the southwest of Mali. The city is relatively flat except to the north, where an escarpment, the remains of an extinct volcano, rises. It first grew on the northern bank, and bridges later joined it to the south, where the largest urbanised area now lies.

The area has evidence of settlement since the Palaeolithic. Fertile land in the Niger Valley supported early chiefdoms that grew wealthy on trade routes across West Africa and the Sahara, in gold, ivory, kola nuts and salt. By the 11th century the Empire of Ghana was the first kingdom to dominate the area, and the Mali Empire later succeeded it. The kafu of Bamako was founded around 1650 by the Niare family, perhaps associated with a Soninke man named Bamba Sanogo. It was a client state of the Segou Empire, and when the Scottish explorer Mungo Park visited in 1806 he estimated its population at 6,000.

In February 1882 Samory Toure defeated the French at the Battle of Samaya. Some leaders of the Dyula community in Bamako, facing his expanding Wassoulou Empire, began to approach the anti-French alliance. The French commander Gustave Borgnis-Desbordes hurried a force to this key point on the Niger and established a fort on 1 February 1883. Samory's brother Kebe Brema led a force against it, and the two sides fought two battles at Woyo Wayanko creek in early April; Kebe Brema won the first but was forced to retreat.

A railway linking Bamako to Kayes was built in 1904, and the city began to grow quickly. The line to Dakar was completed in 1923. After independence in April 1960 the city had about 160,000 people. Moussa Traoré took power in a coup and ruled for 23 years. On 22 March 1991 a large protest march in central Bamako was violently suppressed, with estimates of the dead reaching 300, and four days later a military coup deposed him.

Bamako is the capital and largest city of Mali and its administrative centre, a separate capital district divided into communes. It holds the University of Bamako, the National Museum of Mali and the Grand Mosque.
bamberg: Bamberg lies in Franconia on the Regnitz river, 3 km before it flows into the Main, 63 km north of Nuremberg by rail. From northeast to southwest the town divides into the Regnitz plain, an island district formed by two arms of the river, and the Hill Town. Bamberg extends over seven hills, each crowned by a church, which has led to its being called the Franconian Rome; the hills are Cathedral Hill, Michaelsberg, Kaulberg, Stefansberg, Jakobsberg, Altenburger Hill and Abtsberg.

After the Roman centuries the region was inhabited mostly by Slavs. The town, first mentioned in 902, grew up by the castle Babenberch, which gave its name to the Babenberg family. In 1007 Emperor Henry II made Bamberg a family inheritance and the seat of a separate diocese, to make the Diocese of Würzburg less unwieldy and to strengthen Christianity in the districts of Franconia to the east. The new cathedral was consecrated on 6 May 1012, and in 1017 Henry founded Michaelsberg Abbey, a Benedictine house for training clergy.

Henry and his wife Kunigunde gave large possessions and privileges to the diocese, from which the bishop's secular power grew. Pope Benedict VIII visited in 1020 and placed the diocese directly under the Holy See; for a short time Bamberg was the centre of the Holy Roman Empire. From the middle of the 13th century the bishops were princes of the Empire. The city lost its independence in 1802 with the secularisation of church lands and passed to Bavaria in 1803.

After a communist uprising took control of Bavaria following the First World War, the state government fled to Bamberg and stayed almost two years. Bavaria's first republican constitution, the Bamberger Verfassung, was passed there.

Bamberg has 79,000 inhabitants. Its old town, with around 2,400 timber houses, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1993, and the site includes the Market Gardeners' District, where urban gardening has been practised since the Middle Ages. Bamberg Cathedral, a late Romanesque building with four towers, holds the tombs of Emperor Henry II and Pope Clement II. The old town hall of 1386 stands in the middle of the Regnitz, reached by two bridges.
bamenda: Bamenda, also known as Abakwa and Mankon Town, lies in north-western Cameroon, 366 kilometres north-west of Yaoundé, and is known for its cool climate and hilly setting. The city is made up of three villages, Bamendakwe, Mankon and Nkwen, which form the Bamenda I, II and III sub-divisions, and it is surrounded by fast-growing suburban areas and villages such as Bambui, Bafut and Bali. North of it runs the Bamenda Ring Road, a 367-kilometre circular route through the Cameroon Highlands that passes Mount Oku, the Menchum River waterfalls, the Fon's palace at Bafut and a pyramidal thatched shrine at Akum.

The origins of the city are linked to the Tikar people, who maintained relations with the Kingdom of Bamum in the 1700s. Germany colonised the area in 1884. In 1916 it passed to administration by Great Britain and France, and in 1919 the Northwest Region, and so Bamenda, came under British administration alone. In 1961 the region joined Cameroon.

In the late twentieth century Bamenda became a centre of political opposition. The Social Democratic Front was launched there on 26 May 1990 despite a heavy police presence, and six civilians were killed. The Southern Cameroons National Council, a group seeking restoration of the former Southern Cameroons, was founded in the city in 1994 after the All Anglophone Conference issued the Bamenda Declaration.

Bamenda is the capital of the Northwest Region and has about six hundred thousand people. Many of them are English-speaking, and Cameroonian Pidgin English is the main language of its shops and streets. Its industries include the processing of agricultural produce such as coffee, handicrafts, education and tourism, and its shops and museum display baskets, beads, woodcarvings and bronze statues. Cultural sites include the Mankon Fon's Palace with its museum and the Bali Fon's palace with its ancient architectural structures. The city is linked by road to Yaoundé and Douala, and is the seat of the University of Bamenda and of a Roman Catholic archdiocese.
banabhatta: What is known of Bana's ancestry and early life is reconstructed from his own words: the introductory verses attached to the Kadambari and the first two chapters, or ucchvasas, of the Harshacharita. He was born to Chitrabhanu and Rajadevi in the village of Pritikuta, in a Kanyakubja Brahmin family. His mother died early and left him in the care of his father, who married again and had two more sons.

His father died when Bana was fourteen. For a time he led a colourful, wandering life with his half-brothers, and afterwards he came back to his native village. There, on a summer day, he received a letter from Krishna, a cousin of Harsha, and went to meet the king, who was camping near the town of Manitara. Harsha received him at first with mock signs of anger and then showed him much favour. Bana became the court poet during Harsha's reign at Kanyakubja.

The Harshacharita, whose title means the deeds of Harsha, was Bana's first composition; its third chapter describes the circumstances in which he came to write it. It is considered the first Indian work that may be regarded as a historical biography and the beginning of historical poetic writing in Sanskrit, and it gives a vivid picture of life in the Indian countryside.

Bana died before he could finish the Kadambari, and his son Bhushanabhatta completed it. Two further works are attributed to him, the Chandikashataka and a drama, the Parvatiparinaya. A Sanskrit saying, Banochhistam jagatsarvam, holds that Bana described everything in the world and left nothing out. The Harshacharita was translated into English by E. B. Cowell and F. W. Thomas for the Royal Asiatic Society in 1897.
banat: Banat is a region of the Pannonian Basin bordered by the Danube to the south, the Tisza to the west, the Mureș to the north and the Southern Carpathians to the east, with an area of about 28,526 square kilometres. In the Middle Ages a banate was a frontier province under a military governor called a ban. When the region was divided in 1920, Romania received about two thirds, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes about one third and Hungary about one per cent. Its eastern part lies in western Romania, its western part in north-eastern Serbia and a small northern part in south-eastern Hungary.

Celtic tribes, notably the Scordisci, settled the area in the 4th century BCE. After Trajan's two wars against the Dacians Banat came under Roman rule as a link to the province of Dacia. The Huns, the Gepids and then the Avars followed, and Avar rule lasted until Charlemagne's campaigns in the 9th century. The First Bulgarian Empire administered Banat from the 9th to the 11th century, and Hungary from the 11th century until 1552, when the Ottoman Empire captured Temesvár.

The Ottoman Empire made it the Eyalet of Temeşvar, with Serbs in the west and Romanians in the east. After Prince Eugene of Savoy took it in 1716 and the Treaty of Passarowitz of 1718, it became a Habsburg province with its own administration at Temesvár, not part of the Kingdom of Hungary. In 1778 the civilian part was incorporated into Hungary, while the southern part stayed in the Military Frontier until 1871.

A Banat Republic was proclaimed at Timișoara in October 1918, but Serbian troops invaded two weeks later. In 1919 most of Banat was divided between Romania and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, with a small area near Szeged going to Hungary, and the Treaty of Versailles and the Treaty of Trianon confirmed the borders.

Romanians, Serbs and Hungarians form most of the population. The region's ethnic diversity was severely affected by World War II. The traditional heraldic symbol of Banat is a lion, assumed to derive from the Cuman lion, and it appears in the coats of arms of Romania and Vojvodina. The Timiș is the largest river inside the region, flowing into the Danube at Pančevo.
banda-aceh: Banda Aceh lies on the northwestern tip of Sumatra, at the mouth of the Aceh River, at an elevation of 35 metres. It is a semi-enclave within Aceh Besar Regency, bordering the Andaman Sea to the northwest. The first part of its name comes from the Persian bandar, meaning port or haven. It has been called the porch of Mecca, Serambi Mekkah, from the days when pilgrims travelling by sea from Indonesia stopped there before continuing to Mecca.

Banda Aceh has long been a strategic transport and trading hub in the eastern Indian Ocean. Marco Polo visited in 1292 and called it Lambri, from the Lamuri Kingdom that existed there, noting it as the logical first port of call for travellers from Arabia and India. By the mid-14th century it was under the trading kingdom of Samudera Pasai, which collapsed under declining economic conditions and pressure from the Portuguese, who occupied Malacca in the early 16th century. Sultan Ali Mughayat Syah of the newly founded Sultanate of Aceh expanded aggressively in the 1520s, built the sultanate on the remains of Pasai and other extinct kingdoms, and made the city its capital.

The Dutch declared war on Aceh on 26 March 1873 and bombarded the capital. With British support the city had been modernised and fortified, and the Dutch underestimated its defences. Their commander, General Johan Köhler, was killed in a skirmish near the city and the first expedition failed. A second expedition within months overwhelmed it, and the Dutch entered the capital in January 1874 believing the Acehnese had surrendered, but the conflict moved into the countryside. The city's name was changed back to Banda Aceh on 9 May 1963.

Banda Aceh is the capital and largest city of the Indonesian province of Aceh. On 26 December 2004 a tsunami caused by a 9.2-magnitude earthquake in the Indian Ocean struck the city, which was the closest major city to the epicentre. It destroyed more than 60 per cent of the city's buildings, and figures for the dead run from 60,000 to 167,000 inhabitants. Memorials include mass graves at Ulee Lheue, the Tsunami Museum and PLTD Apung 1, a floating diesel power ship carried inland. The Baiturrahman Grand Mosque, built in the reign of Iskandar Muda (1607 to 1636), was rebuilt in 1875 after burning in the Aceh war.
bandar-abbas: Bandar Abbas stands on flat ground about 9 metres above sea level on the southern coast of Iran, at the narrow Strait of Hormuz, just across from Oman's Musandam. The island of Qeshm lies to the south, and the nearest hills are Mount Geno, 17 kilometres to the north. Because it has always been a port, its names have reflected that function. The commonest was Gamrūn, which Henry Yule derives either from gümrük, "customhouse", or, which he found more convincing, from Persian kamrūn, "shrimp". The present name means "Port of Abbas", after Abbas the Great, who reigned from 1588 to 1629.

The earliest record of the place is from the reign of Darius the Great, between 522 and 486 BCE, when his commander Scylax embarked from here for India and the Red Sea. The Portuguese conquered it in 1514 and made it an important base for protecting their commerce in the Persian Gulf and India, calling it Comorão for the lobsters and crabs on its shores. Shah Abbas took it from them in 1614, and in 1622 he defeated Portuguese troops in the region with the help of the English Navy and the Persian commander Imam Quli Khan. The city was renamed Bandar-e Abbas, and with English naval backing he developed it into a major port.

In 1625 a combined Anglo-Dutch fleet attacked the Portuguese and took the trade posts. The Dutch East India Company soon outcompeted the English, and from 1654 it controlled the local spice and silk trade completely until 1765. From 1794 to 1868 the city was held by the Sultanate of Oman and Zanzibar under a lease from Persia, whose Arabic and Persian versions apparently differed. Persia tried to oust the Omanis in 1823 and recovered the city in 1854. Under British pressure after the Anglo-Persian War of 1856 the lease was renewed, and in 1868 it was renewed once more and cancelled two months later by the Persian government.

An earthquake in July 1902 damaged parts of the city. Under Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi the government invested heavily in the port: in 1955 it was a small fishing port of about 17,000 people, and in 1977 the bulk of the Iranian Navy was moved from Khorramshahr to a new headquarters and naval base here. The city is the capital of Hormozgan Province and has been the southern terminus of Iran's main north-south railway since 1993. Its original inhabitants speak Bandari, a variety of Persian. Its pottery was once exported to England as goombroon ware.
bandar-e-anzali: Bandar-e Anzali lies on the Caspian Sea in Gilan province and consists of an island called Mianposhteh and the surrounding lands. The Anzali Lagoon divides the port in two parts, and the city is connected by two bridges to Beheshti Island. The humid subtropical climate, with heavy autumn and early winter rain and water draining from the Elburz Mountains, allows crops such as rice and tea that need much moisture. Anzali Gulf was a safe harbour for trade ships and fishing boats, and the city was home to the first and biggest port on the southern shores of the Caspian Sea.

The city is described as an old settlement first inhabited by the Cadusii. Its name is given in Middle Persian as Anzalag. It was renamed Pahlavi in 1935. In 1919, after the collapse of General Anton Denikin's White Russian army, eighteen of his ships sought refuge there.

On 18 May 1920 a Soviet flotilla of thirteen ships made a surprise attack on Anzali and captured the British garrison and the eighteen White Russian ships. This allowed the establishment of the short-lived Persian Socialist Republic and the Persian Communist Party. Soviet authorities denied responsibility for the attack and blamed the local Russian naval commander for acting on his own authority.

The people of Anzali speak Gilaki, Azerbaijani and Persian, and the city is the biggest after Rasht where Gilaki is spoken. Most are adherents of Shia Islam, with a sizeable Armenian Christian minority. The 2016 census counted 118,564 people. Historically the townspeople were mostly involved in the fish trade, and the city is a centre of caviar production. Its sights include a clock tower called Manareh, the harbour promenade, the lagoon, and buildings such as the Mian Poshte Palace and the Motamedi Edifice.
bangkok: Bangkok lies in the Chao Phraya River delta in Thailand's central plain. The river flows southwards through the city and empties into the Gulf of Thailand about 25 kilometres south of the centre. The area is flat and low-lying, with an average elevation of 1.5 metres above sea level. Most of it was originally swampland, gradually drained and irrigated by canals (khlong) dug between the 16th and 19th centuries. The origin of the name is unclear. Bang is a Thai word for a village on a stream, and the name may derive from Bang Ko, 'island', or from Bang Makok, after a plant bearing olive-like fruit.

The history of Bangkok goes back at least to the early 15th century, when it was a village on the west bank of the Chao Phraya under Ayutthaya. It served as a customs outpost with forts on both sides of the river, and was the site of a siege in 1688 in which the French were expelled from Siam. After Ayutthaya fell to the Burmese in 1767, King Taksin made the town his capital. The City Pillar was erected on 21 April 1782, regarded as the date of the city's foundation as the capital, and foreign visitors continued to call it Bangkok.

The city was at the heart of the modernisation of Siam in the late 19th century. Charoen Krung Road, the first built by Western techniques, was completed in 1864, and rail transport was introduced in 1893. Through the 20th century the city was at the centre of political struggles, as Siam abolished absolute monarchy and adopted constitutional rule. It became a special administrative area under the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration in 1972.

Bangkok is governed by the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration and is a special administrative area at provincial level, divided into fifty districts. Its landmarks include the Grand Palace and the Buddhist temples Wat Arun and Wat Pho. Thailand's five oldest universities, Chulalongkorn, Thammasat, Kasetsart, Mahidol and Silpakorn, founded between 1917 and 1943, are in the city.
bangladesh-liberation-war: Pakistan came into being in August 1947 in two geographically and culturally separate parts, with India between them. In 1948 Governor-General Muhammad Ali Jinnah declared that Urdu alone would be the federal language, although Bengali speakers made up over 56% of the population. East Pakistan had the larger population but West Pakistan dominated politically and received more from the common budget. The 1970 Bhola cyclone struck the East Pakistan coast on 12 November and killed an estimated 300,000 people, and eleven East Pakistani leaders charged the government with gross neglect.

On the night of 25 March 1971 the Pakistan Army began Operation Searchlight, a planned pacification meant to take the major cities and eliminate all opposition within a month. Foreign journalists were deported beforehand, and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman was arrested. Major Ziaur Rahman broadcast the declaration of independence from the radio station at Chittagong on 26 March. Resistance grew as Bengali soldiers defected and merged into the Mukti Bahini, supplied from India, while Pakistan raised the Razakar, Al-Badr and Al-Shams militias.

India joined the war on 3 December after Pakistani air strikes on northern India. Indian aircraft achieved near-total air supremacy within a week, and the East Pakistan ports were blockaded. On 16 December 1971 the Pakistani commander in East Pakistan signed the Instrument of Surrender in Dhaka, and over 93,000 Pakistani troops surrendered, the largest surrender since the Second World War.

The Pakistani military and supporting militias carried out widespread killings, deportation and rape. Estimates range from 300,000 to 3,000,000 killed and from 200,000 to 400,000 women raped. On 14 December 1971 the army and the Razakars seized at least 100 physicians, professors, writers and engineers in Dacca and murdered them. An estimated 10 million refugees fled to India and 30 million were internally displaced.

Bhutan was the first state to recognise Bangladesh, on 6 December 1971. The Simla Agreement of 1972 between India and Pakistan secured Pakistani recognition of Bangladesh in exchange for the return of prisoners of war. In West Pakistan the defeat discredited Yahya Khan's rule. The war changed the geopolitical landscape of South Asia and became an episode of Cold War tension involving the United States, the Soviet Union and China.
banjarmasin: Banjarmasin lies on a delta island near the confluence of the Barito and Martapura rivers, and the Martapura bisects it. The land is flat and low-lying, and several smaller rivers affected by the tides form its drainage. The city sits in a swampy region, generally below water level, and is prone to flooding by tidal bores. Its climate is tropical monsoon, with heavy rain from November to June.

The name is thought to be a corruption of Bandar Masih, Port Masih, after Patih Masih, who ruled the port and surrounding villages. Dayaks from the interior visited the port to trade, and some settled there.Europeans first met the Banjar through trade, mostly at Banten from 1596. Dutch traders came to the port only after Banten's rulers banned them. On 17 July 1607 the Sultan took revenge on a Dutch ship at Banjarmasin by hijacking it and massacring the crew. A trade agreement gave the Dutch East India Company a monopoly of trade in the port, but the sultan expelled the company in 1638 after waging war and burning much of its property around the port.

The Imperial Japanese Army occupied the city in the Second World War, and control then passed to the Imperial Japanese Navy, whose rule locals described as harsher. Australian forces liberated the city in September 1945. The people opposed the return of Dutch rule, which led to the four-year Kalimantan Physical Revolution between Indonesian nationalists and the Royal Netherlands East Indies Army, ending with Dutch recognition of Indonesia in 1949. The city was granted city status in 1959 and became the capital of the new province of South Kalimantan.

Banjarmasin is the largest city in South Kalimantan, Indonesia, and the centre of Banjarese culture. The provincial capital was legally moved to Banjarbaru on 15 February 2022. The culture of the Banjar people is described as a river culture, influenced by Dayak, Javanese, Malay, Arab and even Persian peoples, and keeps elements of a Hindu-Buddhist past despite a Muslim majority.
banjul: Banjul stands on St Mary's Island, also called Banjul Island, in the Gambia River where it enters the Atlantic Ocean. Bridges connect the island to the mainland, and ferries cross the river. There are several explanations of the name. One tradition says that Bandjougou, son of Barafin, came to the island fleeing the attacks of Soumaoro Kante on the Manding region, and that his name became Bandjoulou. Another derives it from Bang julo, the Mandinka word for the rope fibre gathered on the island.

In 1651 the island was leased from the King of Kombo by the Duke of Courland and Semigallia, as part of the Curonian colonization. On 23 April 1816 Tumani Bojang, the King of Kombo, ceded it to Alexander Grant, the British commandant, in exchange for an annual fee of 103 iron bars. Grant's expedition of 75 men had been ordered by Charles MacCarthy to establish a military garrison. Grant founded a trading post and base to control the entrance to the Gambia estuary and suppress the slave trade.

The British renamed the island St Mary's and called the town Bathurst, after the 3rd Earl Bathurst, Secretary of State for War and the Colonies. The streets were laid out in a modified grid and named after Allied generals at the Battle of Waterloo.

Within a few years the town drew migrants: Africans of various origins, Levantines and Europeans. Most of its people were Muslim, with a significant Christian minority including the Aku. The Wolof, mainly from Gorée and Saint-Louis, were the largest African group, rising from 829 in 1881 to 10,130 in 1944. Islamic schools called dara were founded early, and the first Muslim court in 1905. Bathurst was declared capital of the Protectorate of the Gambia in 1889, and became a centre of British activity in the colony. It was an important Allied naval and air hub in the Second World War, when its population rose from 14,370 in 1931 to 21,154 in 1944. After independence the town was renamed Banjul on 24 April 1973.

Banjul is the capital of the Gambia and its economic and administrative centre, with the Central Bank of the Gambia and a port that ships groundnut products, beeswax, palm oil and hides. The city proper had 26,461 people at the 2024 census, and the Greater Banjul Area, which includes the Kanifing municipality, 405,809. Arch 22, 35 metres tall, was built as an entrance portal to commemorate the bloodless coup of 22 July 1994 and houses a textile museum. The Gambian National Museum, the Albert Market and the State House are in the city.
bank-of-england: After the Revolution of 1688 brought William III and Mary II to the throne, a national bank became possible. During the Nine Years' War the Royal Navy was defeated by the French at the Battle of Beachy Head in 1690, and the government decided to rebuild it, but low public funds and poor credit made it impossible to borrow the £1.5 million it wanted. The idea of a public bank was two decades old. John Locke was an early supporter and, once it was set up, an early investor, and in 1691 the Scottish trader William Paterson proposed a national bank to bolster public finances. It was chartered in 1694.

The Ways and Means Act of 1715 authorised the bank to take subscriptions for a government issue of 5% annuities meant to raise £910,000; this began its role in managing government stocks, which it kept until 1998. The bank has been on Threadneedle Street since 1734, and a satirical cartoon by James Gillray in 1797 gave it the nickname the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street. Its first branches opened in 1826, and by 1829 there were eleven; the last five closed in 1997.

Britain was on the gold standard until 1931, when the Great Depression forced the bank to take it off. Banknotes were issued from 1694, hand-written at first and fully printed from 1855. After the First World War the bank withdrew increasingly from private and commercial accounts to concentrate on central banking. It was privately owned by stockholders until its nationalisation in 1946 by the Attlee ministry.

The Bank of England is the central bank of the United Kingdom and the model on which most modern central banks have been based. It is the world's second oldest central bank, after Sweden's of 1668. In 1998 it became an independent public body, and the Debt Management Office took over government debt. The bank is custodian of the official gold reserves of the United Kingdom and holds a monopoly on issuing banknotes in England and Wales.
banska-stiavnica: Banská Štiavnica stands in the middle of an immense caldera created by the collapse of an ancient volcano, known for its size as the Štiavnica Mountains. Its fate has been closely linked to the exploitation of abundant silver ore. Excavations show that the site was settled in the Neolithic period. The Slavic population named the settlement in the valley Štiavnica, meaning acidic stream, and the settlement on the hill above came to be called Bánya, the mine.

The first mining settlement was founded by Celts in the 3rd century BCE, probably by the Cotini tribe. The site was called terra banensium, the land of miners, as early as 1156. Skilled German settlers began arriving in the 13th century and adapted the local name to Schemnitz. Banská Štiavnica gained the status of a royal town in 1238, one of the first in the Kingdom of Hungary, and in the High and Late Middle Ages it was the main producer of silver and gold in the kingdom.

During the Ottoman Wars the town built powerful fortifications, including two castles, in the 16th century. It was also a centre of mining innovation: in 1627 gunpowder was used in a mine there, one of the first uses in the world. In the 18th century local scientists, among them Jozef Karol Hell, Maximilian Hell and Samuel Mikovíny, designed a system of reservoirs and channels called tajchy to drain flooded mines.

Samuel Mikovíny founded a Mining Academy in 1735, the first mining school in the Kingdom of Hungary. From 1763 it became the Academy of Mining with the support of Queen Maria Theresa, and in 1848 the Academy of Mining and Forestry, described as the first technical university in the world. In 1782 the town was the third biggest in the kingdom, but mining declined progressively from the second half of the 19th century.

Banská Štiavnica is a town in central Slovakia with a population of less than 10,000. The surviving urban centre was formed during the 16th century, and the town and its surroundings were proclaimed a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 11 December 1993. Sixty reservoirs were built between the 15th and 18th centuries, connected by more than 100 kilometres of channels, and they are now used mainly for recreation. The old and new castles have become museums.
banten: Banten lies at the western tip of Java. It is bordered by the Java Sea on the north, the Sunda Strait on the west and the Indian Ocean on the south, and by West Java and Jakarta on the east. The Sunda Strait carries sea lanes linking Australia and New Zealand with Southeast Asia, and Banten forms a link between Java and Sumatra. The province covers 9,355.76 square kilometres and ranges from sea level to 2,000 metres, with lowlands in the north and south and hills in the centre.

In the fourth and fifth centuries the area belonged to the kingdom of Tarumanagara. A Sanskrit inscription found in 1947 in Munjul describes life under Purnawarman. After Tarumanagara fell to an attack by Srivijaya, western Java became part of the Sunda Kingdom. Islam began to spread in the 15th century and by the late 16th century had replaced Hinduism and Buddhism as the main religion, with the establishment of the Banten Sultanate. According to the Babad Banten, Sunan Gunung Jati and Maulana Hasanuddin spread Islam widely.

The Portuguese were established in Banten before the Dutch, and the English, French and Danish also traded there. The Portuguese left in 1601 after the Dutch destroyed their fleet off the coast. The Dutch East India Company gradually weakened the sultanate, and on 22 November 1808 Governor-General Herman Willem Daendels declared it absorbed into the Dutch East Indies. Japan occupied the region from March 1942 and built the Saketi-Bayah railway to carry brown coal, using about 1,000 forced labourers, rōmusha, drawn mainly from Banten; casualties are estimated at 20,000 to 60,000, not counting mine workers. Banten became a separate province on 17 October 2000.

The capital of the province is Serang and its largest city is Tangerang. Most residents are Muslims, and the Bantenese, at 47 per cent, are the largest ethnic group. The Baduy people of Kanekes practise Sunda Wiwitan and keep their ancestral customs. The Great Mosque of Banten and Ujung Kulon National Park, a sanctuary of the Javan rhinoceros, are among its notable sites.
bantu-peoples: The Bantu peoples are a grouping of about 400 distinct Indigenous African ethnic groups who speak Bantu languages, of which there are between 440 and 680 depending on how language and dialect are defined. They are not a single ethnic group. The term Bantu is an artificial one, introduced into modern scholarship by Wilhelm Bleek in 1857 or 1858, based on a reconstructed Proto-Bantu word for people. Proto-Bantu is estimated to have been spoken 4,000 to 3,000 years ago in the area of modern Cameroon. The spread of Bantu speakers across Central, East and Southern Africa, the Bantu expansion, took roughly two millennia, during the 1st millennium BCE and the 1st millennium CE.

In the course of the expansion Bantu-speaking peoples absorbed or displaced many earlier inhabitants. Central African Pygmy groups, the Hadza of northern Tanzania and various Khoisan populations of southern Africa remained. Genetic analysis shows admixture with earlier local populations, and interaction with Cushitic, Nilotic and Central Sudanic speakers. Pioneering groups had reached parts of KwaZulu-Natal before the 3rd century CE and the Northern Cape by 500 CE.

Between the 9th and 15th centuries Bantu-speaking states began to emerge in the Great Lakes region and in the savanna south of the Central African rainforest, and from the 12th century state formation became more frequent. Examples include the Kingdom of Kongo, the Luba Empire, the Lunda Empire, Buganda, Rwanda and the Zulu Kingdom. The Monomotapa kings built the Great Zimbabwe complex, ancestral to the Shona. On the East African coast contact with Arab and Persian traders produced Swahili culture, whose language holds many Arabic loanwords.

Speakers of Bantu languages number in the hundreds of millions, roughly 350 million in the mid-2010s, about 30 per cent of Africa's population. About 90 million are in the Democratic Republic of the Congo alone.

In South Africa the term Bantu came into use in the 1920s in preference to Native. After World War II the National Party governments adopted it officially, and it became identified with apartheid, which named its eleven rural reserves Bantustans. It is now used there only in its linguistic sense.
bantustan: From 1913 successive white-minority South African governments set up reserves to segregate the black population, as the Natives Land Act of 1913 limited black people to seven percent of the land. When the National Party came to power in 1948, Hendrik Verwoerd, Minister for Native Affairs and later Prime Minister, built on this with measures such as the Group Areas Acts and the Natives Resettlement Act of 1954. The creation of homelands was central to the strategy, since the long-term goal was to make them independent, so that black people would lose their South African citizenship and voting rights and whites would remain in control.

The word, first used in the late 1940s, was coined by supporters of the policy to echo Pakistan and Hindustan, and it quickly became a pejorative; the National Party preferred homelands. Nelson Mandela wrote in 1959 that the word was a complete misnomer that helped the Nationalists perpetrate a fraud, since Africans would have no rights outside the reserves.

The Bantu Authorities Act of 1951 established homelands for the black ethnic groups, amounting to 13% of the country's land. The Bantu Self-Government Act of 1959 set out a plan called Separate Development, in four steps: a single Territorial Authority, a legislative assembly with limited powers, self-governing status, and nominal independence. Cooperative chiefs ran the homelands, and uncooperative ones were forcibly deposed. The Black Homelands Citizenship Act of 1970 designated all black South Africans citizens of the homelands, even if they lived in white South Africa, and cancelled their South African citizenship.

By 1984 all ten homelands in South Africa were self-governing, and four, Transkei, Bophuthatswana, Venda and Ciskei, had been declared independent between 1976 and 1981. Only South Africa recognised them. An estimated 3.5 million people were forced from their homes from the 1960s to the 1980s, many resettled in the homelands, yet only about 39% of black South Africans lived in them in 1986. Following the Odendaal commission, ten homelands were also set up in South West Africa from 1968.

The homelands were generally poor, with few local jobs. Bophuthatswana, with deposits of platinum, was the wealthiest, and the casino resort of Sun City was built there, taking advantage of laws that differed from those of South Africa. Homeland leaders were widely seen as collaborators with the apartheid system, though some gained a following. All the Bantustans were dismantled and reincorporated into South Africa on 27 April 1994, when the Interim Constitution came into force; in Ciskei South African security forces intervened in March 1994 to defuse a crisis. The term is now used more generally, in a disapproving sense, for any area where people are forced to live without full civil and political rights.
bao-dai: Bảo Đại was born Nguyễn Phúc Vĩnh Thụy on 22 October 1913, the only child of Emperor Khải Định. The Nguyễn dynasty had ruled Vietnam since 1802, but after the French conquest of 1883 the country was divided into the protectorates of Annam and Tonkin and the colony of Cochinchina, and the dynasty kept only nominal rule of Annam and Tonkin. In 1922 the boy was adopted by a former French Resident-Superior of Annam and sent to France to study. He was the first Vietnamese monarch to receive a full Western education.

Khải Định died in 1925, and on 8 January 1926 Vĩnh Thụy was enthroned at the age of twelve, taking the era name Bảo Đại, meaning keeper of greatness. A regent governed for him while he returned to France to study. He came back to Vietnam in 1932 and began to reform the court, abolishing the kowtow and the rule against looking directly at the emperor.

In March 1945 the Japanese, who had occupied French Indochina since 1940, ousted the French administration and kept Bảo Đại as emperor. On 11 March he signed a declaration of independence, prepared by the Japanese, that cancelled the treaty of 1884 with France and proclaimed the Empire of Vietnam, in practice a client state of Japan. After Japan surrendered, the Viet Minh forced the imperial government to hand over power, and he abdicated, saying that he would prefer to be a citizen of an independent country than emperor of an enslaved one.

Hồ Chí Minh invited him to Hanoi as supreme adviser to the new Democratic Republic of Vietnam, a post he held for nearly a year. In 1946 he left a delegation to China and settled in Hong Kong. From 1949 to 1955 he was chief of state of the French-associated State of Vietnam. He was criticised for being too closely tied to France and for spending much of his time outside Vietnam, and in 1955 Prime Minister Ngô Đình Diệm removed him in a referendum.

Bảo Đại lived in exile in France. He died in Paris on 31 July 1997, aged 83, and was buried in the Passy Cemetery. The Communist Party of Vietnam regarded him as a traitor, and many overseas Vietnamese opposed to communism also judged him weak, though recent studies have questioned both views.
bar-le-duc: Bar-le-Duc, formerly known as Bar, is the capital of the Meuse département in the Grand Est region of north-eastern France. The lower town, the more modern and busier part, extends along a narrow valley shut in by wooded or vine-clad hills, and the Ornain runs through it. The upper town, the Ville Haute, lies on the left bank of a small arm of the river, the Canal des Usines.

Bar-le-Duc was the seat of a county and, from 1354, of the Duchy of Bar. The town is probably of ancient origin but was unimportant until the 10th century, when Frederick I of Upper Lorraine fortified it. Bar was an independent duchy from 1354 to 1480, when the Duchy of Lorraine acquired it.

In 1916, during the Battle of Verdun, Bar-le-Duc was the assembly point for the supplies sent to the besieged city of Verdun. Thousands of trucks carrying men, equipment and food travelled north around the clock on the road linking the two towns, which the writer and politician Maurice Barres named the Voie Sacrée, the Sacred Way, in April 1916.

The Ville Haute is crossed by a long, quiet street lined with houses of the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries, and holds 16th-century remains of the château of the dukes of Bar, dismantled in 1670. The church of Saint-Étienne contains the Cadaver Tomb of René of Châlon, who died in 1544, a carved white stone effigy of a half-decayed corpse by the 16th-century artist Ligier Richier. Among the natives of Bar-le-Duc are Mary of Guise, mother of Mary, Queen of Scots, and the mathematician Henri Poincaré. Bar-le-Duc jelly, made from currants and first mentioned in 1344, is known as Bar caviar.
bar-montenegro: Bar lies on the Adriatic shore in the coastal region of Montenegro, about 53 kilometres from Podgorica, with Lake Skadar, the largest lake in southern Europe, to the east. Its name is thought to be a shortened Slavic form of Antivari, from the Latin Antibarum or Antibari, meaning opposite Bari, for its position across the Adriatic from that Italian city. It is called Tivari in Albanian. Finds from the Neolithic show that people lived there in prehistoric times, and the name Antibarium is first quoted in the 10th century.

In the Middle Ages Bar was linked to the Slavic state of Duklja. Stefan Vojislav, ruler from 1018 to 1043, defeated the Byzantines in a battle on a hill near Bar and made it his seat. His son Mihailo I established the Archdiocese of Antivari, founded in 1089. Byzantium held the town from 1166 to 1183, until Stefan Nemanja conquered and destroyed it. The Nemanjić dynasty ruled it until 1360, then the Balšić family. The Venetians controlled Bar from 1405 to 1412, when it grew most and became a city-state, with its own Statute of Communes and coinage. They ruled again from 1443 to 1571, until the Ottomans captured Antivari and held it until 1878.

The Ottomans ceded Antivari to Montenegro at the Treaty of Berlin in 1878, and the town was made militarily neutral. In the late 1850s it had 4,000 inhabitants, 62.5 per cent of them Muslims; more than half left or were expelled after 1878. On 30 August 1904 Guglielmo Marconi made a radio link between Antivari and Bari, and in 1908 the first railway in this part of the Balkans opened there. In 1914 and 1915 Austro-Hungarian ships bombarded the port, and on 16 August 1914 a French fleet sank the cruiser SMS Zenta off the town in the Battle of Antivari. Bar joined the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in 1918.

The old town of Stari Bar and the newer settlement by the sea are distinct: the district of Pristan was demolished in 1976 to enlarge the port, and its people moved mostly to Topolica. The Port of Bar and the Belgrade–Bar railway, opened in 1976, are the basis of its economy. King Nikola's castle at Topolica, built in 1885, houses the Bar Homeland Museum. Bar is the birthplace of Saint Jovan Vladimir, and has Orthodox and Catholic churches and mosques built by the Ottomans.
bar-sur-aube: The town is old. Remains of an Iron Age oppidum survive, and a coin bearing a horse and the name of Togirix, a chief of the Lingones, was found on the hill of Sainte Germaine. In Roman times it appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana as Segessera, and villas of the 1st to 4th centuries have been found in and around it. Tradition tells that the city was devastated by Attila, and Sainte Germaine is said to have been beheaded on his order in 451. After the division of the kingdom of Clovis it became part of Austrasia, and under Charles the Bald coins were struck with its name on the reverse. The name Bar comes from a Gallic word meaning summit.

Under the counts of Champagne the town was of great importance because of the Champagne fairs, where merchants from Flanders and Italy traded oriental spices and silk for the textiles and raw materials of northern Europe. The town was later joined to the crown of France. In 1318 Philip V the Tall sold it to Jacques de Croÿ; the residents then bought it themselves, so that the king could no longer sell or alienate their lands. A long plague in 1636 ended the fair.

The fortifications were demolished in 1862 and replaced by a boulevard. The French Revolution was well received there, and from 1790 to 1800 the town was the chief town of its district. On 27 February 1814, near the end of the Napoleonic era, the Battle of Bar-sur-Aube was fought in the town and its surroundings.

Bar-sur-Aube is a commune and sub-prefecture in the Aube department of the Grand Est region, about 30 kilometres west-north-west of Chaumont. It lies on the Aube among hills and Champagne vineyards. Its heritage includes the 12th-century church of Saint Maclou, the 16th-century church of Saint Peter, which holds most of the commune's more than 200 registered historical objects, and the chapel of Saint John, held in turn by the Knights Templar and the Knights Hospitaller.
barbastro: Barbastro is a city in the Somontano county of the province of Huesca, at the junction of the rivers Cinca and Vero. It was known originally as Barbastra or Bergiduna. An ancient Celtiberian city called Bergidum or Bergiduna stood there; in Roman times, as Barbastro, it lay within Hispania Citerior and later Hispania Tarraconensis, and after the fall of the Western Roman Empire it belonged to the Visigoth kingdom.

Musa bin Nusair overtook Barbastro and the surrounding Barbitaniya in 717, as part of the Umayyad push into the northern territories of the Marca Hispanica, and the town was called Madyar. It was later settled by the Banu Jalaf, who made it the capital of an emirate of Barbineta and Huesca until 862, and it was known as the Emirate of Brabstra until 882.

In 1064 Sancho Ramírez, King of Aragón, and Frankish Christian forces led by William VIII of Aquitaine and a Norman commander called Le Bon Normand invaded the city, which then belonged to the emirate of Zaragoza. The attack is known as the Siege of Barbastro. Contemporary sources state that 50,000 people were killed or captured, but modern historians regard this as an exaggeration, since the whole population of the town probably did not exceed 8,000. Muslim forces reconquered the city in 1065.

A Sephardic Jewish community flourished in Barbastro in the Middle Ages and suffered little compared with others in Spain; the first written record of it dates from 1144. After the Disputation of Tortosa its members all became conversos, and the old synagogue became a centre of converso life. In June 1837, during the First Carlist War, the French Foreign Legion, attached to the liberal government's army, fought the Carlist foreign legion there, and its commander, Colonel Joseph Conrad, was killed.

In the Spanish Civil War 51 Catholic Claretians, mostly young seminarians, were executed in Barbastro by anarchist militia of the Popular Front, and the diocese suffered the highest proportion of clergy killed in the war. The city's economy flourished until the early 20th century, declined, and recovered from the 1960s with the growth of agricultural production.
barbed-wire: Fencing of flat, thin wire with bristling points was first proposed in France by Leonce Eugene Grassin-Baledans in 1860. In April 1865 Louis François Janin proposed a double wire with diamond-shaped metal barbs. In 1867 alone six patents were issued, only two of them for livestock, one to Lucien B. Smith of Ohio, regarded as the American inventor. After the Civil War the plains were extensively settled, and ranchers, railroads and farmers all needed to fence large open spaces where wood and stone were costly and hedges unreliable.

In 1873 Joseph Glidden, a farmer, saw at a fair in DeKalb, Illinois a display by Henry B. Rose of a wooden strip with metallic points. With the hardware dealer Isaac L. Ellwood and the lumber merchant Jacob Haish he began experimenting, twisting two wires round the barbs with a grindstone and shaping barbs with a coffee mill. Glidden applied for a patent in October 1873; Haish, who held patents of his own, accused him of interference, and approval of Glidden's wire, nicknamed The Winner, was deferred until 24 November 1874.

In 1876 John Warne Gates demonstrated the wire in Military Plaza, San Antonio, showing cattle held by it, and sales rose sharply. Between 1873 and 1899 as many as 150 companies made barbed wire, then consolidated, notably into the American Steel and Wire Company, later part of U.S. Steel. A US District Court upheld the Glidden patent in 1880 and the Supreme Court affirmed it in 1892. Wire cut the cost of enclosing land and set farmers against open-range ranchers in the range wars. Heavy penalties were set for cutting fences, and some historians date the end of the Old West to the wire's spread.

Portuguese troops used barbed wire in the Battle of Magul in 1895, and it was used extensively in the Boer War, where it held the captured Boer population in concentration camps. In the First World War all combatants placed entanglements before their trenches to halt charges or funnel soldiers into machine-gun fire. The tank defeated it, as the Allied breakthrough at Amiens on 8 August 1918 showed.

Barbed wire is still the standard fencing for enclosing cattle in most regions of the United States. Fences are built between heavy braced posts and kept under great tension, often up to half a ton. The wire is galvanized, and high-tensile wire is thinner but resists stretching better. Razor wire, which replaces the barbs with near-continuous cutting surfaces, is used where humans must be kept out.
barbuda: Barbuda lies north of Antigua and covers about 160 square kilometres. Coral limestone makes up most of the island, which has very little variety in its landscape. Hills in the Barbuda Highlands on the eastern side reach about 38 metres, while the northwest corner holds many lagoons, and Codrington Lagoon dominates the western part. Salty ponds and scrubland are spread across the interior. The climate is tropical marine. Codrington, which grew up as the main residential area by 1666, is still the only town and the main settlement.

The first settlers arrived by canoe, as hunter-gatherers, around 2,900 to 3,000 BCE. Sources disagree on whether they came from South America, the Greater Antilles or the Yucatán region. They made cutting blades, hoes and picks from the shells of conch, trumpet and whelk. They were followed by Arawak people, present on Barbuda and Antigua from at least 1,000 BCE, whose numbers on Barbuda peaked between 1,500 and 800 years ago. They probably came from present-day Venezuela and Guyana, grew sweet potatoes, corn, cotton and tobacco, and made pottery in the Saladoid style, with white-on-red designs.

English colonisation was attempted from St. Kitts under a patent of 1625 granted to the Earl of Carlisle, and the island appears there as Barbado. In 1668 about 240 Kalinago attacked the 20 English inhabitants, and eight settlers died. Strong Kalinago resistance and drought caused this attempt to fail. In 1685 the crown granted the island to the brothers John and Christopher Codrington. The colonisers intended Barbuda to be a colony for the forced reproduction of enslaved people, but this never went through. Slavery was abolished there in 1834. Because a single land grant had covered the whole island, Barbudans went on farming communal property on their own account.

Barbuda forms part of the twin-island state of Antigua and Barbuda as an autonomous entity. It gained autonomy in 1976 through the Barbuda Local Government Act, which created the Barbuda Council, and gained independence from the United Kingdom in 1981 as part of Antigua and Barbuda. The Council has eleven members and sits in Codrington. Under the Barbuda Land Acts, land is held communally. The 2011 census counted 1,634 people. Fishing, especially for lobster, supplies most exports, and tourist attractions include the Frigate Bird Sanctuary in Codrington Lagoon, a 19th-century Martello Tower and the ruins of Highland House, the Codrington family home.
barcelona: Barcelona lies on the north-east coast of the Iberian Peninsula, facing the Mediterranean Sea, on a plain about 5 km wide limited by the Collserola mountain range, the Llobregat river to the south-west and the Besòs river to the north. It lies 120 km south of the Pyrenees. The escarpment of Montjuïc overlooks the harbour and is topped by Montjuïc Castle, a fortress built in the 17th and 18th centuries to control the city.

According to tradition Barcelona was founded by Phoenician or Carthaginian settlers, and some historians credit the Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca with naming it Barcino in the 3rd century BCE, though this theory has been questioned. Coins of the 3rd century BCE found at the foot of Montjuïc carry the name Barkeno in Iberian script.

In the Middle Ages Barcelona became the capital of the County of Barcelona. After the union with Aragon it remained capital of the Principality of Catalonia and the most important city of the Crown of Aragon, until Valencia overtook it shortly before 1516. Its industrial rise began in 1833, when Catalonia's textile industry began to use steam power. It became capital of autonomous Catalonia in 1931 and was taken by the fascists in 1939.

Barcelona is the capital of Catalonia and the second most populous municipality of Spain. Its old centre, the Barri Gòtic, has buildings from medieval times and some from the Roman settlement. Works of Antoni Gaudí and Lluís Domènech i Montaner are World Heritage Sites, and the city hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics.
bareilly: Bareilly lies in the Indo-Gangetic Plains on the bank of the Ramganga River, about 252 kilometres north-west of Lucknow and 265 kilometres east of New Delhi. The plain is level and well watered, with fertile alluvial soil, although the lower plain is flood-prone. According to the Mahabharata, the region, called Panchala, was the birthplace of Draupadi, and folklore says that Gautama Buddha visited the ancient fortress city of Ahichchhatra.

The earliest settlement was founded in 1537 by the Rajput chieftain Jagat Singh Katehriya, who named it after his two sons Bansaldev and Baraldev. The town came under Mughal rule in 1569, and in 1657 the Mughal governor Mukrand Rai laid the foundation of the modern city. As Mughal power weakened, the Kingdom of Rohilkhand rose, with Bareilly as a major centre. Under Hafiz Rahmat Khan Barech, Rohilkhand blocked Maratha expansion into northern India at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.

In 1774 the combined forces of Nawab Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and the East India Company defeated Hafiz Rahmat Khan, who was killed in battle, ending Rohilla rule. The Nawab of Awadh surrendered Rohilkhand to the Company in a treaty of 10 November 1801. A military station was established south of the city in 1811, and a fort was built in 1816. Bareilly was freed by rebels during the Indian Rebellion of 1857 and remained independent under Khan Bahadur Khan until the British re-annexed it in 1858.

Bareilly is a city in the Indian state of Uttar Pradesh and the centre of the historical region of Rohilkhand. It is the place of origin of the Barelvi movement, a Sunni Islamic movement formed by the scholar Ahmad Raza Khan to counter the growing influence of the Deobandi movement; his shrine at the Bareilly Dargah is visited by millions of followers each year. The city has been known as Nath Nagri because of its ancient Shiva temples, and is a centre of furniture manufacturing and of trade in cotton, cereal and sugar.
barometer: On 27 July 1630 Giovanni Battista Baliani wrote to Galileo Galilei about a siphon led over a hill about 21 m high that failed to work: the water in the limb sank to about 10 m above the reservoir. Galileo answered that the power of a vacuum held the water up until its weight grew too great, a restatement of the old doctrine that nature abhors a vacuum. After his Discorsi reached Rome in December 1638, Gasparo Berti and Raffaello Magiotti sought a better way to produce a vacuum. W. E. Knowles Middleton places their experiment between 1639 and 1643, with Athanasius Kircher and Niccolò Zucchi present.

Torricelli, who had been Galileo's amanuensis in the last three months of his life, read the results differently. In a letter to Michelangelo Ricci in 1644 he argued that the weight of the atmosphere explained the resistance, and that it was foolish to attribute to a vacuum what followed from another evident cause.

Marin Mersenne was shown the experiment by Torricelli toward the end of 1644, and in 1646 Blaise Pascal and Pierre Petit repeated and perfected it. Pascal tested the Aristotelian claim that vapours from the liquid filled the space above it by comparing water with wine, thought more spiritous. He did so in public, inviting the Aristotelians to predict the result. They expected the wine to stand lower, and it did not.

Mercury barometers broke at sea, and in 1668 Robert Hooke's marine barometer, made by Henry Hunt, was presented to the Royal Society. The compact sympiesometer was widely used on ships in the early 19th century. Leibniz proposed an aneroid barometer around 1700, and Lucien Vidi invented a working one in 1844.

Pressure readings and the pressure tendency, the change over time, have been used in weather forecasting since the late 19th century.
