Combined with wind observations they allow reasonably accurate short-term forecasts, and readings from a network of stations produced maps of air pressure, the first form of the modern weather map. A rapid fall suggests an approaching low-pressure system and more chance of rain, while a rapid rise follows a cold front and goes with clearing skies. Readings are corrected for temperature, since the density of mercury changes, and reduced to sea level.
bartolome-de-las-casas: Bartolomé de las Casas was born in Seville on 11 November 1484. For centuries his birth was dated to 1474, until archival work in the 1970s uncovered records of a contemporary lawsuit showing that he was born a decade later. His father, Pedro de las Casas, was a merchant. He arrived in Hispaniola as one of the first Spanish settlers and took part in the colonial economy built on forced Indigenous labour. In 1513, as a chaplain, he joined the conquest of Cuba, where he witnessed many atrocities against the Ciboney and Guanahatabey. He later wrote that he saw cruelty on a scale no living being has ever seen.

In 1515 he gave up his Indigenous laborers and his encomienda and met King Ferdinand to argue against the encomienda system. He was given the title Protector of the Indians. In his early writings he advocated African slaves to replace Indigenous labour, a position he later retracted, writing that black slavery was as unjust as Indian slavery. His attempt at peaceful settlement in Venezuela failed, and in 1522 he entered the Dominican monastery of Santa Cruz in Santo Domingo, taking vows in 1523.

He worked as a missionary among the Maya of Guatemala and lobbied for the abolition of the encomienda, winning an important victory in the New Laws of 1542. He was consecrated Bishop of Chiapas on 30 March 1544. Conflicts with the encomenderos and colonists forced him back to Spain. In 1550 he took part in the Valladolid debate, in which Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda argued that the Indians were less than human. De Las Casas maintained that they were fully human and that forcible subjugation was unjustifiable.

De Las Casas resigned his bishopric and spent the rest of his life at the imperial court, where he had great influence on matters concerning the Indies. He died on 18 July 1566. A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, written in 1542 and published at Seville in 1552, was one of the first attempts by a colonial-era Spanish writer to describe the mistreatment of Indigenous peoples. His efforts improved the legal status of Indigenous people and sharpened the ethical debate over colonialism, though he did not change Spanish policy as a whole. After his death he was widely venerated, and a cause for beatification was opened.
bartolome-esteban-murillo: Murillo was probably born in December 1617 to Gaspar Esteban, a barber surgeon, and María Pérez Murillo, and was baptised in the parish of Santa María Magdalena in Seville on 1 January 1618. After his parents died in 1627 and 1628 he became the ward of his older sister Ana and her husband Juan Agustín Lagares, and he stayed in their house until his marriage in 1645.

He studied in Seville in the workshop of Juan del Castillo, his uncle and godfather. His first works were also influenced by Francisco de Zurbarán, Jusepe de Ribera and Alonso Cano. According to the painter and art historian Antonio Palomino he travelled to Madrid in 1642, but there is little evidence for this, and Palomino denied claims by Joachim von Sandrart that he went to Italy.

In 1645 Murillo married Beatriz Cabrera y Villalobos, with whom he had ten children. The year of his marriage he received his first major commission, eleven canvases for the convent of San Francisco in Seville, on which he worked until 1648. They show a range from the tenebrism of the Ecstasy of St Francis to the softly luminous style, seen in the Death of St Clare, that became typical of his mature work. Also about 1645 he painted The Young Beggar, now in the Louvre, the first of his many paintings of children, in which the influence of Velázquez is apparent.

After a pair of pictures for Seville Cathedral he specialised in the Virgin and Child and the Immaculate Conception. He was again in Madrid from 1658 to 1660. On returning to Seville he was one of the founders of the Academia de Bellas Artes, sharing its direction in 1660 with the architect Francisco Herrera the Younger. This was his period of most activity, and the paintings for Santa María la Blanca were completed in 1665.

Murillo died in Seville on 3 April 1682, a few months after he fell from a scaffold while working on a fresco at the church of the Capuchines in Cádiz. He had many pupils and followers, and the imitation of his paintings ensured his reputation in Spain and his fame throughout Europe. Before the 19th century his work was more widely known than that of any other Spanish artist, and Gainsborough and Greuze were among those influenced by his style. His paintings of flower girls, street urchins and beggars form an extensive record of the everyday life of his times.
bartolomeu-dias: Dias came from a family with a maritime background. One of his ancestors, Dinis Dias e Fernandes, explored the African coast in the 1440s. Tracing his own biography is complicated by the existence of several Portuguese seafarers of the same name. In 1481 he accompanied an expedition led by Diogo de Azambuja to build the fortress and trading post of São Jorge da Mina in the Gulf of Guinea, and indirect evidence suggests he may have joined Diogo Cão's first expedition to the Congo River. On 10 October 1486 King John II of Portugal granted him an annuity of 6,000 reis for services to come.

Probably in July or August 1487 Dias left Lisbon with three ships, to continue the exploration advanced by Cão and to look for Prester John, a Christian ruler believed to reign somewhere beyond Europe. He carried stone pillars, padrões, to mark landfalls, and six Africans kidnapped by Cão and taught Portuguese, whom he meant to leave along the coast. On 8 December 1487 he reached modern Walvis Bay. The ships then turned southwest, away from land; historians debate whether a storm drove them or they sought better winds. After 30 days at sea, on 4 February 1488, they reached the southern cape of Africa at what became Mossel Bay.

They continued east until 12 March 1488, when they anchored at Kwaaihoek. The crew were restless and the ships battered, and the officers unanimously urged a return, which Dias accepted. In May 1488 he first saw the Cape of Good Hope; tradition says he named it the Cape of Storms and King John II renamed it. He reached Lisbon in December 1488 after 16 months. Almost all maritime records were destroyed in the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, and much comes from João de Barros, writing about sixty years later. His reception at court was muted.

Dias contributed to the design and construction of the São Gabriel and São Rafael used by Vasco da Gama, and accompanied da Gama's fleet to the Cape Verde Islands in 1497. In 1500 he was a captain on Pedro Álvares Cabral's expedition, which reached Brazil on 22 April 1500. He died on 29 May 1500 when four ships, his among them, were lost in a storm off the Cape of Good Hope. His grandson Paulo Dias de Novais founded São Paulo de Luanda in 1576.
baruch-spinoza: Spinoza was born in Amsterdam on 24 November 1632 to a marrano family that had fled Portugal for the more tolerant Dutch Republic. His ancestors, adherents of crypto-Judaism, had faced persecution during the Portuguese Inquisition. His father, Michael, was a prominent merchant whose business had a wide reach and who was elected an administrative officer of the congregation Talmud Torah in 1649. Spinoza attended the congregation's school, where pupils were taught in Spanish to read the prayerbook and the Torah in Hebrew. His name does not appear on the school's registry after the age of fourteen, and he was needed in his father's business after his brother died in 1649.

Between 1654 and 1657 he began studying Latin with Franciscus van den Enden, a former Jesuit and political radical, who likely introduced him to scholastic and modern philosophy, including Descartes. Many of his friends were freethinkers or belonged to dissenting Christian groups such as the Collegiants. In 1654, when his father died, Spinoza became public and defiant in a series of financial and legal clashes with the synagogue, and the community, anxious for its reputation, expelled him permanently in 1656. He then supported himself by grinding lenses.

Around 1660 to 1661 Spinoza moved to Rijnsburg, near Leiden, where he wrote a Short Treatise on God, Man, and His Well-Being, which he never published, and began his Ethics. His Descartes' Principles of Philosophy, a geometric exposition in the manner of Euclid, appeared in 1663. He published sparingly in his lifetime to avoid persecution.

The Tractatus Theologico-Politicus, published in 1670, questioned the divine origin of the Hebrew Bible and argued that ecclesiastical authority should have no role in a secular, democratic state; it caused an uproar across Europe. The Ethics, which he regarded as his chief work, is written in a mathematical form modelled on Euclid. It equates God with nature, a view that scholars interpret as pantheist, panentheist or atheist. Spinoza denied that God has personality, intelligence or will, which is why he was often called an atheist. His unfinished Tractatus Politicus treats forms of government.

Spinoza's health failed in 1676, and he died at The Hague on 21 February 1677, aged 44, of a lung ailment, probably tuberculosis, perhaps worsened by glass dust. His friends published his works after his death. In 1785 Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi condemned his pantheism after Gotthold Ephraim Lessing was thought to have confessed to being a Spinozist, which then meant much the same as atheist, and Moses Mendelssohn disagreed with him. Later he came to be seen as a cultural hero and the first secular Jew. According to his biographer Jonathan I. Israel, thinkers from Lessing and Goethe to Kant, Hegel and Nietzsche remained preoccupied with him throughout their lives.
bas-rhin: Bas-Rhin, meaning Lower Rhine, is a department of Alsace in the Grand Est region of France. The name refers to its lower altitude, since it lies downstream of Haut-Rhin. The Rhine forms its eastern border, and the area includes foothills of the Vosges Mountains. To the north lies the Palatinate Forest in the German state of Rhineland-Palatinate, and to the east the state of Baden-Württemberg. Strasbourg is its prefecture and most populous commune. With Haut-Rhin it formed the traditional region of Alsace, which until 1871 also included the area now called the Territoire de Belfort. It is the last French department to keep the term Bas in its name.

Bas-Rhin is one of the original 83 departments, created on 4 March 1790 during the French Revolution. On 14 January 1790 the National Constituent Assembly decreed that Alsace be divided into two departments with Strasbourg and Colmar as their capitals. Its borders then changed many times. In 1793 it absorbed newly annexed territories such as the County of Sarrewerden and the County of Drulingen. In 1808 some territories east of the Rhine, including the city of Kehl, were annexed, and in 1814 and 1815 the treaties of Paris first gave France the lands north of the Lauter, including Landau, and then took them away. Troops from Baden and Saxony occupied the department from June 1815 to November 1818.

In 1871 the Treaty of Frankfurt annexed it to Germany, and it became the Bezirk Unterelsass in the Reichsland Elsaß-Lothringen. It became French again in 1919 under the Treaty of Versailles and kept the cantons of Schirmeck and Saales that Germany had taken from the Vosges. The Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp operated there between 1941 and 1944. Kehl was attached to Bas-Rhin in 1944 and reassigned to West Germany in 1953. In 1982 the department joined the newly created Alsace region.

Strasbourg is the official seat of the European Parliament and of the Council of Europe. The department had 1,163,810 inhabitants in 2023 and is densely populated, with more than twice the French average density. The Rhine has always been of great historical and economic importance to the area. On 1 January 2021 the departmental councils of Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin merged into the European Collectivity of Alsace. Its inhabitants are known as Bas-Rhinois.
basel-landschaft: Basel-Landschaft, also called Basel-Country, and informally Baselland or Baselbiet, is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation. It is composed of five districts, with Liestal as its capital, and is traditionally considered a half-canton, the other half being Basel-Stadt. It lies essentially south of the Rhine and north of the Jura Mountains, in the northwestern corner of Switzerland, and borders Basel-Stadt, Aargau, Solothurn and Jura, with international borders with France and Germany. The Ergolz and the Birs drain its lands. Its shape is very irregular, and its borders cut across several towns.

In Roman times the area was a centre of Roman activity. The remains of Augusta Raurica, in what is now Augst, show a city of about 20,000 people around 200 CE, and the site includes the best-preserved amphitheatre north of the Alps. With Basel-Stadt, Basel-Landschaft formed the historic canton of Basel, which joined the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1501. Until the end of the 16th century most of its land belonged to the city of Basel, on which the countryside was economically dependent, and the castles and residences of Basel merchants dominated much of the landscape. After Napoleon's visit in 1798 the country achieved equality with the city.

After 1830 political quarrels and armed conflict broke out in the canton, partly over the rights of the rural population. They culminated in the uprising of 1833, including the Battle of the Hülftenschanz near Frenkendorf, and led to the separation of Basel-Landschaft from the city on 26 August 1833.

A movement for reunification gained momentum after 1900, when many parts of Basel-Landschaft became industrialised. The two half cantons agreed in principle to merge, but in 1969 the people of Basel-Landschaft voted down the proposal, perhaps because the economic gap between the two had closed. Since then they have signed agreements to co-operate, such as the canton's contribution to the University of Basel since 1976. In 1988 the canton wrote into its constitution the aim of recognition of the two Basels as full cantons. The population is predominantly German-speaking.
basel-stadt: Basel-Stadt, or Basel-City, is one of the 26 cantons of the Swiss Confederation, composed of three municipalities, Basel, Riehen and Bettingen, with Basel as its capital. It is traditionally a half-canton, the other half being Basel-Landschaft. It is the smallest canton by area, just 37 square kilometres, and one of the northernmost and lowest, lying on both sides of the Rhine. Basel stands at the Rhine knee, where the river turns from a westerly to a northerly flow, marking the change from the High Rhine to the Upper Rhine. The territories of Switzerland, France and Germany meet in the middle of the Rhine, about 150 metres north of the Dreiländereck monument.

Together with Basel-Landschaft, Basel-Stadt was part of the Canton of Basel, which joined the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1501. After political quarrels and armed conflict, partly over the rights of the population of the agricultural areas, the canton was divided and Basel-Landschaft separated from the city on 26 August 1833. A movement for reunification gained momentum after 1900, when many parts of Basel-Landschaft became industrialised, but the people of Basel-Landschaft voted against reunion in 1969 and again in September 2014.

The present constitution of the canton dates from 1889. In 1966 Basel-Stadt became the first German-speaking canton to allow women to vote, five years before the right was extended to all Swiss women in 1971.

The chemical and pharmaceutical industries are the most significant industries in the canton, and Basel is the worldwide seat of the Bank for International Settlements. The port on the Rhine offers landlocked Switzerland its only direct connection to the sea, and the airport of Basel-Mulhouse lies 4 kilometres inside French territory. The Carnival of Basel, whose central tradition, the Morgestraich, begins at 4 a.m. and is followed by 72 hours of festivities, and the Autumn Fair, the biggest in Switzerland, are major events. The canton is known for two biscuits, the Basler Läckerli and the Basler Brunsli.
basf: BASF is an acronym for Badische Anilin- und Sodafabrik, the Baden Aniline and Soda Factory. It was founded by Friedrich Engelhorn on 6 April 1865 in Mannheim, in the state of Baden. Engelhorn had set up a gasworks and street lighting for the town council in 1861, and used the tar it produced as a by-product of coal to extract aniline for dyes. The plant was built across the Rhine at Ludwigshafen because the Mannheim council feared air pollution, and dye production moved there in 1866.

William Henry Perkin's discovery in 1857 that aniline could make intense colouring agents had begun the commercial production of synthetic dyes in England. BASF recruited the chemist Heinrich Caro as its first head of research. He developed a synthesis for the red dye alizarin and applied for a British patent on 25 June 1869, one day before Perkin applied for a virtually identical one; the two companies reached a commercial agreement. A synthetic indigo reached the market in 1897, and in 1901 about 80% of production was dyestuffs.

Other processes followed. In 1890 a unit using the contact process produced sulfuric acid at 98% concentration, the result of research by Rudolf Knietsch. After the Haber process, developed from 1908 to 1912, made it possible to synthesise ammonia, BASF acquired exclusive rights and in 1913 opened a plant at Oppau, adding fertilizers. In 1916 it opened a site at Leuna where explosives were made during the First World War. An explosion at Oppau on 21 September 1921 killed 565 people, the biggest industrial accident in German history.

Under Carl Bosch, BASF founded IG Farben with Hoechst, Bayer and three other companies, losing its independence. After Adolf Hitler became chancellor in 1933, IG Farben cooperated with the National Socialist government and profited from forced labour; by 1943 nearly half its workers were forced labourers, besides concentration camp prisoners supplied by the Nazis. IG Farben built a large chemical factory at Auschwitz and produced Zyklon B, the gas used to kill prisoners in the extermination camps. The Allies dissolved IG Farben in November 1945, and the Ludwigshafen site, bombed 65 times, had been almost completely destroyed.

An explosion at the Ludwigshafen site on 28 July 1948 killed 207 people. BASF was refounded under its name in 1952 and shared in the German economic miracle of the 1950s, adding synthetics such as nylon, and it invented Styropor in 1951. After a change of strategy in 1965 it put more weight on coatings, pharmaceuticals, pesticides and fertilizers, and it expanded production abroad.
bashkirs: The Bashkirs, or Bashkorts, are a Turkic people indigenous to Russia, concentrated in Bashkortostan and the historical region on both sides of the Ural Mountains. The Bashkir group was formed by Turkic tribes of South Siberian and Central Asian origin who wandered for a long time in the Aral-Syr Darya steppes, before migrating to the southern Urals between the end of the 9th century and the beginning of the 10th. The name Bashqurt has been known since the 10th century. Most researchers read it as bash, head or leader, plus qurt, wolf, and a legend tells how a wolf guided the first seven Bashkir tribes from the Syr Darya valley to their land.

The first Arabic and Persian reports of the Bashkirs date from the 9th century, including the account of Sallam al-Tardjuman, who travelled to their territory around 850. In the early 10th century Ahmad ibn Fadlan, an envoy of the Baghdad caliph to Volga Bulgaria, wrote the first ethnographic description, calling them a warlike and powerful people who bred cattle and worshipped twelve gods. By 1226 Genghis Khan had incorporated their lands into his empire, and in the 13th and 14th centuries Bashkortostan was part of the Golden Horde. Afterwards the Bashkirs were divided among the Nogai Horde, the Khanate of Kazan and the Khanate of Sibir.

From the middle of the 16th century the Tsardom of Russia gradually conquered the Bashkirs. They took part in uprisings in 1662–64, 1681–84 and 1704–11, and in 1676 a rebellion under Seyid Sadir gave the Russian army great difficulties. The founding of Orenburg in 1735 brought a fourth insurrection that lasted six years.

In the late 1780s they gained tax-free status in exchange for providing soldiers to the Tsarist army, and in 1798 Russia formed an irregular Bashkir army. On 15 November 1917 the Bashkir Regional Shuro proclaimed the first independent Bashkir Republic, and in March 1919 the Bashkir Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was formed.

The Bashkirs traditionally practised agriculture, cattle-rearing and bee-keeping, and the half-nomadic among them herded cattle through the mountains or the steppes. Before Islam they practised animism and shamanism and incorporated Tengrism; they began converting in the 10th century, and Islam was finally established among them in the 1320s and 1330s. Most are Sunni Muslims of the Hanafi school. Their oral tradition includes the epic poem Ural Batyr, which tells how the hero Ural gives up eternal life and from his body emerge the Ural Mountains. In the 2021 Russian census 1,571,879 ethnic Bashkirs were recorded in Russia.
basic-law-for-the-federal-republic-of-ge: Between February and June 1948 the London Six-Power Conference, of the United States, the United Kingdom and France with the Netherlands, Belgium and Luxembourg, debated the political future of the three western occupation zones of Germany and concluded that a democratic and federal West German state should be established. The West German constitution was adopted in Bonn on 8 May 1949, approved by the western Allies on 12 May and came into effect on 23 May. It was called the Grundgesetz, Basic Law or Fundamental Law, rather than a Verfassung, constitution, because its drafters regarded it as an interim arrangement for a provisional state, pending a definitive constitution for a reunified Germany. It was never put to a popular vote.

The authors sought to ensure that a dictator could never again come to power. The first article protects human dignity, and the fundamental rights of Articles 1 to 19 bind all state authority, whereas the Weimar Constitution had listed them only as state objectives. Article 20 sets out the principles of democracy, republicanism, social responsibility, federalism and the rule of law. Under the eternity clause, Article 79 (3), Articles 1 and 20 cannot be amended. The original text had no emergency powers like those of the Reichstag Fire Decree of 1933, and it allows a right of resistance against anyone seeking to abolish the constitutional order.

It set up a parliamentary democracy with separation of powers. The Federal President is head of state and the Federal Chancellor head of government, who can be dismissed only through a constructive vote of no confidence. The Bundestag is elected by proportional representation, the Bundesrat represents the Länder, and the Federal Constitutional Court guards the Basic Law. Unlike Weimar's, the text names political parties and allows the court to abolish those that violate its democratic foundations.

The Basic Law offered two routes to unity: Article 23, under which other parts of Germany could declare their accession, and Article 146, under which a new constitution could be adopted by the German people. Reunification in 1990 used Article 23, and the Basic Law was kept as the definitive constitution of the united country. Article 23 was then repealed, to reaffirm the renunciation of any claim to land east of the Oder and Neiße, and an article on the European Union was inserted instead. The Basic Law was amended in 1955 to allow federal armed forces, the Bundeswehr, and in 1968 to introduce emergency competencies. Some interpreters see it as an attempt to correct Germany's supposed Sonderweg, or special path.
basil-i: Basil was born to a peasant family at Chariopolis in the theme of Macedonia, in 811 by the usual account, though some scholars place his birth in the 830s. His ethnic origin is disputed: the general scholarly view is that his father was probably of Armenian origin and settled in Thrace, and Basil relied on the support of Armenians in high positions. During his reign a genealogy was produced tracing his ancestors to the Arsacid kings of Armenia, Alexander the Great and Constantine the Great.

According to one story he spent part of his childhood as a captive in Bulgaria and escaped in 836. He entered the service of Theophilitzes, a relative of the Caesar Bardas, as a groom, and caught the notice of Emperor Michael III as a horse tamer and wrestler. He became the emperor's companion and bodyguard, and about 865, on Michael's orders, divorced his wife Maria and married Michael's mistress Eudokia Ingerina.

Basil had Bardas murdered on 21 April 866 and was crowned co-emperor on 26 May 866. When Michael began to favour another courtier, Basiliskianos, Basil organised Michael's assassination on the night of 24 September 867 and became sole ruler. Although he had little formal education and had come to power through murder, he was an effective and respected monarch and kept a reputation for piety throughout his reign.

His legislative work earned him the name of a second Justinian. His laws were gathered in the Basilika, in sixty books, and in the shorter manual known as the Eisagoge; Leo VI completed them, and the Basilika remained the law of the empire until the Ottoman conquest. He built the Nea Ekklesia cathedral and the palace hall called the Kainourgion, and exiled the Patriarch Photios in favour of Ignatios, who was backed by Pope Adrian II.

In 872 his general Christopher defeated the Paulicians, whose leader Chrysocheir died. Allied with Louis II, Basil sent 139 ships against Arab raiders in the Adriatic, and Bari fell in 871, becoming Byzantine territory in 876. Syracuse fell to the Emirate of Sicily in 878, but Nikephoros Phokas the Elder took Taranto and much of Calabria in 880.

The death of Basil's eldest son Constantine in 879 darkened his last years. He disliked his son Leo, whom he probably suspected of being Michael III's child, and imprisoned him for three years after a reported plot. Basil died on 29 August 886 of a fever after a hunting accident, in which his belt caught in the antlers of a deer and he was reportedly dragged 25 kilometres. Leo VI succeeded him and reburied Michael III's remains with great ceremony in the Church of the Holy Apostles.
basil-ii: Basil II was born in 958, a porphyrogennetos, born into the purple, as were his father Romanos II and his grandfather Constantine VII. His mother Theophano was the daughter of a poor tavern-keeper named Krateros. Romanos crowned him co-emperor on 22 April 960 and died on 15 March 963 at the age of 24, a death commonly thought at the time to have been poisoning with hemlock. Nikephoros II and John I then ruled, brilliant commanders but poor administrators. Basil II became sole emperor in 976, and spent his early years learning administration and military science while Basil Lekapenos hoped to use him as a puppet.

The early years were dominated by civil wars against two Anatolian generals, Bardas Skleros and Bardas Phokas, which ended shortly after Phokas died and Skleros submitted in 989. He sent his sister Anna Porphyrogenita to Vladimir I of Kiev in return for military support, forming the Varangian Guard, and the marriage led to the Christianization of the Kievan Rus. After fighting in Syria against the Fatimids, Basil rode through Asia Minor to Aleppo in sixteen days, arriving in April 995, and the Fatimid commander withdrew without battle.

Against Bulgaria he suffered a serious defeat at the Battle of the Gates of Trajan in 986 after besieging Sofia with 30,000 men. Samuel of Bulgaria became his main adversary, and Basil eventually brought the First Bulgarian Empire under complete subjugation after a long struggle. In 1001 he inherited the territories of the Georgian prince David III of Tao, organised as the theme of Iberia, and in 1021 Seneqerim-John of Vaspurakan ceded his kingdom in exchange for estates in Sebasteia.

Basil campaigned with his army rather than sending orders from Constantinople, ate the same rations as his soldiers, and took the children of dead officers under his protection. His laws protected small landowners and lowered their taxes, and he reduced the power of the great landowning families and filled the treasury. He left the empire at its largest territorial extent in four centuries. His successors were largely incompetent, but the empire flourished for decades after his death. Basil is seen as a Greek national hero but is a despised figure among Bulgarians.
basilica-of-saint-denis: The site began as a Gallo-Roman cemetery, with graves showing a mixture of Christian and pre-Christian burial practices. According to the Life of Saint Genevieve, written about 520, Denis was sent by Pope Clement I to evangelise the Parisii and was beheaded on Montmartre about 250; in the legend he carried his head to the place where he wished to be buried. A martyrium was built over the grave about 313, and around 475 Saint Genevieve bought land and built a chapel. In 636, on the orders of Dagobert I, the relics of Denis were reinterred in the basilica.

King Pepin the Short vowed to rebuild the abbey, and the church begun in 754 was consecrated in 775 in the presence of Charlemagne. Abbot Suger, who became abbot in 1122 and served Louis VI and Louis VII as confidant and minister, began rebuilding about 1135, citing the decrepit state of the old church and the crowds of pilgrims. The west front was dedicated on 9 June 1140, and the chevet was built in four years, from 1140 to 1144.

The chevet is a double ambulatory divided by two rows of columns rather than walls, with five radiating chapels and outer walls filled with windows, so that light entered the choir. The tall jamb figures of the west front, destroyed in 1771 and known from drawings, were adopted at the cathedrals of Paris and Chartres and became a feature of almost every Gothic portal. From 1231 Abbot Odo Clement rebuilt the nave and the upper choir in the Rayonnant Gothic style, with walls filled with glass.

The abbey was also the French royal necropolis. Its role as the burial place of kings formally began under Hugh Capet, but earlier kings already lay there. In 1264 the bones of sixteen kings and queens, eight Carolingian monarchs and eight Capetians, were placed in new tombs with carved effigies around the crossing. Nearly every king from the 10th century to Louis XVIII, the last to be entombed, in 1824, is buried there.

The church was pillaged during the Hundred Years' War and the Wars of Religion, though damage was largely limited to tombs and treasure. On 14 September 1792 the monks held their last services and the monastery was dissolved. In 1793 the National Convention ordered the royal tombs destroyed, while a commission chose some monuments to save; most were restored by Viollet-le-Duc in 1860.

Napoleon reconsecrated the church in 1806 and intended it for his own dynasty's tombs. It lost its rank as a cathedral in 1895 and regained it in 1966 with the creation of the Diocese of Saint-Denis. Its organ, completed in 1843, was the first by Aristide Cavaillé-Coll.
basques: The Basques are a Southwestern European ethnic group, characterised by the Basque language, a common culture and shared genetic ancestry with the ancient Vascones and Aquitanians, and are considered among the last remaining direct descendants of Neolithic European populations in Europe. The English word Basque comes from French, itself from Gascon Basco, cognate with Spanish Vasco and ultimately from Latin Vasco, plural Vascones. Because the language predates the Indo-European languages and blood groups and other classical markers are distinctive, a long-held popular view made the Basques living fossils of the earliest modern humans in Europe. Yet although genetically distinctive in some ways owing to isolation, they are typically European in their Y-DNA and mtDNA sequences, which are widespread across the western half of the continent.

Strabo and Pliny mentioned Basque tribes in Roman times, among them the Vascones and the Aquitani, and there is enough evidence to support the hypothesis that they spoke old varieties of the Basque language, known as Aquitanian. In the early Middle Ages the territory between the Ebro and Garonne rivers was known as Vasconia, a vaguely defined ethnic area and political entity struggling to fend off pressure from the Visigothic kingdom and Arab rule to the south and the Frankish push from the north.

By the turn of the first millennium Vasconia had fragmented into feudal regions such as Soule and Labourd. South of the Pyrenees, Castile, Pamplona and the Pyrenean counties of Aragon, Sobrarbe, Ribagorça and Pallars emerged in the 9th and 10th centuries as the main regional entities with a Basque population.

The Basque Country, Euskal Herria in Basque, lies around the western end of the Pyrenees on the Bay of Biscay and is divided into at least three administrative units: the Basque Autonomous Community, made up of Álava, Biscay and Gipuzkoa, and Navarre in Spain, and the Basque Country Agglomeration Community in the French Basque Country. The Basque Autonomous Community has 2,123,000 inhabitants, and its largest cities are Bilbao, San Sebastián and Vitoria-Gasteiz.

The identifying language is Basque, or Euskara, spoken by 25 to 30 per cent of the region's population. Basques call themselves euskaldun, Basque speaker, and their country Euskal Herria, country of the Basque language. Knowledge of the language declined for many years under Franco's dictatorship owing to official persecution. Basques have a close attachment to the home, etxea, especially the traditional self-sufficient family-run farm, the baserri, and many surnames come from farm names, such as Etxeberria, the new house. Gastronomical societies, txoko, are food clubs where men gather to cook. Large numbers have emigrated, often as shepherds, ranchers, fishers and merchants, and Basque descendants live in North America, Latin America, South Africa and Australia.
basra: Basra lies on the banks of the Shatt al-Arab, which empties into the Persian Gulf, near the border with Iran. Its Arabic name, al-Basrah, means the overwatcher, perhaps an allusion to its origin as an Arab military base; others derive it from the Aramaic basratha, a place of huts or settlement. It was built in 636 as a camp for the Arab tribesmen of the armies of the Rashidun caliph Umar. The original site, about 15 km south-west of the modern city, is marked by the Imam Ali Mosque, and Basra is home to the first mosque built outside the Arabian Peninsula.

Under the Abbasids, who took Basra in the late 740s, it became an intellectual centre and home to the Basra School of Grammar, rival and sister of the school of Kufa. Its notable figures include the polymath Ibn al-Haytham, the writer al-Jahiz and the Sufi mystic Rabia Basri. The city was a centre of the slave trade in Mesopotamia until the Zanj rebellion of agricultural slaves, whose forces sacked it in 871. The Qarmatians invaded and devastated it in 923.

After the Mongols under Hulegu Khan sacked Baghdad in 1258, Basra by some accounts capitulated to avoid a massacre. Ibn Battuta visited in the 14th century. Portugal controlled the city from 1526, and the Ottoman Empire captured it in 1668. It was under Safavid control from 1697 to 1701, and the Zand dynasty under Karim Khan Zand occupied it briefly after a long siege. In 1884 the Ottomans created the vilayet of Basra. British forces captured the city in 1914, and it passed to Mandatory Iraq and then to the Kingdom of Iraq, independent in 1932.

Basra is the capital of Basra Governorate and the third largest city in Iraq, after Baghdad and Mosul. Its position on the Gulf makes it a major port, and it is the country's only coastal region, along with its adjoining governorate. During World War II it was an important port through which much equipment sent to the Soviet Union flowed. The University of Basrah was founded in 1964. The population is mostly Arab Shia Muslims, with a large Sunni minority.
basse-terre: Basse-Terre stands at the south-western corner of the island of Basse-Terre, the western half of Guadeloupe, about 100 km north of Dominica. The town grew on a narrow coastal strip between the Caribbean Sea and the first hills of the ridge that divides the island, with the volcanic massif of the Soufrière to the north-east. The name comes from the seamen's vocabulary of the 17th century, which called a land or coast sheltered from the wind a basse-terre.

The site of the present cathedral was first a village of American Indian horticulturists and potters. French settlement began in 1635, when Charles Liénard de l'Olive and Jean du Plessis d'Ossonville landed with 4 missionaries and 550 colonists at Pointe Allègre, and relations with the Native Americans soon turned to war. Charles Houël du Petit Pré moved to the right bank of the Galion and built a fort, a church followed, and the town was organised around the chapel and the fort. English privateers burned it in 1691 and 1703.

A British force captured the island on 23 January 1759, and France recovered it in 1763. Pointe-à-Pitre was founded in 1764 in a better position to receive the ocean swell. In 1794 Victor Hugues recaptured Guadeloupe from the British and abolished slavery. In 1802 General Antoine Richepanse, sent by Napoleon to restore slavery, fought Louis Delgrès, who retreated to the fort on 20 May and left it on 22 May. After the cyclone of September 1928 the architect Ali Tur built the courthouse and a market. In 1976, because of the Soufrière's activity, 73,600 inhabitants of Guadeloupe were evacuated.

Basse-Terre is the prefecture of Guadeloupe, though Pointe-à-Pitre is the larger city, and holds the courts, including the Court of Appeal, and the seat of the diocese. Fort Delgrès, begun by Houël as Fort Saint-Charles and renamed in 1989, is a classified historical monument, as is the Church of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, which marked the town's foundation. The Bologne distillery, producing rum, remains its main local industry.
basses-pyrenees: Pyrénées-Atlantiques, named after the Pyrenees mountain range and the Atlantic Ocean, lies in the south-west corner of metropolitan France, in the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine. It covers the French Basque Country and the Béarn, and its prefecture is Pau. It is bordered by the departments of Landes, Hautes-Pyrénées and Gers, by the Bay of Biscay to the west and by the Spanish provinces of Huesca, Navarre and Gipuzkoa to the south. The Pyrenees cross it from east to west, and the border with Spain follows the chain. Its highest point is the Pic Palas, in the Balaïtous massif, at 2,974 m.

Originally named Basses-Pyrénées, it was one of the 83 departments created during the French Revolution, on 4 March 1790. It comprised Labourd and Soule, in the provinces of Guyenne and Gascony, as well as Lower Navarre, still at least nominally part of the Kingdom of Navarre, and the Béarn. Six districts were set up, with the prefecture first at Navarrenx before it moved to Pau on 14 October 1790.

The reform ended native institutions and laws. All the Basque estates representatives from Labourd opposed the new layout, the representatives of Lower Navarre refused to vote in Paris on the ground that they were not part of the Kingdom of France, and those of Soule voted against. The brothers Garat, representing Labourd, voted yes, thinking it would give them a say in later decisions. In 1800 the six districts were replaced by five arrondissements: Pau, Orthez, Bayonne, Mauléon and Oloron. In 1926 a reform under the government of Raymond Poincaré abolished those of Orthez and Mauléon, leaving the three that remain.

In the 1950s the department formed part of the newly created region of Aquitaine. In 1969 it was renamed Pyrénées-Atlantiques, because its inhabitants found Basses-Pyrénées pejorative compared with the name of the Hautes-Pyrénées.

The west is mainly inhabited by the Basques and the east by the Béarnais, who have shared a department since the Revolution; from 1790 to 1969 the inhabitants were called Bas-Pyrénéens. Gascon, a dialect of Occitan, and Basque, a language isolate, are indigenous in their districts, but French is the predominant native language. Pau and the urban area of Bayonne, Anglet and Biarritz are the two main urban concentrations. The department has 706,564 inhabitants in 2023 and is known for its tourism and its links with Spain. Its coat of arms combines those of Lower Navarre, Béarn, Labourd and Soule.
bastia: Bastia lies in the north-east of Corsica at the base of the Cap Corse, between the sea and the mountain. The city is 35 km from the northern tip of the Cap Corse, 50 km west of the Italian island of Elba and 90 km from continental Italy, which can be seen on a few days a year when visibility is excellent. The climate is Mediterranean, with an average annual temperature of 16.3 °C and about 240 sunny days a year.

In Roman times the north-eastern part of the present commune formed a pieve, the oldest known administrative division, occupied by the Vanacimi people. Bastia did not exist: Ptolemy, Strabo and Pliny do not mention it. At the end of the 9th century the pieve of Mantino depended on the Loretesi lords, driven out in 1072 by the Da Furiani with the help of the Marquis of Massa. Before the Genoese came, the pieve of Orto held several small communities, and on the coast stood a fishing hamlet called Porto Cardo.

The Genoese soon felt the need to protect Bastia from attack by sea and began to build a bastiglia and a citadel in the time of the governor Leonello Lomellini. The settlement grew, prospered and became more important than Cardo, and it was the capital during Genoese rule. The sea and the mountains decided where houses stood, and the town spread later onto the slopes, drawn toward the water at the Place Saint-Nicolas.

Bastia is a commune of Haute-Corse and the department's capital, with the second-highest population of any commune on the island after Ajaccio. It is the island's principal port and commercial town. The Old Port, in a narrow cove that gives good protection from the weather, was at the heart of the first development. The centre consists mainly of the citadel, also called Terra Nova, the Palace of the Governors, the Old Port and the market place, and the buildings along the Paoli Boulevard. The Church of Sainte-Marie, a former cathedral built in 1495 and heavily remodelled in the early 17th century, stands in the citadel.
batavian-republic: After the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War, the Patriot party revolted against Stadtholder William V but was struck down in September 1787 when Frederick William II of Prussia intervened. Most Patriots went into exile in France, and the Dutch Republic became in effect an Anglo-Prussian protectorate, formalised by the Act of Guarantee in 1788. The French Revolution embraced many Patriot ideas, and the Patriots hoped to be treated as a sister republic rather than conquered territory. In the severe winter of 1794 and 1795 a French army under General Charles Pichegru, with a Dutch contingent under General Herman Willem Daendels, crossed the frozen rivers. Many cities rose before the French arrived, and William fled to England on 18 January 1795.

The republic was proclaimed on 19 January 1795. The harsh Treaty of The Hague of 16 May 1795 imposed territorial concessions, a large indemnity and a French army of occupation of 25,000 men, and it made the state a French client, the first of the sister republics. Even so, the programme of reform was driven mostly by Dutch needs. A National Assembly met at The Hague on 1 March 1796, divided between unitary democrats such as Pieter Vreede and federalists such as Rutger Jan Schimmelpenninck.

The constitution of 1798 was the first in Dutch history of a democratic character. France supported coups in turn: Daendels seized the Assembly on 12 June 1798 and arrested its members, and a coup in 1801 brought a new regime and a revised constitution.

From October 1801 the state was called the Batavian Commonwealth. Napoleon disliked the Dutch government, partly because Amsterdam bankers had refused him a large loan in 1800. After a clash over French customs men in November 1804 he settled on a new constitution, and Schimmelpenninck became Grand Pensionary. This regime also failed to satisfy him. The republic ended on 5 June 1806 with the accession of his brother, Louis Bonaparte, as king of Holland.

The Kingdom of Holland lasted four years: Louis refused to follow French dictates, abdicated on 2 July 1810 and the territory was incorporated into the French Empire. After the French defeat the independent Netherlands re-emerged in 1813, and William VI of Orange landed at Scheveningen on 30 November. The republic's reforms outlasted it. The confederal structure of the old Dutch Republic was replaced for good by a unitary state, a type of ministerial government appeared for the first time, and many present government departments date their history to this period. Its influence also eased the move to the more democratic constitutional revision of 1848 by Johan Rudolph Thorbecke.
bathsheba: Bathsheba is called the daughter of Eliam in 2 Samuel 11:3 and the daughter of Ammiel in 1 Chronicles 3:5, where she is named Bathshua. Because a man named Eliam is listed in 2 Samuel 23:34 as a son of Ahithophel, a counsellor of David, Jewish tradition and several scholars take her to be Ahithophel's granddaughter, though some doubt that Ahithophel was old enough. According to the Hebrew Bible she had five children with David, among them Shimea, Shobab, Nathan and Solomon.

The account in 2 Samuel 11 says David saw her bathing from the roof of his palace, learned that she was Uriah's wife, and slept with her. When Uriah, away on campaign, would not go home to his wife, David ordered his general Joab to place him on the front lines, and Uriah was killed during the siege of Rabbah. Bathsheba mourned him, and David then took her into his house.

David's act displeased God, who sent the prophet Nathan to reprove him with a parable of a rich man who took a poor man's lamb. David confessed, but the first child born to Bathsheba fell ill and died after seven days. She later bore Solomon. In David's old age she secured Solomon's succession to the throne in place of David's older surviving sons, on the strength of promises David had made to her. Nathan's prophecy was held to be fulfilled when Absalom rebelled and took ten of his father's concubines in public.

Scholars disagree on how to read her part. Some, among them David J. Zucker, see her as a victim of what he calls power rape, and Michael D. Coogan notes that the text faults David from its first verse; Kenneth E. Bailey argues instead that she displayed herself deliberately. The story affected how David's later decline was understood. In Christianity she appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1:6 and in medieval typology is linked with the Virgin Mary, and the Ethiopian Orthodox Church venerates her as a saint. Islam does not mention her in the Quran, and some tradition rejects the story as incompatible with the infallibility of prophets. Artists often showed her at her bath, as in Rembrandt's painting in the Louvre.
battambang: Battambang lies on the Sangkae River, which winds through the province of the same name. The province is considered the rice bowl of Cambodia, and the city has many mills that process rice for national and international markets; its jasmine rice is well known. The river long served as the main link to Phnom Penh and Saigon, and the city is also joined to Phnom Penh and Bangkok by National Highway 5.

Battambang began as a fishing village on the Sangkae River in the 11th century, founded under the Khmer Empire. In 1795 Siam annexed much of north-western Cambodia as the province of Inner Cambodia and ruled Battambang as a provincial capital through the Abhaiwongse family. By 1880 it was an important trading city of about 2,500 residents. The Siamese built one road, a fort for the governor, a market, several pagodas and a Catholic hospital.

In 1907 the province was ceded to France and rejoined Cambodia within French Indochina. The French laid out a grid of streets, canals and bridges in what is now the Heritage Conservation Area, linked both riverbanks by two bridges in 1917 and in 1926 began a second phase of building, with a railway to Phnom Penh, villas, the central market and state buildings.

In 1953 Prince Norodom Sihanouk chose Battambang as the centre of Cambodia's independence movement. It was Cambodia's second largest city in the 20th century, with garment factories, an airport, schools and a university. Under Democratic Kampuchea its population was forcibly evacuated into labour camps and land tenure was abolished; the Battambang Provincial Museum became a prison, and the Phnom Sampeau killing caves, a Khmer Rouge execution site, lie about six kilometres from the city. A Vietnamese invasion toppled the Khmer Rouge in 1980, but the province remained a Khmer Rouge stronghold into the 1990s. Guerrillas besieged the city in 1990 without taking it, and conflict around it continued until 1997.

Battambang is the capital of its province and one of Cambodia's larger cities. The municipality established a Heritage Protection Area in 2009 to safeguard around 800 historic buildings, among them French colonial architecture and the Art Deco central market, Psar Nath, built in 1936. Wat Damrei Sar, built in the 19th century, is the oldest pagoda in the city. UNESCO named it a City of Gastronomy in 2023, the first Cambodian city in its Creative Cities Network.
battering-ram: A battering ram is a siege engine designed to break open the masonry walls of fortifications or to splinter their wooden gates. In its simplest form it is a large, heavy log carried by several people and driven against an obstacle. Later rams enclosed the log in an arrow-proof, fire-resistant canopy mounted on wheels, with the log swung inside from chains or ropes. Many canopies had curved or slanted wooden roofs covered in fresh wet hides, which reduced the risk of fire and protected the crew from arrows and javelins.

Rams worked because stone and brick were weak in tension and cracked under force. With repeated blows the cracks grew until a breach opened. A capped ram had an iron or steel head, sometimes shaped like the head and horns of a sheep, which did more damage but weighed more to carry.

The earliest depiction of a possible ram is in the tomb of Khety, a noble of the 11th Dynasty of Egypt, where two soldiers advance on a fortress under a mobile roofed shelter, carrying a long pole. In the Iron Age in the ancient Middle East and the Mediterranean the log was slung from a wheeled frame. An Assyrian image of the 9th century BCE shows defenders trying to burn a ram with torches and to trap it with a chain, while the wet hides on the canopy protect it from the flames.

The first confirmed use in the Occident was in 503 to 502 BCE, when the Roman consul Opiter Verginius attacked Pometia, according to Livy. The Spartans used rams at the siege of Plataea in 427 BCE, and rams with siege towers appeared in Sicily at the siege of Selinus in 409 BCE.

Defenders answered rams by dropping obstacles such as a sack of sawdust in front of the head, by catching the log with grappling hooks, by setting the ram on fire, or by making a sudden sally. Some rams ran on rollers instead of hanging, so that they gained more speed, and Vitruvius describes one used by Alexander the Great.

Rams influenced the design of defensive walls, and they were used in sieges of major cities, among them the Roman destruction of Jerusalem, the Crusades, the Sack of Rome in 410 and the sieges of Constantinople. The siege cannons of the later Middle Ages ended their use. A story that the rhyme about Humpty Dumpty concerns a ram at the siege of Gloucester in 1643 is almost certainly untrue, and began in a spoof essay of 1956.
battle-of-actium: The Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Mark Antony and Lepidus was renewed in 37 BCE but broke down. Antony left his wife Octavia Minor, Octavian's sister, and settled in Egypt with Cleopatra VII. In 34 BCE he and Cleopatra raised her son Caesarion, said to be Julius Caesar's, to power as King of Kings, which was seen as a threat to Roman republican tradition. Octavian, whom Caesar had adopted, began a propaganda war, claiming that Antony meant to set up a monarchy and move the capital to Alexandria.

In 32 BCE both consuls and a third of the Senate sided with Antony and left Rome. Antony divorced Octavia and went to Ephesus with Cleopatra, where a vast fleet gathered. The publication of Antony's will provoked an outburst of feeling in Rome, and Antony was deprived of the consulship. The Senate declared war on Cleopatra, which was understood to mean Antony, and left him without legal authority.

Antony's fleet lay in the Ambracian Gulf and his army camped near Actium. In 31 BCE Octavian's general Marcus Agrippa raided the Greek coasts and cut Antony's communications with Egypt. Disease and desertion afflicted Antony's camp, and malaria left many ships short of rowers. One of his generals, Quintus Dellius, defected with his battle plans. His heavy ships were hard to board but less manoeuvrable than Octavian's smaller Liburnian vessels.

On 2 September the fleets met outside the gulf. Octavian refused to be drawn out, and the battle raged through the afternoon without result. Cleopatra's squadron then retreated without fighting, and Antony, believing all was lost, followed her in a smaller vessel. The ships left behind fought on until after nightfall, and were captured or sunk. J. M. Carter gives a different account, in which Antony deliberately broke through a gap in Octavian's line.

Some 19 legions and 12,000 cavalry left Antony in the night, and his camp was occupied the next day. Antony was defeated at Alexandria in 30 BCE and stabbed himself on false news that Cleopatra was dead; she killed herself on 12 August. Octavian had Caesarion killed, and Egypt became a Roman province, ending the Ptolemaic Kingdom. He took the title Princeps, and in 27 BCE the Senate gave him the name Augustus. Historians generally regard this as the end of the Roman Republic. He founded the city of Nicopolis, meaning City of Victory, opposite Actium.
battle-of-agincourt: Henry V of England claimed the title of King of France through his great-grandfather Edward III, although English kings had in practice been prepared to renounce the claim if the French acknowledged English rights in Aquitaine and other lands. After a Great Council in the spring of 1414 the lords insisted that Henry negotiate further.

He offered to give up the claim if the French paid the 1.6 million crowns outstanding from the ransom of John II and conceded Anjou, Brittany, Flanders, Normandy, Touraine and Aquitaine, with a marriage to Charles VI's daughter Catherine and a dowry of 2 million crowns. When negotiations failed, the English resumed the war in 1415. Disease killed many soldiers during the Siege of Harfleur, and the weakened army tried to withdraw to Calais, where its path was blocked by a considerably larger French army.

On 25 October 1415 Henry drew up his army, about 1,500 men-at-arms and 7,000 longbowmen by one reckoning, across a narrow strip of open land between woods. The archers drove pointed stakes into the ground to turn aside cavalry. The French, under Constable Charles I d'Albret, had about 10,000 men-at-arms and several thousand other troops, since King Charles VI, who suffered from mental illness, did not command. For three hours after sunrise neither side attacked, the French expecting reinforcements.

The French cavalry then charged, but could not outflank the archers because of the woods or break through the stakes. Wounded horses panicked and trampled their own infantry, and the charge churned up recently ploughed ground. The men-at-arms who followed walked several hundred yards through thick mud in armour weighing 50 to 60 pounds, with visors lowered, and were so closely packed that those in the third rank could scarcely use their swords.  The French also attacked the English baggage train, and the sources disagree on whether this came at the start or the end. Fearing that the French were regrouping, Henry had French prisoners killed.

Around 6,000 French fighting men were killed, among them the constable, three dukes (Alençon, Bar and Brabant), nine counts and the Archbishop of Sens. Entire noble families were wiped out in the male line. The victory boosted English morale and began a period of English dominance in the war that lasted until the Siege of Orléans in 1429.

Historians disagree about the numbers. Most contemporary accounts have the English outnumbered several times over, while Anne Curry argued from administrative records for about 12,000 French and 9,000 English. Juliet Barker, Jonathan Sumption and Clifford J. Rogers criticised her reliance on those records. The exact location of the field is also debated. The battle is the setting of Act IV of William Shakespeare's Henry V, written in 1599.
battle-of-albulena: Skanderbeg had fought the Ottoman Empire since 1444, and after more than a decade of war his resources were worn out. His siege of Berat in 1455 ended in catastrophe when an Ottoman counterattack fell on the Albanians during his temporary absence. Afterwards some of his most trusted officers deserted. Moisi Golemi returned in May 1456 at the head of an Ottoman force, was defeated at the Battle of Oranik and was taken back without punishment.

A graver loss was his nephew Hamza Kastrioti, one of his most important officers, who had grown dissatisfied with Skanderbeg's increasing power and was promised control of much of Albania once it was conquered. Relations with Venice were at their lowest point. Alfonso V of Aragon and Pope Calixtus III, his allies, could not provide for him fully, and a fleet the pope promised in 1457 did not arrive.

By the end of May 1457 an Ottoman army of between 50,000 and 80,000 men approached, against which Skanderbeg had between 8,000 and 10,000. He stalled the akıncı vanguard marching through Dibër, then withdrew before the main force. Since both Ottoman commanders knew his usual ambushes, he split his army into several groups and ordered them to march through the forests and mountains in different directions, supplied by the local people and by depots, and not to assemble or attack without his word.

The Ottomans pillaged the Mat valley and camped at Albulena, north of Mount Tumenishta and south of modern Laç. Through July and August Skanderbeg stayed out of sight, and rumours spread that he had fled. On 2 September his reassembled army attacked the camp in three groups with a great noise of clashing metal. The Ottomans, believing the attackers more numerous than they were, panicked. Their dead may have been as many as 30,000, though it is unlikely that more than 15,000 were killed; 15,000 were taken prisoner and twenty-four standards were captured.

Hamza Kastrioti was captured and sent as a prisoner to Naples. An Ottoman envoy came to ransom the standard bearers and forty distinguished prisoners and proposed a truce, which Skanderbeg would accept only if Svetigrad and Berat were restored to him. In 1460 Sultan Mehmed II and Skanderbeg signed an armistice that lasted three years, giving Skanderbeg the opportunity to cross to Italy and help Ferdinand I of Naples. The historian Franz Babinger called the battle Skanderbeg's most brilliant victory. Desertions from his army became rare afterwards, but the war continued until the fall of Krujë in 1478.
battle-of-ankara: Timur, a Turco-Mongol from Transoxiana, had built an empire in Central Asia and sought to rebuild the Mongol Empire. In the 1380s and 1390s he conquered parts of Persia, ravaged southern Russia and Ukraine in 1395–96 and sacked Delhi in 1398. Relations with the Ottomans were tense but no cause of war existed until Bayezid demanded tribute from an emir loyal to Timur, which Timur took as a personal affront. In 1400–01 he took Sivas from the Ottomans and parts of Syria from the Mamluks, and then turned towards Anatolia. In 1402 Bayezid broke off his blockade of Constantinople and marched to Ankara.

The armies are reliably estimated at 140,000 for Timur, mostly cavalry, with 32 war elephants, and no more than 85,000 for Bayezid. Contemporary figures of 800,000 and 1.6 million are exaggerations. The Ottoman force included Janissaries, Anatolian Muslim vassals and Balkan Christian vassals, among them Serbian vassals under Stefan Lazarević. Bayezid's tired army marched through the midsummer heat, and his generals advised him to take up defensive positions. Instead he marched east, while Timur's army secretly marched round to the Ottoman rear and occupied the camps and water sources they had left.

The battle was fought on 28 July 1402 on the Çubuk plain near Ankara. Timur's horse archers met the Ottoman attack with swarms of arrows. Stefan Lazarević and his knights, in heavy black plate armour, cut through the Timurid ranks three times, and Timur said of them that they fight like lions. Timur diverted Çubuk creek, the main water supply of both armies, leaving the Ottomans without water. The Black Tatars and the sipahis of the Anatolian beyliks deserted to Timur. Bayezid escaped to the mountains with a few hundred horsemen but was surrounded and captured, and died in captivity three months later.

Timur moved through western Anatolia to the Aegean coast and took Smyrna, a stronghold of the Christian Knights Hospitalers. The battle was catastrophic for the Ottoman state, bringing near collapse and a civil war among Bayezid's sons that continued until 1413. It is also remembered as the only occasion on which an Ottoman sultan was captured in person.
battle-of-austerlitz: Britain declared war on France in May 1803, after the Treaty of Amiens broke down over Malta and the return of captured colonies. In December 1804 an Anglo-Swedish agreement created the Third Coalition. Britain and Russia signed an alliance by April 1805, and Austria, twice defeated by France and eager for revenge, joined a few months later. In August 1805 Napoleon turned his army from the English Channel to the Rhine, and 23,000 Austrians surrendered at Ulm on 20 October. Vienna fell in November.

Napoleon retreated from the dominant Pratzen Heights near Austerlitz and gave every sign that his army was in poor state. He deliberately weakened his right flank to tempt the Allies to attack it, and hid his main force in dead ground. The Allies adopted the plan of the Austrian chief of staff Franz von Weyrother, a main drive against the French right. Napoleon began with some 72,000 men against about 85,000, since the corps of Marshal Davout was still far to the south.

The battle began about 8 am on 2 December 1805 with Allied attacks on the village of Telnitz, where Davout's first men arrived in time to hold the French right. At about 8:45 am Napoleon saw the weakness of the Allied centre, which had been stripped to extend against his right, and ordered Marshal Soult's corps to storm the Pratzen Heights, saying that one sharp blow would end the war.

The Allies lost about 36,000 men, 186 guns and 45 standards; the French lost around 9,000. France and Austria agreed an armistice at once, and the Treaty of Pressburg of 26 December took Austria out of the war. It confirmed Austria's loss of lands in Italy and Bavaria to France and in Germany to Napoleon's German allies, and imposed an indemnity of 40 million francs. The victory also allowed the creation of the Confederation of the Rhine.

The battle is often cited by military historians as one of Napoleon's tactical masterpieces, in the company of Hannibal's Cannae and Alexander the Great's Gaugamela. It did not establish a lasting peace, since neither Russia nor Britain was driven to settle. The battlefield has been protected by law as a landscape monument zone since 1992.
battle-of-bir-hakeim: Bir Hakeim was a fortress built by the Ottomans at the crossing of two Bedouin paths. It stood at the southern end of the Gazala line, a series of brigade-sized defensive boxes that the British Eighth Army held west of Tobruk. On 14 February 1942 the 1st Free French Brigade took over the box, which was surrounded by 50,000 mines. The brigade had a fighting strength of 3,000 men, with the 13th Demi-Brigade of the Foreign Legion as its backbone, and by mid-May it had dug 1,200 entrenchments, foxholes and gun emplacements. The Axis plan sent the armour around the box while the Italian 132nd Armoured Division Ariete neutralised it.

On the morning of 27 May an Italian tank battalion of the Ariete Division, with 60 tanks, charged the minefield and wire. It lost 31 tanks and a self-propelled gun, and ten tanks that got through were knocked out by 75 mm anti-tank guns. From 2 June the position was shelled and bombed, and Stuka dive-bombers raided it more than twenty times, but the well-built positions were almost invulnerable. On 6 June the 90th Light Division attacked with pioneers, who cleared passages through the minefields.

From 8 June Rommel directed attacks from the north with part of the 15th Panzer Division, and the perimeter was forced back. On 10 June, with ammunition almost gone, the fort took the largest air raid of the siege, by 100 Stukas. After dark sappers cleared a narrow passage through the mines on the western face. Kœnig left at the head of the column in a car driven by Susan Travers, an Englishwoman serving with the Foreign Legion, and most of the brigade broke through troops of the 90th Light Division to reach lorries and ambulances sent by the British 7th Motor Brigade.

Thomas Buell and Ken Ford give the French losses as 141 dead, 229 wounded and 814 taken prisoner, with 53 guns and 50 vehicles; the Axis lost 3,300 dead or wounded and 227 captured, with 164 vehicles destroyed and 49 aircraft shot down. The defence had lengthened the Axis supply route around the Gazala line and gave the British time to recover from their defeat in the Cauldron, and the delay influenced the cancellation of Operation Herkules, the Axis invasion of Malta. Tobruk still fell ten days later. Both sides used the battle for propaganda, and Winston Churchill declared the Free French to be the Fighting French.
battle-of-britain: Germany had rapidly overwhelmed France and the Low Countries in the Battle of France, leaving Britain to face the threat of invasion by sea. The German high command recognised the difficulty of a seaborne attack while the Royal Navy controlled the English Channel, and its primary objective was to compel Britain to accept a negotiated peace. On 16 July 1940 Adolf Hitler ordered preparation of Operation Sea Lion, an amphibious and airborne assault to follow once the Luftwaffe had air superiority over the Channel. Britain officially dates the battle from 10 July to 31 October 1940.

The Luftwaffe first attacked coastal convoys and ports. On 1 August it was directed to achieve air superiority and incapacitate RAF Fighter Command, and twelve days later it shifted its attacks to airfields and infrastructure. The RAF's Hurricanes and Spitfires faced the Bf 109, and Fighter Command relied on the Chain Home radar and a system of reporting chains named for Hugh Dowding. About 20 per cent of the pilots were from outside Britain, among them 145 Poles, 127 New Zealanders and 112 Canadians.

On 7 September the Luftwaffe began the night attacks on London and other cities known as the Blitz. At a conference on 14 September Hitler acknowledged that it had not gained the air superiority that Sea Lion required. On 15 September the Luftwaffe made its largest bombing attack yet, which forced the whole of the RAF to defend London and the south-east and ended in a decisive British victory. In September RAF Bomber Command night raids also disrupted the German preparation of converted barges.

On 19 September Hitler ordered a reduction in work on Sea Lion. The Luftwaffe proved unable to sustain daylight raids, though its night bombing continued until 11 May 1941. By 2 November the RAF fielded 1,796 pilots, over 40 per cent more than in July. The battle was the first major military campaign fought entirely by air forces and the first major defeat of Germany's military forces. Churchill summed it up with the words, Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few, and the pilots have been known as The Few ever since.
battle-of-cannae: Hannibal crossed the Pyrenees and the Alps in 218 BCE and beat the Romans at the Trebia and at Lake Trasimene. The Romans then appointed Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus dictator, and he avoided pitched battles and cut Hannibal's supplies. The policy grew unpopular, and Rome feared its allies would defect. In 216 BCE the consuls Gaius Terentius Varro and Lucius Aemilius Paullus were given a newly raised army of unprecedented size, about 86,000 Roman and allied troops, and told to engage Hannibal.

In the spring Hannibal seized the supply depot at Cannae in Apulia, between the Romans and their supplies. The consuls found him on the left bank of the Aufidus. Roman law made them alternate command daily, and Varro commanded on the day of the battle. The sources, none contemporary, make him reckless, though some historians suggest he was made a scapegoat.

The Romans massed their infantry in a deeper formation than usual to break through Hannibal's centre. Hannibal advanced his centre, held by Hispanics and Celts, into a crescent and kept his African infantry on the flanks. As the Roman centre pressed forward, the Africans wheeled in on its flanks while Carthaginian cavalry closed behind, surrounding most of the army, which was slaughtered.

The figures are uncertain. Polybius gives 70,000 Roman and allied infantry killed and 10,000 captured; Livy gives a considerably lower count of the dead. Among the dead were the consul Paullus and 29 of 48 military tribunes. Only about 15,000 Romans survived, mostly from the camp garrisons.

Rome was gripped by panic. The authorities consulted the Sibylline Books, sent Quintus Fabius Pictor to the Delphic oracle and buried four people alive as a sacrifice. They lowered the draft age and enlisted criminals, debtors and slaves. Capua and other Italian cities went over to Carthage, but Rome refused Hannibal's offer to ransom prisoners and fought on until victory at Zama 14 years later. The defeat led Rome to adopt smaller, more flexible infantry units, and Cannae became the model of a battle of annihilation, studied by later commanders such as Alfred von Schlieffen.
battle-of-dien-bien-phu: By 1953 the First Indochina War had defeated a succession of French commanders, who had been unable to suppress the Viet Minh insurrection. In 1952 and 1953 the Viet Minh overran much of Laos. Navarre looked for a way to protect it, and Colonel Louis Berteil formulated the hedgehog concept: a fortified airhead, supplied by air, beside Viet Minh supply lines to Laos.

In June 1953 Major General René Cogny proposed Dien Bien Phu, which had an old airstrip built by the Japanese. Navarre chose it, and every major subordinate officer protested; Cogny warned of a new Nà Sản under worse conditions. Operation Castor began on 20 November 1953, when the French dropped or flew about 9,000 troops into the area in three days.

The French had assumed that the Viet Minh had no anti-aircraft capability. Under General Võ Nguyên Giáp the Viet Minh surrounded the camp and hauled heavy artillery, anti-aircraft guns among it, up the rear slopes of the mountains, where tunnels let them pull the guns out, fire and withdraw. Their attack began on 13 March 1954 against the outpost Béatrice. On 14 March the airstrip was put permanently out of commission, so supplies had to come by parachute. On 17 March most of the Tai troops defending Anne-Marie left or defected.

Fighting then centred on the strong points Eliane and Dominique, and from 5 April Giáp changed to entrenchment and sapping. By the end of April the outpost Isabelle was nearly out of water and ammunition. On 6 May the Viet Minh used Katyusha rockets for the first time and exploded a mine under Eliane 2. The garrison was overrun, and the survivors surrendered on 7 May.

Dien Bien Phu was the decisive battle of the First Indochina War, and the loss of the garrison cost roughly one-tenth of the French Union manpower in Indochina. The Viet Minh counted 11,721 prisoners on 8 May, of whom 4,436 were wounded. The able-bodied were force-marched over 600 km to prison camps, and hundreds died of disease on the way.

The Geneva Conference opened on 8 May, and its agreement in July partitioned Vietnam into a communist North and the State of Vietnam in the south, temporarily, with elections in 1956 that were never held. The last French forces left Vietnam in 1956. The defeat did not significantly alter the strategic situation, but it brought a profound psychological shock to France.
battle-of-france: France and Britain declared war on Germany on 3 September 1939, after the German invasion of Poland. The French army began the limited Saar Offensive but by mid-October had withdrawn to its start line, and a period of inaction known as the Phoney War followed. In the 1930s the French had built the Maginot Line along the border with Germany, intended to divert a German invasion into Belgium, where the best French divisions would meet it. The hills and woods of the Ardennes were thought to cover the area to the north of the line.

The German plan, Fall Gelb, was reshaped on the advice of Manstein and Heinz Guderian, who proposed concentrating most of the armour at Sedan. The invasion began on 10 May 1940 with attacks on Belgium, Luxembourg and the Netherlands, and the French sent their best forces north into Belgium. German armour advanced through the Ardennes, crossed the Meuse and raced down the Somme valley, cutting off the units that had gone into Belgium. British, French and Belgian forces were pushed back to the sea, and the British and French navies evacuated much of the British Expeditionary Force and the French and Belgian armies from Dunkirk in Operation Dynamo.

The Germans began Fall Rot on 5 June against the Somme and Aisne, where the French resisted strongly but were beaten by German air superiority and armoured mobility. Italy declared war on 10 June. Paris was declared an open city and occupied by German forces on 14 June. Paul Reynaud resigned as Prime Minister on 16 June and was succeeded by Philippe Pétain, who asked for an armistice.

The armistice was signed at Compiègne on 22 June 1940, the site Hitler chose because the 1918 Armistice had been signed there. France was divided into a German occupation zone in the north and west and a zone libre in the south. Pétain's Vichy government replaced the Third Republic, and De Gaulle refused to accept its legitimacy; his Appeal of 18 June was the beginning of Free France. German losses are commonly put at 27,074 killed, 111,034 wounded and 18,384 missing, little more than a third of those at Verdun in the First World War.
battle-of-gaugamela: Darius III had lost the Battle of Issus to Alexander in November 333 BCE, and his wife, mother and two daughters were captured. Alexander then took the Levant after the Siege of Tyre and Egypt, whose satrap Mazaces surrendered peacefully. Ancient historians report that Darius tried diplomacy three times, finally offering land west of the Euphrates, joint rule, a daughter in marriage and 30,000 talents of silver. The accounts differ in detail. Diodorus Siculus has Parmenion say he would accept, and Alexander reply that so would he, if he were Parmenion. Alexander refused, insisting there could be only one king of Asia.

In the summer of 331 BCE Alexander crossed the Euphrates and followed a northern route, easier for foraging and cooler. He crossed the Tigris with great difficulty, and captured scouts told him that Darius waited at Gaugamela, where the ground was being levelled. Calculations put the battle on 1 October 331 BCE.

Modern scholars reject the very high ancient figures for Darius's army and accept Arrian's for Alexander's: 7,000 cavalry and 40,000 infantry. Darius cleared the ground for scythed chariots and placed himself at the centre with his best infantry, with Bessus commanding the left flank and Mazaeus the right. Alexander took the right wing himself with the Companion cavalry and left Parmenion to hold the left.

Alexander led the Companions toward the right, drawing the Persian cavalry to the flanks and forcing Darius to attack. A long cavalry battle followed, in which the outnumbered Macedonians held on by careful use of reserves. The scythed chariots were intercepted by javelin-throwers, and those that got through were let pass between gaps in the ranks. Alexander then formed a wedge and struck the weakened centre, and Arrian says Darius was the first to turn and flee.

Alexander went first to help Parmenion, whose wing was encircled, and the fiercest fighting of the day followed against the Persian right. Babylon was surrendered by Bagophanes, and 4,000 talents and the war elephants were captured. Darius escaped east with a small force, but Bessus murdered him. Alexander gave him a full burial at Persepolis and executed Bessus the next year. The Achaemenid Empire is traditionally considered to have ended with Darius's death. The site of the battlefield is uncertain, and the most commonly accepted location is Karamlesh in the Nineveh Plains.
battle-of-gettysburg: After the Confederate victory at the Battle of Chancellorsville, General Robert E. Lee decided on a second invasion of the North. It would upset the Union's plans for the summer, might reduce the pressure on the besieged Confederate garrison at Vicksburg, and would let his army live off Northern farms while Virginia rested. His army of about 72,000 men could also threaten Philadelphia, Baltimore and Washington and might strengthen the growing peace movement in the North. Lee began to move north from Fredericksburg on 3 June, and on 28 June President Abraham Lincoln replaced Major General Joseph Hooker with Major General George Meade as commander of the Army of the Potomac.

On 1 July the armies met northwest of Gettysburg. Brigadier General John Buford's Union cavalry delayed the Confederates until infantry arrived, but two large Confederate corps broke the hastily formed Union lines, which fell back to the hills south of the town. On 2 July the Union line stood in a fishhook shape.
