Lee attacked the Union left, with fierce fighting at Little Round Top, the Wheatfield, Devil's Den and the Peach Orchard, and assaulted Culp's Hill and Cemetery Hill on the right, but the Union held its lines.

On 3 July around 1 p.m. 150 to 170 Confederate guns opened what was probably the largest bombardment of the war, which did little to the Union position. About 3 p.m. between 10,500 and 12,500 Confederate soldiers advanced three-quarters of a mile towards Cemetery Ridge in the assault known as Pickett's Charge. Union artillery and rifle fire devastated them, and the few who briefly reached the ridge were driven back. On 4 July Lee began his retreat.

Union casualties were 23,055, of whom 3,155 were killed, and the Confederates lost 23,231 by one recent count, though many authors give as many as 28,000. Nearly a third of Lee's general officers were killed, wounded or captured. On 4 July the Vicksburg garrison surrendered to Major General Ulysses S. Grant, and news of Gettysburg ended lingering hopes of European recognition of the Confederacy.

Historians often call Gettysburg the turning point of the war, usually together with Vicksburg, since Lee conducted no more strategic offensives afterwards, though it was not seen as decisive at the time and the war went on for almost two years. On 19 November 1863 Lincoln spoke at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery, now Gettysburg National Cemetery, in his Gettysburg Address of 271 words.
battle-of-grunwald: In 1230 the Teutonic Order, a crusading military order, moved to Chełmno Land and launched the Prussian Crusade, conquering and converting the pagan Prussians by the 1280s. It then turned on the pagan Grand Duchy of Lithuania and for about 100 years raided its lands, particularly Samogitia, which separated the order's lands in Prussia from its branch in Livonia, but gained very little territory. In May 1409 an uprising began in Teutonic-held Samogitia, which Lithuania and Poland supported. Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen declared war on both on 6 August 1409.

The Polish and Lithuanian troops gathered at Czerwińsk and crossed the Vistula over a pontoon bridge between 24 and 30 June 1410. They then marched towards Marienburg (Malbork), the capital of Prussia, and crossed the Prussian border on 9 July. No contemporary source gives reliable troop counts; the highest estimates, 39,000 Polish–Lithuanian and 27,000 Teutonic men, are often cited as commonly accepted. The Teutonic army was outnumbered but had advantages in discipline, training and equipment.

On 15 July the armies met between the villages of Grünfelde, Tannenberg and Ludwigsdorf. Vytautas attacked the Teutonic left flank, and after more than an hour the Lithuanian light cavalry retreated. Heavy fighting between Poles and Teutons followed, and Jungingen led 16 banners to the Polish right flank. The Lithuanians returned and struck from the rear, Jungingen was killed, and the leaderless Teutonic forces retreated to their camp, where the defence was broken. The battle lasted about ten hours.

The victors delayed three days on the battlefield and reached Marienburg only on 26 July, which gave Heinrich von Plauen time to organise its defence. Many Teutonic fortresses surrendered, but the siege of Marienburg failed, and the Peace of Thorn of 1411 cost the order minimal territory. The order never recovered its former power, and the burden of war reparations caused internal conflicts and an economic downturn in its lands.

The battle shifted the balance of power in Central and Eastern Europe towards the Polish–Lithuanian union. It is regarded as one of the most important victories in the history of Poland and Lithuania and is also commemorated in Ukraine and Belarus. In 1914 Germany named a victory over Russia the Battle of Tannenberg and framed it as revenge for 1410.
battle-of-hastings: King Edward the Confessor died childless on 5 January 1066, leaving several claimants to the throne. Harold Godwinson, Earl of Wessex, was elected king by the Witenagemot and crowned by Ealdred, the Archbishop of York. Duke William of Normandy claimed that Edward had promised him the throne and that Harold had sworn to agree, and the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada also made a claim.

Hardrada and Harold's exiled brother Tostig Godwinson defeated an English army at the Battle of Fulford on 20 September 1066, and Harold defeated them at the Battle of Stamford Bridge on 25 September. Three days later William landed at Pevensey. Harold marched about 200 miles south in roughly a week and camped on Caldbec Hill on the night of 13 October.

The armies met on Saturday 14 October 1066 about 7 miles north of Hastings, near the present town of Battle. The fighting began at 9 am and lasted until dusk. The numbers are unknown; most modern historians argue for 7,000 to 8,000 English troops. The English were almost entirely infantry, in a shield wall at the top of a steep slope, with few archers. About half of William's army was infantry, and the rest was split between cavalry and archers.

Norman arrows shot uphill had little effect, and attacks by infantry and then cavalry failed to break the shield wall. A retreat began on William's left, and a rumour spread that he was dead; he rode through his men showing his face and led a counter-attack. The Normans then used the tactic of feigned flight. Accounts of Harold's death conflict, and the traditional arrow in the eye is first mentioned in the 1080s. He appears to have died late in the battle, and most of his army then retreated.

Some historians estimate that 2,000 invaders died, along with about twice that number of Englishmen. Harold's body was identified the day after the battle. William was crowned king on Christmas Day 1066. Rebellions and resistance continued, but Hastings effectively marked the culmination of his conquest of England. William founded a monastery on the site, with the high altar of the abbey church said to mark the spot where Harold died.
battle-of-hattin: The Kingdom of Jerusalem was divided. Guy of Lusignan became king in 1186 in right of his wife Sibylla, and his court faction, which included Raynald of Châtillon, Gerard of Ridefort and the Knights Templar, was opposed by a nobles' faction led by Raymond III of Tripoli. Saladin, who had become vizier of Egypt in 1169, had taken Damascus in 1174 and Aleppo in 1183 and controlled the southern and eastern flanks of the crusader states. In 1187 Raynald raided a Muslim pilgrim caravan while a truce was in force. Saladin's son al-Afdal and the emir Gökböri then raided around Acre, and in May 1187 they heavily defeated the Templars at the Battle of Cresson.

Saladin assembled about 40,000 men and crossed the Jordan on 30 June. On 2 July he stormed Tiberias, where Raymond's wife Eschiva of Bures held out in the citadel, hoping to draw the Crusader army away from its well-watered camp at La Saphorie. Raymond advised against marching, but Gerard and Raynald accused him of cowardice, and Guy resolved to advance.

On 3 July the Crusaders marched under constant attack by mounted archers and found the springs inadequate. They were forced to camp on a dry plateau near Meskenah, surrounded overnight, while Muslim troops set fire to dry grass. On 4 July, blinded by smoke and tormented by thirst, they were blocked from the water. Raymond broke through to the lake with two charges and escaped to Tyre. Most of the infantry fled onto the Horns of Hattin. The knights made three charges on Saladin's position and were broken when Guy's tent fell.

Guy, Raynald and other barons were captured. Saladin had Raynald killed for breaking the truce, assuring Guy that kings do not kill kings. About 200 captive Templar and Hospitaller Knights were beheaded, except the Grand Master of the Temple, and the captured turcopoles were executed. Other prisoners were sold into slavery, while the high-ranking barons were treated well; Guy was released in 1188.

Having sent most of their men to the field, the Crusaders had little left to defend their castles. Fifty-two towns and fortifications fell, among them Acre, Nablus, Jaffa and Beirut, and Queen Sibylla, Patriarch Heraclius and Balian negotiated the surrender of Jerusalem on 2 October. Tyre held, saved by Conrad of Montferrat. The defeat led Pope Gregory VIII to call a new crusade, and the Third Crusade began in 1189. Crusader military power in Outremer finally collapsed at La Forbie in 1244.
battle-of-issus: Alexander the Great crossed into Asia in 334 BCE and defeated the Persian satraps of Asia Minor at the Battle of the Granicus. He then occupied most of Asia Minor and took the coastal settlements, in order to negate the power of the superior Persian fleet. While he was at Tarsus he heard that Darius III was massing a great army at Babylon. Alexander sent Parmenion ahead to occupy the coast around Issus. Darius took a northern route and captured Issus without opposition, cutting off the hands of the sick and wounded Alexander had left there. In doing so he put his army behind Alexander's and cut his supply lines.

The two armies met on either side of a small river, the Pinarus, on a coastal plain only 2.6 kilometres wide between the sea and the mountains, where Darius could not use his superior numbers. Ancient writers gave Persian totals from 250,000 to 600,000, but most modern historians estimate no more than 100,000. Alexander's army may not have exceeded 40,000. The fighting is dated to 5 November 333 BCE.

The Persian cavalry charged first against Parmenion. In the centre the Macedonian phalanx suffered severely crossing the river against the Greek mercenaries. Then Alexander's hypaspists broke through the Persian line, and Alexander led the Companions in a direct assault on Darius and his bodyguard, who fled. Alexander then turned on the rear of the Greek mercenaries, who also gave way. The Persians, seeing their king gone, fled in rout, and the cavalry pursued them while the light lasted.

The battle was a decisive victory for Alexander and marked the beginning of the end of Persian power. It was the first time the Persian army had been defeated with the king present. The Macedonians captured Darius's wife, his daughters and his mother, who had accompanied the campaign. Alexander, who later married the younger daughter Stateira, treated the women with great respect. The Spartan king Agis III later recruited 8,000 of the Greek mercenary survivors, and in 331 BCE he defeated a Macedonian general but was finally beaten at the Battle of Megalopolis.
battle-of-iwo-jima: After the American capture of the Marshall Islands in early 1944, Japanese commanders expected a drive toward the Marianas and set up an inner line of defences running north to Japan through the Volcano Islands. The American invasion, called Operation Detachment, aimed to capture Iwo Jima and its two airfields. In June 1944 Lieutenant General Tadamichi Kuribayashi took command of the defence. He knew his garrison could not win, but hoped to inflict such casualties that the Americans would reconsider invading Japan.

The Japanese positions were heavily fortified, with bunkers, hidden artillery and 18 kilometres of tunnels. Major General Harry Schmidt, commanding the Marine landing force, asked for a ten-day bombardment, but Rear Admiral William H. P. Blandy insisted on three days, a decision the Marines resented.

The landings began on 19 February 1945. After about an hour, once men and equipment crowded the beach, the Japanese opened fire with machine guns, mortars and heavy artillery. Loose volcanic ash stopped the amphibious tractors, and the Marines had to go forward on foot. The 28th Marines crossed the island at its narrowest, about 800 metres, and isolated Mount Suribachi. Kuribayashi had forbidden banzai charges as a waste of resources, and the Japanese fought from their fortifications.

On 23 February six Marines raised a flag on Suribachi, in the second flag-raising there that day, and Joe Rosenthal's photograph of it won a Pulitzer Prize. The north was harder: rocky terrain favoured the defenders, and the Motoyama Plateau became what the Marines called the meatgrinder. Flamethrowers were used to clear pillboxes and caves.

Of some 21,000 Japanese on the island, only 216 were taken prisoner, and 3,000 or more kept fighting in the caves until they were hunted down. The 36-day assault cost more than 26,000 American casualties, including 6,800 dead. It was the only Marine battle in which American casualties exceeded Japanese. Two Japanese soldiers held out until January 1949. The value of the island remains disputed: William V. Pratt, a retired Chief of Naval Operations, called it useless to the Army and the Navy, though its airfield served escort fighters and emergency landings of B-29s. Lessons from it guided the Battle of Okinawa.
battle-of-jutland: The German High Seas Fleet had 16 dreadnought-type battleships against the Royal Navy's 28 and stood little chance of a head-on clash, so the Germans planned to lure out and destroy parts of the British fleet. In January 1916 Vice-Admiral Reinhard Scheer took command. His plan was to use Vice-Admiral Franz Hipper's five battlecruisers to draw Vice-Admiral Sir David Beatty's battlecruisers into the path of the main fleet, with submarines across the likely British routes. The British, however, held a copy of the German codebook, taken in 1914 from the cruiser SMS Magdeburg, and usually knew of German activities. Admiral Sir John Jellicoe sailed with the Grand Fleet on 30 May 1916 to meet Beatty.

On the afternoon of 31 May Beatty met Hipper earlier than the Germans expected, and in the exchange he lost two battlecruisers. When at 16:40 he sighted the German battleships, he turned back north, drawing the Germans towards Jellicoe. At 18:30 the main fleets engaged for the first time, with Jellicoe crossing the T of Scheer's line. Scheer, taken by surprise and hampered by poor visibility, ordered a turn away at 18:33. Jellicoe crossed his line again at 19:15, and the leading German battleships were badly damaged.

At 21:00 Jellicoe, aware of the fleet's weakness in night fighting, chose to avoid a major engagement until dawn and moved south to block Scheer's escape. Scheer instead crossed Jellicoe's wake and escaped by Horns Reef, and most of the British light forces failed to report their night encounters with the Germans. Fourteen British and eleven German ships were sunk.

Both sides claimed victory, and historians have not agreed on who won, or whether anyone did. The British lost more ships and far more sailors, but the German fleet had not broken the blockade. By the end of 1916 the German navy accepted that its surface ships had been contained and turned to unrestricted submarine warfare, which together with the Zimmermann Telegram led to the United States declaring war in April 1917.

Jellicoe was criticised for caution in letting Scheer escape, became First Sea Lord, and was replaced as commander of the Grand Fleet by Beatty. His supporters blamed Beatty for the failure to achieve a complete victory. The Admiralty's own review found that British armour-piercing shells often exploded outside German armour instead of penetrating it.
battle-of-kadesh: After expelling the Hyksos around 1550 BCE, the rulers of the Egyptian New Kingdom reclaimed their borders and fought as far north as the Orontes, but Egyptian influence in Syria declined in the late Eighteenth Dynasty, as the Amarna letters show. In the Nineteenth Dynasty Seti I set out to restore the empire. He reoccupied abandoned posts, made an informal peace with the Hittites and captured Kadesh and Amurru, with his son Ramesses II campaigning beside him. In his fourth year Ramesses marched into Syria, and in the spring of his fifth year, in May 1274 BCE, he set out from his capital Pi-Ramesses. The Hittite king Muwatalli II gave the recovery of Amurru as his reason for marching south.

Ramesses led four divisions, named Amun, Re, Set and Ptah, together with Sherden troops and a contingent called the Ne'arin. Muwatalli had gathered allies, and Ramesses recorded nineteen of them. Two captured nomads, who were Hittite spies, told Ramesses that the Hittite army was far off at Aleppo, and he hurried towards Kadesh with the Amun division while the others were strung out behind him. Hittite chariots then crossed the river and struck the Re division in the open, scattering it, and went on to attack the Egyptian camp.

Ramesses, by his own account abandoned and surrounded, rallied his bodyguard and the survivors and led several charges. The Hittites stopped to plunder the camp and were driven back towards the Orontes. Muwatalli sent another thousand chariots, but the Ne'arin arrived suddenly and the Ptah division threatened the Hittite rear. After six unsuccessful charges the Hittites were pinned against the river, and many drowned trying to swim it. They kept Kadesh itself.

Unable to besiege the walled city, Ramesses went south and then back to Egypt, proclaiming victory. Hittite records tell a different story, and modern historians regard the battle as a draw. Muwatalli went on to capture the Egyptian province of Upi. Ramesses took Dapur and Tunip in his eighth and ninth years, but they returned to Hittite control within a year. A peace treaty with Hattusili III was signed in the twenty-first year of Ramesses's reign, about 1258 BCE. It was inscribed on a silver tablet; a clay copy was found at Hattusa and an Egyptian version survives on papyrus.

More texts and wall reliefs record this battle than any other in the Ancient Near East, almost all from the Egyptian side. The main sources are the Poem and the Bulletin, repeated in temples at Abydos, Luxor, Karnak, Abu Simbel and the Ramesseum, and the bombastic nature of Ramesses's version is recognised.
battle-of-karbala: After the assassination of the third caliph Uthman ibn Affan in 656, Ali ibn Abi Talib was proclaimed caliph, but Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan, governor of Syria, denounced his legitimacy. After Ali was assassinated in 661, his son Hasan handed power to Mu'awiya by treaty, on condition that Mu'awiya rule justly and let his successor be chosen by consultation. After Hasan's death in 670 his brother Husayn became head of the Banu Hashim clan. Before his death in 680, Mu'awiya named his son Yazid successor, making the caliphate hereditary.

Husayn declined to pledge allegiance to Yazid and went to Mecca. There the people of Kufa sent him many letters inviting him to overthrow Umayyad rule, and his cousin Muslim ibn Aqil reported favourably on their support. Husayn set out for the city on 9 September 680 with about fifty men and his family.

On the way Husayn learned that Muslim ibn Aqil had been executed in Kufa, and told his followers they could leave. Most who had joined him on the road did, and his companions from Mecca stayed. A force of 1,000 sent by the caliph intercepted his caravan, and he camped at Karbala on 2 October, where a further 4,000 Umayyad troops arrived. The governor Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad refused safe passage unless Husayn submitted to his authority, which Husayn rejected.

On 10 October 680 Husayn addressed his opponents, reminding them that he was Muhammad's grandson. Al-Hurr ibn Yazid al-Tamimi went over to his side. Husayn was struck by an arrow and then surrounded and killed. Seventy or seventy-two died on his side, and the surviving women and children were taken to Kufa and then Damascus.

Kufan supporters felt guilty at having abandoned Husayn and formed the Tawwabin movement, with the slogan Revenge for Husayn, which was crushed in January 685. Mukhtar al-Thaqafi then ruled much of Iraq for eighteen months, killing several of those responsible for Husayn's death. Heinz Halm writes that there was no religious aspect to Shi'ism before 680 and that the deaths at Karbala created it. Shia commemorate Husayn's martyrdom in the ten days of Muharram, ending on Ashura, and the Imam Husayn Shrine at Karbala is a holy site of Shia Islam, the destination of the Arba'in pilgrimage.
battle-of-koppam: From his accession Rajadhiraja Chola I sought to subdue the Chalukyas, who ruled parts of northern Karnataka and the south of present-day Maharashtra, and to add their lands to the Chola Empire. His first invasion, in 1047–48, had failed. On the second expedition he led a large army north and plundered the province of Rattamandalam, with his brother and heir-apparent Rajendra Chola II following in the rear.

According to the Chola sources and the Thiruvalandur copper plate, Rajadhiraja had personally led the attack on Kalyanapura, also called Kalyani, the modern Basavakalyan. Someshvara I fled when the city was attacked, returned with an army and was beaten again, and the Chola king then withdrew towards Kollapura. The copper plate says that Someshvara gathered a huge army and called out for battle as the Chola withdrew, and that the Chola turned to meet him at the place called Koppam.

The copper plate describes columns of foot soldiers, horses and elephants engaging their counterparts, with Rajadhiraja fighting from his elephant until a downpour of Chalukya arrows killed him. The Chola troops, who had been holding the upper hand, panicked and began to retreat. Rajendra II, commanding the reserve, took over the army, rallied it and inflicted heavy losses, forcing Someshvara to flee. Chola sources record that the elephants, horses and camels of the Chalukyas, a large booty and the queens of Someshvara fell into Chola hands. Rajendra is reported to have set up a victory pillar at Kolhapur before returning to his country.

The battle is known chiefly from the Chola side: an inscription dated to 1054 and Rajendra Chola II's Manimangalam record of 1055. The latter gives the victory to Rajendra and says that Ahavamalla, as it calls the Chalukya king, became afraid, incurred disgrace and ran away. The year is given as 1054, or as 1052 by the historian Sen. The site is also uncertain. The Manimangalam inscription places Koppam on the bank of the great river; the scholar Fleet identified it with Khidrapur, 30 miles south-east of Kolhapur, taking the river to be the Krishna, while other historians have put it near Maski.
battle-of-kosovo: After the death of Stefan Uroš V in December 1371 and the Ottoman victory at the Battle of Maritsa earlier that year, the Serbian Empire had broken into virtually independent principalities. Prince Lazar, ruler of Moravian Serbia, the northern part of the former empire, prepared for a campaign against the Ottomans. After Ottoman defeats at Pločnik in 1386 and Bileća in 1388, Sultan Murad I moved his troops through Kratovo and Kumanovo to Pristina, where he arrived on 14 June 1389. Lazar gathered troops near Niš and moved to Kosovo, a crossroads that let him control the routes Murad could take. Lazar's army included his own troops, a contingent under his son-in-law Vuk Branković and Bosnian forces under Vlatko Vuković sent by King Tvrtko I.

Reliable accounts are scarce, and no first-hand account from a participant exists. The army sizes are disputed; the leading estimate accepted by Western scholars is 15,000 to 20,000 for Lazar and 27,000 to 30,000 for Murad. Murad's son Bayezid commanded the right wing and his son Yakub the left. It is believed that the battle began with Ottoman archers shooting at the Serbian cavalry, which broke through the Ottoman left wing, but light Ottoman cavalry and infantry then counterattacked and the Serbian heavy armour became a disadvantage. Bayezid led a counterattack and the Ottomans routed the Serbian infantry.

Lazar was captured and Murad was killed. Murad's death is attributed to a Serbian knight named Miloš Obilić, and accounts of how he did it differ. In popular tradition Vuk Branković betrayed Lazar by fleeing, a theory first presented by Mavro Orbini in 1601 that is largely seen as unfounded. Both armies were largely destroyed, and the battle is the only time an Ottoman sultan was killed in battle.

Bayezid killed his brother Yakub on hearing of their father's death and became sole heir. The Serbs had too few men left to field large armies, while the Ottomans could draw on reserves from the east. Hungary tried to expand in northern Serbia, and the Ottomans renewed their campaign in the south in 1390 to 1391. Some Serbian principalities that were not already vassals became so in the following years, and Lazar's daughter married Bayezid. Serbia became an Ottoman province, and the capture of Smederevo on 20 June 1459 marks the end of medieval Serbian statehood.

The battle was mythologised soon afterwards, and the Kosovo Myth became central to Serbian folklore. In the 19th century Vuk Karadžić collected the epic poems of the Kosovo cycle. The battle is seen in Serbian public discourse as important to Serbian history, tradition and national identity, and Vidovdan commemorates it.
battle-of-kulikovo: After the Mongol invasion of Rus' in the 13th century the Russian principalities became vassals of the Golden Horde. Moscow grew in power and often challenged its neighbours, and in 1300 it seized Kolomna from Ryazan. After the killing of Khan Berdi Beg in 1359 the Golden Horde fell into what were called the Great Troubles, and the commander Mamai, Berdi Beg's son-in-law, took power in its western part and enthroned khans of his own. He was not a descendant of Genghis Khan, so his hold on power was tenuous, and he had to fight both for supremacy and against separatism while Lithuania, Moscow and Ryazan rose as new powers.

In August 1380 Dmitry of Moscow learned that Mamai's army was approaching. Mamai's envoys demanded a tribute raised to the level of the time of Khan Jani Beg, and Dmitry agreed only to the amount of his earlier agreement. He gathered an army at Kolomna and marched south, reaching the Don on 6 September. Jogaila of Lithuania was marching to join Mamai. On the morning of 8 September, in thick fog, the Russian army crossed the Don.

The early sources give few details of the fighting. The fullest account, The Tale of the Rout of Mamai, dates from the 16th century, and it is unknown whether it rests on an earlier source. It describes six regiments, with an ambush regiment hidden in an oak grove and Dmitry exchanging his coat and helmet with a boyar so as to fight unrecognised. The main forces clashed at about 10.35 in the morning, and Russian sources agree that a long and cruel melee followed in which many died on both sides. A third of the commanders of the banners were killed. Dmitry survived, wounded and exhausted, and was found among the corpses.

Jogaila turned back on hearing of Mamai's defeat. Dmitry made Prince Oleg of Ryazan accept him as his older brother. Mamai escaped to the Genoese stronghold of Caffa in Crimea and raised a new army, but without a legitimate khan his nobles went over to his rival Tokhtamysh, who gained full power and ended the twenty-year split of the Golden Horde. Mamai fled to Caffa again and was killed.

The victory did not end Mongol domination, but it is traditionally regarded as the turning point at which Mongol influence began to fade and Moscow's power to rise. Only five primary sources survive, none from the Tatar side, yet the battle produced a larger body of medieval Rus' literature than any other event, the Kulikovo cycle, which includes the epic Zadonshchina.
battle-of-kursk: After Stalingrad the Red Army moved to a general offensive in the south, and by February 1943 the southern sector of the German front was in strategic crisis. Kursk was retaken by the Soviets on 8 February. Short of infantry and artillery, the Germans would have to rely chiefly on their panzer divisions for any offensive in 1943. On 10 March Manstein presented a plan to pinch off the Kursk salient. Hitler believed that a victory would reassert German strength and improve his prestige with allies he thought were considering withdrawing from the war.

The Soviets had foreknowledge of the German plans through the Lucy spy ring in Switzerland and the spy John Cairncross at Bletchley Park. Georgiy Zhukov and other officers recommended a strategic defensive before going on the offensive. The Germans delayed the attack to build up their forces, which gave the Red Army time to construct a series of deep defensive belts and a large reserve.

Operation Citadel began on 5 July 1943, with attacks from north and south on the base of the salient. In the north, Model's 9th Army attacked the Central Front, and the fighting around Ponyri and Olkhovatka became a battle of attrition that troops called a mini-Stalingrad. In the south, Hoth's 4th Panzer Army advanced against the Voronezh Front, and the Soviets committed their strategic reserves, including the 5th Guards Tank Army, which advanced to Prokhorovka, where a large armoured clash took place from 12 July.

The Western Allies invaded Sicily on 10 July, and on 12 July Hitler decided to stop the offensive and move forces to Italy, though Manstein objected that his forces were on the verge of breaking through. The same day the Soviets launched Operation Kutuzov against the Orel salient, and on 3 August they began Operation Polkovodets Rumyantsev, liberating Belgorod by 5 August.

For the first time a major German offensive was stopped before it broke through; the Germans advanced at most 8 to 12 kilometres in the north and 35 kilometres in the south. The Soviet victory was costly, but the Soviet Union's industry and manpower allowed it to replace its losses. The battle was the last strategic offensive the Germans were able to launch on the Eastern Front, and the Red Army held the strategic initiative for the rest of the war. It is the single largest battle in the history of warfare and the single deadliest armoured battle.
battle-of-leipzig: Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 ended in disaster, and in June 1813 the Duke of Wellington routed the French at Vitoria in Spain. The allies regrouped as the Sixth Coalition, which included Prussia, Russia, Sweden, the United Kingdom and smaller German states whose rulers no longer felt loyal to the French emperor. Napoleon raised another large army, but it consisted largely of teenagers and inexperienced conscripts, and his cavalry was weak. The Coalition followed the Trachenberg Plan, defeating his marshals with weaker forces while wearing out his own corps in chases across Germany.

Two attempts to take Berlin failed, at Großbeeren and Dennewitz. Napoleon withdrew westward and gathered his army around Leipzig to protect his supply lines, while the Coalition armies converged on the city. He was outnumbered but held Leipzig and its bridges, which let him shift troops between sectors faster than the Allies could.

The fighting lasted from 16 to 19 October 1813. On the first day the French won small victories at Lindenau and Wachau and had a reverse at Möckern, and the day ended in a draw. Reinforcements then favoured the Allies: 145,000 arrived by 17 October, against 14,000 for the French. On 18 October Napoleon offered to surrender his fortresses on the Oder and Vistula in return for an armistice and a withdrawal behind the Saale. Alexander I, Francis I and Frederick William III declined.

On 19 October the Allies attacked the retreating French, while Marshal Oudinot's rearguard of 30,000 fought street by street in Leipzig. A corporal blew up the only bridge over the Elster while it was crowded with retreating troops, and the rout cost thousands of French lives and 30,000 prisoners. Prince Józef Poniatowski drowned.

Leipzig was the bloodiest battle of the Napoleonic Wars, with estimates of 80,000 to 110,000 killed, wounded or missing. It ended French power east of the Rhine and brought Baden, Saxony and Württemberg over to the Coalition. Napoleon told the Senate that a year before all Europe had marched with him and now all Europe marched against him. The Coalition invaded France in 1814, and Napoleon abdicated in May and was exiled to Elba. A 91-metre Monument to the Battle of the Nations was completed in Leipzig in 1913.
battle-of-lepanto: Pope Pius V promoted the Christian coalition to rescue the Venetian colony of Famagusta on Cyprus, which the Turks were besieging in early 1571. On 1 August the Venetians surrendered after being promised they could leave freely, but the Ottoman commander Lala Kara Mustafa Pasha broke his word, imprisoned them and had Marco Antonio Bragadin flayed alive. The Holy League included Venice, the Spanish Empire, the Papal States, Genoa and other states. Its banner reached Naples on 14 August 1571, where it was consigned to John of Austria, half-brother of Philip II of Spain, the overall commander.

The Holy League fleet had 206 galleys and six galleasses, large Venetian galleys with heavy artillery. The Ottoman admiral Ali Pasha commanded 211 war galleys and 63 galliots; the oarsmen were virtually all slaves, many of them captured Christians. The Christians had an estimated 1,815 guns against 750 Ottoman guns with insufficient ammunition, and their arquebusiers faced Ottoman composite bowmen.

On the morning of 7 October 1571 the Christian fleet formed up in four divisions on a north–south line, with the Venetian Agostino Barbarigo on the left, John of Austria in the centre and the Genoese Gianandrea Doria on the right, and met the Ottoman fleet in the Gulf of Patras. John of Austria had the galley slaves freed from their chains. The battle was in essence an infantry battle on floating platforms, and the Ottoman fleet was almost completely destroyed.

It was the largest naval battle in Western history since classical antiquity, with more than 450 warships, and the last major engagement fought almost entirely between rowing vessels. The Ottomans, who had not lost a major naval battle since the fifteenth century, rebuilt quickly, with about 250 ships built within six months. The League failed to capitalise, since friction among the Christian leaders ended further operations and it regained none of the territories lost earlier. The loss of qualified crews led to a sharp decrease in Ottoman naval initiative after 1580.

The victory confirmed the de facto division of the Mediterranean between an Ottoman east and a west under the Spanish Crown and its Italian allies. The League credited the victory to the Virgin Mary, and Pius V instituted the feast of Our Lady of Victory, now kept as the feast of Our Lady of the Rosary.
battle-of-manzikert: Byzantine strength in the east weakened under Constantine IX Monomachos, who about 1053 disbanded the Iberian Army of 50,000 men, a step that contemporaries judged catastrophic for the eastern defences. A truce with the Seljuks lasted until 1064, when Alp Arslan took Ani. Romanos IV Diogenes came to power in 1068 and campaigned against the Seljuks, retaking Hierapolis but winning no decisive victory in 1069.

While Alp Arslan besieged Aleppo, Romanos led a large army into Armenia to recover lost fortresses. It numbered around 40,000, with professional troops from the western and eastern provinces, Frankish and Norman mercenaries under Roussel de Bailleul, Turkic and Bulgarian mercenaries, Georgian and Armenian troops and part of the Varangian Guard. Andronikos Doukas, son of his rival John Doukas, commanded the rear guard. Romanos took Manzikert on 23 August 1071 but had detached part of his army to Khliat, halving his force.

Alp Arslan was nearby with a large cavalry force, and his scouts knew exactly where Romanos was. Seljuk horse archers harassed the Byzantines, some Turkic mercenaries deserted, and Romanos rejected a Seljuk peace emissary. On 26 August the Byzantines advanced against a Seljuk crescent whose wings moved to surround them. They captured Alp Arslan's camp, but the Seljuk cavalry avoided a pitched battle.

At nightfall Romanos ordered a withdrawal. The right wing misunderstood, and Doukas ignored the order to cover the retreat and marched back to camp. The Seljuks attacked the confused army, the right wing and then the left broke, and the emperor and the Varangian Guard were surrounded. Romanos was wounded and taken prisoner.

Alp Arslan treated Romanos with considerable kindness and, after about a week, agreed terms. Back in the empire Romanos was defeated three times by the Doukas family, deposed, blinded and exiled, and died of an infection from the blinding. Modern scholars think Byzantine losses in the battle were relatively low, and that the civil war that followed did more harm. By 1080 the Seljuks had gained 78,000 square kilometres of Anatolia. Byzantine writers such as Anna Komnene saw the battle as a disaster, and historians date the loss of Anatolia from it.
battle-of-marathon: Athens and Eretria had each sent a force to support the Ionian cities in their revolt against Persian rule, and the Athenians and Eretrians captured and burned Sardis before retreating with heavy losses. Darius I swore to burn down the two cities. After the Persian victory at the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE crushed the revolt, he began planning to subjugate Greece. In 490 BCE he sent a naval force under Datis and Artaphernes across the Aegean, which captured Eretria and then landed at the bay of Marathon, about 27 kilometres north-east of Athens.

Under Miltiades, the Athenian general with most experience of fighting the Persians, the Athenian army marched to block the two exits from the plain. The Spartans, in the middle of a religious festival, said they could not march until the full moon, but 1,000 hoplites from Plataea joined the Athenians.

Ancient sources give the Athenians and Plataeans as about 10,000 men, a figure modern historians generally accept. Modern estimates for the Persian infantry run from 20,000 to 100,000, with a consensus of perhaps 25,000. The Athenians, probably outnumbered at least two to one, had no need to seek battle, since each day brought the Spartans closer, and the marshes and mountains kept the Persian cavalry from joining the infantry.

Miltiades ordered a general attack. The Greeks thinned their centre, perhaps so that their line was as long as the Persian line, and ran for the last stretch under the Persian arrows. The Persian centre prevailed against the thin Greek centre, but on both wings the Athenians and Plataeans routed the Persian levies and turned inwards to surround the Persian centre. The Persians broke in panic towards their ships, and some ran into the swamps, where an unknown number drowned. The Athenians captured seven ships.

Herodotus records 6,400 Persian bodies counted on the battlefield and 192 Athenian dead, among them the war archon Callimachus. The Persian fleet then sailed towards Athens, but the Athenian army marched back quickly and arrived in time to prevent a landing, and the Persians returned to Asia. The Spartan army reached Marathon the next day and agreed that the Athenians had won a great victory. Darius's son Xerxes I began the second invasion in 480 BCE.

The defeat barely touched the resources of the Persian Empire, yet it was the first Greek victory over the Persians and showed that resistance was possible. It also showed that Greeks could win without the Spartans, and it raised Greek esteem for Athens.
battle-of-midway: Japan had quickly won its first goals in the Pacific, taking Hong Kong, the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies. After the Doolittle air raid on Tokyo in April 1942, Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto planned Operation MI, an attack on Midway Atoll meant to draw out and destroy the American Pacific Fleet, above all its carriers. The plan was complex, scattered its forces over hundreds of miles of sea, and assumed that only two American carriers were available.

The United States had an advantage in intelligence. Cryptanalysts under Commander Joseph Rochefort had partly broken the Japanese naval code JN-25b and learned of an operation against a target called AF. To confirm that AF was Midway, the base broadcast an uncoded message that its water supply had failed, and a Japanese message soon reported AF short of water. Admiral Chester Nimitz sent forces under Frank Jack Fletcher and Raymond Spruance, and the carrier Yorktown, damaged at the Coral Sea, was made battle-ready in 72 hours.

On 4 June 1942 Japanese aircraft bombed Midway. Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo, who had kept half his aircraft in reserve, ordered them rearmed with bombs for land targets, and then received a report of an American fleet. American carrier aircraft reached his force while his carriers were rearming and refuelling. Akagi was set ablaze by a single hit that exploded among armed and fuelled aircraft, and Kaga and Sōryū were also sunk.

The last carrier, Hiryū, counterattacked and hit Yorktown with three bombs, but that afternoon American dive bombers left her unable to operate aircraft. All four Japanese fleet carriers were sunk, as was the heavy cruiser Mikuma. Japan lost 3,057 men, including many pilots hard to replace. The United States lost Yorktown and the destroyer Hammann.

American forces withdrew once pursuit became too hazardous, and returned to Pearl Harbor after 10 June. Three American airmen captured during the battle were killed by their captors. After Midway and the Solomon Islands campaign, Japan could not replace its losses in ships and trained men, while American industrial and training capacity grew. The depth of the sea made the wrecks hard to find: Robert Ballard located Yorktown in 1998, and in 1999 an expedition found wreckage of Kaga. In 2000 the atoll was designated the Battle of Midway National Memorial.
battle-of-mohacs: After the death of King Matthias Corvinus in 1490, the Hungarian magnates secured the accession of the weak-willed Vladislaus II, who gave away most royal estates and revenues. The nobility cut its own taxes by 70 to 80 per cent, the Black Army of Matthias was dissolved and border garrisons went unpaid. A peasant rebellion under György Dózsa in 1514 was crushed by the nobles under John Zápolya, leaving the country divided. In 1521 the Ottomans took Nándorfehérvár, present-day Belgrade, the strongest Hungarian fortress on the Danube.

King Louis II married Mary of Habsburg in 1522, and the Ottomans saw the alliance as a threat. After Suleiman I came to power in 1520 they offered peace at least once, and Louis refused for reasons that are unclear. Help from Europe was scarce, since the western powers were absorbed in the Italian wars. Francis I of France, defeated at Pavia in 1525, asked Suleiman to make war on the Habsburgs, and the road lay across Hungary. An Ottoman army left Constantinople on 16 April 1526.

The Hungarian nobles were slow to answer their king's call. The army that took the field numbered around 25,000 to 30,000 men, with 85 cannons against about 300 for the Ottomans. The battle was fought on the afternoon of 29 August 1526 on a waterlogged plain near Mohács. Pressed by nobles who wanted immediate battle, the Hungarians relied on heavy cavalry to break the Ottoman line.

Archbishop Pál Tomori led a charge that at first drove back the Ottoman front line. The grand vizier Ibrahim Pasha drew his centre back into a crescent, exposing the flanks of the cavalry, and Ottoman cavalry and light infantry attacked from both wings while Janissaries and artillery fired from prepared positions. The Hungarian army was encircled, and its lines collapsed within two hours. King Louis and much of the aristocracy were killed.

Suleiman did not at first grasp the scale of his victory. During four more days on the field about 2,000 captured nobles were executed. Queen Mary fled Buda, and the Ottomans pillaged the abandoned castle and left. The nobility elected two kings, John Zápolya and the Habsburg Archduke Ferdinand, and the Ottomans occupied Buda in 1541, dividing Hungary into Habsburg, Ottoman and Transylvanian parts. Many Hungarians regard Mohács as the turning point of their history, and the saying More was lost at Mohács is still used for any great loss.
battle-of-okinawa: The battle, codenamed Operation Iceberg, followed a long campaign of island hopping. The Allies planned to use Kadena Air Base on Okinawa as a staging point for Operation Downfall, the invasion of the Japanese home islands 550 kilometres away. The United States formed the Tenth Army, combining Army and Marine divisions, with its own tactical air force. Against it stood Lieutenant General Mitsuru Ushijima's Thirty-Second Army, a mixed force of regular troops, naval infantry and conscripted local Okinawans, about 100,000 Japanese troops in all at the start.

The 77th Infantry Division captured the Kerama Islands from 26 March 1945. On 28 March, 394 civilians on Tokashiki island were forced by Japanese soldiers to kill themselves after American troops landed. The main landing took place on 1 April on the Hagushi beaches on the west coast, and the Tenth Army quickly took the Kadena and Yomitan airbases. The 6th Marine Division cleared the north, while two Army divisions turned south and met fierce resistance at fortified outposts guarding the Shuri Line. The Japanese fought from prepared cave positions, and the advance cost many lives on both sides. The land battle lasted about 81 days.

At sea, Japanese attacks came in waves. Between 1 April and 25 May seven major kamikaze attacks involved more than 1,500 planes. In April the battleship Yamato and nine other warships sailed from Japan on a suicide sortie, Operation Ten-Go; American carrier aircraft sank Yamato and five other warships before they reached Okinawa.

The Americans suffered some 48,000 casualties, more than 12,000 of them killed or missing. Lieutenant General Simon Bolivar Buckner Jr., the commander of the Tenth Army, was killed by artillery fire four days before the campaign ended, the highest-ranking American officer killed by enemy fire in the war. Okinawa had a large civilian population, and about 40,000 of the Okinawans killed had been drafted or impressed by the Japanese army. The Cornerstone of Peace at Mabuni, erected in 1995, lists the names of all the known dead, civilian and military, Japanese and foreign.

Japan surrendered soon after, so the planned invasion of the home islands never took place. Some military historians hold that the cost of Okinawa led American planners to seek an alternative in the atomic bombings, while others point to the Soviet invasion of Manchuria and Japan's depleted resources.
battle-of-plassey: Siraj-ud-Daulah, who succeeded his maternal grandfather Alivardi Khan as Nawab of Bengal in 1756, ordered the British to stop extending their fortifications. He attacked British-controlled Calcutta, an episode that included the Black Hole massacre. The British sent reinforcements from Madras under Colonel Robert Clive and Admiral Charles Watson, recaptured Calcutta, and then seized the French fort at Chandannagar. The conflict took place during the Seven Years' War, and a small French contingent fought against the British. The Nawab also feared attack from the Afghans under Ahmad Shah Durrani in the north and from the Marathas in the west, so he could not commit his whole army against the British.

The British formed a conspiracy with Siraj-ud-Daulah's demoted commander-in-chief Mir Jafar, with Yar Lutuf Khan, Rai Durlabh and others. Clive promised to make Mir Jafar Nawab. He marched on Murshidabad with about 3,000 men, and the Nawab's army, about 50,000 strong with 40 cannons and 10 war elephants, took position at Plassey by 21 June 1757.

On 23 June the Nawab's artillery opened fire at 8:00, and Clive withdrew into a grove sheltered by an embankment. After a heavy rainstorm, in which the British covered their ammunition and the Nawab's army did not, Mir Madan Khan led a cavalry charge that was driven back with grapeshot. Siraj, disturbed, appealed to Mir Jafar, who sent word of it to Clive, and on the advice of Rai Durlabh the Nawab withdrew and left for Murshidabad. Clive's troops took the French position at 15:00. Mir Jafar, Rai Durlabh and Yar Lutuf Khan had made no move to join the battle, which lasted about eleven hours.

On 24 June Clive greeted Mir Jafar as Nawab of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, and on 29 June he placed him on the throne at Murshidabad. The French were no longer a significant force in Bengal. By 1759 Mir Jafar resented his subordination to the British and encouraged the Dutch to send ships from Java; Clive defeated them at the Battle of Chinsura on 25 November 1759, and the British then deposed Mir Jafar and installed Mir Qasim. The British used the revenue and concessions they gained to increase their military strength, and historians judge Plassey one of the pivotal battles in the colonial control of the subcontinent.
battle-of-plataea: Xerxes I began preparing an invasion of Greece soon after his accession in 486 BCE, and a congress of city states, probably at Corinth, formed an alliance known as the Allies in 481 BCE. In August 480 BCE a small Allied army under the Spartan king Leonidas I held the pass of Thermopylae for three days before being outflanked. The Persians then occupied the evacuated city of Athens. The Allied navy won a decisive victory at Salamis, and Xerxes retreated to Sardis with a small part of his army, leaving his general Mardonius to finish the conquest the following year.

Mardonius retreated into Boeotia, hoping to draw the Greeks onto ground suited to his cavalry, and built a fortified camp on the north bank of the Asopos river. The Greek army, commanded by Pausanias, the regent of Sparta, crossed Mount Cithaeron and took positions on high ground opposite. According to Herodotus the Spartans sent 45,000 men, among them 5,000 full citizens and 35,000 helots. Estimates of the Persian army, drawn from the size of its camp, range from about 70,000 to 120,000, though modern historians differ widely.

The Greeks refused to descend to the plain, and a stalemate lasted eleven days. Persian cavalry then cut the Greek supply lines. On the thirteenth day the Greeks tried to withdraw, and their line broke up. Mardonius took this for a full retreat and ordered a pursuit. The Spartans, Tegeans and Athenians turned and fought, routed the lightly armed Persian infantry and killed Mardonius. Much of the Persian army was trapped in its camp and killed.

According to Herodotus the Battle of Mycale was fought on the same day, destroying what remained of the Persian fleet. After the two victories the second Persian invasion was over, and the Persian desire to conquer Greece gradually diminished. The sale of the loot paid for buildings such as the Athenian Treasury at Delphi.

A bronze column of intertwined snakes, the Serpent Column, was made from melted Persian armour and set up at Delphi, listing the 31 city-states that fought; most of it now stands in the Hippodrome of Constantinople. The poet Simonides of Ceos wrote an elegy and an encomium on the battle, and in Spartan tradition the victory avenged Thermopylae.
battle-of-poltava: King Charles XII of Sweden had defeated most of the anti-Swedish coalition, and Tsar Peter I was the only enemy still fighting. Peter offered to return the Baltic provinces Russia had occupied since 1703, except Ingria, where he had begun to build St. Petersburg, but Charles refused. In the autumn of 1707 Charles marched towards Moscow with almost 44,000 men. Russian scorched-earth tactics and harsh weather forced him south into Ukraine, where he hoped for help from Ivan Mazepa, the Cossack hetman who had decided to rebel against Peter. The winter of 1708 to 1709 was the coldest in Europe in over 500 years.

By spring 1709 Charles had about 20,000 soldiers and 34 cannons. He besieged the fortress of Poltava on the Vorskla on 2 May, and Peter marched to relieve it with about 80,000 men and built a fortified camp north of the town. On 20 June Charles was shot in the foot, so Field Marshal Carl Gustav Rehnskiöld took operational command. Peter had built ten redoubts across the corridor between two woods.

The Swedish attack began before dawn, but the cavalry arrived late and the Russians sounded the alarm. The Swedes overran the first two redoubts, but a column under General Carl Gustaf Roos became isolated at the third and surrendered at 9:30 a.m. At 9:45 the Swedes advanced on Peter's 42 battalions and nearly broke the first line, but their cavalry could not reform in time and the infantry on the left flank fled. The Russians filled the gap, and Aleksandr Menshikov's cavalry outflanked the Swedes.

Charles retreated south that evening. Lewenhaupt led the survivors towards the Dnieper but, pursued by Russian cavalry and Kalmyk auxiliaries, was forced to surrender at Perevolochna on 11 July. Peter sent many Swedish prisoners to Siberia. Charles and Mazepa escaped with about 1,500 men to Bendery in Moldavia, then controlled by the Ottoman Empire, where Charles stayed five years.

The battle revived the anti-Swedish coalition, which attacked the weakened Swedish Empire on several fronts. It was the largest battle of the Great Northern War, and Sweden lost its dominant position in the Baltic, which the Russian Empire took over.
battle-of-salamis: Athens and Eretria had supported the Ionian Revolt against the Persian king Darius I, and a Persian force destroyed Eretria in 490 BCE but was defeated by the Athenians at Marathon. In 480 BCE Xerxes I invaded Greece with a vast force. A small Greek force held Thermopylae, where the Spartan rearguard was annihilated, while the allied fleet fought at Artemisium and retreated with heavy losses. The Persians took Phocis, Boeotia, Attica and Euboea. The allies prepared to defend the Isthmus of Corinth, and the fleet withdrew to Salamis.

The Persians needed to finish the conquest in one campaigning season, since so large a force could not be supplied for long. To outflank the Isthmus they needed their navy, so destroying the allied fleet offered Xerxes the best hope. Herodotus has Queen Artemisia of Caria warn him that fighting at sea was an unnecessary risk.

The Athenian general Themistocles persuaded the allies to fight at sea again. By a ruse, a message telling Xerxes that much of the Greek fleet lay at Salamis, he drew the Persian navy into the straits to block both entrances. Herodotus gives the Greek fleet as 378 triremes, while Aeschylus, who fought there, says 310. Herodotus puts the Persian fleet at 1,207 ships at the outset, but most modern historians favour 600 to 800 at Salamis.

Ancient sources describe the fighting poorly. In the cramped waters Persian numbers became a hindrance, as ships struggled to manoeuvre and fouled their own lines. The Persian admiral Ariabignes, a brother of Xerxes, was killed early, and the Phoenician squadrons were pushed against the coast, many running aground. In the centre a wedge of Greek ships split the Persian fleet in two.

Xerxes tried to build a causeway across the straits, but the Greek fleet now patrolled them. He retreated to Asia with much of his army and left Mardonius to complete the conquest. The next year the Persians lost at Plataea and Mycale and made no further attempt on the Greek mainland, and over thirty years Thrace, the Aegean islands and Ionia were removed from their control. Many historians count Salamis among the most significant battles in history. In 2017 archaeologists announced the discovery of the anchorage used by the Greek warships before the battle.
battle-of-stalingrad: By the spring of 1942 the Wehrmacht held Ukraine, Belarus and the Baltic republics, and Adolf Hitler chose the south of the Soviet Union as the target of the summer campaign. Germany's fuel supplies had dwindled, and the plan, code-named Fall Blau, aimed to seize the Soviet oil fields in the Caucasus. Stalingrad was one of the largest industrial centres of the Soviet Union and a transport hub on the Volga River, and controlling it would block Soviet shipments along the river. The city also carried the name of the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin. Hitler split the army group, sending one part south to the Caucasus and the other, including Paulus's 6th Army, east towards the Volga.

German forces first met the Red Army's Stalingrad Front on 17 July 1942. On 23 August the 6th Army and part of the 4th Panzer Army began their offensive, supported by Luftwaffe bombing that reduced much of the city to rubble. The fighting became house-to-house. The Soviet commander Chuikov kept his front line as close to the Germans as possible, so that German artillery and aircraft could not strike without risking their own men, and used small units moving through the city's sewers. After 27 September the struggle moved to the factory district, and by November the Germans held 90 per cent of the ruined city, with the Soviet defenders confined to two narrow pockets on the Volga's west bank.

On 19 November the Red Army launched Operation Uranus against the Romanian armies guarding the German flanks. The flanks were overrun and about 330,000 Axis troops were trapped. Hitler forbade a breakout; attempts to supply the army by air failed, and Manstein's relief attempt, Operation Winter Storm, did not reach it. On 7 January 1943 Soviet envoys offered terms of surrender, which Hitler refused to let Paulus accept. On 2 February 1943 the 6th Army, out of ammunition and food, capitulated, the first of Hitler's field armies to do so.

The Axis suffered between 800,000 and 1,500,000 casualties, killed, wounded or captured, among the German armed forces and their allies. Of the troops trapped in the pocket, 105,000 eventually surrendered and 60,000 died. The German public was told of the disaster only at the end of January 1943; on 31 January state radio broadcast the Adagio of Anton Bruckner's Seventh Symphony before announcing the defeat. On 18 February Joseph Goebbels gave his Sportpalast speech calling for total war.

The defeat ended Germany's 1942 summer offensive and passed the strategic initiative on the Eastern Front to the Soviet Union. It is generally regarded as the turning point of the war in Europe. Stalingrad was named a Hero City in 1945, and the monument The Motherland Calls was erected on Mamayev Kurgan in 1967.
battle-of-stamford-bridge: The death of the childless King Edward the Confessor in January 1066 set off a struggle for the English throne among contenders from across north-western Europe, among them Harald Hardrada of Norway. The Norwegian army, with reinforcements from Orkney, most likely numbered between 7,000 and 9,000 men. Hardrada was joined by forces Tostig Godwinson had recruited in Flanders and Scotland. Tostig, exiled in 1065 after being ousted as Earl of Northumbria, was at odds with his brother Harold, who had been elected king. On 20 September the invaders defeated the northern earls Edwin and Morcar at the Battle of Fulford and received the surrender of York.

Harold was in southern England awaiting an invasion by William, Duke of Normandy. On hearing of the Norwegians he marched north with his housecarls and as many thegns as he could gather, covering about 185 miles from London to Yorkshire in four days. On 25 September he took the Norwegians completely by surprise at Stamford Bridge, where they had gone to collect hostages and supplies. According to Snorri Sturluson's saga, Harold himself rode up beforehand and offered Tostig his earldom.

A Norwegian with an axe was said by the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Henry of Huntingdon to have blocked the narrow bridge alone and cut down more than 40 Englishmen. The delay allowed the Norse to form a shield wall, but they had left their armour behind. The battle raged for hours and went far beyond the bridge. When the shield wall broke, Hardrada was killed by an arrow in the throat and Tostig was slain. Eystein Orre's men ran 16 miles from the ships at Riccall and briefly checked the English, but were overwhelmed.

Harold granted a truce to the survivors, among them Hardrada's son Olaf and Paul Thorfinnsson, Earl of Orkney, who pledged not to attack England again. Only 24 ships of a fleet of over 300 were needed to carry them home. Three days later, on 28 September, William landed at Pevensey, and Harold marched south and was defeated and killed at Hastings on 14 October. The battle has traditionally marked the end of the Viking Age, although major Scandinavian campaigns in Britain followed, such as Sweyn Estrithson's in 1069–1070 and Magnus Barefoot's in 1098.
battle-of-the-atlantic: At its core was the Allied naval blockade of Germany, announced the day after the declaration of war, and Germany's counterblockade. The United Kingdom was an island highly dependent on imports and needed more than a million tons of imported material a week to survive and fight, so the battle became a tonnage war. The Germans targeted merchant shipping, and from 1942 the Axis also sought to stop the build-up of Allied supplies in Britain for an invasion of occupied Europe. The name came into use in 1941, when the First Lord of the Admiralty, A. V. Alexander, asked Parliament on 5 March for more ships and men to fight the Battle of the Atlantic.

The Kriegsmarine lacked the strength in 1939 to challenge the British and French navies directly, and relied on commerce raiding. The German occupation of Norway and France in 1940 gave U-boats bases on the Atlantic coast, and from June to October 1940 over 270 Allied ships were sunk, a period U-boat crews called the Happy Time. The British answered with permanent escort groups, and the Royal Canadian Navy grew from a handful of destroyers into a large escort force. United States ships and aircraft began to aid convoys on 13 September 1941.

In February 1942 the U-boats changed to a new four-rotor Enigma key that the Allied codebreakers could not read for ten months, and the Germans read about 80 per cent of the Admiralty messages sent in Naval Cipher 3 from March 1942 to June 1943. Against this the Allies developed shipborne direction-finding radio, the Leigh Light for night attacks by aircraft and long-range B-24 Liberator aircraft that closed the mid-Atlantic gap. In March 1943, 120 ships were sunk and 12 U-boats destroyed; by mid-1943 the U-boats had been defeated, although losses continued until the end of the war.

The German tonnage war failed, and the supplies and troops needed for the D-Day landings were built up in Britain. Between 1939 and 1945, 72,200 Allied naval and merchant seamen died. The Germans lost about 30,000 U-boat sailors, three quarters of a force of 40,000. United States yards built 2,710 Liberty ships of 38.5 million tons, far more than the 14 million tons the U-boats sank in the whole war.

Historians disagree about which measures mattered most. Max Hastings holds that in 1941 alone Ultra saved between 1.5 and two million tons of shipping, while a former U-boat commander writing for the Admiralty after the war attributed the defeat first to Allied radar developments.
battle-of-the-bulge: After the breakout from Normandy at the end of July 1944, the Allies advanced toward Germany faster than expected, leaving troops tired and supply lines stretched thin. They captured Antwerp intact in September, but it was not operational until 28 November. Adolf Hitler believed that a blow in the west could split the Allies and force the Americans and British to a separate peace, giving Germany time to produce new weapons and concentrate in the east. After the war this was generally judged unrealistic given Allied air superiority.

The offensive aimed to stop Allied use of Antwerp and to split their lines. The Germans called it Unternehmen Wacht am Rhein, a name implying a defensive posture. The name Battle of the Bulge came from the press, from the way the Allied line bulged inward on wartime news maps.

At 5:30 on 16 December 1944 the Germans opened with a 90-minute barrage along a front of 130 kilometres. They achieved total surprise, through Allied overconfidence, poor air reconnaissance in bad weather and faulty intelligence. The region was a rest area held thinly by tired troops and inexperienced replacements. In the north the 2nd and 99th Infantry Divisions held Elsenborn Ridge and forced the German spearhead onto less favourable routes. Waffen-SS troops under Joachim Peiper shot American prisoners near Malmedy.

In the centre the Germans encircled two regiments of the 106th Division at the Schnee Eifel, the most serious American reverse of the campaign. Bastogne was surrounded, and the farthest German advance, to Foy-Notre-Dame, was stopped by the 2nd Armored Division on 24 December. The weather improved from 23 December, letting Allied aircraft strike, and on 26 December the lead element of George S. Patton's Third Army reached Bastogne from the south.

The offensive was effectively broken by 27 December, but fighting went on for another month as Patton attacked north and Bernard Montgomery south to reduce the bulge. On 1 January 1945 the Luftwaffe attacked Allied airfields in Operation Bodenplatte, destroying about 465 aircraft but losing 277, and was left ineffective for the rest of the war. It was the largest and bloodiest single battle fought by the United States in the war. German casualties are put at 81,000 to 103,900 by Allied estimates. The battle destroyed much of Germany's armoured strength and set back the Allied advance into Germany by several weeks.
battle-of-the-catalaunian-plains: By 450 the Romans had restored their authority in much of Gaul, though control of the provinces beyond Italy was diminishing. Germanic peoples occupying Roman territory were bound by treaty as foederati under their own leaders: the Visigoths on the Garonne were restive, the Burgundians awaited an opening for revolt, and the Alans on the Loire were more loyal. When Attila invaded, the general Flavius Aetius moved his army rapidly from Italy to Gaul and tried to persuade the Visigothic king Theodoric I to join him. Theodoric hesitated, and Aetius turned to the former Praetorian Prefect of Gaul, Avitus, who according to tradition persuaded the Visigoths and other wavering peoples.

The coalition assembled at Arles and Toulouse and marched to Orléans, reaching it on 14 June. Jordanes lists among Aetius's allies Franks, Burgundians, Alans and other Celtic or German tribes; Peter Heather suggests the Visigoths may have fielded about 25,000 men.

Attila was leaving Gaul with most of his objectives achieved when Aetius and his allies pursued him from Orléans. The armies met on the Catalaunian Plains on or about 20 June. The exact site is uncertain; scholars place it near Châlons-en-Champagne or Troyes, and the ridge at Montgueux, west of Troyes, is the most thoroughly researched proposal.

The account of Jordanes, who wrote long afterwards and is described as notoriously unreliable on Gothic history, tells of a struggle for the ridge, with the Alans in the centre. Theodoric was killed on the right, and his son Thorismund attacked the Hunnic centre and nearly killed Attila. Darkness fell in confusion, and neither side knew the outcome until morning. Hydatius says almost 300,000 men are said to have fallen. Attila withdrew.

From Cassiodorus in the early sixth century the battle was increasingly seen as a Roman allied victory. Edward Gibbon called it the last victory achieved in the name of the Western Roman Empire, and Edward Shepherd Creasy called it a triumph of Christian Europe. Most modern authors have moved away from this view. J. B. Bury held that its significance had been enormously exaggerated, since the decisive moment was the defence of Orléans and the battle was fought as Attila retreated, though it damaged his prestige and weakened his forces.

In 452 Attila invaded Italy and razed Aquileia after a three-month siege; Pope Leo I took part in an embassy that brought a treaty, and Attila retreated, most likely because of famine and disease in his army. Attila died in 453, and after the Battle of Nedao in 454 the coalition of the Huns and their Germanic vassals gradually disintegrated.
battle-of-the-somme: The Chantilly Conference of December 1915 agreed on simultaneous offensives in 1916 by the Russian, Italian, British and French armies. The Somme offensive was the Franco-British share, with the French army to take the main part, supported on the northern flank by the British Fourth Army. When the Germans began the Battle of Verdun on 21 February 1916, French commanders diverted many of the divisions intended for the Somme, and the British attack became the principal effort. The British force was a mixture of wartime volunteers from the Territorial Force and Kitchener's Army with the remains of the pre-war army.

A five-day artillery bombardment preceded the attack, which began on 1 July 1916. The French Sixth Army and the right wing of the British Fourth Army inflicted a considerable defeat on the German Second Army, but from the Albert–Bapaume road north to Gommecourt, where the Germans had made their main defensive effort, the British attack was a disaster. British casualties on the first day were 57,470, including 19,240 killed, the worst in the history of the British Army.

Douglas Haig abandoned the attack north of the road to reinforce the success in the south, and the offensive became the capture of fortified villages and woods that offered observation for artillery. The Battle of Flers–Courcelette on 15 to 22 September saw the first use of tanks on the Somme and the debut of the Canadian Corps and the New Zealand Division. The battle is dated to 18 November.

More than three million men fought in the battle, and more than one million were wounded or killed. The Anglo-French operational objectives were not achieved, since they failed to capture Péronne and Bapaume. In March 1917 the Germans made a strategic retreat of about 25 miles to the Hindenburg Line in Operation Alberich.

In the United Kingdom and Newfoundland the Somme became the central memory of the First World War, commemorated on 1 July each year at the Thiepval Memorial to the Missing of the Somme. Some historians see it as the beginning of modern all-arms warfare, in which Kitchener's Army learned to fight a mass-industrial war. Debate continues over the necessity, significance and effect of the battle.
battle-of-the-teutoburg-forest: Julius Caesar conquered most of western Europe in the Gallic Wars and twice crossed the Rhine, but his engagements with Germanic tribes were inconclusive. Rome then neglected the continent for two decades, and the Gauls rebelled when troops left in 31 BCE. Publius Quinctilius Varus, appointed by Augustus to command in Germania in 7 CE, had been consul and governor of Africa and Syria. The historian Michael McNally judges that he was sent for his political skill in handling the Germanic factions rather than for military ability.

Arminius of the Cherusci had been taken to Rome as a hostage as a boy, received an aristocratic education, joined the Roman cavalry and commanded auxiliaries. He then returned home, still nominally loyal to Rome. His Roman training let him anticipate Roman tactics and deceive Varus.

Varus planned a simple campaign for 9 CE: the army would cross the Rhine and set up a summer camp in nominally pacified Cherusci territory. Sources say he took little military action that summer and held court instead, though the only contemporary account comes from Velleius Paterculus, who had reason to dislike him. In late summer Arminius invented reports of a local rebellion. Others advised Varus that there was too little time to suppress it, but Arminius proposed a shorter route through the territory of the Angrivarii, and Varus took it.

The army set out on 8 September, strung out for 15 to 20 kilometres on forest tracks, and Arminius meant to lead it toward Kalkriese, where the Angrivarii lay in ambush. In the late morning his Bructerii allies attacked along the line in a brief skirmish aimed at tiring the Romans. A torrential downpour began, and Varus ordered a camp. The fighting went on between 8 and 11 September.

Suetonius records that Augustus struck his head against the palace walls, shouting for Varus to give him back his legions. The numbers XVII, XVIII and XIX were never used for Roman legions again. Tiberius took effective control, and Germanicus raided Germania in 14 CE. Arminius was poisoned by fellow Germans in 21 CE. Since the 15th century the battle has been seen as the event that ended Roman expansion at the Rhine, and in the 19th century it became part of German nationalist mythology. Recent scholars point to other reasons for the frontier, such as supply from the Mediterranean by river and the greater wealth of the Rhine lands.
battle-of-the-yarmuk: Emperor Heraclius had defeated the Sasanian Empire in 627 and restored the True Cross to Jerusalem in 629. The Muslims had seized Emesa, a march from Aleppo and from Antioch, where Heraclius resided. Alarmed, he prepared a counteroffensive, and in 635 Yazdegerd III of Persia sought an alliance, planning a simultaneous attack in Iraq. When Heraclius launched his offensive in May 636, Yazdegerd could not coordinate with it. The Muslims learned of the preparations from Byzantine prisoners, and on Khalid ibn al-Walid's advice Abu Ubayda pulled the army back from Palestine and Syria and concentrated it on the plain near Jabiyah and the Yarmuk River.

Estimates of the armies are uncertain. Early accounts give the Muslims 36,000 to 40,000 men and the Byzantines 60,000 to 70,000, while some modern estimates put the Byzantine army at 40,000 at most or even 15,000 to 20,000, and Warren Treadgold suggests 80,000 to 100,000 or more. The only early Byzantine source is Theophanes, who wrote a century later. Heraclius had told his commander Vahan to avoid battle until diplomacy was exhausted, and negotiations delayed the fighting for a month.

The battle began on 15 August 636 and lasted six days. On the first days the Byzantines tried limited attacks and then thrusts against the Muslim right wing and centre, which fell back, but Khalid used his mobile guard of cavalry to counterattack and the Byzantines made no breakthrough. On 20 August, with some 8,000 cavalry massed, Khalid rode round the Byzantine left wing and drove the Byzantine cavalry from the field. The infantry was left exposed and was forced towards the ravine to the west.

Khalid pursued the survivors towards Damascus. Vahan, who had escaped the fighting, was probably killed there, and Khalid entered Damascus, where he was welcomed. When news reached Heraclius at Antioch, he accepted that the defeat was God's decision and a result of the sins of the people, himself included. Lacking men and money to defend Syria, he sailed for Constantinople by night and, according to tradition, bade farewell to Syria.

The battle effectively ended Byzantine rule in Syria and is regarded as one of the most decisive in military history. It marked the culmination of the first great wave of early Muslim conquests after the death of Muhammad, which saw the Rashidun Caliphate advance into both the Sasanian and the Byzantine empires. It was also the most important victory of Khalid ibn al-Walid.
battle-of-thermopylae: Athens and Eretria had aided the Ionian Revolt against Darius I in 499–494 BCE, and Darius vowed to punish them. His first invasion of Greece ended in 490 BCE with the Greek victory at the Battle of Marathon. A decade later his son Xerxes had assembled a very large land and naval force to conquer Greece. The Athenian general Themistocles proposed that the allied Greeks block the Persian army at the pass of Thermopylae while the fleet held the Straits of Artemisium. The Spartans sent an advance force under King Leonidas I, with the 300 men of the royal bodyguard, to block the pass.

The Greek force numbered approximately 7,000. Ancient authors gave the Persian army in the millions; modern scholars estimate between 120,000 and 300,000. Xerxes attacked on the fifth day after the Persians reached the pass, first with 5,000 archers, whose arrows the Greeks' shields and bronze helmets deflected, then with waves of about 10,000 men. The Greeks fought at the narrowest part of the pass in a phalanx of overlapping shields, and the Persians could make no headway on the first day or the second.

On the second day Ephialtes, a local man motivated by the desire for a reward, told Xerxes of a mountain path around the pass. His name came to mean nightmare in Greek and to stand for the archetypal traitor. On the third day a Persian column bypassed the Phocians guarding the path. Leonidas, aware that he was being outflanked, dismissed most of the Greek army and stayed to guard the retreat with 300 Spartans and 700 Thespians; up to 900 helots and 400 Thebans are also reported to have remained. Most of the Thebans reportedly surrendered, and the others fought to the death.

The Persians now held the pass, and the Greek fleet at Artemisium withdrew to Salamis. The Persians overran Boeotia and captured the evacuated city of Athens, but the Greek fleet defeated them at the Battle of Salamis in late 480 BCE. Xerxes withdrew to Asia with much of his army, leaving Mardonius, who was decisively defeated at the Battle of Plataea the following year. Writers ancient and modern have used Thermopylae as an example of an army defending its native soil.
battle-of-tours: The Umayyad troops under Al-Samh ibn Malik al-Khawlani, governor-general of al-Andalus, overran Septimania by 719 and made Narbonne their capital from 720. Duke Odo the Great broke the siege of Toulouse, taking them by surprise, and Al-Samh ibn Malik was mortally wounded, but the Umayyads raided into Burgundy in 725. When Odo was later defeated, he appealed to the Franks for help, which Charles Martel granted only after Odo agreed to submit to Frankish authority.

In 732 the Umayyad advance force under Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi was heading north towards the Loire, having outpaced its supply wagons and part of its army. It was caught off guard to find a large Frankish force sitting directly in its path to Tours. Charles chose not to attack but to take up a defensive formation, and according to Arab sources the Franks drew up in a large square with hills and trees in front of them to break up cavalry charges. For a week the armies skirmished.

The battle was fought on 10 October 732 at a site between Poitiers and Tours that the sources do not fix exactly. Abd al-Rahman trusted in his cavalry and had it charge repeatedly through the day. According to Arab sources the cavalry broke into the Frankish square several times, but the Franks did not break. Al-Ghafiqi was killed in combat, and the Umayyad army withdrew.

The Umayyad army retreated south over the Pyrenees, and Charles continued to expand southwards. The Umayyads remained in control of parts of Septimania for another 27 years; Charles failed to take Narbonne in 737, and his son Pepin the Short forced its surrender in 759. Ninth-century chroniclers gave Charles the nickname Martel, the hammer.

Historians disagree about the battle's importance. Edward Gibbon and others held that it halted the spread of Islam in Western Europe. Alessandro Barbero writes that historians now tend to play down its significance, since the Muslim force aimed to pillage the monastery of St-Martin of Tours rather than conquer the Frankish kingdom. Arab historians who mention it at all present it as a minor skirmish. Most historians agree the battle helped lay the foundations of the Carolingian Empire.
battle-of-trafalgar: In 1805 Napoleon Bonaparte's First French Empire dominated the European continent by land, while the Royal Navy held the seas through blockades.
