Napoleon renewed his determination to invade Britain, and to bring his invasion flotilla across the English Channel he needed to wrest control of it from the Royal Navy. Vice-Admiral Villeneuve's fleet evaded Horatio Nelson's blockade of Toulon, joined the Spanish fleet at Cádiz and sailed for the Caribbean. Nelson pursued it across the Atlantic and missed it by a few days. Villeneuve returned to Europe and ended at Cádiz, where Napoleon ordered him in September to sail to Naples.

Villeneuve changed his mind several times, and on 18 October he ordered the combined fleet to sail, though the winds were very light. On 21 October, off Cape Trafalgar, it met Nelson's fleet of 27 ships of the line, against Villeneuve's 33. Nelson sailed at the flank of the Franco-Spanish line in two columns, hoping to break it up and force a melee in which his well-trained crews could fight ship to ship, instead of the usual parallel lines of battle.

At 11:45 Nelson signalled to the fleet, England expects that every man will do his duty. The light winds meant the leading British ships were under heavy fire for almost an hour before their own guns could bear. Nelson's flagship HMS Victory led one column and was almost knocked out of action; Nelson was shot by a French marksman and died shortly before the battle ended. The columns split the Franco-Spanish fleet into three groups and isolated the rear, which was overwhelmed. The British lost no ships, and Villeneuve was captured.

A storm followed the battle and wrecked or sank several of the captured ships. On 4 November 1805 a British squadron under Sir Richard Strachan captured four French ships that had escaped the battle. The victory confirmed Britain's naval supremacy and ended any real effort by Napoleon to invade Britain; Britain's command of the sea was not tested for over a century. Nelson's death in victory secured his place as a British national hero.
battle-of-tsushima: The Russo-Japanese War began on 8 February 1904, when Japanese destroyers made a surprise attack on the Russian Far East Fleet at Port Arthur. Japan needed to neutralise Russian naval power in order to secure its supply lines to the mainland and fight a ground war in Manchuria. After the Russian First Pacific Squadron fell inactive and Port Arthur came under siege, the Tsar agreed to form a Second Pacific Squadron from the Baltic Fleet, including 11 of its 13 battleships. The voyage lasted over seven months and covered 18,000 nautical miles. In the Dogger Bank incident the squadron mistook British fishing trawlers for Japanese torpedo boats, killing several fishermen.

Admiral Zinovy Rozhestvensky revealed his choice of the Tsushima Strait, the shortest route, only on 25 May 1905. The fleet approached in radio silence, but a Japanese ship located it early on 27 May and reported by wireless, and Admiral Tōgō Heihachirō sailed with the Combined Fleet. In the afternoon Tōgō turned his line in sequence across the Russian course. The Russian gunnery proved surprisingly good, but Rozhestvensky was wounded and knocked unconscious, and four Russian battleships were sunk by sunset.

At night 21 destroyers and 45 torpedo boats attacked for three hours without a break, and the Russians dispersed into small groups. On the morning of 28 May the Japanese surrounded the squadron of Admiral Nebogatov, who ordered the four remaining battleships to surrender. Tōgō's greater battle experience, extensive Japanese gunnery practice, high-explosive shells, wireless telegraphy and British help with guns, ships and intelligence are all credited with the result.

All 11 Russian battleships were lost, seven sunk and four captured. Only a cruiser and two destroyers reached Vladivostok. Russian losses were 216 officers and 4,614 men killed, with about 6,000 taken prisoner. Japan lost three torpedo boats and 117 men killed, and none of its heavy ships.

The loss forced Russia to seek peace, and the Treaty of Portsmouth was signed in September 1905. In Japan Tōgō was revered as a national hero, and his flagship Mikasa is preserved as a museum ship at Yokosuka. It was the only decisive engagement ever fought between modern steel battleship fleets and the first in which wireless telegraphy played a critical role. It showed that faster battleships with long-range big guns were superior to mixed batteries, which led to the dreadnought arms race. Russia's prestige was badly damaged and the defeat was a blow to the Romanov dynasty.
battle-of-uhud: After the Muslims migrated to Medina, hostilities with the Quraysh of Mecca grew, largely because of Muslim raids on Meccan caravans. In 624 the Muslims defeated a more numerous Meccan force at Badr, where several Quraysh leaders were killed, including Amr ibn Hisham. Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, chosen as their leader, vowed revenge, and wealthy Meccans who had lost relatives gave money for another expedition. He mobilised more than 3,000 men against Medina.

Muhammad had meant to stay in Medina and use its fortifications, but many Muslims who had missed Badr wanted open battle, and he gave way. Shortly before the battle Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, chief of the Khazraj, withdrew with 300 men. The Muslim force of around 700 took position on the slopes of Mount Uhud, which protected its rear. Muhammad posted 50 archers on a nearby hill to guard the flank against the Meccan cavalry and ordered them not to leave their places.

The battle took place on 23 March 625. It opened with duels in which the Meccan standard-bearer Talha ibn Abi Talha was killed by Ali ibn Abi Talib, and others of his family who took up the banner fell one after another. In the general engagement the Muslims swept through the Meccan ranks. Believing the battle won, most of the archers left the hill to collect spoils. Khalid ibn al-Walid, commanding the Meccan cavalry, attacked the few who stayed and then struck the Muslim flank and rear.

Many Muslims were killed, among them Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, Muhammad's uncle. Rumour spread that Muhammad had died, but he had been wounded in the face. Umar ibn al-Khattab rallied the troops, and a counter-charge drove Khalid's men from the slopes. The Meccan cavalry could not climb the slope, and Abu Sufyan returned to Mecca without attacking the wounded Muslims again.

Scholars differ on the result. Chase F. Robinson writes that a disheartening Muslim defeat is clear enough, while William Montgomery Watt notes that the Meccans failed to destroy Muhammad and his followers. The Qur'an, in a verse revealed soon after, attributes the setback to disobedience and desire for loot and treats it as a test. Abu Sufyan then sought alliances with nomadic tribes, and the Quraysh returned in 627 with a larger confederate force at the Battle of the Trench. Khalid ibn al-Walid's leadership at Uhud was an early sign of the career that made him one of the best-known Arab generals of the later conquests.
battle-of-verdun: By late 1914 the war of movement on the Western Front had ended, and offensives gained little ground at heavy cost. According to his memoirs, the German Chief of the General Staff, Erich von Falkenhayn, believed that the French army could still be defeated if it suffered enough casualties. He offered five corps for an offensive at Verdun, but only on the east bank of the Meuse. Verdun, a town that had played an important part in the defence of France for centuries, was ringed by a double line of 28 forts, but in 1915 guns and ammunition had been removed from many of them.

Bad weather delayed the German attack from 12 to 21 February 1916. It began with a ten-hour bombardment by 808 guns, which fired about 1,000,000 shells, and German stormtroopers followed with flamethrowers and grenades. The Germans captured Fort Douaumont four days later. Philippe Pétain ordered that there be no retreat and that German attacks be counter-attacked. The Germans extended the offensive to the west bank of the Meuse to eliminate the French artillery there, but the attacks failed to reach their objectives.

The Germans captured Fort Vaux in June and came within 4 kilometres of the Verdun citadel, but the Brusilov Offensive and the opening of the Battle of the Somme on 1 July forced them to transfer artillery from Verdun. In September and December French counter-offensives recaptured much ground on the east bank, including Fort Douaumont and Fort Vaux. The battle lasted 302 days, the longest of the First World War.

In 2000 Hannes Heer and Klaus Naumann calculated that the French suffered 377,231 casualties and the Germans 337,000, a total of 714,231. Rain and constant bombardment turned the clay soil into mud full of debris and human remains, and forests were obliterated. Accounts of men breaking down with insanity and shell shock were common.

In France, Verdun came to symbolise the determination of the French Army and the destructiveness of the war, and it has become for the French the representative memory of the First World War, as the Somme is for the British. In 1920 a ceremony was held in the citadel of Verdun to choose the body for the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at the Arc de Triomphe.
battle-of-vienna-1683: Capturing Vienna had long been an Ottoman aim, because the city controlled the Danube and the trade routes to Germany. Suleiman's advance had been stopped at Szigetvár in 1566, and Vienna was not threatened again until 1683. Under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha the Ottomans made extensive preparations. In Habsburg Hungary, unrest against Leopold I's Counter-Reformation had grown into rebellion, and in 1681 the Ottomans reinforced the forces of Imre Thököly. A peace had held between the two empires for twenty years.

The Ottomans laid siege to Vienna on 14 July 1683. Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg, commanding the garrison, refused to surrender, having heard of the massacre at Perchtoldsdorf, where townspeople who had surrendered were killed. The Viennese demolished houses near the walls, and the Ottomans dug trenches and mines towards the city.

Delays in the siege gave a relief force time to arrive. Poles and Imperial troops assembled in only six days under King John III Sobieski, with money from bankers, noblemen and the Pope. Kara Mustafa left his rear to the Khan of Crimea, who refused to attack the relief force as it crossed the Danube. The Wallachian prince Șerban Cantacuzino, sympathetic to the Christian side, also proved unreliable.

On 12 September the Ottomans attacked at 4:00 in the morning to disturb the deployment. Charles of Lorraine's Imperial troops counterattacked and took the villages of Nussdorf and Heiligenstadt, and ten Ottoman mines under the walls were found and disarmed. In the afternoon Polish infantry advanced on the Ottoman right and took Gersthof, and as the Imperial troops closed in, the Polish cavalry charged, in what is noted as the largest cavalry charge in history.

Ottoman losses in the battle itself are put at 8,000 to 15,000 dead, and the relief force lost about 3,500 killed and wounded. The Ottoman raiding of 1683 in the Austrian and Hungarian border zone took 57,220 people as slaves. Kara Mustafa was executed in Belgrade on 25 December. The war continued until 1699, when the Treaty of Karlowitz ceded most of Ottoman Hungary to the Habsburgs. Historians see the battle as the end of Ottoman expansion into Europe, and Pope Innocent XI extended the feast of the Holy Name of Mary to the whole Church in commemoration.
battle-of-waterloo: When Napoleon I returned to power in March 1815, at the start of the Hundred Days, the powers at the Congress of Vienna declared him an outlaw, and the United Kingdom, Russia, Austria and Prussia mobilised armies as the Seventh Coalition. Critically outnumbered, Napoleon judged that his only chance was to attack before the coalition was ready. Wellington's and Blücher's armies were cantoned close to the north-eastern border of France, and he planned to strike them separately. On 16 June he defeated the bulk of the Prussian army at the Battle of Ligny, while a smaller French force fought the Battle of Quatre Bras. The Prussians withdrew in good order, and Wellington fell back in parallel to the ridge of Mont-Saint-Jean near Waterloo.

On Sunday 18 June the French army of around 74,500 men and 254 guns faced a multinational army under Wellington. Napoleon had sent a third of his forces after the Prussians, and they were held at the Battle of Wavre. The French attacked the farm of Hougoumont in the morning, then bombarded the centre with the 80 guns of the grande batterie and sent infantry columns forward. British heavy cavalry charged in support of the hard-pressed infantry. Around 16:00 Marshal Ney, mistaking the movement of wounded to the rear for a retreat, led massed cavalry, about 9,000 horsemen, against Wellington's centre, but they could not break the infantry squares. The French later captured the farm of La Haye Sainte.

At about 13:15 Napoleon had seen Prussian columns approaching his right flank, and from about 16:30 Prussian corps under Bülow, Zieten and Pirch arrived in strength and fought through Plancenoit. At about 19:30 Napoleon committed his last reserve, the Imperial Guard. Wellington's line repulsed it, the Prussians broke through on the French right, and the French army was routed.

Wellington lost around 17,000 killed or wounded and Blücher some 7,000. Napoleon lost between 24,000 and 26,000 killed or wounded, including 6,000 to 7,000 captured, and about 15,000 more deserted in the following days. Wellington called the battle the nearest-run thing you ever saw in your life. Napoleon abdicated four days later, and coalition forces entered Paris on 7 July. The defeat ended the Hundred Days and the First French Empire.

Later generations in Europe saw Waterloo as the turning point that ended the wars convulsing Europe since the French Revolution and ushered in the Concert of Europe, a period of relative peace often called the Pax Britannica. The battlefield lies about 15 kilometres south of Brussels. In 1820 King William I of the Netherlands ordered a monument there, and the Lion's Mound, a hill built from 300,000 cubic metres of earth taken from the ridge, now dominates the site.
battle-of-zama: In 218 BCE, at the start of the Second Punic War, Hannibal invaded Italy and campaigned there for 16 years. In 210 BCE Scipio took command of the Roman war effort in Iberia and cleared the peninsula of Carthaginians in five years. He was elected consul in early 205 BCE at the age of 31, though the minimum age was 42, and had made an ally of the Numidian leader Masinissa. In 204 BCE his army landed near Utica. Scipio attacked the Numidian and Carthaginian camps at night, setting fire to the Numidian reed barracks, and inflicted heavy losses on both. Carthage opened peace talks and recalled Hannibal from Italy. The Roman Senate ratified a draft treaty, but Carthage repudiated it when Hannibal arrived.

Scipio probably had 29,000 or 30,000 men, including 4,000 Numidian cavalry under Masinissa; the Carthaginians had 40,000 or 50,000 and 80 war elephants. The battle opened with a charge by the elephants, which was repulsed. Some fled through the Carthaginian cavalry on the wings and disordered it, and the Roman cavalry routed their opponents and chased them from the field.

The heavy infantry of both armies stood in three lines. The first lines fought hard until the Carthaginians broke, and their second line then drove back the Roman first line until Scipio committed his second. After a pause, in which the Romans formed one long line to match Hannibal's veterans, the two lines charged each other fiercely, and for some time neither gained the advantage. The Roman cavalry then returned and attacked the Carthaginian line from behind, and it was destroyed.

Polybius states that 20,000 Carthaginians were killed and as many taken prisoner, and that the Romans lost 1,500 dead. Hannibal reached Hadrumetum and advised the Carthaginian Senate to make peace on whatever terms it could. The peace treaty dictated by Rome stripped Carthage of its non-African territories and some of its African ones, and it was clear that Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.

Masinissa later raided and seized Carthaginian land, and Rome always backed him. In 149 BCE Carthage sent an army against him, in breach of the treaty, and Rome used this as a pretext for the Third Punic War. In 146 BCE the Romans destroyed the city and sold 50,000 survivors into slavery.
batu-khan: Batu was a son of Jochi and so officially a grandson of Genghis Khan, although Jochi's paternity is highly uncertain. After Jochi died, Genghis Khan divided his lands between Batu and his older brother Orda and installed Batu as khan. Orda's White Horde ruled the lands between the Volga and Lake Balkhash, while Batu's Golden Horde ruled the lands west of the Volga. According to Giovanni da Pian del Carpine, Batu was kind enough to his own people but greatly feared by them, and most cruel in fight.

At a kurultai after the war against the Jin, the Great Khan Ögedei ordered Batu to conquer western nations. In 1235 he was given an army of possibly 130,000, which was actually commanded by the general Subutai. It crossed the Volga and invaded Volga Bulgaria in 1236. In November 1237 Batu demanded the allegiance of Yuri II of Vladimir-Suzdal. When Yuri refused, the Mongols besieged Ryazan, which was destroyed after six days and never restored to its former glory. They took Vladimir after a siege that began on 4 February 1238 and burned it, and on 4 March destroyed the army Yuri had raised on the Sit' River. Kiev was stormed in December 1240, and the Rus' principalities became vassals of the Mongol Empire.

The Mongols then invaded central Europe in three groups. One devastated Poland and defeated Henry II the Pious, Duke of Silesia, and the Grand Master of the Teutonic Order at Legnica. Batu's own army defeated King Béla IV of Hungary and his allies at the Battle of Mohi on 11 April. Plans to invade Austria, Italy and Germany were under way when news came of Ögedei's death in December 1241, and the Mongols withdrew in late spring 1242 as the princes were recalled to Karakorum for the kurultai.

Batu made his camps on the Volga and, as one of the oldest of the descendants of Genghis Khan, became viceroy over the western parts of the empire. He controlled routine affairs among the Rus' princes, among them Yaroslav II of Vladimir, whom he confirmed as suzerain, while Michael of Chernigov was put to death for refusing to bow before the tablets of Genghis Khan. Danylo of Halych submitted to him at Sarai. Batu delayed the election of Güyük, who became Great Khan in 1246, and in 1250 he called a kurultai on his own territory that offered the throne to him; he nominated Möngke instead, who was proclaimed Great Khan in 1251.

Batu died in 1255 and left affairs of state to his son Sartaq. His brother Berke inherited the Golden Horde after a brief regency. The Golden Horde ruled the steppes of what is now Ukraine, Russia and Kazakhstan, and Batu's line held the throne until 1360.
bauchi-state: Bauchi State lies in north-eastern Nigeria and covers 49,119 square kilometres. It borders Jigawa, Yobe, Gombe, Taraba, Plateau, Kaduna and Kano. It spans two vegetation zones, Sudan savanna in the south and semi-desert Sahel savanna in the north, with a mountainous south-west where the Bauchi Plateau continues. Rainfall falls from about 1,300 millimetres a year in the south to about 700 in the far north. The Gongola River crosses the south and east, and the Jama'are River runs through the north. Farming and livestock are the base of the economy, with cotton, groundnuts, millet and yams, and tin and columbite mining.

According to tradition the city of Bauchi was named after a hunter called Baushe, who settled in the region before the arrival of Yakubu, first traditional ruler of the Bauchi emirate. In the early 1800s the Fulani jihad seized much of the area and formed the Bauchi Emirate under the Sokoto Caliphate. About 90 years later a British expedition occupied it and made it Bauchi Province in the Northern Nigeria Protectorate. Nigeria became independent in 1960, and the area passed from the Northern Region to the North-Eastern State in 1967.

Bauchi State was formed on 3 February 1976, when the North-Eastern State was divided and ten other states were created. It then included the area of today's Gombe State, which became a separate state in 1996. The Ajawa language, once spoken there, became extinct by 1940 as speakers shifted to Hausa.

The state takes its name from its capital, the historic city of Bauchi, and has twenty local government areas. It has 55 tribal groups, among them the Bolewa, Fulani, Kanuri, Karai-Karai, Jarawa and Gerawa, and most of its people are Muslim, with Christian and traditionalist minorities. The Durbar Festival is a major annual event, and there are twenty traditional institutions, nineteen emirates and one chiefdom. Yankari National Park in the south is a large wildlife park with a population of hippopotamus, buffalo and roan antelope, and its Wikki Warm Springs attract visitors. Abubakar Tafawa Balewa, the first and only Prime Minister of Nigeria, is among the state's notable people.
baudouin-of-belgium: Baudouin was born on 7 September 1930 at Laeken, north of central Brussels, the elder son of Prince Leopold and Princess Astrid of Sweden. His grandfather King Albert I was killed in a climbing accident in 1934, and Leopold became king. His mother died in a car accident in 1935, and in 1941 his father married Mary Lilian Baels. Germany invaded Belgium in May 1940, and Leopold surrendered on 28 May and stayed under house arrest. After the Normandy landings the family was deported to Germany and then Austria, and was freed in May 1945.

The Royal Question, over whether Leopold had collaborated, kept the family out of Belgium. It rested on his surrender, his refusal to join the government in exile, his visit to Adolf Hitler in November 1940 and his marriage to Lilian. Prince Charles served as regent, and the family lived in Switzerland.

A referendum in March 1950 narrowly favoured Leopold's return, but parliamentary dissent and public protests forced him to delegate his powers to Baudouin on 11 August 1950 and then to abdicate. Baudouin took the oath on 17 July 1951. In 1960 he declared the Belgian Congo independent. At the ceremony he praised Leopold II as a genius, and the prime minister Patrice Lumumba answered with a speech citing the killings, insults and slavery the Congolese had suffered under Belgian rule.

Katanga Province seceded with Belgian support, and Lumumba was executed there on 17 January 1961. A Belgian parliamentary investigation of 2001 concluded that Baudouin knew of the plot against Lumumba and did nothing to oppose it, though it found no conclusive evidence that he ordered its details. Baudouin married Doña Fabiola de Mora y Aragón in 1960; they had no children. In 1990 he refused to sign a law liberalising abortion, and the government declared him temporarily unable to reign for a day so that it could sign the bill.

Baudouin died of a heart attack on 31 July 1993 at Motril in Spain, after a reign of 42 years. About 500,000 people came to see his body in Brussels. He was buried at the Church of Our Lady of Laeken, and his brother succeeded him as Albert II. The King Baudouin Foundation, formed in 1976 on his silver jubilee, works to improve living conditions in Belgium.
bauhaus: Walter Gropius founded the school on 1 April 1919 by merging the Grand Ducal Saxon Academy of Fine Art with the Grand Ducal Saxon School of Arts and Crafts. Gropius was strongly influenced by William Morris and the British Arts and Crafts Movement, and his pamphlet for an exhibition in April 1919 declared the aim of creating a new guild of craftsmen without the class distinctions that raise an arrogant barrier between craftsman and artist. The name joins the German words for building and for the Bauhütte, a premodern guild of stonemasons.

The first faculty was Johannes Itten, Lyonel Feininger, Gerhard Marcks and Gropius. Oskar Schlemmer joined in 1920 to head the theatre workshop, and Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky came in 1922. The first major joint project was the Sommerfeld House, built in 1920–1921.

The school moved to Dessau in 1925, and its new buildings, designed by Gropius, opened in late 1926. It offered no classes in architecture until 1927. Gropius resigned in February 1928 and Hannes Meyer became director; under him the school won commissions for five apartment buildings in Dessau and for the ADGB Trade Union School at Bernau bei Berlin, and it turned its first profit in 1929.

In 1930 the mayor of Dessau, Fritz Hesse, dismissed Meyer after a scandal over alleged use of school funds for communist causes, and appointed Ludwig Mies van der Rohe. Nazi writers had labelled the Bauhaus un-German, and the Dessau school was closed in 1932 after the Nazi party took over the local government of the Free State of Anhalt. Mies rented a derelict factory in Berlin and ran the school there for ten months. In 1933 the Gestapo closed it; Mies protested and obtained permission to reopen, but he and the faculty chose to shut it voluntarily.

The Bauhaus became one of the most influential currents in modern design and architecture. Many of its artists fled or were exiled by the Nazi regime, and it had a major effect in Western Europe, Canada, the United States and Israel in the following decades. German Jewish architects who emigrated to the British Mandate of Palestine built more than 4,000 buildings in the Bauhaus or International Style in Tel Aviv, whose White City UNESCO proclaimed a World Heritage site in 2003. In 1996 four major Bauhaus sites in Germany were inscribed on the World Heritage List, and two more in 2017.
bautzen: Bautzen, known in Upper Sorbian as Budyšin, lies on the River Spree about 50 km east of Dresden, in the bilingual Sorbian settlement area of Lusatia. The old town stands on a plateau above the river, topped by Ortenburg Castle and bordered by the city walls. Until 1868 its German name was Budissin, when the Saxon government changed it to Bautzen.

An eastern Germanic settlement existed here in the 3rd century, and Sorbs arrived in the 6th. The first written mention, as Budusin, dates from 1002. In 1018 the Peace of Bautzen between the German king Henry II and the Polish ruler Bolesław I the Brave left the town under Polish rule. In 1032 it passed to the Margraviate of Meissen, in 1075 to the Duchy of Bohemia, which became a kingdom in 1198.

In 1346 the town joined the Lusatian League with Görlitz, Kamenz, Lauban, Löbau and Zittau. The Hussites besieged it unsuccessfully in 1429 and 1431. In 1547 Ferdinand I, as King of Bohemia, imposed the Upper Lusatian Pönfall on it after disobedience in the Schmalkaldic War, and the town lost its self-governing privileges. The Swedes destroyed it in 1634 during the Thirty Years' War, and in 1635 it fell to the Electorate of Saxony.

The Battle of Bautzen was fought here in 1813 during the Napoleonic Wars. Sorbian life centred on the town in the 19th century: the student society Societas Slavica Budissenensis was founded in 1839, the Sorbian national anthem was first performed in public in 1845, and the Sorbian House opened in 1904. Under the Nazi regime political prisoners were held in the prisons Bautzen I and II, and a subcamp of the Groß-Rosen concentration camp operated here. Bautzen II held political prisoners in East Germany and has been a memorial since 1993.

Bautzen had about 38,000 inhabitants in 2021. It is the political and cultural centre of the Sorbs, with the Domowina, Sorbian Radio and the Sorbian Institute, and about 10 percent of its people speak Upper Sorbian. The medieval centre keeps its walls, the leaning Reichenturm, the Old Waterworks of 1558 and St Peter's Cathedral, the only historic interdenominational church building in eastern Germany.
bavaria: Bavaria is a landlocked state of Germany. It borders Baden-Württemberg, Hesse, Thuringia and Saxony within Germany, and Switzerland across Lake Constance, Austria to the south and the Czech Republic to the east. Two major rivers, the Danube and the Main, flow through it, and the Bavarian Forest and the Bohemian Forest form most of the frontier with the Czech Republic. Its modern borders take in Altbayern and parts of the historical regions of Franconia and Swabia, and it is divided into seven administrative regions: Upper Palatinate, Upper Bavaria and Lower Bavaria in Altbayern, Upper, Middle and Lower Franconia, and Swabia.

Humans have lived in Bavaria since the Paleolithic era, and Celtic tribes of the Bronze Age, such as the Boii, were the first documented inhabitants of the Bavarian Alps. Archaeologists know of a large Celtic Iron Age settlement at Feldmoching-Hasenbergl, north of Munich, where up to 500 people lived from 450 BCE. At Manching in Upper Bavaria an unfortified, semi-urban society prospered from the 3rd century BCE until the early 1st century CE, with food ovens, pottery kilns and metallurgical furnaces. By 200 BCE it was trading, and finds of coins and a golden tree suggest contact with distant Italo-Greek communities.

In the first century CE the Roman Empire incorporated the territory into the provinces of Raetia and Noricum. After the empire collapsed, the Duchy of Bavaria was created in Francia in 555 CE. It later became part of East Francia and controlled land in modern Austria, Slovenia and Italy. Within the Holy Roman Empire Bavaria gained elector status in 1623, during the Thirty Years' War, and it became the Kingdom of Bavaria in 1806. After the unification of Germany it stayed a kingdom within the German Empire until the end of the First World War. The modern state was established in 1945 and became part of West Germany in 1949.

The capital and largest city is Munich; other major cities are Nuremberg, Augsburg, Regensburg and Ingolstadt. With an area of 70,550 square kilometres it is the largest German state, and it has about 13 million inhabitants. The official name is the Free State of Bavaria. Its culture is strongly shaped by its Catholic heritage, and the Bavarian language, a group of German dialects spoken in Bavaria and Austria by around 12 million people, is the largest German dialect. It has two official flags of equal status, one striped white and blue and one with white and blue lozenges.
bavay: Bavay lies in the Nord department in the Hauts-de-France region of northern France, some 20 km east-south-east of Valenciennes and 10 km west of Maubeuge. It has about 3,200 inhabitants. Several roads radiate from the town, and the commune is otherwise entirely farmland. Its inhabitants are called Bavaisiens in French.

Bavay grew out of the reorganisation of Gaul by Augustus, probably between 16 and 13 BCE. It became the capital of the Nervii, whose territory lay between the Scheldt, the Sambre and the Meuse, under the name Bagacum or Bavacum, in the province of Gallia Belgica. It was a junction of seven roads, linking Germania with Boulogne-sur-Mer, the port from which Britain could be reached, and with the capitals of neighbouring peoples such as Amiens, Tongeren, Cassel, Trier and Reims. The future emperor Tiberius passed through with his armies about 4 CE.

The city grew from the Claudian period and especially under the Flavians in the late 1st century, when a forum, baths supplied by an aqueduct from a spring near Floursies, 20 km away, and other official-looking buildings were built. The Tabula Peutingeriana names the town as Baca Conervio. Medieval chroniclers told another story of its origin. In a 15th-century manuscript Jean Wauquelin, following Jacques de Guise, wrote that Bavo, a cousin of Priam, fled Troy and founded a city called Belges, the present Bavay. Most historians since the 19th century have treated this as a fable.

Excavations in the Roman forum found ceramics of the 9th and 10th centuries, but the town's history in this period is unclear. In the 12th century the area belonged to the County of Hainaut and Bavay was the seat of a provost, and in the 13th and 14th centuries it was fortified. Hainaut passed to the Burgundian Netherlands in 1433, to the Holy Roman Empire of Charles V in 1519 and, in 1555, to Philip II of Spain. The Treaty of Nijmegen in 1678 confirmed the union of Bavay with France after the conquests of Louis XIV. Austrian troops took the town on 21 July 1792.

The Gallo-Roman archaeological site in the town includes a forum of the 1st century, whose importance was revealed when the bombing of 1940 destroyed the buildings above it. Several hypocausts have been found beneath the church and some houses, among them signs of important baths. A column replaced the Roman milestone that marked the meeting of the roads, destroyed in the 17th century. The poet Jean Lemaire de Belges was born at Bavay in 1473.
bay-of-biscay: The bay, also called the Gulf of Biscay or the Gulf of Gascony, lies south of the Celtic Sea. The International Hydrographic Organization defines its limits as a line joining Cap Ortegal to Penmarch Point. Its average depth is 1,744 metres and its maximum depth 4,735 metres. Parts of the continental shelf extend far into the bay, producing shallow waters in many areas and the rough seas for which it is known. Heavy storms occur especially in winter, and it was long a regular occurrence for merchant vessels to founder in Biscay storms. The Gulf Stream enters the bay and keeps temperatures moderate throughout the year, and a fog triangle fills its southwestern half in late spring and early summer.

The Romans named the bay in the 1st century BCE as Sinus Cantabrorum, the Bay of the Cantabri, and also as Mare Gallaecum, the Sea of the Galicians. The southern part is still called the Cantabrian Sea in Spain. On some medieval maps it is marked as the Basque Sea. Its name differs by shore: in Spain it is the Gulf of Biscay, and in France the Gulf of Gascony.

The bay has been the site of many naval engagements. In 1592 the Spanish defeated an English fleet in the Battle of the Bay of Biscay. The Biscay campaign of June 1795 consisted of manoeuvres and two battles between the British Channel Fleet and the French Atlantic Fleet off the southern coast of Brittany, during the second year of the French Revolutionary Wars. On 12 April 1970 the Soviet submarine K-8 sank in the bay after a fire, with the death of forty sailors. North Atlantic right whales once came to the bay to feed and probably to calve, but whaling by Basque people almost wiped them out sometime before the 1850s.

The main cities on or near its shores include Lorient, Vannes, Saint-Nazaire, Nantes, Bordeaux, Bayonne, San Sebastián, Bilbao, Santander, Gijón and Avilés. Many rivers empty into it, among them the Loire, the Charente, the Garonne, the Dordogne, the Adour, the Nervión and the Nalón. Car ferries cross it between ports on its Spanish shore and other ports.
bay-of-kotor: The bay is about 28 kilometres long, with a shoreline of 107.3 kilometres, and is closed in by two massifs of the Dinaric Alps, the Orjen mountains to the west and the Lovćen mountains to the east. It is a ria, the drowned valley of the vanished Bokelj River, and consists of several broad bays joined by narrower channels: the Bay of Herceg Novi at the main entrance, then the Bay of Tivat, and beyond the Verige Strait, which is only 340 metres wide at its narrowest, the inner bays of Risan and Kotor. The steep mountains make it one of the wettest places in Europe, and cold Bora winds blow down from them in winter.

The bay has been inhabited since antiquity, and South Slavs settled the Balkans from the 6th century. In 1171 Stefan Nemanja sided with Venice against the Byzantine Empire and launched an offensive towards Kotor, after which the bay came under the Nemanjić dynasty. In 1219 Saint Sava founded the seat of the Eparchy of Zeta on Prevlaka, and Kotor became a major centre of the salt trade. After 1371 local lords and the King of Bosnia contended for the region, and Kotor was a city-state from 1391 until it accepted Venetian rule in 1420.

Venetian rule lasted until 1797. The Ottomans took Novi in 1482 and held the northern parts of the bay until the end of the 17th century, when the whole area became Venetian. In 1654 the people of Perast defended their town against an Ottoman attack. The Treaty of Campo Formio gave the bay to Habsburg rule in 1797; French rule followed after the Treaties of Tilsit in 1807, as part of the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy and the Illyrian Provinces. A union with Montenegro was declared in 1813, but in 1815 the bay was annexed by the Austrian Empire and placed in the province of Dalmatia. The Serbian army entered it on 7 November 1918, and since 1945 it has been part of Montenegro.

The well-preserved medieval towns of Kotor, Risan, Tivat, Perast, Prčanj and Herceg Novi, with their surroundings, were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979. The bay has a long maritime tradition: Kotor had a naval academy, the Scuola Nautica, and the fleet of the Boka peaked at 300 ships in the 18th century. Its people, the Bokelj, are a South Slavic community, most of them Orthodox Christians and some Catholics, and its many Orthodox and Catholic churches and monasteries draw pilgrims and visitors.
bayda-libya: Bayda, also written Elbeida, lies in northern Cyrenaica and is the capital of the Jabal al Akhdar district. The Green Mountains take their name from the dense forests and woodlands that cover them; the highest point is about 850 metres. The range is part of the larger Jabal al Akhdar Plateau, which covers some 15,000 square kilometres, and a network of natural springs makes it one of the most fertile areas of the coastal Maghreb.

The city has a mild Mediterranean climate, with average annual precipitation of about 540 millimetres, and is known for recurring snowfalls. Fruit trees, thyme, rosemary and other herbs grow in the district, which is noted for its honey. The ruins of the ancient Greek colony of Cyrene, some 2,000 years old, lie nearby at Shahat.

In classical antiquity the place was known as Balagrae. It was later called Sidi Rafaa, after the tomb there of Ruwaifi bin Thabit al-Ansari, a companion of the prophet Muhammad. When Muhammad ibn Ali as-Senussi arrived in the area in the 19th century and a white-painted zawiya was built on a high hill, visible from afar, the town was renamed az-Zawiyat al-Bayda, the White Monastery, and in time simply al-Bayda. The Senussi zawiyas taught jurisprudence, had the young memorise the Quran and helped settle local and tribal disputes.

Under Fascist Italian rule the town was called Beda Littoria, after the fascio littorio, the main fascist symbol. The modern city, which dropped that name under the Kingdom of Libya, was built as the intended new capital of Libya, and most of the necessary government buildings were constructed there. The plan to move the capital from Tripoli was eventually abandoned.

Bayda is a commercial and industrial city with a population of about 250,000, the fourth largest in Libya after Tripoli, Benghazi and Misrata. It is home to Omar Al-Mukhtar University, the second university established in the country, and to one of the country's most successful football clubs, Alakhdhar.

The Senussi zawiya still stands near the university at the western entrance to the city. Bayda lies on the Libyan Coastal Highway and serves as a base for visits to Cyrene and Apollonia. The seaside resort of Susa is close by.
bayeux: Bayeux stands 7 kilometres from the English Channel and 30 km north-west of Caen, at elevations of 32 to 67 metres, and the River Aure runs through it. It is the capital of the Bessin, the area that was the bailiwick of the province of Normandy until the French Revolution. The Bajocian Age of the Jurassic period takes its name from the Latinised name of its inhabitants, the Bajocassi.

Augustodurum was founded as a Gallo-Roman settlement in the 1st century BCE. Fortified Celtic camps show earlier occupation, but there is no evidence of a major Celtic town before Gaul was organised into Roman civitates. Titus Sabinus, a lieutenant of Julius Caesar, brought the Bessin under Roman rule. Ptolemy names the town Noemagus Biducassium. Baths, a head of Minerva and the blocks of a Roman building found at the cathedral show the adoption of Roman culture. By the end of the 3rd century a wall enclosed the city; it stood until the 18th century. Bayeux formed part of the Roman coastal defence against pirates, and a legion was stationed there.

Viking raids largely destroyed the city in the late 9th century, and it was rebuilt in the early 10th. In the middle of that century it was held by Hagrold, a pagan Viking who defended it against the Franks, and the poet Benoît de Saint-Maure remarked that Danish was commonly spoken there. Odo of Bayeux, half-brother of William the Conqueror, completed the cathedral, dedicated in 1077, but the city lost prominence when William made Caen his capital. After Henry I of England defeated his brother Robert Curthose, Bayeux was burned as an example to the duchy. Under Richard the Lionheart it grew rich enough to buy a municipal charter.

Bayeux was repeatedly pillaged until Henry V of England captured it in 1417. After the Battle of Formigny Charles VII of France retook it and granted its people a general amnesty in 1450. New families replaced those the war had destroyed and built about 60 mansions, with stone replacing wood.

Bayeux is a sub-prefecture of Calvados. It is the home of the Bayeux Tapestry, which shows the events leading to the Norman Conquest of England in 1066. French tradition credits the attendants of Matilda of Flanders with making it, though it was almost certainly designed and stitched in England, as its English spellings show. The Norman-Romanesque and Gothic cathedral of Notre-Dame preserved it for centuries. The town was the first major one liberated in the Battle of Normandy, on 7 June 1944, by British troops of the 50th Infantry Division, and Charles de Gaulle made the first of two major speeches there on 16 June 1944. Its war cemetery, with 4,648 graves, is the largest British Second World War cemetery in France.
bayezid-i: Bayezid was the son of Murad I and his Greek wife Gülçiçek Hatun. His first major role was as governor of Kütahya, which he gained by marrying the daughter of a Germiyanid ruler. An impetuous soldier, he earned the nickname Thunderbolt (Yıldırım) in a battle against the Karamanids. He came to the throne after his father was killed by the Serbian knight Miloš Obilić during or just after the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. Soon afterwards Serbia became a vassal of the Ottomans, and Bayezid had his younger brother strangled to avoid a plot. In 1390 he married Olivera Despina, daughter of Prince Lazar of Serbia, and recognised Lazar's son Stefan Lazarević as the new Serbian leader.

In Anatolia Bayezid first secured fatwas from Islamic scholars to justify wars against Muslim states, since he needed the gazis as warriors. In a single campaign in 1390 he conquered the beyliks of Aydin, Saruhan and Menteshe, and then overwhelmed Hamid, Teke and Germiyan and took Konya from Karaman. He made peace with Karaman in 1391, then took Kastamonu and Sinop before Kadi Burhan al-Din stopped him at the Battle of Kırkdilim. In Europe he captured Skopje in 1391, and from 1389 to 1395 conquered Bulgaria and northern Greece. He crossed the Danube against Wallachia under Mircea the Elder but was stopped at the Battle of Rovine.

He adopted the title Sultan-i Rûm and besieged Constantinople in 1394, and again from 1395 to 1402. A crusade organised after appeals by the Byzantine emperor Manuel II Palaeologus, led by Sigismund of Hungary, was defeated at the Battle of Nicopolis in 1396; Bayezid built the Ulu Cami in Bursa to celebrate. At this time his realm included Thrace except Constantinople, Macedonia, Bulgaria and parts of Serbia in Europe, and in Asia reached the Taurus Mountains. In 1397 he killed the emir of Karaman at Akçay and annexed his territory, and in 1398 he conquered the Djanik emirate and Burhan al-Din's lands, violating an accord with Timur.

In 1400 Timur roused the Turkic beyliks that had been Ottoman vassals to attack Bayezid. Bayezid lifted his siege of Constantinople, and on 20 July 1402 the Ottoman army was defeated at the Battle of Ankara. Bayezid was captured and died in captivity on 8 March 1403.

A European legend held that he was kept in a cage and humiliated, with his wife serving Timur at dinner. Early accounts, among them the traveller Johann Schiltberger and Timur's court historian Sharafaddin Yazdi, mention no cage and report respectful treatment. The cage first appears in later writers such as the Ottoman historian Mehmed Neshri. Four of his sons escaped the battlefield and fought the civil war known as the Ottoman Interregnum, which ended with the coronation of Mehmed I.
bayezid-ii: Bayezid was born at Demotika, the first son of Şehzade Mehmed, the future Mehmed II, and his concubine Gülbahar Hatun. His birth is dated 3 December 1447 or 1448. Around 1454 to 1456 he was appointed governor of Amasya and held the post for 27 years, until he became the eighth Ottoman sultan. In 1473 he fought at the Battle of Otlukbeli against the Aq Qoyunlu.

His first concern was the quarrel with his brother Cem Sultan, who claimed the throne and sought backing from the Mamluks in Egypt. Defeated by Bayezid's armies, Cem sought protection from the Knights of St. John at Rhodes, who handed him to Pope Innocent VIII. The pope thought of using him to drive the Turks out of Europe, but the crusade never came about, and Cem died in Naples. Bayezid worked to keep domestic politics running smoothly, which earned him the epithet the Just. He returned to their former owners most of the waqf properties Mehmed had taken for the state.

In 1484 he led a campaign against the Moldavian Black Sea ports of Kilia and Akkerman, supported by Wallachian troops and Crimean Tatars. Kilia surrendered about 14 July 1484 and Akkerman fell in early August. A first Ottoman-Mamluk war was fought against Qaitbay from 1485 to 1491 over the southern Anatolian frontier. Rebellions of the Qizilbash, often backed by Ismail I of Iran, troubled his reign.

In July 1492 Spain expelled its Jewish and Muslim populations. Bayezid sent the navy under Kemal Reis to carry the refugees to Ottoman lands and ordered governors to receive them, threatening death for any who treated them harshly. Many settled in Salonica.

In his last years Bayezid suffered from gout and left government largely to his viziers, while his sons Ahmed, Selim and Korkut rivalled each other. An earthquake on 10 September 1509, called the Little Apocalypse, killed several thousand people in Istanbul. He abdicated in favour of Selim I and died on 26 May 1512. Historians describe the reign as one of consolidation.
bayonne: Bayonne lies in south-western France near the Spanish border, at the confluence of the Nive and the Adour, in the northern part of the Basque Country and the southern part of Gascony. Its Basque and Gascon name is Baiona. The Nive divides it into Grand Bayonne and Petit Bayonne, and both quarters are still backed by Vauban's walls. The Adour valley narrows there, so the river was easier to cross at this point than anywhere else along its estuary.

The site on the left bank was probably occupied before ancient times. A fortified enclosure is attested in the 1st century, when the Tarbelli held the territory, and a Roman castrum stood there in the 4th and 5th centuries. In 1023 Bayonne was capital of Labourd. It came under English control in 1152 through the marriage of Eleanor of Aquitaine, and Richard the Lion Heart took it in 1177. Maritime trade made it important commercially. Jean de Dunois, a former companion of Joan of Arc, captured it on 20 August 1451 for the French Crown, at the price of a war indemnity of 40,000 gold écus.

The loss of English trade was followed by the silting of the river. In 1578 dredging under Louis de Foix returned the Adour to its former mouth, and trade revived. Sephardic Jewish refugees fleeing the Spanish expulsions settled in Saint-Esprit and brought skill in chocolate making. In the 17th century Vauban fortified the city, and his works served as models of defence for a hundred years. Activity peaked in the 18th century, with trade with Spain, the Netherlands and the Antilles and the cod fishery off Newfoundland. In 1814 Napoleon's troops fought a Spanish-Anglo-Portuguese coalition led by the Duke of Wellington in and around Bayonne, the last time it was besieged.

The railway from Paris reached Bayonne in 1854, and the city turned to the steel industry while its port declined. The discovery of the Lacq gas field in 1951 gave the port new activity. Bayonne forms a conurbation with Anglet and Biarritz and is the seat of the Communauté d'agglomération du Pays Basque. Its heritage includes the cathedral, the walls, the Basque half-timbered houses along the Nive and the Fêtes de Bayonne.
bayreuth: Bayreuth lies in northern Bavaria on the Red Main, in a valley between the Franconian Jura and the Fichtel Mountains. The town is believed to have been founded by the counts of Andechs, probably around the mid-12th century, and was first mentioned in 1194 as Baierrute, in a document of Bishop Otto II of Bamberg. The syllable rute may mean a clearing, and Baier indicates settlers from the Bavarian region. In December 1457 Margrave Albert Achilles, who was also Elector of Brandenburg, gave the town the coat of arms it still bears, with the black and white of the Hohenzollerns.

Bayreuth was the seat of the margraves, and the New Palace and its court garden served as their residence from 1753. The Margravial Opera House, opened in 1748, is one of the finest Baroque theatres in Europe and a World Heritage Site. From 1701 the Crown Prince and later Margrave George William founded the then independent town of St Georgen am See with a castle, town hall and barracks. In 1705 he founded the Order of Sincerity, renamed the Order of the Red Eagle in 1734, and in 1716 a princely porcelain factory was set up there.

Electric street lights came in 1892, a municipal electricity station in 1908 and the first cinema in the same year. After the First World War a Workers' and Soldiers' Council briefly took power, and on 17 February 1919 a three-day coup, the Speckputsch, interrupted an otherwise staid town.

Bayreuth is the capital of Upper Franconia and is best known for its link with the composer Richard Wagner, who lived there from 1872 until his death in 1883. His villa Wahnfried was built with the sponsorship of King Ludwig II of Bavaria and became a Wagner Museum after the Second World War. The Festival Hall in the north of the town is used only for the annual Bayreuth Festival, at which only his works are performed. The premieres of Siegfried and Götterdämmerung, of the Ring cycle as a whole and of Parsifal took place there.
beaune: Beaune stands on a plain beside the hills of the Côte d'Or and is served by a small river, the Bouzaise, whose source lies in a public park on the north-east edge of the town. The name derives from the Latinised Gaulish Belena, the name of a spring around which the settlement grew, itself derived from Belenos, a god of fast-flowing water. The climate is semi-continental with an oceanic influence, with frequent rain in every season.

A Roman fort was built at the site in the first century CE, and the town has features from pre-Roman and Roman times through the medieval and Renaissance periods. The region was already a wine-growing area in the 13th century, and the cellars of producers have stood in the historic centre since Roman times. Beaune is a walled city: much of its battlements, ramparts and moat survives in good condition, and the old town inside the walls is extensive. Historically it is closely connected with the Dukes of Burgundy.

The Hospices de Beaune were founded in the 15th century by Nicolas Rolin, chancellor of the Duke of Burgundy, who was encouraged by his wife Guigone de Salins. They are a charity running hospitals and other services for the needy, and through the gifts of benefactors they own vineyards in Burgundy. At the end of the First World War the American Expeditionary Forces University was established in Beaune under Brigadier General Robert I. Rees, with its own chapter of Phi Beta Kappa.

Beaune is a commune and sub-prefecture of the Côte-d'Or department, in the region of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, and is regarded as the wine capital of Burgundy. Many major négociants have their houses there, and the appellation Beaune was created in 1936. An annual charity wine auction is held for the Hospices. Landmarks include the Hospices, the old market, the Beffroi clock tower and the collegiate church of Notre Dame, and the town is the main centre of the polychrome Burgundian tile roofing of the Renaissance. In 2015 it was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Climats, terroirs of Burgundy.
beauvais: Beauvais is a town and commune in northern France, the prefecture of the Oise département in the Hauts-de-France region, 75 kilometres north of Paris. It lies at the foot of wooded hills on the left bank of the Thérain at its confluence with the Avelon. Its ancient ramparts have been destroyed and it is now surrounded by boulevards. The region around it is called the Beauvaisis.

The Romans knew it by the Gallo-Roman name Caesaromagus, the capital of the Belgic tribe of the Bellovaci. Some hold that it was the fortified town of Bratuspantium that surrendered to Julius Caesar, as De Bello Gallico reports, while others identify that town with Vendeuil-Caply or Bailleul sur Thérain. In the ninth century it became a county, which passed in about 1013 to the bishops of Beauvais, who became peers of France from the twelfth century. At royal coronations the Bishop of Beauvais wore the royal mantle and, with the Bishop of Langres, raised the king from his throne to present him to the people.

The town defended itself against the English in 1346 and was besieged by them again in 1433. The siege by the Duke of Burgundy in 1472 was noted for the heroism of the town's women under Jeanne Hachette, remembered in a procession on 27 June in which women take precedence over men. Beauvais was extensively damaged in World War I and again in June 1940; much of the older part was all but destroyed, and the cathedral was badly damaged before British forces liberated the town on 30 August 1944.

The cathedral of Saint-Pierre, begun in 1247 under Bishop William of Grès, was raised an extra 5 metres to make it the tallest cathedral in Europe, and the vaulting of the interior exceeds 46 metres. Work stopped in 1284 when the vaulting of the choir collapsed, and the fall of a too-ambitious central tower in 1573 halted it again. The building consists only of a transept and choir with an apse and seven apse chapels; a small Romanesque church of the 10th century, the Basse Oeuvre, occupies the site meant for the nave. Its stained glass of the 13th, 14th and 16th centuries includes work by Engrand Le Prince.

The state tapestry manufactory dates from 1664. The church of Saint-Étienne is a Romanesque and Gothic building of the early 12th to late 16th centuries, and a former episcopal palace of the 16th century houses the departmental museum. Beauvais–Tillé Airport, dating from the 1930s, serves as a gateway to Paris.
bede: Almost everything known of Bede's life comes from the last chapter of his Ecclesiastical History of the English People, completed in about 731. He gives his birthplace as the lands of the twin monastery of Monkwearmouth and Jarrow. Bede says nothing of his origins, but his connections with men of noble ancestry suggest that his family was well-to-do.

At the age of seven he was sent to Monkwearmouth to be educated by Benedict Biscop and later by Ceolfrith. Jarrow was founded by Ceolfrith in 682, and Bede probably moved there with him that year. In 686 a plague broke out at Jarrow, and the Life of Ceolfrith records that only two surviving monks could sing the full office, one of them a young boy, almost certainly Bede. In about 692 he was ordained a deacon by John, Bishop of Hexham, and in about 702 he became a priest.

Bede began writing in about 701 with two classroom works, De Arte Metrica and De Schematibus et Tropis, and eventually completed over 60 books, most of which survive. He wrote on music, metrics, chronology, history and theology, knew some Greek, and read Pliny the Elder, Virgil, Ovid and Horace. In his own time he was as well known for his biblical commentaries as for his history.

The Ecclesiastical History opens with Caesar's invasion and a brief account of Christianity in Roman Britain, then tells of Augustine's mission of 597, the progress of the faith in Kent and Northumbria, the reigns of Oswald and Oswy, and the Council of Whitby. He also studied computus, the calculation of calendar dates, above all the date of Easter, a subject of controversy, and helped to popularise dating forward from the birth of Christ.
His last surviving work is a letter to Ecgbert of York, written in 734. He died on 26 May 735. A cult formed around him by the 10th century and was widespread in England by the fourteenth.

His body was moved to Durham Cathedral in 1020 and placed in the tomb of Saint Cuthbert, then in 1370 to a shrine of its own. The shrine was demolished during the English Reformation, and Bede was reburied in the cathedral. In 1899 Pope Leo XIII declared him a Doctor of the Church, the first native of Great Britain to hold the title.
bedrich-smetana: Smetana was born on 2 March 1824 in Litomyšl, east of Prague near the traditional border between Bohemia and Moravia, then provinces of the Habsburg Empire. He was the third child, and first son, of František Smetana, a brewer in the service of Count Waldstein, and his third wife Barbora Linková. German was the official language of Bohemia, and the children did not learn correct Czech until much later in their lives.

He gave his first public performance at the age of six. He came to Prague in the autumn of 1839 and soon began missing classes at his school in favour of concerts and the opera, convinced after hearing Franz Liszt that he wanted a musical career. His father saw music only as a pastime. Smetana later studied under Josef Proksch, and in 1848 he helped man the barricades on the Charles Bridge as a member of the Citizens' Army, where he met the writer Karel Sabina.

After failing to establish himself in Prague, Smetana left for Gothenburg, where within weeks he gave a recital, opened a music school that was soon overwhelmed by applications and became conductor of the Gothenburg Society for Classical Choral Music. A visit to Liszt at Weimar in the summer of 1857 shaped his later orchestral work and led to the three Gothenburg symphonic poems, Richard III, Wallenstein's Camp and Hakon Jarl.

The announcement in 1861 of a Provisional Theatre for Czech opera drew him back to Prague. The conductorship went to Jan Nepomuk Maýr, because the conservative faction considered Smetana a dangerous modernist in thrall to Liszt and Wagner. His first two operas, The Brandenburgers in Bohemia and The Bartered Bride, were premiered there in 1866, and he then became the theatre's principal conductor, though his years in the post were marked by controversy.

By the winter of 1882–83 Smetana suffered depression, insomnia and hallucinations. By the middle of February 1884 he had ceased to be coherent, and on 23 April his family removed him to the Kateřinky Lunatic Asylum in Prague, where he died on 12 May 1884.

Most commentators agree that he created a canon of Czech opera where none had existed and a musical style matching the emergent Czech national spirit. Relatively few of his works are in the international repertory, and most foreign commentators regard Antonín Dvořák as the more significant Czech composer.
beijing: Beijing is situated at the northern edge of the roughly triangular North China Plain, which opens to the south and east of the city. Mountains to the north, northwest and west shield the city and northern China's agricultural heartland from the encroaching desert steppes. The Great Wall of China across the northern part of the municipality was built on the rugged topography to defend against nomadic incursions from the steppes. The highest point of the municipality is Mount Dongling, at 2,303 metres, in the Western Hills on the border with Hebei.

The name Beijing means 'Northern Capital' and was applied to the city in 1403, during the Ming dynasty, to distinguish it from Nanjing, the 'Southern Capital'. The older English spelling Peking was used by the Jesuit missionary Martino Martini in an atlas published in Amsterdam in 1655. Over the past 3,000 years the city has had numerous other names.

The earliest traces of human habitation in the municipality were found in the caves of Dragon Bone Hill near the village of Zhoukoudian, where Peking Man lived. Homo erectus fossils from the caves date to 230,000 to 250,000 years ago, and Homo sapiens lived there more recently, about 27,000 years ago. Neolithic settlements have been found throughout the municipality, including in Wangfujing in central Beijing.

The first walled city in the area was Ji, the capital of the state of Ji, located around the present Guang'anmen area in the south of Xicheng District. During the early Zhou period the settlement was conquered by the state of Yan, which made it its new capital. Its original capital lay 45 kilometres to the southwest in Fangshan District. Yan eventually became one of the seven major states of China in the Warring States period.

Beijing is the capital of China and is governed as a provincial-level municipality with 16 districts. In 2024 its population was about 21.8 million. Its traditional housing consists of siheyuans, courtyard houses, and the narrow alleys between them called hutongs. It has eight UNESCO World Heritage Sites, among them the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace, the Ming Tombs, the Zhoukoudian Peking Man Site and parts of the Great Wall and the Grand Canal. Beijing opera is its best-known traditional form of theatre.
belarus: Belarus is a landlocked country of 207,600 square kilometres, lying between latitudes 51° and 57° N and measuring 560 kilometres from north to south and 650 from west to east. It is relatively flat, with large tracts of marshy land, about 40% forest, and 11,000 lakes.

Three major rivers run through it: the Neman flows west toward the Baltic Sea, the Pripyat flows east to the Dnieper, and the Dnieper flows south toward the Black Sea. The highest point is Dzyarzhynskaya Hara, at 345 metres. About 70% of the radiation from the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster in neighbouring Ukraine entered Belarusian territory, and about a fifth of the land was affected by fallout.

Baltic tribes first permanently settled the region in the 3rd century, and around the 5th century the Slavs took it over, and the gradual assimilation of the Baltic settlers into Slavic culture was peaceful. In the 9th century it became part of Kievan Rus', a vast East Slavic state ruled by the Rurikids, which split into independent principalities on the death of Yaroslav the Wise in 1054.

The Battle on the Nemiga River in 1067 is considered the founding date of Minsk. The lands avoided the brunt of the 13th-century Mongol invasion and joined the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; the annals affirm an alliance and united foreign policy between Polotsk and Lithuania for decades. The duchy fought alongside Poland against the Teutonic Knights at the Battle of Grunwald in 1410.

By the 14th century the lands had come fully under the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and later the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, a period lasting 500 years until the partitions of 1792–1795 placed Belarus within the Russian Empire for the first time. The Byelorussian SSR, formed after the Russian Revolution, became a founding republic of the Soviet Union in 1922. After the Polish-Soviet War (1918–1921) Belarus lost almost half its territory to Poland, and in the Second World War it lost about a quarter of its population and half of its economic resources. Many prominent Belarusian intellectuals were exiled or killed in Stalinist purges in the 1930s.

Belarus proclaimed its sovereignty on 27 July 1990 and gained independence on 25 August 1991. Belarus and Russia signed a treaty in 2000 forming the Union State. The official languages are Russian and Belarusian. Francysk Skaryna's Bible, published between 1517 and 1525, was the first book printed in Belarus or anywhere in Eastern Europe.
belarusians: Balts historically inhabited most of the territory of present-day Belarus, and many ancient place names there are of Baltic origin. Slavic settlement began around the 6th and 7th centuries, and the Balts were gradually absorbed, a process that ended in eastern and central Belarus around the 12th century. In the 8th and 9th centuries most of the land was held by three tribal unions, the Kryvichs, Dryhavichs and Radzimichs. The Kryvichs were the most important, and Polotsk and Smolensk, which they founded, were the chief cultural and political centres. The principalities formed there belonged to Kievan Rus'.

Beginning with Mindaugas and Gediminas, Lithuania expanded rapidly east and south, and by the mid-14th century most of modern Belarus, including Polotsk, Vitebsk, Minsk, Turov and Pinsk, belonged to the Lithuanian state. These lands kept their Orthodox Christian and East Slavic traditions, and the Ruthenian nobility took full part in Lithuania's political life. Polish influence grew after the Union of Lublin in 1569 and the Union of Brest in 1596, and Polish replaced Ruthenian in official use in the late 17th century. A modern Belarusian national identity did not yet exist.

After the Third Partition of 1795 the Russian Empire took most of these lands. In 1839 Tsar Nicholas I banned the word Belarus and replaced it with Northwestern Krai. A short-lived Belarusian Democratic Republic was declared in March 1918. By the Peace of Riga in 1921 the territory was split between the Second Polish Republic and Soviet Russia, which created the Belarusian Soviet Socialist Republic. More than two million people, about a quarter of the population, were killed in Belarus during the three years of German occupation.

Before 1991 Belarusians were known as Ruthenians, Litvins and White Ruthenians, and in the Soviet era as Byelorussians. The name White Rus' was first used in the Middle Ages for the area of Polotsk. The Republic of Belarus has existed since the Belovezha Accords ended the Soviet Union in 1991. Belarusians form the majority of its population, with minorities in Ukraine, Poland, Russia and Lithuania, and many emigrated to the United States, Brazil and Canada in the early 20th century. Most are Eastern Orthodox.
belem: Belém lies about 100 km upriver from the Atlantic Ocean, on the Pará River, which belongs to the greater Amazon River system and is separated from the larger part of the Amazon delta by Marajó Island. It is the gateway to the Amazon, with a busy port. The climate is tropical rainforest, with more than 60 mm of rain on average in every month and a wetter season from December to May. The city is called the City of Mango Trees because of the many mango trees in it, and it is named after Santa Maria de Belém in Lisbon.

In 1615 the Portuguese captain-general Francisco Caldeira Castelo Branco led a military expedition, sent by the Governor General of Brazil, to check the trading excursions of French, Dutch and English up the Amazon. On 12 January 1616 he anchored in Guajará Bay, where the Pará and Guamá rivers meet. Mistaking the bay for the main channel, he built a wooden fort covered with straw, which he called Presépio, meaning nativity scene, now known as Forte do Castelo. The colony it formed was named Feliz Lusitânia and became the beginning of Belém. The fort failed to suppress Dutch and French trading but did ward off colonisation. Belém was the first European colony on the Amazon, and was given city status in 1655.

Sugar was important in the region until the end of the 17th century, followed by cattle ranching and, in the 18th century, rice, cotton and coffee. Belém then became the main exporting centre of the Amazon rubber industry, and its position was further enhanced in 1866 when the Amazon, Tocantins and Tapajós rivers were opened to navigation, although the Port of Manaus upriver reduced its importance somewhat. The rubber era ended after the boom of 1910–12, but Belém remained the main commercial centre of northern Brazil.

Belém is the capital and largest city of the state of Pará, in northern Brazil. Its colonial quarter keeps tree-filled squares, churches and traditional blue tiles. On the second Sunday in October it holds the Círio of Nazaré, described as the largest religious event in Brazil, a procession that follows a statue of the Virgin and Child and is regarded as the Christmas of the Amazon; its river pilgrimage honours the water men, who regard the Virgin of Nazareth as their patron saint. The Federal University of Pará and the State University of Pará are in the city.
belfast: Belfast stands on the banks of the River Lagan and is connected to the open sea through Belfast Lough and the North Channel. Its name comes from the Irish Béal Feirste, "mouth of the Farset", a river whose name means a sandbar or tidal ford. The Farset flowed into the Lagan, until it was culverted in the late 18th century, along what is now High Street, and the early settlement developed at the low-water crossing near the present Queen's Bridge. The site has been occupied since at least the Neolithic, and the Giant's Ring, a 5,000-year-old henge, lies near the city.

In 1613, under a commission from King James VI, Sir Arthur Chichester undertook the Plantation of Belfast and its surroundings, building a new castle and attracting mainly English and Manx settlers. Scottish Presbyterians followed, and in 1649 an English Parliamentarian army temporarily expelled them in the town's only recorded siege. Their descendants' disaffection with Ireland's Anglican establishment contributed to the rebellion of 1798 and the union with Great Britain in 1801.

From the 1820s Belfast expanded rapidly in industry. After a cotton boom and bust it became the global leader in linen goods, earning the name Linenopolis, and shipbuilding led to heavier industry. When it was granted city status in 1888 it was the world's largest centre of linen manufacture, and by the 1900s its shipyards were building up to a quarter of all United Kingdom tonnage.

New industry drew large numbers of Catholics from rural districts to a largely Protestant town, and sectarian tensions grew. They erupted in sustained violence in 1920–22, as Belfast became the capital of the six north-eastern counties that kept the British connection.

In the spring of 1941 the German Luftwaffe attacked the city four times, damaging or destroying more than half its housing and killing more than a thousand people, the heaviest loss of life in any air raid outside London. The Troubles began in the late 1960s, and the British Army was on the streets from August 1969 in the longest continuous deployment in its history.

Belfast is the capital, largest city and main port of Northern Ireland, the second largest city on the island of Ireland after Dublin, with 345,418 people recorded in 2021. A division of working-class Protestant and Catholic districts by barriers remains a legacy of the conflict. The port still has commercial and industrial docks and a reduced Harland and Wolff shipyard, and the Titanic Quarter has been developed on former dockland. Ulster University and Queen's University Belfast are in the city.
belgium: Belgium covers 30,689 square kilometres in the Low Countries, bordered by the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg, France and the North Sea. It has three main geographical regions: the coastal plain in the northwest, with sand dunes and polders; the central plateau, a slowly rising landscape of fertile valleys and the sandy plain of the Campine; and the forested, rugged Ardennes in the southeast. The highest point is the Signal de Botrange, at 694 metres. The climate is maritime temperate, with significant precipitation in all seasons.

In his account of the conquest of Gaul, Julius Caesar described the Belgae as inhabiting northern Gaul between the Seine and Marne rivers and the Rhine, and as the bravest of the Gauls. The northernmost tribes, including the Menapii, Nervii and Atuatuci, held most of modern Belgium. After Caesar's conquests the Roman province of Gallia Belgica covered most of northern Gaul, and the eastern part of modern Belgium lay in Germania Inferior. As Roman central government collapsed, the provinces were inhabited by Romanised populations and Germanic-speaking Franks, who came to dominate military and political life.

The region was later part of the Carolingian Empire, the Holy Roman Empire and the Burgundian Netherlands, and was ruled by Habsburg Spain (1556–1714), the Austrian Habsburgs (1714–1794) and Revolutionary France (1794–1815). Most of it joined the United Kingdom of the Netherlands after the Congress of Vienna in 1815. Being contested by so many powers gave Belgium the name the Battlefield of Europe.

An independent Belgium was established in 1830 after the Belgian Revolution. It was the first country in continental Europe to industrialise, and mining and steelmaking in Liège Province and around Charleroi made it one of the three most industrialised nations in the world from 1830 to 1910, although Flanders suffered famine from 1846 to 1850.

Belgium is a parliamentary constitutional monarchy and a federal state of three regions, Flanders, Wallonia and the Brussels-Capital Region, with Dutch-speaking, French-speaking and small German-speaking communities. Tensions between Dutch-speakers and French-speakers rose in the second half of the twentieth century and led to reforms that turned a unitary state into a federal one between 1970 and 1993. After the 2010 federal election the country went a record 589 days without forming a government. Brussels hosts the seats of several European Union institutions, and the country's colonies, the Belgian Congo and Ruanda-Urundi, became independent between 1960 and 1962.
belgrade: Belgrade lies 116.75 m above sea level at the confluence of the Danube and Sava rivers, at the crossroads of the Pannonian Plain and the Balkan Peninsula. Its historical core, Kalemegdan, stands on the right banks of both rivers. Since the 19th century the city has expanded to the south and east, and after World War II New Belgrade was built on the left bank of the Sava, connecting Belgrade with Zemun. The name in Serbian, Beograd, means White City.

Chipped stone tools found in Zemun show that nomadic foragers lived around Belgrade in the Palaeolithic and Mesolithic eras. The first farmers belonged to the Neolithic Starčevo culture, which flourished between 6200 and 5200 BCE, and the Vinča culture (5500-4500 BCE) grew out of their settlements and is known for very large settlements. In antiquity Thraco-Dacians inhabited the region, and after 279 BCE Celts settled the city and named it Singidūn. The Romans conquered it under Augustus and awarded it city rights in the mid-2nd century.

Slavs settled the city in the 520s. It then changed hands several times between the Byzantine Empire, the Frankish Empire, the Bulgarian Empire and the Kingdom of Hungary before becoming the seat of the Serbian king Stefan Dragutin in 1284. It was the capital of the Serbian Despotate under Stefan Lazarević, and his successor Đurađ Branković returned it to the Hungarian king in 1427. Noon bells rung in support of the Hungarian army during the siege of 1456 against the Ottoman Empire remain a widespread church tradition.

After the Serbian Revolution Belgrade was named capital of Serbia again in 1841. Northern Belgrade remained the southernmost Habsburg post until 1918, when former Austro-Hungarian territories joined the new Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Belgrade was the capital of Yugoslavia from its creation to its dissolution. Placed in a strategic position, it has been battled over in 115 wars and razed 44 times, and has been bombed five times and besieged many times.

Belgrade is the capital and largest city of Serbia and the seat of its central government. The 2022 census counted 1,197,114 people in the city proper and 1,682,720 in its administrative area. The University of Belgrade, founded in 1808 as the Velika škola, is the oldest institution of higher learning in Serbia. The author Ivo Andrić wrote The Bridge on the Drina in the city, and it hosted the first Non-Aligned Movement Summit in 1961.
belize-city: Belize City stands at the mouth of Haulover Creek, a distributary of the Belize River, which empties into the Caribbean Sea eight kilometres from the city. The city proper is usually divided into two areas: Northside, bounded by Haulover Creek and ending in the east at the Fort George area, and Southside, which includes downtown and the port. Four bridges, among them the Swing Bridge at Market Square, link the divisions, and the main canals are Haulover Creek, Burdon Canal and Collet Canal. The climate is tropical monsoon, with a long wet season from May through February, and the city is susceptible to flooding in the rainy season.

The city was founded as Belize Town in 1638 by English lumber harvesters, on the site of a small Maya settlement called Holzuz. The place suited the English as a central post because it was on the sea and was a natural outlet for the local rivers and creeks down which they shipped logwood and mahogany. It also became the home of the thousands of African slaves brought in by the English, and later the British from 1707, to work in the forestry industry.

Belize Town was the coordination site for the Battle of St. George's Caye in 1798, which the British won against would-be invaders, and the home of the local courts and government officials until the 1970s. For this reason historians often say that the capital was the colony, since the centre of British control lay there. Antonio Soberanis Gómez, George Price and Evan X Hyde all lobbied to take their movements outside the city, but people continued to look to it for guidance.

Belize City was directly struck by hurricanes in 1931 and 1961, and fires have burnt out stretches of housing at various times. Hurricane Hattie swept ashore in October 1961 and almost entirely destroyed the city. The government was moved to the new capital, Belmopan, in 1970.

Belize City is the largest city in Belize, with a population of 63,999 at the 2022 census, and it is the country's principal port and its financial and industrial hub. It has branches of all the major banks and the Central Bank, and the Supreme Court of Belize still sits there.

St John's Cathedral, begun in 1812 and completed in 1820 of orange bricks that came on British ships as ballast, is the oldest Anglican church in Central America and the only Anglican cathedral outside England where kings have been crowned.
ben-jonson: Jonson was born in June 1572, possibly on the 11th, in or near London.
