His father, a Protestant who had lost his property and been imprisoned under Queen Mary, became a clergyman after his release and died a month before his son's birth; what is known of him comes from the poet's own account. His widow married a master bricklayer two years later. A family friend paid for his studies at Westminster School, where the antiquarian William Camden was one of his masters; their friendship and Camden's wide scholarship left a lasting mark on Jonson's style until Camden's death in 1623.

A play he wrote with Thomas Nashe, The Isle of Dogs, was suppressed in 1597 after causing great offence, and Jonson was jailed in Marshalsea Prison. In 1598 he killed the actor Gabriel Spenser in a duel on 22 September and was imprisoned in Newgate; he pleaded guilty to manslaughter but was released by benefit of clergy, forfeiting his goods and being branded on the left thumb.

His public plays were mainly comedies, among them Every Man in His Humour, Volpone, The Alchemist and Bartholomew Fair; his two tragedies, Sejanus and Catiline, largely failed to impress audiences. His comedies show a keen eye for absurdity and hypocrisy. When James VI and I came to the throne in 1603 he quickly adapted to the demand for masques and entertainments encouraged by the king and Anne of Denmark, and enjoyed the patronage of Elizabeth Sidney and Lady Mary Wroth, which led to his country house poem To Penshurst.

According to a contemporary letter, Jonson died in London on 18 August 1637, and his funeral was attended by all or the greater part of the nobility then in town. He is buried in the north aisle of the nave of Westminster Abbey, with the inscription O Rare Ben Johnson over his grave; John Aubrey records that a passer-by, John Young, paid a workman eighteen pence to cut it. The upright burial was taken as a sign of his reduced circumstances.

Younger poets such as Robert Herrick, Richard Lovelace and Sir John Suckling called themselves the Sons or Tribe of Ben. After the Restoration his comedies and his theory of humour characters were the blueprint for many Restoration comedies, and his work, with Shakespeare's and Fletcher's, formed the core of the repertory when the theatres reopened. He has been called the first poet laureate, and many critics since the 18th century have ranked him below only Shakespeare among English Renaissance dramatists. Of Shakespeare he wrote in Timber that he was not of an age, but for all time.
benedict-xiv: Prospero Lambertini was born into a noble family of Bologna, the third of five children of Marcello Lambertini and Lucrezia Bulgarini. At thirteen he began attending the Collegio Clementino in Rome, where he studied rhetoric, Latin, philosophy and theology, and he often read the works of Thomas Aquinas, his favourite author. In 1694, at nineteen, he received the degrees of Doctor of Sacred Theology and of both ecclesiastical and civil law.

As Promoter of the Faith from 1708 he secured the canonization of Pope Pius V and wrote a treatise on the process of beatification and canonization of saints. Created a cardinal in 1726, he was named Archbishop of Bologna in 1731 and wrote there a three-volume treatise on the diocesan synod, De synodo dioecesana.

After Clement XII died in February 1740 the conclave lasted six months. Lambertini arrived late and was not among the favourites of any faction; he was put forward as a compromise and is reported to have said, 'If you wish to elect a saint, choose Gotti; a statesman, Aldrovandi; an honest man, me.' He was elected on the 255th ballot on 17 August 1740.

His pontificate began amid disputes with Catholic rulers over their demand to nominate bishops, and he settled the quarrels of the Holy See with Naples, Sardinia, Spain, Venice and Austria. The papal government was heavily in debt, by 56,000,000 scudi, and he cut the army and the pay of its officers and soldiers, though the administration still ran a deficit at his death. He encouraged agriculture and free trade, revived anatomical studies at the University of Bologna and added about 3,300 of his own books to the Vatican Library.

On 22 December 1741 the bull Immensa Pastorum Principis excommunicated anyone who enslaved the indigenous peoples of Brazil, though it went unenforced. In the bulls Ex quo singulari of 1742 and Omnium sollicitudinum of 1744 he condemned the accommodation of Chinese and Indian customs by the Jesuit missions, and many converts left the Church.

Benedict XIV had suffered from kidney problems for years. After a battle with gout he died on 3 May 1758, at the age of 83, lucid to the end, and was buried in Saint Peter's Basilica. He was noted for his modesty and humour and was also an avid gambler who used profane language.

His intellectualism and advocacy of science education earned him the nickname the Enlightenment Pope. Horace Walpole described him as a pope without nepotism and an author without vanity, a man whom neither intellect nor power could corrupt.
benevento: Benevento stands on a hill 130 metres above sea level at the confluence of the Calore and the Sabato rivers in Campania. As Maleventum it was one of the chief cities of Samnium, on the Appian Way 51 kilometres east of Capua. Ancient writers ascribed its foundation to Diomedes after the Trojan War, a legend its inhabitants adopted, and in the time of Procopius they claimed to display the tusks of the Calydonian Boar as proof. Another tradition names Auson, a son of Ulysses and Circe, as founder.

The city first appears in history as a Samnite town, strong enough that the Romans did not attack it in their first two wars with the Samnites. Its theatre, completed under Caracalla between 200 and 210, reflects its growing importance after the Via Appia Traiana opened. After Totila sacked it and razed its walls in 545, Benevento became the seat of a powerful Lombard duchy, whose creation is disputed. Arechis I, who died in 640, captured Capua and Crotone. After his reign the Eastern Roman Empire held only Naples, Amalfi, Gaeta, Sorrento, the tip of Calabria and the maritime cities of Apulia in the south.

Benevento passed peacefully to the papacy when Emperor Henry III ceded it to Leo IX in exchange for the pope's consent to the founding of the Diocese of Bamberg. In 1806 Napoleon gave the principality to Talleyrand, who never ruled it, and in 1815 it returned to the papacy. It was united with Italy in 1860. A Jewish community lived there from at least the fifth century, and was expelled in 1569 under Paul IV.

Benevento is the capital of its province and the seat of an archbishop. Its Lombard church of Santa Sofia, a circular building of about 760, was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2011 as one of seven buildings called Longobards in Italy. The Arch of Trajan, the Roman theatre and the castle called the Rocca dei Rettori also survive. Allied bombing in the summer of 1943 killed 2,000 people, destroyed half the town and almost all of the cathedral, which was rebuilt by 1965.
bengaluru: Bengaluru lies in the south-east of Karnataka on the Mysore Plateau, part of the Deccan Plateau, at an average elevation of 900 m. The topography is generally flat, with small hills of granite and gneiss to the south. No major river runs through the city, though six rivers rise at the Nandi Hills about 60 km to the north, and most of its water comes from the Kaveri. Because of its elevation the climate is moderate, with distinct wet and dry seasons. The city is known as India's Garden City because of its parks and greenery.

Stone Age artefacts indicate human settlement around 4000 BCE, and Roman coins of the first century CE show that the region took part in trans-oceanic trade. The earliest known reference to the name Bengaluru is an Old Kannada hero stone of 890 CE at Begur. In 1537 Kempe Gowda I, a local chieftain aligned with the Vijayanagara Empire, built a mud-brick fort that became the centre of the modern city. He divided the town into pētēs and built tanks such as Kempambudhi for water storage. In 1638 an Adil Shahi army defeated Kempe Gowda III, and the Mughals later sold the city to the Maharaja of Mysore. Hyder Ali seized the kingdom after 1759, and the city passed to his son Tipu Sultan.

After the Anglo-Mysore Wars the city returned to the Maharaja of Mysore, and in 1809 the British formed a military garrison and set up the cantonment outside the old city. By the late 19th century Bengaluru was essentially two cities, the Pete and the Cantonment. A plague epidemic in 1898 claimed nearly 3,500 lives and led to better sanitation. The two settlements merged under one urban administration in 1949, and the city became the capital of Mysore State, renamed Karnataka in 1973.

Bengaluru is the capital and largest city of Karnataka, with 8.4 million inhabitants at the 2011 census. Its official name was Bangalore until 1 November 2014. Kannada is the official language of the state and the mother tongue of 42.1 percent of the city's people at that census, and many other languages are spoken. The city was among the first in India to have electric power, in 1905. Lal Bagh, established in the 1760s, is a botanical garden of 97 hectares with a glass house of 1889 modelled on the Crystal Palace in London.
benito-juarez: Benito Pablo Juárez García was born on 21 March 1806 in the village of San Pablo Guelatao, Oaxaca, in New Spain, a settlement of about two hundred people. He came from a poor rural Indigenous family and was orphaned as a child. At the age of 12 he moved to Oaxaca City, where he worked as a domestic servant.

His employer, a lay Franciscan, sponsored him, and he enrolled for a time in a seminary before switching to law, becoming active in liberal politics. As a lawyer he took cases of Indigenous villagers and was imprisoned after helping villagers of Loxicha accuse a priest of abuses. He sat in the Oaxaca state legislature from 1832, married Margarita Maza on 31 October 1843, and later became governor of Oaxaca.

After the Plan of Ayutla ousted Antonio López de Santa Anna, President Juan Álvarez made Juárez his Minister of Justice. He was instrumental in the Juárez Law, part of the reforms known as La Reforma, which ended the separate courts of clerics and soldiers. As head of the Supreme Court he succeeded to the presidency when Ignacio Comonfort resigned early in the Reform War, and he led the Liberals to victory after three years. Liberal troops entered Mexico City on Christmas Day 1860.

The Second French Intervention followed at once. French troops took Puebla on 17 May 1863 and entered Mexico City on 10 June 1863, and Juárez moved his government north to San Luis Potosí, Monterrey and Chihuahua City. The Second Mexican Empire collapsed after the last French troops left on 12 March 1867. Maximilian and his generals were captured at Querétaro on 14 May 1867, and Juárez re-entered the capital on 15 July.

In his last years Juárez faced opposition from Liberals who thought him autocratic. He stood for re-election in 1871, and when he lacked the required majority, Congress decided for him on 12 October 1871. Porfirio Díaz rebelled against him in the Plan de la Noria. Juárez died of a heart attack in 1872 and was given a state funeral.

He is seen as a symbol of Mexican nationalism and resistance to foreign intervention, and his policies favoured civil liberties, equality before the law and the authority of civilian power over the Church and the army. After his death the city of Oaxaca added "de Juárez" to its name, and his birthday, 21 March, is a national holiday.
benito-mussolini: Benito Amilcare Andrea Mussolini was born on 29 July 1883 in Dovia di Predappio, in Romagna. His father, Alessandro, was a blacksmith and socialist, and his mother, Rosa Maltoni, a devout Catholic schoolteacher. He was named after the Mexican president Benito Juárez, and his middle names honoured the Italian socialists Amilcare Cipriani and Andrea Costa. He became a journalist for the Italian Socialist Party newspaper Avanti! and was expelled for advocating military intervention in the First World War. He served in the army from 1915 until wounded in 1917, and during the war turned to nationalism.

On 23 March 1919 Mussolini founded the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in Milan, often considered the world's first fascist movement. It became the National Fascist Party in 1921, and after fascist militants marched on Rome King Victor Emmanuel III appointed him prime minister in 1922. He founded the secret police OVRA in 1927, outlawed strikes and, through measures such as the Acerbo Law, turned a parliamentary democracy into a one-party state. By the end of 1925 press censorship had tightened and appointed podestàs had replaced elected mayors. He signed the Lateran Treaty in 1929, establishing Vatican City, and ordered the Pacification of Libya, which some scholars characterise as a genocide.

His invasion of Ethiopia brought condemnation from the League of Nations, which isolated Italy and pushed him towards Adolf Hitler and the Rome-Berlin Axis of 1936. The Pact of Steel followed in 1939. In June 1940, believing a German victory imminent, he joined the Second World War on Germany's side.

After defeats and the Allied landing in Sicily, the Grand Council of Fascism voted the Grandi motion, and in July 1943 the king dismissed Mussolini and placed him in custody. After the armistice of September 1943 German forces rescued him, and Hitler made him figurehead of the Italian Social Republic, a collaborationist puppet state in German-occupied northern Italy. In April 1945 he and his mistress Clara Petacci tried to flee to Switzerland, were captured by communist partisans and were summarily executed on 28 April 1945.
benjamin-franklin: Benjamin Franklin was born on Milk Street in Boston on 17 January 1706 and baptised at the Old South Meeting House. His father, Josiah Franklin, born at Ecton in Northamptonshire, was a tallow chandler and soap and candle maker. Benjamin was his fifteenth child and tenth and last son. His mother, Abiah Folger, was born in Nantucket, and both parents were pious Puritans.

His father could afford to send him to school for only two years, and he continued to educate himself by reading. At 12 he became an apprentice to his brother James, a printer. When James founded The New-England Courant, Franklin wrote letters in the name of Silence Dogood, a middle-aged widow, and neither the readers nor his brother knew the author. He later left the apprenticeship without permission and so became a fugitive.

Franklin became a successful printer and editor in Philadelphia, publishing The Pennsylvania Gazette at 23 and Poor Richard's Almanack under the pseudonym Richard Saunders. In 1736 he created the Union Fire Company, and in 1743 he founded the American Philosophical Society. In 1749 he printed Proposals Relating to the Education of Youth in Pensilvania and was appointed president of the Academy, which opened in 1751.

His electrical research began in the 1740s. He proposed that vitreous and resinous electricity were one fluid under different pressures, was the first to call them positive and negative, and discovered the principle of conservation of charge. He invented the lightning rod, the Franklin stove and bifocal glasses and never patented them. As an agent in London he led the repeal of the Stamp Act, and as the first United States ambassador to France he secured French support for the Revolutionary War. He served as President of Pennsylvania from 1785 to 1788.
Franklin owned at least seven slaves from 1735 and advertised slaves for sale in his newspaper, but by the late 1750s he had begun to argue against slavery and later became an active abolitionist.

Franklin died of a pleuritic attack at his home in Philadelphia on 17 April 1790, aged 84. About 20,000 people attended his funeral, and the assembly of revolutionary France went into mourning for three days. He left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia, to gather interest for 200 years. He is the only person to have signed the Declaration of Independence, the Treaty of Paris with Britain and the Constitution.
beowulf: Beowulf is an epic in the tradition of Germanic heroic legend, composed in alliterative verse by an anonymous author called the Beowulf poet. The only certain dating is that of its manuscript, produced between 975 and 1025, and scholars disagree about when the poem was composed. Some place it in the 8th century, J. R. R. Tolkien among them, since he held that it keeps too genuine a memory of Anglo-Saxon paganism to be much later than the Christianisation of England. Others link it with the courts of King Alfred the Great or King Cnut the Great, and some suggest a 7th-century origin at Rendlesham in East Anglia.

The story is set in pagan Scandinavia in the 5th and 6th centuries. Beowulf, a hero of the Geats, helps Hrothgar, king of the Danes, whose mead hall Heorot has been attacked for twelve years by the monster Grendel. He kills Grendel with his bare hands, and then kills Grendel's mother, who has taken revenge by killing Hrothgar's advisor Æschere, with a giant's sword found in her lair.

Beowulf returns home and becomes king of the Geats. Fifty years later a slave steals a golden cup from a dragon's lair, and the dragon burns the land. Beowulf resolves to fight it alone, but only his young Swedish relative Wiglaf stays to help him. They kill the dragon, but Beowulf is mortally wounded, and his body is cremated and a barrow visible from the sea is raised for him. Digressions on the Swedish–Geatish wars, the fight at Finnsburg and biblical tales give the poem historical depth.

The poem survives in a single manuscript, the Nowell Codex, now British Library, Cotton Vitellius A.XV, copied by two scribes. It has no title in the manuscript and takes its name from its hero. A fire at Ashburnham House in London in 1731 charred its margins and cost some readings. Grímur Jónsson Thorkelin made the first transcriptions in 1786, which are prized because the manuscript has crumbled since. Some verses were first translated into modern English in 1805, and nine complete translations followed in the 19th century. Tolkien's 1936 lecture argued that its literary value had been overlooked in favour of its historical content.
berkshire: Berkshire, officially the Royal County of Berkshire, is a ceremonial county in South East England, with Reading as its county town and largest settlement. The whole county is drained by the Thames. The Berkshire Downs, a chalk upland, lie in the west and are the source of the River Kennet, which flows east through Newbury to meet the Thames at Reading. In the south-east lies Swinley Forest, a remnant of Windsor Forest. The historic county included the parts of Oxfordshire south of the Thames, such as Wantage, where Alfred the Great was born, and the Iron Age Uffington White Horse.

According to Asser's biography of King Alfred, written in 893, the county takes its name from a wood of box trees called Bearroc, a Celtic word meaning hilly, west of Frilsham near Newbury. In the Anglo-Saxon period the region was contested between Mercia and Wessex, and Alfred's campaign against the Danes included the battles of Englefield, Ashdown and Reading. Windsor Castle, built after the Norman Conquest, became the official country residence of the British monarch, since William the Conqueror established Windsor as a royal residence.

The county saw several battles in the First English Civil War, with Reading and Wallingford besieged and two battles fought at Newbury, in 1643 and 1644. A second Battle of Reading, on 9 December 1688, was the only substantial military action in England during the Glorious Revolution. Reading replaced Abingdon as county town in 1867. The county received the title Royal County in 1957 because of Windsor Castle, and its boundaries changed on 1 April 1974, when the northern part passed to Oxfordshire and Slough and Eton came from Buckinghamshire.

Berkshire is divided into six unitary authority areas: Bracknell Forest, Reading, Slough, West Berkshire, Windsor and Maidenhead, and Wokingham. Its population is concentrated in the east, nearest London, while the west is rural and its largest town is Newbury. Proximity to London led to development from the 19th century, when Slough became an industrial centre and Bracknell was designated a new town. Software and high-technology industry dominate the economy in the east, and the west remains agricultural.
berlin: Berlin lies in low-lying marshy woodland on the Northern European Plain, along the Spree, which empties into the Havel in the western borough of Spandau. The Spree follows the Berliner Urstromtal, an ice-age glacial valley between the Barnim Plateau to the north and the Teltow plateau to the south, formed by meltwater at the end of the last glaciation. About a third of the city's area is forests, parks, gardens, rivers, canals and lakes. The name has roots in the language of the West Slavs and may be related to the Old Polabian stem berl-/birl-, 'swamp'. Five of the twelve boroughs bear Slavic-derived names, among them Pankow and Spandau.

The area has been settled for millennia: a deer mask of about 9,000 BCE is attributed to the Maglemosian culture, and dense settlement along the Spree and Havel gave rise to the Lusatian culture around 2,000 BCE. Germanic tribes settled from about 500 BCE, the Burgundians followed the Semnones after about 200 CE, and in the 7th century Slavic tribes, later known as the Hevelli and Sprevane, reached the region.

Berlin was first documented in the 13th century, at the crossing of two important trade routes. It was capital of the Margraviate of Brandenburg from 1417, the Kingdom of Prussia from 1701 and the German Empire from 1871. In 1685 the Edict of Potsdam granted religious freedom and tax-free status to French Huguenot refugees.

The Greater Berlin Act of 1920 raised the population from 1.9 million to 4 million, and in the 1920s Berlin was the third-largest city in the world. It was capital of the Weimar Republic and of Nazi Germany until 1945. After the Second World War it was split into West Berlin and East Berlin, divided by the Berlin Wall, and Bonn became the West German capital. Berlin again became the capital of all Germany after reunification on 3 October 1990.

Berlin covers 891 km2 and is the most populous city proper in the European Union. Since 1990 it has been one of three city-states among the 16 states of Germany, governed by the Senate and the 141-seat Abgeordnetenhaus. The bombing of the Second World War devastated the city, and many surviving buildings were later demolished; after reunification many heritage structures were reconstructed.

Museum Island, designated a district dedicated to art and antiquities by royal decree in 1841, is one of three UNESCO World Heritage Sites. The Charité hospital traces its origins to 1710, and Robert Koch and Rudolf Virchow worked in Berlin. The city hosted the 1936 Summer Olympics.
bermuda: Bermuda is an archipelago of 181 islands, though the most significant are connected by bridges and appear to form one landmass. Its land area is 54 square kilometres. The nearest land is the coast of North Carolina, about 1,035 kilometres to the west-northwest. The islands lie in the west of the Sargasso Sea and have a tropical climate; a coral reef gives them some protection from tropical cyclones. When discovered, they had no human population and were dominated by forests of Bermuda cedar.

Bermuda was discovered in the early 1500s by the Spanish explorer Juan de Bermúdez and appears on Spanish charts of 1511. Spanish and Portuguese ships used it to take on fresh meat and water. Legends of spirits and devils, now thought to stem from the calls of birds and the noises of introduced wild hogs, together with storms and dangerous reefs, gave it the name Isle of Devils, and neither Spain nor Portugal tried to settle it.

In 1609 a flotilla bound for the Jamestown colony was broken up by a storm, and its flagship, the Sea Venture, was driven onto Bermuda's reef to prevent her sinking, so that all aboard survived. Having heard the true conditions in Jamestown, the settlers were unwilling to move on and made several attempts to rebel and stay. The new settlement became a prison labour camp and built two ships, the Deliverance and the Patience. The Somers Isles Company suppressed shipbuilding, wanting the colonists to farm, but the islanders turned to maritime trades, and in 1684 the company's charter was revoked. The House of Assembly dates from 1620.

After the American Revolution the Royal Navy began improving the harbours, and in 1811 work began on the Royal Naval Dockyard on Ireland Island, guarding the western Atlantic shipping lanes. In the War of 1812 the British attacks on Washington, D.C., and the Chesapeake were planned and launched from Bermuda. In the early 20th century it became a popular destination for tourists, and the Smoot–Hawley Tariff Act of 1930 ended its agricultural export trade to America and encouraged tourism.

Bermuda is a British Overseas Territory and a self-governing parliamentary democracy, with a bicameral parliament in the capital Hamilton; the United Kingdom is responsible for foreign affairs and defence. It is divided into nine parishes. An independence referendum in 1995 produced a large majority against independence. The historic Town of St. George's is a World Heritage Site.
bernard-of-clairvaux: Bernard's parents, Tescelin de Fontaine, lord of Fontaine-lès-Dijon, and Alèthe de Montbard, belonged to the highest nobility of Burgundy. He was the third of seven children, six of them sons. At nine he was sent to a school at Châtillon-sur-Seine run by the secular canons of Saint-Vorles, where he was drawn to literature and rhetoric. After his mother died he decided to go to Cîteaux, the abbey founded near Dijon in 1098 by a group led by Robert of Molesme to live by a literal reading of the Rule of St Benedict.

Three years after entering Cîteaux, Bernard was sent with twelve monks to found a new house at the Vallée d'Absinthe in the diocese of Langres, which he named Clairvaux on 25 June 1115. Its beginnings were austere, but candidates flocked to it, and more than sixty abbeys followed in his lifetime. He defended the Cistercians against criticism from the Benedictines of Cluny in his Apology, and Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, answered with admiration and friendship.

At the Council of Troyes in 1128 he traced the outlines of the Rule of the Knights Templar. When Honorius II died in 1130 and the election of Innocent II and the Antipope Anacletus II split the Church, Bernard was chosen at the council of Étampes to judge between them and decided for Innocent, then spent years winning over rulers and cities; the schism ended with Anacletus's death in 1138. In 1141 he secured the condemnation of Peter Abelard at a council at Sens.

In 1146 Pope Eugene III commissioned him to preach the Second Crusade, and on 31 March, with King Louis VII present, he preached to an enormous crowd at Vézelay. He also opposed attacks on Jews in the Rhineland and silenced the monk Radulf, who was inspiring them.

The failure of the Second Crusade saddened his last years and put the whole responsibility on him; he wrote that the sins of the crusaders had caused it. He died on 20 August 1153, aged sixty-three, and was buried at Clairvaux. After his remains were destroyed in 1792 by the French Revolutionary government, they were transferred to Troyes Cathedral.

He was canonized 21 years after his death and declared a Doctor of the Church in 1830. Against the rational approach of the scholastics he preached poetically and stressed personal friendship with Christ, and he helped spread devotion to Mary. His sermons on the Song of Songs are his best known. Bernard appears as Dante's last guide in the Divine Comedy.
bertrand-russell: Russell was born on 18 May 1872 at Ravenscroft, a country house in Trellech, Monmouthshire, to John Russell, Viscount Amberley, and Katharine, Viscountess Amberley, both early advocates of birth control. His mother died of diphtheria in June 1874, followed shortly by his sister Rachel, and his father died in January 1876. He was raised by his paternal grandparents at Pembroke Lodge in Richmond Park, chiefly by his grandmother, the Countess Russell, whose progressive views on social justice and standing up for principle remained with him all his life.

He began at Trinity College, Cambridge, in 1890 on a scholarship to read for the Mathematical Tripos, graduating seventh Wrangler in 1893 and becoming a Fellow in philosophy in 1895. His first major publication was An Essay on the Foundations of Geometry (1897).

Russell started in British idealism, the dominant philosophy of the time, but his friendship with G. E. Moore led him to analytic philosophy, and the two led a revolt against idealism. With Whitehead he wrote Principia Mathematica, published in 1910–1913. His article On Denoting has been considered a paradigm of philosophy. In 1916 he was convicted under the Defence of the Realm Act 1914 for his pacifist activity in the First World War and dismissed from Trinity. After a campaign by the Fellows, he was offered reinstatement and accepted it in 1920, but he resigned in 1921.

In August 1920 he visited Soviet Russia as part of a delegation and met Vladimir Lenin, whom he found disappointing. The visit ended his tentative support for the revolution, and he wrote The Practice and Theory of Bolshevism. He opposed rearmament against Nazi Germany, but changed his view in 1940 and in 1943 adopted a position he called relative political pacifism, that war may in extreme circumstances be the lesser of two evils. His History of Western Philosophy (1945) was a best-seller.

Russell is credited as one of the founders of analytic philosophy, and Willard Van Orman Quine named his work as a chief influence on his own. He made language a central part of philosophy and influenced Ludwig Wittgenstein, Gilbert Ryle, J. L. Austin and P. F. Strawson. In lectures of 1918 he set out logical atomism, the view that knowledge can be reduced to atomic propositions and their truth-functional compounds.

He argued that religion is largely harmful and was a member of the advisory council of the British Humanist Association. He became the 3rd Earl Russell in 1931 and held the title until his death on 2 February 1970.
bethlehem: Bethlehem stands in the Judean Mountains at about 775 metres above sea level, some 30 metres higher than Jerusalem, which lies about ten kilometres to the north. The Arabic name Bēt laḥm means house of meat, while the Hebrew Bet Leḥem means house of bread or house of food. Beit Jala and Beit Sahour form an urban cluster with the city, and the refugee camps of Aida and Azza lie within its limits.

A possible earliest reference is in the Amarna correspondence of ancient Egypt, where Abdi-Heba, the Egyptian-appointed governor of Jerusalem, appeals for help in retaking a town near Jerusalem called Bit-Lahmi after attacks by Apiru mercenaries. The reading is uncertain and has met with objections. The Hebrew Bible names Bethlehem as the birthplace of David. In 2012 excavators in the City of David found a clay seal impression reading From the town of Bethlehem to the King, which they date to the 8th or 7th century BCE and take to have sealed a tax shipment.

The Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Luke place the birth of Jesus in Bethlehem, though scholars regard the two accounts as contradictory and are divided on his actual birthplace. Under the Roman Empire Hadrian destroyed the city, and Constantine the Great later commissioned the Church of the Nativity in 327 CE. It was heavily damaged in 529 by Samaritans in revolt and rebuilt by Justinian I. In 1009 the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah ordered it demolished, but local Muslims, who were permitted to worship in its southern transept, spared it.

Crusaders took Bethlehem in 1099 and replaced the Greek Orthodox clergy with Catholic ones. The Mamluk Sultanate demolished its walls in the mid-13th century, and the Ottoman Empire rebuilt them in the 16th. From 1517 the Catholic and Greek Orthodox churches bitterly disputed custody of the basilica. Bethlehem was part of Mandatory Palestine from 1920 to 1948, was held by Jordan after the 1948 Arab–Israeli War and was captured by Israel in 1967. Refugees from the 1947–48 war settled near the city and helped turn its Christian majority into a Muslim one.

Bethlehem is the capital of the Bethlehem Governorate and had 28,591 inhabitants in 2017. Its economy is closely tied to tourism and to pilgrimage to the Church of the Nativity at Christmas, and it is known for olive wood and mother-of-pearl carving, a craft said to have been introduced by Franciscan friars from Italy in the 15th century. Bethlehem University, founded in 1973, was the first university established in the West Bank.
beziers: Béziers stands on a small bluff above the River Orb, about ten kilometres from the Mediterranean coast and 75 kilometres south-west of Montpellier. It is a subprefecture of the Hérault department. The Canal du Midi crosses the Orb here by the Pont-canal de l'Orb, an aqueduct claimed to be the first of its kind. Its inhabitants are called Biterrois, after Baeterrae, the Roman name of the town.

Béziers is one of the oldest cities in France. Research published in March 2013 dates its ancient Greek colony to 575 BCE. The Romans refounded it as a colony for veterans in 36–35 BCE, as Colonia Julia Baeterrae Septimanorum, and it exported wine to Rome. It was conquered by Muslims and remained part of Islamic Iberia between 720 and 752. From the 10th to the 12th centuries it was the centre of a viscounty, whose rulers controlled the coastal plain and the main east–west route through Languedoc. The Trencavels ruled for 142 years, until the Albigensian Crusade.

Béziers was a stronghold of Catharism, which the Catholic Church condemned as heretical. The crusaders arrived on 21 July 1209 and offered the Catholics of the town the choice of handing over the heretics or leaving; many refused. The town was sacked the next day, and no one was spared, not even priests or those sheltering in the churches. The papal legate Arnaud-Amaury reported to Pope Innocent III that almost 20,000 people were put to the sword. The Cathedral of Saint Nazaire burned and collapsed on those inside. Other accounts give a handful of survivors.

The city was repopulated, and repairs to the cathedral began in 1215. Béziers joined the royal domain in 1247. In 1632 the Edict of Béziers abolished the privileges of Languedoc, restored in 1649. In the 18th century it prospered through vine growing. On 12 May 1907, 150,000 people gathered in Béziers to defend southern winegrowing, and in June soldiers of the 17th regiment, sent to Agde, mutinied and returned to the town.

The Gothic Cathedral of Saint-Nazaire, rebuilt in the 14th century, rises above the town; its nave is 32 metres high. The park of the Plateau des Poètes dates from 1867, and the allées Paul Riquet carry a statue of the creator of the Canal du Midi. Every August the town holds the Feria de Béziers, centred on bullfighting.
bharatiya-janata-party: The party's origins lie in the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, founded in 1951 by Shyama Prasad Mukherjee in collaboration with the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and widely regarded as its political arm. Its aims included protecting India's Hindu cultural identity and countering what it saw as the appeasement of Muslims and of Pakistan by the Congress party under Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. The RSS lent it several full-time workers, among them Deendayal Upadhyaya, who became General Secretary. The Jana Sangh won three Lok Sabha seats in 1952 and kept a minor presence in parliament until 1967.

After Prime Minister Indira Gandhi imposed a state of emergency in 1975, thousands of Jana Sangh members were imprisoned in the protests. In 1977 the party merged with the Socialist Party, the Congress (O) and the Bharatiya Lok Dal to form the Janata Party, which won a majority and formed a government under Morarji Desai. The former Jana Sangh supplied 93 of its seats, and Atal Bihari Vajpayee became Minister of External Affairs.

The Janata Party dissolved in 1980, and the former Jana Sangh members formed the Bharatiya Janata Party, with Vajpayee as its first president. It first softened the Hindutva stance of its predecessor and stressed Gandhian socialism, and won only two Lok Sabha seats in 1984, an election held soon after Indira Gandhi's assassination, when the Congress won 414 seats. The party then grew through the Ram Rath Yatra in Uttar Pradesh and victories in several state elections, and in 1996 became the largest party in parliament; its government under Vajpayee lasted 13 days.

After the 1998 election the BJP led a coalition, the National Democratic Alliance (NDA), and Vajpayee returned as Prime Minister. The coalition broke up in May 1999 when J. Jayalalithaa withdrew her support, and fresh elections followed. The next NDA government under Vajpayee served a full term, the first non-Congress government to do so, and lost the 2004 election. In the 2014 general election the BJP won 282 seats, the NDA 336 of 543, and Narendra Modi was sworn in as Prime Minister on 26 May 2014.

The party's official philosophy is integral humanism, first formulated by Deendayal Upadhyaya in 1965. It follows Hindutva, a Hindu nationalist ideology, and keeps organisational and ideological links with the RSS. During its first period in national government it set its Hindutva priorities aside and concentrated on economic growth.

The name means Indian People's Party. Its symbol is the lotus, the national flower of India, which has cultural significance in Hinduism and was used by Indian nationalists during the independence movement. Its flag is mostly saffron with a green stripe, and the lotus is set within the saffron part.
bhubaneswar: Bhubaneswar lies in the Khordha district of Odisha, in the eastern coastal plains along the axis of the Eastern Ghats, in the Mahanadi River Delta, at an average altitude of 45 metres. The Daya River is 4 kilometres to the south and the Kuakhai 4 kilometres to the east. The name is the anglicisation of the Odia Bhubanēśwara, from Tribhubanēśwara, the Lord of the Three Worlds, which in this context refers to Shiva. The old town was historically often called Chakra Khetra and Ekamra Khetra, the area adorned with a mango tree.

Bhubaneswar stands near the ruins of Sisupalgarh. At Dhauli, near the city, the Kalinga War of about 262 to 261 BCE took place, in which the Mauryan emperor Ashoka invaded and annexed Kalinga. One of the most complete edicts of Ashoka, dating from between 272 and 236 BCE, remains carved in rock 8 kilometres southwest of the modern city. After the decline of the Mauryan empire the area came under the Mahameghavahana dynasty, whose best-known ruler is Kharavela; his Hathigumpha inscription is at the Udayagiri and Khandagiri caves near the city. Several dynasties followed, including the Satavahanas, Guptas, Matharas and Shailodbhavas.

Cuttack, the capital of British-ruled and independent Orissa, was vulnerable to floods and short of space, and in September 1946 a proposal to build a new capital was introduced in the Legislative Assembly of the Odisha Province. The German architect Otto Königsberger designed the modern city in 1946, and with Jamshedpur and Chandigarh it was one of modern India's first planned cities. The foundation of the new capital was laid on 13 April 1948 and the Legislative Assembly moved from Cuttack in 1949. The first census of independent India, in 1951, counted just 16,000 people. A municipality was established on 12 March 1979, and the Bhubaneswar Municipal Corporation on 14 August 1994.

Bhubaneswar is the capital and largest city of Odisha and is called the Temple City. Its temples are built in the Kalinga architectural style, with a curving spire over the sanctum housing the presiding deity and a pyramid-roofed hall where people sit and pray. They include the Lingaraja, Muktesvara, Rajarani and Ananta Vasudeva temples, and the small Kukutesvara Siva Temple, a shrine to Shiva about a thousand years old. At the festival of Ashokashtami the image of Lingaraja is taken in procession to the Mausima Temple. The area formed by Bhubaneswar and Cuttack, often called the twin cities of Odisha, had a population of 1.7 million in 2011. The main language is Odia, and Utkal University is the oldest university in Odisha.
bibliotheque-nationale-de-france: The library traces its origin to the royal library founded at the Louvre Palace by Charles V in 1368, from manuscripts he had received from his predecessor John II. The first librarian of record was Claude Mallet, the king's valet de chambre, who made a catalogue of the books. After the death of Charles VI the collection was bought by the English regent of France, the Duke of Bedford, who took it to England in 1424, and it was apparently dispersed at his death in 1435.

The invention of printing led to a new collection at the Louvre, inherited by Louis XI in 1461. Later kings added to it: Charles VIII seized part of the collection of the kings of Aragon, Louis XII brought in the library at Blois, and Francis I merged it with his private library at Fontainebleau in 1534.

The collection moved several times in Paris, and many treasures were lost. Under the librarian Jacques Auguste de Thou it became the largest and richest collection of books in the world, and it grew rapidly under Louis XIII and Louis XIV, in great part through the interest of the minister Jean-Baptiste Colbert. The library moved in 1666 to two houses in the Rue Vivienne and opened to the public in 1692. Jean-Paul Bignon reformed its system, and from 1721 the Richelieu site, the main location for 275 years, began to take shape.

After the French First Republic was established in September 1792 the Assembly declared the Bibliothèque du Roi national property and it became the Bibliothèque Nationale. Its collections passed 300,000 volumes as the private libraries of aristocrats and clergy were seized. Napoleon ordered provincial libraries to send it any book it lacked and added spoil from his conquests, some of it returned after his fall. In 1868 it moved into new buildings on the Rue de Richelieu designed by Henri Labrouste, and in 1896 it was still the largest repository of books in the world.

The library is a public establishment under the Ministry of Culture and the national repository of all that is published in France, which by law must be deposited there. President François Mitterrand announced a new library on 14 July 1988; the architect Dominique Perrault designed it, and after cost overruns that earned it the nickname Très Grande Bibliothèque it was inaugurated on 15 December 1996.

Its Manuscripts department houses the largest collection of medieval and modern manuscripts worldwide, including about 5,000 Ancient Greek manuscripts. Gallica, its digital library established in October 1997, makes freely available millions of books, manuscripts, newspapers, images, maps and recordings.
bicycle: The dandy horse, also called the Draisienne or Laufmaschine, was invented by the German Baron Karl von Drais, who introduced it to the public in Mannheim in 1817 and in Paris in 1818. It was the first means of human transport to use only two wheels in tandem and is regarded as the first bicycle, though it had no pedals: the rider sat astride a wooden frame and pushed it along with their feet while steering the front wheel. A Scottish blacksmith, Kirkpatrick MacMillan, may have built the first mechanically propelled two-wheeled vehicle in 1839, although the claim is often disputed.

In the early 1860s the Frenchmen Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement added a mechanical crank drive with pedals to an enlarged front wheel, the velocipede, which was the first to be mass-produced. In 1869 the Scotsman Thomas McCall built a rod-driven velocipede with rear-wheel drive, and Eugène Meyer of Paris patented a method of tensioning wire spokes that allowed stronger, lighter wheels. The velocipede developed into the penny-farthing, with a metal frame, wire-spoked wheels and solid rubber tyres. Britain's first cycle factory grew from the Coventry Sewing Machine Company's order for a Michaux cycle in 1868, which led to the Coventry Model.

A bicycle is a human-powered or motor-assisted, pedal-driven, single-track vehicle with two wheels attached to a frame, one behind the other. The basic shape of the upright or safety bicycle has changed little since the first chain-driven model was developed around 1885. Most have a diamond frame, a truss of two triangles. Historically, women's frames had a top tube joined lower on the seat tube, so that a rider could mount and dismount in a skirt or dress; this is called a step-through or open frame.

It is the most efficient human-powered means of transport in terms of the energy a person must spend to cover a distance. Up to 99 per cent of the energy the rider puts into the pedals reaches the wheels, though gearing may reduce this by 10 to 15 per cent. Cycling takes about four-fifths less energy than walking the same distance.

The bicycle had a considerable effect on society, in both culture and industry. Around the turn of the 20th century it reduced crowding in inner-city tenements by letting workers commute from more spacious suburban homes, and it reduced dependence on horses. It also allowed people to travel into the country for leisure, being three times as energy efficient as walking and three to four times as fast.

Several components that played a key role in the development of the car were first invented for the bicycle: ball bearings, pneumatic tyres, chain-driven sprockets and tension-spoked wheels. The first bicycle sharing scheme was the White Bicycle plan in Amsterdam in 1965.
biella: Biella is the capital of the province of the same name in Piedmont, about 80 kilometres north-east of Turin and at about the same distance west-north-west of Milan. It lies in the foothills of the Alps, in an area of springs and lakes fed by glaciers and watered by the streams Elvo, Oropa and Cervo. The first inhabitants were Ligurians and Celts. A Ligurian people, the Victimuli, exploited gold veins near the Elvo on the plain of the Bessa, an activity that continued into the early Middle Ages.

The name appears for the first time as Bugella in a document of 826, recording the donation of Bugella to Count Busone by Louis the Pious. On 12 April 1160 Uguccione, bishop of Vercelli, granted trade privileges to anyone living on the Piazzo hill as a refuge from the warfare between Guelphs and Ghibellines of Vercelli, which was the birth of the Borgo del Piazzo. A revolt destroyed the bishop's castle in the 14th century, and Biella and its dependent communes came under the House of Savoy.

In the 14th and 15th centuries the Visconti family competed with Savoy for the region. The French occupied Biella in 1704, and in 1706 the Biellese soldier Pietro Micca saved nearby Turin from a siege, but died doing so. The French occupied the town again in 1798 and annexed it after the Battle of Marengo, and the Congress of Vienna returned it to Savoy. In 1859 Biella was besieged by the Austrians until Garibaldi ended the siege.

The statutes of Biella already refer to the guilds of wool workers and weavers in 1245, and the region's high pastures and abundant water suited the trade. A silk factory built in 1695 was converted in 1835 into a wool factory with mechanical looms, putting Biella at the forefront of the industry.

Biella remains an important wool processing and textile centre; Ermenegildo Zegna and Cerruti 1881 are among its firms. Its cathedral grew around the Romanesque baptistery of the 10th and 11th centuries, which houses 13th-century frescoes. Nearby, the Sanctuary of Oropa, a site of pilgrimage, became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003.
biscay: Biscay lies on the south shore of the Bay of Biscay and is bordered by Cantabria and the province of Burgos to the west, Gipuzkoa to the east and Álava to the south. The southern ranges of the Basque Mountains form a continuous barrier, with passes no lower than 600 metres, and the water divide between the Atlantic and Mediterranean basins. The middle section is occupied by the valleys of the Nervión, the Ibaizabal and the Kadagua. The coast is usually high, with cliffs and small inlets, and its main features are the estuary of Bilbao and the estuary of Gernika. The climate is oceanic, with high precipitation all year.

Biscay has been inhabited since the Middle Paleolithic, and its caves hold cave paintings, those of Santimamiñe showing bison, horses, goats and deer. Roman geographers placed two tribes there, the Caristii and the Autrigones, who are thought to have spoken Basque. The Roman presence had little impact, and the Basque language and traditions survived. The name Biscay first appears in the Chronicle of Alfonso III in the late 9th century, and the territory was then controlled by the Kingdom of Navarre.

The house of Haro, leaders of the pro-Castilian lords, was granted the rule of the newly created Biscay, and tradition names Iñigo López as its first Lord in 1043. The lordship later passed by inheritance to John I of Castile and became one of the titles of the king of Castile. Each lord had to swear to defend the fuero, the Biscayan laws derived from Navarrese and Basque customary rights, which held that sovereignty lay with the Biscayans. Lords and later kings swore the statutes to the oak of Gernika, where the assembly of the lordship sits.

In 1511 the kings granted the port of Bilbao privileges for trade with the ports of the Spanish Empire, and it was already the main Castilian harbour, shipping wool to Flanders. The Carlist Wars of the 19th century grew in part from the desire to keep foral rights, and the victory of the anti-Carlists brought successive cuts to Biscay's autonomy. Iron ore discovered in the 1850s brought foreign investment and rapid industrialization. In 1937 German aircraft under Franco's control destroyed the town of Gernika, and Bilbao fell some months later. The 1979 Statute of Guernica created the Autonomous Community of the Basque Country.

Biscay is a province of the Basque Autonomous Community with its capital and largest city at Bilbao. Its name is Bizkaia in Basque and Vizcaya in Spanish, and its institutions are the Juntas Generales and the Foral Diputation. Its population is 1,167,233.
bishkek: Bishkek stands at an altitude of about 800 metres, just off the northern fringe of the Kyrgyz Ala-Too Range, an extension of the Tian Shan whose peaks rise to 4,895 metres. North of the city a fertile, gently undulating steppe stretches far into Kazakhstan, and the river Chüy drains most of the area. The central city is laid out on a rectangular grid, with wide boulevards, marble-faced public buildings and many Soviet-style apartment blocks, and narrow irrigation channels line most streets to water the shade trees.

The site began as a caravan rest stop on a branch of the Silk Road through the Tian Shan, possibly founded by the Sogdians. In 1825 the khan of Kokand fortified it with a mud fort, Pishpek, to control the caravan routes and collect tribute from the Kyrgyz. Russian forces under Colonel Apollon Zimmermann later took and razed the fort, and a Russian settlement with the original name Pishpek was established on the site in 1868, within the General Governorship of Russian Turkestan.

In 1925 the Kara-Kirghiz Autonomous Oblast was created and Pishpek became its capital. In 1926 the city was renamed Frunze after Mikhail Frunze, a Bolshevik military leader and associate of Lenin who was born there. It became capital of the Kirghiz Soviet Socialist Republic in 1936. Until the mid-1990s Russians and other people of European descent were the majority of the population; in the 1970 census the Kyrgyz were only 12.3 per cent. The city was renamed Bishkek on 5 February 1991, and Kyrgyzstan became independent later that year. One tradition derives the name Bishkek from the paddle used to churn fermenting milk.

Bishkek is the capital and largest city of Kyrgyzstan and of the Chüy Region, with about 1.2 million people, near the border with Kazakhstan. It is the country's financial centre and its most important cultural city, with the National Library, the Kyrgyz State Historical Museum on Ala-Too Square and the Frunze House Museum. Most residents are ethnic Kyrgyz, with a sizeable Russian minority. The Dordoy Bazaar on the north-eastern edge is a major wholesale and retail market.
bissau: Bissau lies on the estuary of the Geba River, off the Atlantic Ocean. The land around the city is extremely low-lying, and the river is accessible to ocean-going vessels for about 80 kilometres beyond it despite its modest discharge. The climate is tropical savanna, with almost no rain from November to May. The name may come from the name of a clan, N'nssassun, in its plural form Bôssassun.

From well before the arrival of Europeans until the early 20th century the island of Bissau was a kingdom of the Papel people. By oral tradition Mecau, a son of the king of Quinara, founded it and moved to the area with his pregnant sister, six wives and subjects of his father's kingdom. The kingdom had seven clans and was highly stratified, and the throne passed to the Bossassun clan, descended from the sister. When the Portuguese began to trade there in the 16th century the king of Bissau was among the most supportive monarchs of the region.

The city was founded in 1687 as a Portuguese trading post. The French were also active, and although King Bacompolco refused them leave to build a fort he granted them a trading factory, from which they shipped thousands of slaves. By 1696 the town had a fort, a church and a hospital. When the Portuguese tried to enforce a monopoly against the Papel policy of free trade, King Incinhate surrounded the unfinished fort, and they soon abandoned it. The Grão Pará and Maranhão Company rebuilt it in 1775 to store more slaves for shipment to Brazil, though real control stayed with the Papel kings.

Around the turn of the 20th century the Papels fiercely resisted Portuguese pacification campaigns. In 1915, after 30 years of war, the Portuguese under Teixeira Pinto and the warlord Abdul Injai defeated the Kingdom of Bissau and incorporated it into Portuguese Guinea. In 1941 the capital was moved from Bolama to Bissau. A dockworkers' strike was bloodily repressed in 1959 and pushed the nationalists towards armed resistance. After the military coup in Lisbon on 25 April, Bissau became the capital of the newly independent state.

Bissau is the capital and largest city of Guinea-Bissau, its main port and its administrative and military centre. Its attractions include the Fortaleza de São José da Amura, built by the Portuguese in the 18th century and containing the mausoleum of Amílcar Cabral, and the Pidjiguiti Memorial to the dockers killed in the strike of 3 August 1959.
bitola: Bitola lies in the southwestern part of North Macedonia, in the southern part of the Pelagonia valley, surrounded by the Baba, Nidže and Kajmakčalan mountain ranges and 14 kilometres north of the Medžitlija-Níki border crossing with Greece. The Dragor River flows through the city, which stands at 615 metres above sea level at the foot of Baba Mountain. It stands at an important junction connecting the south of the Adriatic region with the Aegean Sea and Central Europe.

The earliest organised settlements nearby are early Neolithic tells near the village of Porodin, first inhabited around 6000 BCE. In antiquity the region was Lynkestis, part of Upper Macedonia, and Heraclea Lyncestis was founded by Philip II of Macedon by the middle of the 4th century BCE. Slavic tribes settled the area in the 6th and 7th centuries and built a fortress around their settlement. Bitola was part of the First Bulgarian Empire from the middle of the 8th to the early 11th centuries and was its last capital, in 1015 to 1018; the Bitola inscription is related to the fortress built in 1015. It then returned to the Byzantine Empire and was briefly part of the Serbian Empire in the 14th century.

The Ottomans conquered the city in the mid-1380s, and it was part of the Ottoman Empire as Monastir until 1912. It was the last capital of Ottoman Rumelia, from 1836 to 1867, and the many European consulates earned it the name City of Consuls. The region was a stronghold of the Ilinden Uprising of 1903, planned in Smilevo in May. In the First Balkan War the Battle of Monastir, from 16 to 19 November 1912, led to Serbian occupation, and the Treaty of Bucharest in 1913 ceded Monastir to Serbia, when its official name became Bitola.
In World War II the Germans took control on 9 April 1941, and on 11 March 1943 Bulgarian forces deported the vast majority of its Jewish community, 3,276 people, to Treblinka extermination camp.

Bitola is an administrative, cultural, industrial, commercial and educational centre of southwestern North Macedonia. Its population was historically diverse: about 37,500 at the end of the 19th century, including Aromanians, a Muslim population, a Jewish community of Sephardic origin and Slavic speakers divided between the Bulgarian Exarchate and the Greek Patriarchate.

The ruins of Heraclea Lyncestis lie 2 kilometres from the centre. Ottoman monuments include the covered bazaar, the Gazi Hajdar Kadi Mosque of the early 1560s, ascribed to the architect Mimar Sinan, and the Deboj Bath. The Church of Saint Demetrius was built in 1830 with contributions from local merchants and craftsmen. The St. Clement of Ohrid University of Bitola was founded in 1979.
black-forest: The Black Forest is a large forested mountain range in Baden-Württemberg, bounded by the Rhine Valley to the west and south and close to the borders with France and Switzerland. It is the source of the Danube and the Neckar. It is about 160 kilometres long and up to 50 kilometres wide, with an area of about 6,009 square kilometres, and its highest peak is the Feldberg at 1,493 metres. The gentle eastern slopes contrast with the steeply falling terrain in the west that drops into the Upper Rhine Graben. It consists of a cover of sandstone on a core of gneiss and granite, and it was covered by glaciers in the last glacial period, which left tarns such as the Mummelsee.

In ancient times the range was known as Abnoba mons, after the Celtic deity Abnoba, and in Roman times as Silva Marciana, from the Germanic marka, border; it probably marked the border area of the Marcomanni, a part of the Suebi. Apart from Roman settlements on the perimeter, such as the baths at Badenweiler, mines near Badenweiler and Sulzburg and the Roman road of the Kinzig valley, the colonization was carried out not by the Romans but by the Alemanni. They settled the valleys first and then increasingly higher areas, so that by the end of the 10th century the first settlements stood in the red sandstone region. Rötenbach, for example, was first mentioned in 819.

The ore deposits supported mining, and for several centuries logs were rafted down the Enz, Kinzig, Murg, Nagold and Rhine. This trade boomed in the 18th century and led to large-scale clearances. Most of the long, straight pine logs went to the Netherlands for shipbuilding and were called Dutchmen; used there as piles for houses, they support many historic buildings in Amsterdam. Rafting largely ended in the late 19th century with the railways and roads.

Charcoal burners, potash boilers and glassmakers also lived from the timber. Because the valleys were relatively inaccessible, industrialization arrived late. In winter many farmers made wooden cuckoo clocks, which developed in the 19th century into a precision engineering and watch industry, and the Baden state government founded a clockmaking school at Furtwangen in 1850.

The Black Forest is mainly rural, with many scattered villages and a few large towns, and the main dialect is Alemannic. It is known for its farmhouses with sweeping half-hipped roofs, the Bollenhut headdress worn in villages of the Kinzig valley, wood carving, the cuckoo clock, Black Forest ham and the Black Forest gâteau. In the 19th and early 20th centuries its rural beauty attracted artists such as Hans Thoma. Tourism is now the primary industry, and several ruined military fortifications date back to the 17th century.
blantyre: Blantyre lies in the Shire Highlands, at the geographical centre of Malawi's Southern Region, and covers an area of 228 km2. The city stands in hilly country at elevations from about 780 to 1,612 metres. Mount Soche, Ndirande mountain, Chiradzulu mountain and Michiru Mountain surround it, and rivers and streams rise in these hills and radiate from the city. The rainy season runs from November to April, and the dry season from May to October.

The mission was founded in 1876 by the Church of Scotland. The site was chosen by the British missionary Henry Henderson, who was joined there on 23 October 1876 by Dr T. T. Macklin and others. Macklin took over the leadership and began building. The first ordained minister, Rev. Duff MacDonald, arrived in 1878. The first missionaries faced local opposition, and three of them were recalled. From 1881 to 1898 the mission was run by David Clement Scott, who built the Church of St Michael and All Angels between 1888 and 1891 with a team of local workmen who had no knowledge of European building techniques. Scott also compiled an Encyclopaedic Dictionary of the Mang'anja Language, later edited by his successor Alexander Hetherwick.

A trading company grew up beside the mission. The Livingstonia Central Africa Trading Company, founded in Glasgow in 1877 and renamed the African Lakes Corporation in 1878, moved in 1881 to Mandala, across the River Mudi. Its Mandala House survives as a National Monument and is the oldest building in Malawi. Blantyre became a British consular station in 1883 and a municipality by 1895, Malawi's oldest. Its commerce began with the colonial trade in ivory, and by the First World War its people included Africans from neighbouring districts and South Asian traders.

Until 1905 the town's growth was confined to three areas within 2 km of each other: the mission, Mandala, and the government and commercial triangle. Limbe began to develop in 1906, after the Shire Highlands Railways Company set up its headquarters and workshops there and the Imperial Tobacco Group built a packaging and grading factory nearby. Indian wholesale and retail shops multiplied, and by 1910 Limbe had surpassed Blantyre. The two towns were merged into one city in 1956.

Blantyre is Malawi's centre of finance and commerce and its second largest city, with 800,264 people at the 2018 census. It is the capital of the Southern Region and of Blantyre District. The Malawi Stock Exchange, opened in November 1996, stands on Victoria Avenue. The city holds eight National Monuments, mostly historic buildings, and the Michiru Mountain Conservation Area lies among its hills.
blood-transfusion: Recorded research into blood transfusion began in the 17th century, after William Harvey's experiments on the circulation of the blood, with successful experiments in transfusion between animals. Working at the Royal Society in the 1660s, the physician Richard Lower devised methods of cross-circulation in animals, using closed arteriovenous connections to prevent clotting. In his own account, towards the end of February 1665 he drew blood from a medium-sized dog until its strength was nearly gone, then introduced blood from a larger mastiff fastened alongside it. The animal recovered with no sign of discomfort. Attempts to transfuse animal blood into humans gave variable and often fatal results.

Blood transfusion is the intravenous transfer of blood products into a human or other animal. Except in major trauma, whole blood is rarely used in modern practice, and instead components such as red blood cells, plasma and platelets are transfused. Donated blood is separated by centrifugation into red cells, plasma and platelets, and plasma can be processed further into albumin, clotting factor concentrates and immunoglobulins. Red cells are typically stored at 1 to 6 °C, platelets at 20 to 24 °C with continuous agitation, and plasma frozen at −18 °C or lower.

Only in 1901, when the Austrian Karl Landsteiner discovered three human blood groups, O, A and B, did transfusion gain a scientific basis and become safer. He found that mixing incompatible blood provokes an immune response in which the red cells clump. He won the Nobel Prize in Physiology and Medicine in 1930. George Washington Crile is credited with the first surgery using a direct transfusion, in 1906 at St. Alexis Hospital in Cleveland.

Before a transfusion the recipient's blood is typed for its ABO and Rh status and screened for antibodies. Most acute haemolytic reactions come from clerical errors or mistaken typing. Blood type O negative is compatible with anyone and is kept for emergencies.
blue-nile: The Blue Nile rises at Gish Abay in Ethiopia, where it is called the Abay, and flows through Lake Tana and out into a canyon about 400 kilometres long. The canyon, cut in the Ethiopian Highlands to a depth of some 1,500 metres, is a tremendous obstacle to travel between northern and southern Ethiopia. The Blue Nile Falls, called Tis Abay, meaning great smoke, lie at its start. The river then runs about 650 kilometres through Sudan and joins the White Nile at Khartoum. It supplies 80 to 86 percent of the Nile's water in the rainy season, and its floods contributed to the fertility of the Nile Valley and so to the rise of ancient Egypt.

The Egyptian fear that Ethiopia might block the river shaped the long relationship between the two countries. Ethiopia depended on the Coptic Orthodox Patriarchate of Alexandria for its metropolitan, and from the 11th century the threat to block the river helped secure the appointment of Egyptian metropolitans, though neither diversion nor large-scale use of the water was ever attempted. Emperor Amda Seyon I first occupied the basin and began spreading Christianity there. Later Solomonic emperors, among them Dawit II, Yeshaq I and Zara Yaqob, used their control of the river as a diplomatic tool and identified it with the biblical Gihon.

The Spanish Jesuit Pedro Páez reached the source on 21 April 1618, and the Scottish explorer James Bruce reached the source of the Nile in 1770. The canyon defeated outsiders' attempts to follow the river, from Frédéric Cailliaud in 1821 to W. W. Macmillan in 1902. In 1968 a team of 60 British and Ethiopian servicemen and scientists, led by John Blashford-Snell at the request of Haile Selassie, made the first full descent from Lake Tana to a point near the Sudanese border.

The Blue Nile is vital to Egypt, which receives over 85 percent of its Nile streamflow from it. Its floods in lower Egypt ended with the completion of the Aswan Dam in 1970. In Sudan the Roseires and Sennar dams supply hydroelectric power and irrigate the Gezira Scheme, noted for its cotton. The river's summer floods carry a great amount of silt, which turns its water dark brown or almost black.
bob-marley: Robert Nesta Marley was born on 6 February 1945 at the farm of his maternal grandfather in Nine Mile, in Saint Ann Parish, then the Colony of Jamaica. His father, Norval Sinclair Marley, was a white Englishman who supervised a subdivision of land for war veteran housing. His mother, Cedella Malcolm, was an Afro-Jamaican aged 18 when they married. Norval gave little financial support and died when Marley was 10. Marley began to play music with Neville Livingston, later known as Bunny Wailer, at school in Nine Mile.

In 1963 Marley, Bunny Wailer, Peter Tosh and others formed a group called the Teenagers, which became the Wailing Rudeboys, the Wailing Wailers and finally the Wailers. Their single Simmer Down for Coxsone Dodd's label became a Jamaican number one in February 1964, and they recorded regularly at Studio One. By 1966 the core of the group was the trio of Marley, Wailer and Tosh.

In 1972 Chris Blackwell of Island Records offered the Wailers an advance of £4,000 to record an album, seeing in Marley the rebel image needed to reach a rock audience. They recorded Catch a Fire at Harry J's studio in Kingston, and with Burnin', both 1973, it brought them international attention. Marley then carried on as Bob Marley and the Wailers, with the I Threes, Judy Mowatt, Marcia Griffiths and his wife Rita, as backing singers. A live version of No Woman, No Cry was his first hit outside Jamaica, in 1975.

Marley survived an assassination attempt at his home in Jamaica in 1976, believed to have been politically motivated. He left Jamaica at the end of that year and spent two years in England, where he recorded Exodus. His album Survival in 1979 reflected his support for African struggles, and in April 1980 he was invited to perform at Zimbabwe's independence celebration.

In July 1977 Marley was diagnosed with acral lentiginous melanoma, a skin cancer beneath the nail of his right big toe. He declined to have the toe amputated, citing religious beliefs, and continued to tour. A longtime follower of Rastafari, he was baptised into the Ethiopian Orthodox Church on 4 November 1980 and died on 11 May 1981. He received a state funeral in Jamaica.
bodhisattva: Bodhisattva combines the Sanskrit words bodhi, awakening or enlightenment, and sattva, being. The etymology of the Indic terms is not fully understood, but many modern scholars read the compound as a being seeking or destined for awakening. In the early Buddhist discourses the Buddha regularly speaks of himself as an unawakened bodhisatta, and the term refers to Gautama Buddha in his previous lives and as a young man working towards liberation.

By the time the tradition had divided into competing schools, the idea of a bodhisattva vehicle as a distinct path, separate from that of the arhat and the solitary buddha, was widespread among the Theravāda, Sarvāstivāda and Mahāsāṃghika schools. It appears in sources of the 2nd century CE such as the Avadānaśataka and the Divyāvadāna. The Theravāda Buddhavaṃsa, from the 1st or 2nd century BCE, tells how Gautama received from the past Buddha Dīpaṃkara a prediction of his future Buddhahood.

In the early schools and in modern Theravāda Buddhism a bodhisattva is someone who has resolved to become a Buddha and has been confirmed in this by a living Buddha, and such people are seen as rare. In Mahāyāna Buddhism the term refers to anyone who has generated bodhicitta, the compassionate wish to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of all beings. The path is open to everyone, and Mahāyāna Buddhists encourage all to follow it.

The bodhisattva practises the perfections (pāramitās), including the perfection of wisdom and skilful means, and the four divine abodes of loving-kindness, compassion, empathetic joy and equanimity. The Mahāyāna sutras generally depict the path as lasting many lifetimes across many aeons. Some texts say a bodhisattva must postpone final nirvana until all beings are liberated, and the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra gives the vow: I shall not enter into final nirvana before all beings have been liberated. Mahāyāna writers held this path to be higher than that of the arhat.

Mahāyāna Buddhists venerate advanced bodhisattvas, among them Avalokiteshvara, Maitreya and Manjushri. Guanyin, a female form of Avalokiteshvara, is the most widely revered bodhisattva in East Asian Buddhism, and Tara is the most important female bodhisattva in Tibetan Buddhism. Followers of Tibetan Buddhism consider the Dalai Lamas and the Karmapas to be emanations of Chenrezig, and several Japanese schools regard their founders, such as Kukai and Nichiren, as bodhisattvas.

Four mountains in Chinese Buddhism are held to be places of awakening for bodhisattvas: Mount Putuo for Guanyin, Mount Emei for Samantabhadra, Mount Wutai for Mañjuśrī and Mount Jiuhua for Kṣitigarbha. Bodhisattvas are also venerated in Theravāda lands, and the recounting of the Jataka tales of Gautama's past lives remains popular there.
bodleian-library: The first purpose-built library known at Oxford was founded in the 14th century under the will of Thomas Cobham, Bishop of Worcester (d. 1327): a small collection of chained books kept above the north side of the University Church of St Mary the Virgin. When Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester, gave a great collection of manuscripts between 1435 and 1437 a larger room was needed, and one was built above the Divinity School and completed in 1488; it is still known as Duke Humfrey's Library.

In the later 16th century the library declined. Its furniture was sold, and only three of Duke Humphrey's original books remained. In 1598 Thomas Bodley, a former fellow of Merton College, wrote to the Vice Chancellor offering to restore it at his own cost. The room was refitted, Bodley gave some of his own books, and the library was formally reopened on 8 November 1602 with around 2,000 books.

In 1610 Bodley made an agreement with the Stationers' Company, suggested by the first librarian, Thomas James, that a copy of every book registered with the company would be placed in the library. The collection grew so fast that the building was extended between 1610 and 1612, and the Schools Quadrangle was built between 1613 and 1619. By 1620 there were 16,000 items. John Selden left his books and manuscripts to the library in 1654. Until the establishment of the British Museum in 1753 the Bodleian was effectively the national library of England.

The library took over the neighbouring Radcliffe Camera in 1860, and the Copyright Act of 1911 continued the Stationers' agreement by making it a library of legal deposit. Its holdings passed one million books in 1914. The New Bodleian, designed by Sir Giles Gilbert Scott, was completed in 1940; rebuilt behind its original façade, it reopened as the Weston Library on 21 March 2015.

The Bodleian works principally as a reference library, and documents may not be taken from the reading rooms. New readers must agree to a formal declaration not to remove, mark or damage anything in the library, nor to bring fire or flame into it. Its head is known as Bodley's Librarian; 25 people have held the office. Since 2000 it has been the largest member of a group of Oxford libraries, called the Bodleian Libraries since 2010. With over 13 million printed items it is the second-largest library in Britain after the British Library, and its principal store is at South Marston.
boethius: Boethius was born in Rome to the Anicii, a wealthy and influential family that included the emperors Petronius Maximus and Olybrius, though it had lost much of its influence in the years before his birth. His grandfather of the same name died in 454 during the palace plot against Flavius Aetius, and his father, Manlius Boethius, consul in 487, died while he was still young. The patrician Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus adopted and raised him, introduced him to philosophy and literature, and later became his father-in-law.

Taking inspiration from Plato's Republic, Boethius left his scholarly pursuits to enter the service of Theodoric the Great, whom he had first met in 500 when the king stayed in Rome for six months. He became a senator by the age of 25 and a consul in 510. His earliest documented tasks were to investigate a charge that the paymaster of Theodoric's bodyguards had debased the coins of their pay, to produce a water clock as a gift for King Gundobad of the Burgundians and to recruit a lyre player for Clovis, King of the Franks.

Boethius set out to translate all the works of Aristotle and Plato from Greek into Latin and to reconcile their teaching with Christian theology. His completed translations of Aristotle's works on logic were the only significant portions of Aristotle available in Latin Christendom from the sixth century until the 12th. He also wrote commentaries, treatises on logic, handbooks on arithmetic and music, and theological treatises, among them one against Eutyches and Nestorius.

In 523 Boethius fell from power. At a meeting of the Royal Council in Verona the referendarius Cyprianus accused the former consul Caecina Decius Faustus Albinus of treasonous correspondence with Justin I, and Boethius defended him, declaring that if Albinus was guilty then so was the whole senate. Imprisoned at Pavia, he was executed in 524. In prison he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, a dialogue with Philosophy personified as a woman, which King Alfred translated into Old English and Chaucer later into English.

Boethius was regarded as a Christian martyr by later generations; his feast day is 23 October, and his cult at Pavia was confirmed in 1883. Edward Kennard Rand called him the last of the Roman philosophers and the first of the scholastic theologians.
bohemia: Bohemia is the westernmost and largest historical region of the Czech Republic, with an area of 52,065 square kilometres. The name derives from the Boii, a Celtic people; Roman authors refer to their former land as Boiohaemum, the earliest mention being in Tacitus. After the Boii left, Suebic peoples, among them the Marcomanni under their king Marobodus, became dominant there. Slavic tribes arrived from about the sixth century, and the Czech name Čechy comes from the Czechs who settled the area. Its borders were mostly marked by mountain ranges such as the Bohemian Forest, the Ore Mountains and the Giant Mountains.

In the 9th century Bohemia was part of Great Moravia under Svatopluk I, and when that state collapsed the Přemyslid dynasty ruled, entering semivassalage to the Frankish rulers. After the victory at Lechfeld in 955 Boleslaus I of Bohemia was granted Moravia by Otto the Great. The title of king became hereditary under Ottokar I in 1198, and Ottokar II conquered a short-lived empire containing modern Austria and Slovenia. Substantial German immigration began in the mid-13th century. The House of Luxembourg took the throne with John I in 1310, and his son Charles IV, king from 1346, founded Charles University in Prague two years later and was the first king of Bohemia elected Holy Roman Emperor.

Jan Hus was executed on 6 July 1415, despite a promise of protection from Emperor Sigismund, and the Hussite Wars followed, led first by Jan Žižka and then by Prokop the Great. The Utraquists defeated the Taborites at Lipany in 1434. After Louis II died at Mohács in 1526, Ferdinand I of Austria became king and Bohemia joined the Habsburg monarchy. The Bohemian Revolt of 1618 began the Thirty Years' War; after the defeat at White Mountain in 1620, 27 leaders of the estates and the rector Jan Jesenius were executed on 21 June 1621. A Czech National Revival began at the end of the 18th century.

After the First World War all of Bohemia became the core of Czechoslovakia. The Munich Agreement of 1938 gave the Sudetenland to Nazi Germany, and in 1939 the rest was occupied as the Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia. After 1945 the vast majority of the Bohemian Germans were expelled. In 1949 the country was divided into administrative regions that did not follow the historical borders, and since the breakup of Czechoslovakia in 1993 Bohemia has lain in the Czech Republic. It has about 6.9 million of the republic's 10.9 million inhabitants, and the historical land names survive in municipal and geographical names.
