bokmal: Until about 1300 the written language of Norway, Old Norwegian, was essentially the same as the other Old Norse dialects. In 1380 Norway entered a personal union with Denmark, and by the early 16th century it had lost its separate political institutions. The Reformation, which prompted Christiern Pedersen's translation of the Bible into Danish, helped a Danish written language standardise, and it displaced the remnants of written Old Norse and Norwegian in virtually all administrative documents.

Danish was used in Norway mainly in writing, but urban elites also spoke it on formal occasions. By the time the ties with Denmark were cut in 1814, a Dano-Norwegian vernacular, often called the educated daily speech, had become the mother tongue of the elites in cities such as Bergen, Kristiania and Trondheim. It was Danish with regional Norwegian pronunciation, some Norwegian vocabulary and simplified grammar.

Bokmål, literally book-tongue, is one of the two official written standards of Norwegian, alongside Nynorsk. It is a Norwegianised variety of Danish and is adopted by around 90 percent of the population of Norway. There is no countrywide standard of pronunciation: the government does not regulate spoken Bokmål, and Urban East Norwegian is generally accepted as the de facto spoken standard in Eastern Norway.

The first Bokmål orthography was officially adopted in 1907 under the name Riksmål, after being under development since 1879; its architects were Marius Nygaard and Jacob Jonathan Aars. It adapted written Danish to the Dano-Norwegian koiné of the urban elite. The school reformer Knud Knudsen, whose work was important for the 1907 orthography and a reform in 1917, is often called the father of Bokmål.

Bjørnstjerne Bjørnson proposed the name Riksmål in 1899, and a movement under his leadership organised to resist the growing influence of Nynorsk. When Aftenposten adopted the 1907 orthography in 1923, Danish writing was practically out of use in Norway. The name Bokmål was adopted by parliament in 1929, after a proposal to call the language Dano-Norwegian lost by a single vote in the Lagting.

Official policy then aimed to merge the written standards into a common Samnorsk through spelling reforms. The 1938 reform, which made many forms mandatory, was harshly criticised by the Riksmål movement, and resistance under Arnulf Øverland culminated in the 1950s. The Norwegian Academy for Language and Literature, founded in 1953, regulates the more conservative standard still called Riksmål. After the Samnorsk policy was abandoned, Riksmål and Bokmål converged, and the Academy's online dictionary covers both.
bolivia: Bolivia is a landlocked country of 1,098,581 square kilometres in central South America, the fifth largest in the continent. Its geography consists of an Andean region in the west and tropical lowlands in the east and north, and it includes the Altiplano plateau, temperate valleys, the Gran Chaco and part of the Amazon plain. Elevations range from 6,542 metres at Nevado Sajama to nearly 70 metres along the Paraguay River.

In the Andean southwest lie Lake Titicaca, the highest commercially navigable lake in the world and the largest lake in South America, and the Salar de Uyuni, the largest salt flat in the world and an important source of lithium.

Tiwanaku, with its capital at Tiwanaku in western Bolivia, dates back as early as 1500 BCE, when it was a small agricultural village. It grew to urban proportions between 600 and 800 CE and, around 400 CE, began expanding its reach into the Yungas by creating colonies, fostering trade agreements and instituting state cults. As rainfall gradually decreased, food stores shrank and the elites lost power, and Tiwanaku disappeared around 1000 CE. Between 1438 and 1527 the Inca Empire expanded from Cusco into the region.

The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire began in 1524 and was mostly completed by 1533. The territory was known as Charcas, with local government from the Audiencia de Charcas at La Plata, modern Sucre. Potosí, founded in 1545 as a mining town, became the largest city in the New World, with a population exceeding 150,000. After an unsuccessful rebellion in Sucre on 25 May 1809, sixteen years of fighting preceded the establishment of the republic. Antonio José de Sucre chose to create a new state rather than join Peru or the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata, and on 6 August 1825 named it in honour of Simón Bolívar.

The name Bolivia was approved on 3 October 1825. In the 19th and early 20th centuries the country lost peripheral territories, among them the Pacific coastal region seized by Chile in 1879. The Bolivian National Revolution of 1952 established universal suffrage and nationalised the tin mines.

La Paz is the seat of government and Sucre the constitutional capital, while Santa Cruz de la Sierra is the largest city. Bolivia is a constitutionally unitary state divided into nine departments, and since 2009 its official name has been the Plurinational State of Bolivia. Spanish is the official and predominant language, and 36 indigenous languages also have official status, of which Guaraní, Aymara and Quechua are most commonly spoken. Major archaeological ruins include Tiwanaku, El Fuerte de Samaipata, Inkallaqta and Iskanwaya.
bolsheviks: The split began with Lenin's support for a smaller party of professional revolutionaries, set out in his pamphlet What Is to Be Done?, written in 1901. At the Second Congress of the Russian Social Democratic Labour Party, held in Brussels and then London in August 1903, Lenin and Julius Martov disagreed over membership rules. Lenin, supported by Georgi Plekhanov, wanted to limit membership to those who supported the party full-time and obeyed its elected leadership; Martov would admit anyone who recognised the programme and gave regular help.

The factions were first called hard and soft. Lenin's side won the votes on most important issues and so came to be called Bolsheviks, from the Russian word for majority, and Martov's side Mensheviks, from the word for minority, though Martov's supporters had won the vote on membership and the Congress was in the end evenly split.

Between 1903 and 1912 the balance between the factions shifted and members changed sides; Plekhanov had parted ways with the Bolsheviks by 1904, and Leon Trotsky joined them only in August 1917. The Bolsheviks played a relatively minor part in the 1905 Revolution, although the Moscow Soviet was dominated by them. Attempts at reunion in 1906 and 1910 failed. In January 1912 a Prague conference of the Bolsheviks alone expelled the Mensheviks and declared the faction an independent party, the RSDLP(b).

After the February Revolution of 1917 Lenin returned to Russia and issued his April Theses, calling for no support for the Provisional Government and all power to the soviets. During the summer large numbers of radicalized workers joined, and the Bolsheviks planned the October Revolution that overthrew the government. They at first governed in coalition with the Left Socialist-Revolutionaries but increasingly centralized power and suppressed opposition during the Russian Civil War, and after 1921 the party was the sole legal party.

The Bolsheviks rested on the Leninist principles of vanguardism and democratic centralism. In 1907 most members were young: 22 percent were under 20 and 37 percent between 20 and 24. By 1905 some 62 percent were industrial workers, and 78 percent were Russian and 10 percent Jewish in 1907. Membership was 8,400 in 1905 and 46,100 by 1907.

Lenin held that revolutions must be led by people who gave their whole lives to the cause, and he paid them salaries. Unlike the Mensheviks, who relied on membership dues, the Bolsheviks also raised money through robberies, among them a bank robbery in 1907 that yielded over 250,000 roubles.
bonaventure: Bonaventure was born at Civita di Bagnoregio, not far from Viterbo, then part of the Papal States. Almost nothing is known of his childhood except the names of his parents, Giovanni di Fidanza and Maria di Ritella. He reported that in his youth he was saved from an untimely death by the prayers of Francis of Assisi, which was the main reason he later wrote the life of Francis. After entering the Franciscan Order he studied at the University of Paris, possibly under Alexander of Hales and certainly under John of Rochelle. He became a friend of Thomas Aquinas.

After defending his order against the anti-mendicant party he was elected Minister General of the Franciscans. On 24 November 1265 he was chosen Archbishop of York, but he was never consecrated and resigned in October 1266. The General Chapter of Narbonne in 1260 forbade publication of any work outside the order without permission. Modern writers have judged Roger Bacon's superiors harshly because of it, but the ban was general and aimed at Gerard of Borgo San Donnino, whose Introduction to the Eternal Gospel had been judged heretical.

Bonaventure helped secure the election of Pope Gregory X, who made him Cardinal Bishop of Albano and insisted that he attend the Second Council of Lyon in 1274. There, after contributions that led to a union of the Greek and Latin churches, he died suddenly and in suspicious circumstances. The 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia has citations suggesting poison, but the 2003 New Catholic Encyclopedia does not mention it.

His major work is the Commentary on the Sentences, written at his superiors' command when he was twenty-seven. Others include The Mind's Road to God, the Breviloquium and, for fellow Franciscans, The Tree of Life and The Triple Way. His philosophy is deeply influenced by Augustine, with Aristotelian principles added. He thought of Christ as the one true master, offering knowledge that begins in faith, develops through reason and is perfected by mystical union with God. Like Aquinas he vigorously opposed the Aristotelian notion that the world is eternal.
bonn: Bonn lies on both banks of the Rhine in North Rhine-Westphalia, about 24 kilometres south-south-east of Cologne, in the southernmost part of the Rhine-Ruhr region. It covers 141.2 square kilometres, and almost three quarters of the city lie on the left bank. In 1969 the independent towns of Bad Godesberg and Beuel and several villages were incorporated into Bonn, producing a city more than twice as large as before. Earlier, on 1 June 1904, Poppelsdorf, Endenich, Kessenich and Dottendorf had been incorporated.

People lived in the area long before the city. Evidence includes a 14,000-year-old double burial at Oberkassel and a trench and wooden palisades on the Venusberg dating to about 4080 BCE. The Roman governor Agrippa had settled the Ubii there in 38 BCE, and in 12 BCE the first fortified Roman camp on the Rhine was built. In 1989 the city marked its 2,000th anniversary, counting from that camp. Bonn was later part of the Roman province Germania Inferior.

From 1597 to 1794 it was the capital of the Electorate of Cologne and the residence of the Archbishops and Prince-electors of Cologne. The Altes Rathaus, in Rococo style, was built in 1737 under Clemens August of Bavaria, and the Kurfürstliches Schloss, the prince-elector's residence, is now the main building of the University of Bonn.

Bonn served as the capital of West Germany from 1949 until 1990 and as the seat of government of reunified Germany until 1999, when the government moved to Berlin. Historians often call the period of West Germany's capital there the Bonn Republic. The Basic Law, Germany's constitution, was made in the city. A political compromise after reunification, the Berlin-Bonn Act, kept a significant federal presence in Bonn.

Bonn is a federal city, with the title Bundesstadt, and a population exceeding 320,000. It holds the primary seats of six federal ministries and twenty federal authorities, and the global headquarters of Deutsche Post DHL and Deutsche Telekom. Twenty United Nations institutions have their seats there, among them the secretariats of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the Convention to Combat Desertification. Beethoven's birthplace stands in Bonngasse near the market place, and he was baptized at St Remigius.
book-of-genesis: The name Genesis comes from the Greek for origin, the title of the book in the Septuagint; in Hebrew it is called Bereshit, In the beginning, after its first word. Genesis was written anonymously. Jewish and Christian tradition attributes the whole Pentateuch to Moses, but modern scholars believe it was the work of many authors and editors writing much later. Internal contradictions suggest this, among them two creation narratives.

By the end of the 19th century most scholars held the documentary hypothesis, in which four sources, the Yahwist, the Elohist, the Deuteronomist and the Priestly source, were combined by editors. Since the 1980s revisions have been proposed. Most scholars now agree that Genesis reached its final form after the Babylonian exile. The original manuscripts are lost, and surviving copies vary across the Masoretic Text, the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint and the Dead Sea Scrolls.

Genesis falls into the primeval history of chapters 1 to 11 and the ancestral history of chapters 12 to 50. The first includes two creation stories, Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, Cain and Abel, the Flood and the Tower of Babel. God sends the Flood because human sin has corrupted the world, sparing the righteous Noah and his family in an ark, and then makes a covenant with Noah marked by the rainbow.

The second part follows Abraham, who at God's command travels from Ur of the Chaldees to Canaan, then his son Isaac and his grandson Jacob, whose name is changed to Israel. Through Jacob's son Joseph, sold into slavery by his brothers and later made second in command in Egypt, the family goes down to Egypt, where the book ends. Scholars generally see a divine promise of offspring, blessing and land as the theme of the patriarchal stories.

Jewish and Christian chronologers added up the spans in its genealogies to calculate the age of the world, and this reckoning underlies the Hebrew and Byzantine calendars. From the 16th to the 19th century scholars in Europe treated Genesis as factual and tried to fit new findings in geology to its account; Johann Jakob Scheuchzer took fossils to be creatures killed in the Flood. This reading lost favour as evidence mounted that the Earth was far older. Its statement that humanity is created in the image of God became a foundational theme within Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
book-of-jeremiah: The Book of Jeremiah is the second of the Latter Prophets in the Hebrew Bible. Its opening verses name it as the words of Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, a priest from the town of Anatot, to whom the word of God came in the days of King Josiah. His career covered the last years of the kingdom of Judah: Josiah's reforms, Babylon's destruction of Assyria, a brief period in which Egypt made Judah a vassal, and Babylon's defeat of Egypt in 605 BCE, which left Judah a Babylonian vassal. Judah revolted twice more, and the second revolt ended with the fall of Jerusalem and the end of the kingdom.

The book falls roughly into six parts: the core of Jeremiah's message in chapters 1 to 25, biography and encounters with other prophets in 26 to 29, promises of restoration in 30 to 33, the fall of Jerusalem in 34 to 45, oracles against the nations in 46 to 51, and an appendix retelling the Second Book of Kings. Its poetic oracles speak of Israel's unfaithfulness and call for repentance. Jeremiah presents the covenant between God and Israel as conditional, and chapter 31 looks to a new covenant that will not be broken. The book also records sign-acts, such as wearing an ox yoke and buying a field at Anathoth, and shows the prophet taunted, jailed and thrown into a pit.

The book survives in two related versions, the Masoretic Hebrew text and the Greek of the Septuagint, which is about one eighth shorter. Both forms were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, and most scholars hold that the Hebrew behind the Greek is older. Authentic oracles are probably in the poetic sections of chapters 1 to 25, while the whole has been heavily edited by followers, perhaps including the scribe Baruch, and by later Deuteronomists. Second Temple Judaism attributed to Jeremiah the Book of Baruch, Lamentations and the Letter of Jeremiah. Early Christians based their understanding of Jesus as the bearer of a new covenant on chapter 31.
bora-bora: The main island is the remnant of an extinct volcano that was active in the Upper Pliocene, between 3.45 and 3.10 million years ago, and was later partly depressed and strongly eroded. It measures only 8 km from north to south and 5 km from east to west. Mount Otemanu, at 727 metres, is its highest point, and Mount Pahia rises to 661 metres. The bay of Tuuraapuo was the volcano's main crater, and its collapsed south-western edge survives as the islets Toopua and Toopua-iti.

A lagoon surrounds the island and is separated from the sea by a barrier reef with a single opening, the Teavanui Passage, west of the main island. To the east and north the reef carries islets of coral debris and sand, called motu. The main settlement, Vaitape, lies on the western side.

The island's old name in Tahitian, Porapora mai te pora, means created by the gods, often shortened to Porapora, first born. The Dutch explorer Jacob Roggeveen sighted it in 1722, and he and his crew adopted the form Bora Bora, which has stood on Western maps since. Polynesian settlers had arrived around the 3rd century CE. James Cook sighted the island on 29 July 1769 with the help of the Tahitian navigator Tupaia. The London Missionary Society arrived in 1820, and a Protestant church was founded in 1890. Bora Bora was an independent kingdom until 1888, when France annexed it as a colony and forced its last queen, Teriimaevarua III, to abdicate.

In the Second World War the United States chose Bora Bora as a supply base for the South Pacific. Under Operation Bobcat, nine ships brought 18,000 tonnes of equipment and nearly 7,000 soldiers, who built an oil depot, an airstrip, a seaplane base and defences, including at least eight 7-inch guns served by the 13th Coast Artillery Regiment. The island saw no combat and the American presence went uncontested throughout the war. The base closed officially on 2 June 1946. The airstrip, on Motu Mute, was never enlarged for large aircraft but was French Polynesia's only international airport until Faa'a International Airport opened next to Papeete in 1960.

Bora Bora forms part of the commune of Bora-Bora, which also includes the atoll of Tupai, in the Leeward Islands of the Society Islands of French Polynesia. Its land area is 30.55 km2, and Tahitian and French are the main languages. The economy rests almost wholly on tourism. Hotel Bora Bora opened in 1961, and the first over-water bungalows were built nine years later. The eight American guns remain in the area.
bornholm: Bornholm lies in the Baltic Sea east of the rest of Denmark, south of Sweden, north-east of Germany and north of Poland. It is known as the sunshine island for its weather and the rock island for its geology, which is granite except along the southern coast. In Old Norse the island was Borgundarholmr, a name related to words for height and rock, because it rises high from the sea. Its early names include Burgendaland in the 9th century, and some scholars believe the Burgundians took their name from it.

Strategically placed, Bornholm has been fought over for centuries. It has usually been ruled by Denmark but also by Sweden and by Lübeck, to which Frederick I of Denmark pawned it for fifty years from 1525, in payment for its support in his winning the Danish throne. Swedish forces conquered it during the Torstenson War in 1645, but it was returned to Denmark. In 1658 Denmark ceded it to Sweden under the Treaty of Roskilde, along with the rest of Skåneland, Bohuslän and Trøndelag. A revolt broke out the same year and culminated on 8 December 1658, when Villum Clausen shot the Swedish commander Johan Printzensköld. The islanders then handed the island back to the Danish kings.

German forces occupied Denmark on 9 April 1940. On 22 August 1942 a V-1 flying bomb crashed on the island during a test, one of the first signs to British Intelligence of German flying-bomb development. Soviet aircraft bombed the main towns on 7 and 8 May 1945, and Soviet troops landed on 9 May, when the German garrison of about 12,000 surrendered after a short fight. The Soviet forces left on 5 April 1946. Sweden afterwards gave aid to rebuild Rønne and Nexø.

Bornholm is a Danish island, and Rønne is its largest town and seat. With Ertholmene it is the last remaining Danish territory in Skåneland east of Øresund. The ruin of Hammershus at the north-western tip is the largest medieval fortress in northern Europe. The island has 15 medieval churches, four of them round churches, and at Rispebjerg are remains of Neolithic sun temples and Iron Age earthworks. In the early 20th century it drew artists who formed the Bornholm school of painters.
borobudur: Borobudur stands in Magelang Regency in Central Java, about 40 kilometres northwest of Yogyakarta, between the twin volcanoes Sindoro-Sumbing and Merbabu-Merapi and the Progo and Elo rivers. Scholars following de Casparis conclude that the Sanjaya and Sailendra dynasties shared power in central Java for a century and a half, with alternating succession traced from 732 until 882, and that many Hindu and Buddhist monuments rose around the Kedu Plain in that period. Evidence suggests that Borobudur was built in the 8th century and later abandoned.

Its abandonment remains a mystery, and it is not known when pilgrimage ceased. Some sources name the period between 928 and 1006, when King Mpu Sindok moved the capital of the Mataram kingdom to East Java after volcanic eruptions. A poet of the Majapahit era mentions the vihara in Budur in the Nagarakretagama, written around 1365.

Borobudur is built as a single large stupa and, seen from above, takes the form of a giant tantric Buddhist mandala representing Buddhist cosmology. Its square foundation measures about 118 metres on each side, and it has nine platforms, the lower six square and the upper three circular, topped by a central dome. About 55,000 cubic metres of andesite were laid without mortar and joined by knobs, indentations and dovetails, and the reliefs were carved in place after the building was complete.

Pilgrims climb through stairways and corridors lined with 1,460 narrative relief panels. Reliefs on the hidden base illustrate the law of karma, others tell the life of Prince Siddhartha from the Lalitavistara, the Jataka stories of the Buddha's earlier lives, and Sudhana's search for truth. The temple holds 432 Buddha statues in niches on the square platforms, and 72 more sit inside perforated stupas on the circular platforms.

Under British administration from 1811 to 1816, Stamford Raffles was told in 1814 of a big monument deep in the jungle near the village of Bumisegoro. He sent the Dutch engineer Hermann Cornelius, who with 200 men cut down trees, burned vegetation and dug away the earth, though he could not uncover all the galleries. Raffles did not visit the site himself but is credited with bringing it to the world's attention. In 1885 Jan Willem IJzerman found that the base enclosed a hidden foot, and a commission formed in 1900 proposed protection. A major renovation funded by UNESCO took place in 1973.
bosniaks: Slavs settled the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the sixth century, during the Migration Period, as small tribal units of the Slavic group the Byzantines called the Sclaveni. The first mention of a Bosnian entity, in the De Administrando Imperio of about 960, calls Bosnia a small land belonging to Byzantium, a geographical rather than a national entity. By the 12th century Bosnia had become independent of Hungarian overlordship under Kulin Ban, who ruled from 1180 to 1204.

Bosnia lay between Catholic and Orthodox areas, with rugged terrain and poor communications, and it developed its own church, the Bosnian Church, which both Rome and Constantinople condemned as heretical. Hungary invaded Bosnia between 1235 and 1241 but withdrew. Scholars disagree on whether the Bosnian Church was dualist; John Fine stresses evidence that it kept basic Catholic theology.

After the Ottoman conquest of the Kingdom of Bosnia in 1463 a distinct community of Bosnian Muslims began to form as the local Slavic population embraced Islam. Mass conversion came in the 1480s in central Bosnia and later elsewhere, at its fullest in the 16th century. At its height Muslims were up to three-fourths of the population, but wars and plagues later reduced them, since they lived in densely populated towns and had to serve in Ottoman campaigns. In the late 17th and early 18th centuries around 130,000 Muslim refugees arrived from Ottoman lands lost in Hungary, Slavonia, Croatia and Dalmatia.

Under Ottoman rule life was structured along religious lines, and the term Bosniak was mainly a territorial designation. Austria-Hungary promoted a non-confessional unitary Bosniak identity, but only a small circle of Muslim notables favoured it, among them Mehmed Kapetanović. In the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes Bosnian Muslims were not acknowledged as a distinct ethnic group. In the Bosnian War they were subjected to ethnic cleansing and genocide, and hundreds of thousands fled. The Dayton Agreement recognises Bosniaks as one of the three constituent nations of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

Most Bosniaks speak the Bosnian language, a variety of Serbo-Croatian mutually intelligible with Croatian and Serbian, with more loanwords from Ottoman Turkish, Arabic and Persian. They are traditionally and predominantly Sunni Muslim, and Sufi orders such as the Naqshbandiyya and Qadiriyya have played a significant role. Traditional culture includes the melancholic folk songs called sevdalinka. Their traditional symbol is a coat of arms with six golden lilies, derived from that of the medieval Kingdom of Bosnia.
bosnian-war: The war arose from the breakup of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The League of Communists of Yugoslavia had lost its ideological force at the end of the Cold War, and ethnic nationalism had revived in the 1980s after violence in Kosovo. After Slovenia and Croatia seceded in 1991, the multi-ethnic Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, inhabited mainly by Muslim Bosniaks (44%), Orthodox Serbs (32.5%) and Catholic Croats (17%), held a referendum on independence on 29 February 1992. Bosnian Serb representatives boycotted it and rejected the result, having already proclaimed their own Serb republic on 9 January 1992.

The war is commonly dated from 6 April 1992, when the new republic was internationally recognised. Bosnian Serb forces led by Radovan Karadžić, supported by the government of Slobodan Milošević in Serbia and supplied by the Yugoslav People's Army, seized about 70% of the country in a campaign marked by widespread ethnic cleansing. Serb forces began shelling Sarajevo on 6 April. Croat forces formed the Croatian Defence Council on 8 April, and tensions between Croats and Bosniaks led to the Croat-Bosniak War in early 1993.

In 1994 the Washington Agreement created the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and allied Bosniaks and Croats against the Republika Srpska. After the Srebrenica and Markale massacres, NATO's Operation Deliberate Force in 1995 targeted the Serb army and proved key in ending the war. The Dayton Accords were initialled on 21 November 1995.

Estimates of the dead range widely, from 25,000 to 329,000, depending on who is counted. A database published in Sarajevo in 2007 names at least 97,207 people killed or missing, and over 2.2 million people were displaced. An estimated 12,000 to 50,000 women were raped, mostly Bosniak women and mainly by Serb forces. The killing of over 8,000 Bosniak males at Srebrenica in July 1995 by Serb forces is the only incident in Europe since the Second World War recognised as a genocide. In 2007 the International Court of Justice found that Serbia had failed to prevent it.
boston: Boston stands on the Shawmut Peninsula, beside Boston Harbor, an arm of Massachusetts Bay. Its highest point is Bellevue Hill, at 330 feet above sea level. Since independence the city has expanded well beyond the original peninsula by filling in land and annexing neighbouring towns. Boston Common, near Beacon Hill, is part of the Emerald Necklace, a string of parks designed by Frederick Law Olmsted.

Before European colonisation the surrounding region was inhabited by the Massachusett people, who built small seasonal communities there. When settlers led by John Winthrop arrived in 1630 they found the Shawmut Peninsula nearly empty of Native people, most of whom had died of diseases brought by earlier settlers and traders.

The first European to live there was William Blaxton, an Anglican cleric educated at the University of Cambridge. He invited Isaac Johnson, a leader of the Puritans, to cross from the failing colony of Charlestown and share the peninsula, and in September 1630 the Puritans made the crossing. Johnson, in one of his last acts before his death on 30 September 1630, named the settlement after his hometown of Boston, Lincolnshire. Puritan ethics and their focus on education shaped the early city, and Boston Latin School, the first public school in America, was founded in 1635.

Boston was home to several seminal events of the American Revolution: the Boston Massacre of 1770, the Boston Tea Party of 1773, the Battle of Bunker Hill in 1775 and the Siege of Boston from 1775 to 1776. After independence it became an important port and manufacturing centre as well as a centre of education and culture, and it has been called the Athens of America for its literary culture. Its firsts include Boston Common in 1634, the oldest public park in the United States, and the Tremont Street subway of 1897, the first subway system.

Boston is the capital and most populous city of Massachusetts and a cultural and financial centre of New England. The Boston Red Sox play at Fenway Park, built in 1912, which is the oldest stadium in active use among the four major American professional sports leagues.
botswana: Botswana has a total area of 581,730 square kilometres and is topographically flat, with approximately 70% of its territory part of the Kalahari Desert. It borders South Africa, Namibia, Zambia and Zimbabwe. The terrain consists of sandy soils, rocky hill ranges and grasslands, and the climate is generally semi-arid, with highly seasonal rainfall. The north and east receive more rain than the dry southwest, and much of the population lives in the southeast.

In the northwest the Okavango River spreads across the Kalahari in a vast inland delta of channels, lagoons, islands and seasonal wetlands, rather than flowing to the sea. The Chobe River in the north forms part of the border with Namibia.

Stone tools in present-day Botswana date back two million years, and the ancestors of the Khoe and the San lived in the region 30,000 to 40,000 years ago. Rock art dates back approximately 30,000 years. Around 2,000 years ago people introduced cattle, sheep, pottery and agriculture. Bantu-speaking peoples migrated into the region between 2,000 and 1,500 years ago: the Kalanga arrived around 200 CE and the ancestors of the Tswana around 400 CE, bringing iron and copper tools and establishing permanent settlements. Trade expanded from the seventh century, and the Toutswe people, the Kingdom of Mapungubwe and later Great Zimbabwe became important regional powers, with cattle and gold playing major economic roles.

From the fifteenth to the eighteenth century Tswana and Kalanga peoples formed new political communities. Tswana society was organised into merafe, governed by chiefs called dikgosi. The Difaqane of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth century caused widespread warfare and migration, and by the 1840s many states had been re-established and were governed through the kgotla, a traditional community council. Missionaries arrived in 1816, followed by British traders and explorers, and David Livingstone established a mission in 1845. The discovery of the Tati Goldfields in 1868 led to a gold rush and the growth of Francistown. In 1885 the British declared the protectorate of Bechuanaland, which became independent on 30 September 1966.

Gaborone is the capital and largest city. Botswana is a parliamentary republic, and its government draws on both the Westminster system and the tribal governments of the Tswana. English is the official language and Setswana is widely spoken. The Tswana make up about 79% of the population, the Kalanga about 11% and the San about 3%. Botswana is a member of the Southern African Development Community, the Commonwealth of Nations and the United Nations.
boudica: Boudica was the consort of Prasutagus, king of the Iceni, a tribe living in what is now Norfolk and parts of neighbouring counties. The Iceni had revolted against the Romans in 47 and afterwards kept their independence. Prasutagus ruled as a nominally independent ally of Rome and had two daughters with Boudica. In his will he made both the daughters and the emperor Nero his heirs. The name may be an honorific title, and the name she bore for most of her life is unknown.

Accounts of the revolt come from Tacitus, Suetonius and Cassius Dio. Dio wrote the longest, about 140 years after her death, and his text survives only in an epitome by the 11th-century monk John Xiphilinus. His details are often fictitious, and the speeches both Tacitus and Dio give her were never recorded.

When Prasutagus died, the Romans ignored his will and absorbed the kingdom into the province of Britannia. Tacitus tells of pillaging and of the flogging of Boudica and rape of her daughters. Dio mentions none of this and gives other causes, among them the recall of loans by Seneca. The Iceni and the Trinovantes raised an army reported at 120,000 men and attacked Camulodunum, a colony for retired soldiers. The Legio IX Hispana tried to relieve the town and was overwhelmed.

The governor Gaius Suetonius Paulinus reached Londinium before the rebels but, outnumbered, abandoned it, and they burned it. They also sacked Verulamium. Modern estimates put the dead at 70,000 to 80,000 Romans and Britons.

Suetonius gathered nearly 10,000 men and took a stand in a narrow pass with a wood behind. His javelins, wedge formation and cavalry crushed the larger British army. Tacitus says that Boudica poisoned herself, while Dio says she fell ill and died and was given a lavish burial. The crisis made Nero consider withdrawing from Britain, but the victory confirmed Roman control of the province. Interest in Boudica revived in the English Renaissance and brought her fame in the Victorian era.
boulogne-sur-mer: Boulogne-sur-Mer stands on the English Channel at the mouth of the river Liane, in the department of Pas-de-Calais, on the Côte d'Opale. The French name derives from the Latin Bononia, also the Roman name of Bologna in Italy. Both are thought to come from native Celtic place-names, with bona possibly meaning foundation, citadel or granary. The epithet sur-Mer, on sea, distinguishes the city from Boulogne-Billancourt near Paris.

The foundation of Gesoriacum is credited to the Celtic Boii. A tall lighthouse, the Tour d'Ordre, was built there around 39 CE on the order of Caligula, possibly in preparation for an invasion of Britain, and fell into the sea through coastal erosion in 1644. From Claudius's invasion in 43 the town was the major port linking the empire with Britain and the chief base of the Roman navy's British fleet until its admiral Carausius rebelled in 286. The junior emperor Constantius Chlorus besieged it by land and sea in 293, and its name changed to Bononia by 310.

In the Middle Ages Boulogne was capital of an eponymous county founded in the mid-9th century. Count Eustace II helped William the Conqueror conquer England, and his wife founded the church that became Notre-Dame cathedral, a pilgrimage site from the 12th century. The English occupied the town several times during the Hundred Years War, and again from 1544 to 1550, when France bought it back for 400,000 crowns. In 1805 Napoleon gathered the Grande Armée there for a planned invasion of Britain. The railway to Paris, completed in 1848, made it a bathing resort for wealthy Parisians.

Boulogne was one of the three base ports most used by Commonwealth armies on the Western Front in the First World War. Allied bombing on 15 June 1944 completely destroyed the harbour and surrounding area, and Canadian troops liberated the town in September 1944. It is France's largest fishing port, specialising in herring, and its 12th-century belfry is a World Heritage Site.
bourges: Bourges stands in central France where the Auron flows into the Yèvre, in the region of Centre-Val de Loire. Its name derives either from the Bituriges, its original inhabitants, or from a Germanic word burg, meaning a hill or village. The Celts called it Avaricon and Latin speakers Avaricum. In the fourth century BCE, and still in Caesar's time, the area around it was the centre of a Gallic confederacy.

In 52 BCE the Gauls adopted a scorched-earth policy to deny Caesar's forces supplies, but the inhabitants of Avaricum persuaded the council not to burn their town. Its marshes, a river that nearly encircled it and a strong southern wall spared it for a time. Caesar's forces nevertheless captured and destroyed it, killing all but 800 of its inhabitants. Rome rebuilt it with a monumental gate, aqueducts, baths and an amphitheatre, and the Roman town grew larger than the medieval one. Saint Ursinus, of the third century, is considered its first bishop.

In the 8th century Bourges lay on the northern edge of the Duchy of Aquitaine and was the first town to face Frankish attacks across the Loire. Charles Martel captured it in 731, and Duke Odo the Great retook it. Pepin the Short destroyed much of it in a siege in 762. It was capital of the Viscounty of Bourges until 1101 and of the Duchy of Berry from 1360. Charles VII sought refuge there in the 1420s, and his son Louis XI was born there in 1423. In 1438 Charles issued the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges. A fire in 1487 destroyed a third of the town, and its economic decline began.

Bourges is the capital of the department of Cher and was capital of the former province of Berry. Its Gothic cathedral, built from 1195 to 1255 and one of the earliest examples of High Gothic, was added to the World Heritage list in 1992. The 15th-century Palais Jacques Cœur and a sixty-five-hectare district of half-timbered houses also survive. From the 1860s the town became an important centre of artillery production, after Napoleon III moved the École de pyrotechnie militaire there from Metz.
boxer-rebellion: After the First Sino-Japanese War, villagers in North China feared the growth of foreign spheres of influence and resented Christian missionaries, who ignored local customs and used their power to protect their followers in court. Shandong, where the Righteous and Harmonious Fists arose, had long been troubled by social unrest, religious sects and martial societies. In 1897 and 1898 drought and floods forced farmers into the cities, and the movement blamed these disasters on foreign and Christian influence. American missionaries probably first called its members Boxers, because of the martial arts they practised. Their main rite was a spiritual possession with whirling swords and incantations, and they claimed invulnerability to cannon, rifle shot and blade.

From 1899 the movement spread across Shandong and the North China Plain, destroying foreign property such as railways and attacking or murdering Chinese Christians and missionaries. In January 1900 Empress Dowager Cixi, with a majority of conservatives at court, issued edicts in its defence. In the spring it moved north towards Beijing, burning churches and intimidating officials. Diplomats, missionaries, soldiers and some Chinese Christians took refuge in the Legation Quarter, which the Boxers besieged.

On 17 June 1900 the Eight-Nation Alliance, of American, Austro-Hungarian, British, French, German, Italian, Japanese and Russian troops, stormed the Dagu Forts at Tianjin. On 21 June Cixi issued a decree that was in effect a declaration of war on the powers. Officials were divided, and those in the southern provinces ignored the order to fight. The Alliance defeated the Imperial Army at Tianjin and reached Beijing on 14 August, ending the 55-day siege of the Legations.

Looting of the capital and countryside followed, together with summary executions of suspected Boxers. The Boxer Protocol of 7 September 1901 required the execution of officials who had supported the movement, allowed foreign troops to be stationed in Beijing and imposed an indemnity of 450 million taels of silver, more than the government's annual tax revenue, to be paid over 39 years to the eight nations. The Qing dynasty's handling of the rebellion further weakened its credibility and its control over China. It led to the Late Qing reforms and, to a greater extent, to the Xinhai Revolution.
bracara-augusta: The site lies in the heart of Minho, in a transitional region between east and west, between mountains, forests, valleys and plains. Human occupation there dates back thousands of years, with vestiges of monumental structures from the Megalithic era. During the Iron Age the Castro culture extended into the northwest, and the Bracari occupied high ground in fortified settlements called castrum. The region became the domain of the Callaici Bracarii, a Celtic tribe who occupied what is now northern Portugal, Galicia and Asturias.

The Romans began their conquest of the region around 136 BCE and finished it, by conquering the northern regions, in the reign of Augustus. The civitas was founded in 16 BCE and, in the administrative reorganization of the new acquisitions, Bracara was rededicated to the emperor and took the name Bracara Augusta. The city developed greatly during the 1st century and reached its maximum extent around the 2nd. Towards the end of the 3rd century Diocletian promoted it to a capital within the newly founded Roman province of Gallaecia. The poet Ausonius described it as prosperous in the 4th century.

Between 402 and 470 the Suebi conquered the area. In 410 they established a kingdom in the northwest of Iberia, founded by Hermeric and lasting over 150 years, with Bracara as its capital. The old Roman amphitheatre was converted into a fortress. In 455 the Visigothic king Theodoric II sacked the city, destroying many historical and archaeological records, while the Suebi king Rechiar escaped, wounded, to Porto. A list of dioceses and parishes of Braga made in 570 still exists, and by about 584 the Visigoths took permanent control of Gallaecia.

The site is the city of Braga in northwestern Portugal, capital of the district of Braga and of the historical Minho Province. It hosts the oldest Portuguese archdiocese, the Archdiocese of Braga, and is the seat of the Primacy of the Spains. In the Middle Ages it was a main centre of Christianity in Iberia. Archbishop Paio Mendes was a contributor to the recognition of Portugal as an independent kingdom under Afonso I Henriques in 1179, and the city was later handed to the Church's direct control, giving it the nickname Paiz Bracarense. The medieval castle in the city centre was destroyed in 1905.
brahmi-script: Early theories derived Brahmi from Egyptian hieroglyphs on a pictographic model, but these have lost credence as purely imaginative and speculative. Many scholars link it to Semitic scripts, particularly Aramaic, which was the bureaucratic language of the Achaemenid empire and lay close to the Indian subcontinent. Georg Bühler connected it to Phoenician and proposed an early 8th century BCE borrowing. A difficulty is that Aramaic is also the accepted source of the Kharoṣṭhī script, which looks very different, and why two such scripts arose from it is unexplained.

Other scholars, among them John Marshall and G. R. Hunter, saw similarities with the undeciphered Indus script. Kenneth Norman proposed that Brahmi was devised over a longer period before Ashoka, citing sherds from Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka dated to perhaps two centuries earlier, though those finds are controversial.

Brahmi is an abugida: vowels are attached to consonant signs by diacritical marks. It changed relatively little from the Mauryan period in the 3rd century BCE to the early Gupta period in the 4th century CE. Sometime afterwards the ability to read it was lost. Its name is a feminine Sanskrit word meaning of Brahma. The Lalitavistara Sūtra lists 64 scripts with Brahmi first. The earliest full inscriptions are in Prakrit, from the 3rd to 1st centuries BCE, and the earliest in Sanskrit date from the 1st century BCE.

The Edicts of Ashoka were written in Brahmi and, in the northwest, sometimes in Kharoshthi. Both scripts had died out by about the 4th century CE, so the edicts could not be read when scholars began to study them in the 19th century. James Prinsep, secretary of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, deciphered Brahmi in a series of articles in the Society's journal in the 1830s, building on the work of Christian Lassen, Edwin Norris, H. H. Wilson and Alexander Cunningham.
From the 6th century CE the script diversified into local variants, the Brahmic family. One survey found 198 scripts that ultimately derive from it, used across South and Southeast Asia.
braila: Before the 14th century a small village stood on the site, probably of fishermen and small merchants. It fell to the Mongols in the invasion of 1241. The origin of the name is unknown and thought to be a personal name. The first certain mention is a privilege from Vladislav I of Wallachia exempting German merchants of Brașov from customs duties on the road to the Danube through Braylan. After the fall of Vicina, Brăila became the main harbour of Wallachia and gained town status around 1400. Foreign merchants had to unload their goods there.

In 1462 the fleet of Mehmed the Conqueror, 25 triremes and 150 other ships, burned it to the ground, and the Moldavians under Stephen the Great destroyed it in a campaign against the Wallachian prince Radu the Fair. Bogdan III of Moldavia burned it again in 1512, yet it recovered each time as the gateway for Levantine goods into Wallachia. Around 1538 to 1540 it passed to the Ottoman Empire, which built a stone stronghold there. Michael the Brave of Wallachia held it briefly in 1595 and 1596.

A Wallachian-Russian army conquered it in 1711 during the Pruth River Campaign, and the siege of 1828 preceded its award to Wallachia by the Treaty of Adrianople in 1829. In the 19th century it was one of the three most important Danube ports of Wallachia, and its prosperity peaked at the end of that century and the start of the next.

Brăila is the capital of Brăila County in Muntenia, eastern Romania, and a port on the Danube accessible to small and medium-sized oceangoing ships, with large grain-handling and warehousing facilities. Streets radiating from the port are crossed by concentric streets that follow the geometry of the old Ottoman fortifications. Landmarks include the Greek Church of 1863 to 1872 and the Church of the Holy Archangels Michael and Gabriel, a former mosque and the oldest church in the city.
brandenburg: Brandenburg lies in northeastern Germany and surrounds Berlin. It borders Poland and the states of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, Lower Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Saxony, and the Oder forms part of its eastern border. Its main rivers are the Spree and the Havel. The name comes from the town of Brandenburg an der Havel, and its origin is unclear: it is thought to derive from the Slavic branyi, marshy, or the Germanic branda, fire. In the extinct local language Polabian the town was called Branibor.

By the 7th century Slavic peoples are believed to have settled the area, the two principal groups being the Hevelli in the west and the Sprevane in the east. From the early 10th century Henry the Fowler and his successors conquered territory up to the Oder, and in 948 Emperor Otto I established margraves over the pagan Slavs there. A great uprising of the Wends drove the imperial forces out in 983. In 1134 Emperor Lothar III granted the Northern March to Albert the Bear, who inherited the town of Brandenburg and the lands of the Hevelli from Pribislav in 1150 and proclaimed himself ruler of the new Margraviate of Brandenburg.

The Ascanian line ended in 1320, and from 1323 to 1415 Brandenburg was under the Wittelsbachs of Bavaria, under whom its margrave gained the status of prince-elector of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1415 Emperor Sigismund granted the Electorate to the House of Hohenzollern, which ruled until the end of the First World War and made Berlin its capital. Brandenburg converted to Protestantism in 1539, and the Hohenzollerns acquired the Duchy of Prussia in 1618, forming Brandenburg-Prussia.

The Great Elector, Frederick William, rebuilt and consolidated the state after the Thirty Years' War, and in 1701 his son took the title King in Prussia as Frederick I. Brandenburg remained the core of the Kingdom of Prussia and, from 1815 to 1947, was a province of Prussia. After the Second World War the lands east of the Oder–Neisse line were ceded to Poland. East Germany dissolved the state in 1952, and it was re-established in the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990.

Brandenburg is a landlocked state of Germany with Potsdam as its capital and about 2.5 million residents. Other major towns are Cottbus, Brandenburg an der Havel and Frankfurt (Oder). In the southeast, part of the historical Lower Lusatia has two official languages, German and Lower Sorbian. A proposal to unify Berlin and Brandenburg was rejected in a referendum in 1996, and the two states still cooperate on many matters.
brandenburg-an-der-havel: Brandenburg an der Havel lies on the banks of the River Havel, which is navigable here as a European Waterway. The name combines two Slavic words, braniti, to protect or defend, and bor, forest or wood. The town gave its name to the medieval Bishopric of Brandenburg, the Margraviate of Brandenburg and the present German state, and it was the original nucleus of the realms of Brandenburg and Prussia. It was capital of the Margraviate until Berlin replaced it in 1417.

Brenna was a Slavic fort, conquered in 929 after the Battle of Lenzen by King Henry the Fowler of Saxony, and first mentioned in documents then as Brennaburg. At the Magdeburg Assembly of Princes in 948 the bishoprics of Brandenburg and Havelburg were established under the control of Otto I. A major Slavic uprising in 983 returned the area east of the Elbe to Slavic chiefs of the Hevelli until the middle of the 12th century. The last of them, Pribislav, died in 1150.

His widow Petrissa enabled Albert I of Brandenburg to take over Brenna. Jaksa of Kopanica drove him out, and he returned in 1157 after a long siege, by agreement and with a joint German and Slav garrison, and styled himself Margrave of Brandenburg. By 1160 nobles, burghers and peasants from the Harz, the Netherlands, the Rhineland and Westphalia were settling the Elbe, Havel and Spree basin. The foundation stone of a cathedral was laid on the cathedral island in 1165, and it was consecrated five years later. In 1314–1315 the Old and New Towns joined the Hanseatic League. Plundering and destruction in the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) led the court to leave. The two towns merged in 1715.

In the late 19th century the town became an industrial centre, making steel, toys and bicycles under brands such as Brennabor. In 1933–1934 one of the first Nazi concentration camps stood here. The Brandenburg-Görden Prison later became a euthanasia centre where the Nazis murdered people with psychiatric disorders, including children, in Action T4, and it was one of the first places where they experimented with killing by gas. Heavy bombing, partly because of the Arado aircraft factory, destroyed 70 percent of the city by 1945.

The Dominsel, the cathedral island, is its historic heart, with the Cathedral of St Peter and Paul, begun in the Romanesque style in 1165 and completed as a Gothic cathedral in the 14th century; the Wagner organ of 1725 is one of the best-known Baroque organs in Germany. Other sights are the brick Gothic Katharinenkirche of 1401, the Old Town Hall with its statue of the knight Roland of 1474, and parts of the medieval wall with four watchtowers.
brasilia: Brasília sits at an elevation of 1,000 metres on the Brazilian Highlands in the Central-West region of Brazil. Paranoá Lake, a large artificial lake, was built to increase the available water and to maintain the region's humidity. The name comes from the Latin translation of Brazil, suggested for the country's capital in 1821 by José Bonifácio de Andrada e Silva.

Brazil's first capital was Salvador, and in 1763 Rio de Janeiro became the capital and remained so until 1960. Resources tended to be concentrated in the southeast, and most of the population lived near the Atlantic coast. A geographically central capital would be more regionally neutral. The idea of moving the capital was conceived in 1827 by José Bonifácio, an adviser to Emperor Pedro I, who presented a plan to the General Assembly for a new city called Brasília, to the west of the heavily populated southeastern corridor. It was to stand upstream on the São Francisco River rather than in the region of Goiás chosen later. The bill was not enacted because Pedro I dissolved the Assembly.

According to a legend, the Italian saint Don Bosco dreamed in 1883 of a futuristic city that roughly fitted Brasília's location, and many references to him, including a church parish, are found in the city today. After the Proclamation of the Republic, the third article of the 1891 Constitution stated that the Union would own, in the central plateau, an area of 14,400 square kilometres, to be demarcated to establish the future federal capital.

The city was developed in 1956 by Lúcio Costa, Oscar Niemeyer and Joaquim Cardozo, in a scheme to move the capital from Rio de Janeiro to a more central location chosen through a committee, with Roberto Burle Marx as landscape architect. President Juscelino Kubitschek founded it on 21 April 1960 to replace Rio de Janeiro.

Brasília is the capital of Brazil and of the Federal District, and all three branches of the federal government sit there. It is laid out in the shape of an airplane: the fuselage is the Monumental Axis, a pair of wide avenues flanking a large park, and the cockpit is the Praça dos Três Poderes. Its white modern architecture is by Oscar Niemeyer. UNESCO inscribed it as a World Heritage Site in 1987 for its modernist architecture and urban planning. It is an administrative region rather than a municipality, and the Federal District is divided into 35 administrative regions.
bratislava: Bratislava lies in southwestern Slovakia at the foot of the Little Carpathians, on both banks of the Danube and the left bank of the Morava. It is on the border of Slovakia, Austria and Hungary, the only national capital with land borders with two other sovereign states, and only 60 kilometres from Vienna. The Danube, along which the city developed, was for centuries the chief transportation route.

The first known permanent settlement began with the Linear Pottery Culture around 5000 BCE. About 200 BCE the Celtic Boii tribe founded the first significant settlement, a fortified town known as the Bratislava oppidum, and established a mint that produced gold and silver coins known as biatecs. From the 1st to the 4th century CE the area fell under Roman influence as part of the Danubian Limes, a border defence system. The Romans introduced grape growing.

The Slavs arrived from the east between the 5th and 6th centuries. In response to attacks by the Avars, local Slavic tribes rebelled and established Samo's Empire (623-658), the first known Slavic political entity. In the 9th century the castles at Bratislava (Brezalauspurk) and Devín (Dowina) were important centres of the Principality of Nitra and Great Moravia. The medieval settlement Brezalauspurc, meaning Braslav's castle, was first mentioned in 907, but its actual location is under scholarly debate. The name Pozsony first appears in 1002.

From 1536 to 1783 the city was the coronation site, legislative centre and capital of the Kingdom of Hungary, and eleven Hungarian kings and eight queens were crowned in St Martin's Cathedral. Most Hungarian parliament assemblies were held there from the 17th century until the Hungarian Reform Era. The Diet used the University Library building, erected in 1756, from 1802 to 1848, and much significant legislation of the Reform Era, such as the abolition of serfdom and the foundation of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences, was enacted there.

Bratislava is the capital and largest city of Slovakia and the seat of the president, parliament and government. The Old Town holds most historical buildings, among them the Town Hall, built in the 14th and 15th centuries, and Michael's Gate, the only gate preserved from the medieval fortifications. The Grassalkovich Palace, built around 1760, is the president's residence. Its history was shaped by Austrians, Bulgarians, Croats, Czechs, Germans, Hungarians, Jews and Slovaks.
brazil: Brazil covers 8,515,767 square kilometres, nearly half of the land area of South America (47.7%), and borders every South American country except Ecuador and Chile. Its Atlantic coastline is 7,491 kilometres long. The country contains most of the Amazon basin, with the world's largest river system and most extensive tropical forest, together with wetlands, savannas, plateaus and low mountains. It is the only country that both the equator and the Tropic of Capricorn cross, and it spans four time zones. Most of its territory is tropical, with equatorial rainforest in the north, semiarid land in the northeast and temperate forest in the south.

Human remains found at Pedro Leopoldo, in Minas Gerais, show habitation going back at least 11,000 years, and the earliest pottery found in the Western Hemisphere, near Santarém, was dated to over 8,000 years ago. The Marajoara culture flourished on Marajó from 400 to 1400 CE. When the Portuguese arrived, the territory had an estimated Indigenous population of 7 million people, mostly semi-nomadic, among them the Tupis, Guaranis and Gês.

The land was claimed for Portugal on 22 April 1500 by the fleet of Pedro Álvares Cabral, after the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494. São Vicente was founded in 1532, and in 1534 King John III of Portugal divided the territory into fifteen private captaincies. The system failed, and in 1549 the king created the Governorate General of Brazil at Salvador. In the first two centuries Indigenous and European groups lived in constant war, forming opportunistic alliances.

Brazil became a united kingdom with Portugal in 1815, after the Portuguese court moved to Rio de Janeiro. Prince Pedro of Braganza declared independence in 1822 and founded the Empire of Brazil after a war with Portugal. The constitution of 1824 set up a bicameral legislature, and slavery was gradually abolished until its final abolition in 1888. A military coup in 1889 made the country a presidential republic. A revolution in 1930 brought Getúlio Vargas to power, and his self-coup of 1937 began the authoritarian Estado Novo. Democracy returned after 1945, a military dictatorship ruled from 1964 to 1985, and the present constitution dates from 1988.

Brazil is a federation of 26 states and a Federal District, which holds the capital, Brasília; São Paulo is the most populous city. The 2022 census counted 203 million people, and 45.3% described themselves as Pardo, 43.5% as White, 10.2% as Black and 0.6% as Indigenous. Its culture derives mainly from Portuguese culture, shaped also by African, Indigenous and other European traditions and by Italians, Germans, Japanese, Jewish and Arab immigrants in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.
brazilian-national-anthem: From the proclamation of independence in 1822 until the abdication of Pedro I in 1831, the national anthem was one composed by Pedro I himself, which remains an official patriotic song as the Independence Anthem. After the abdication its popularity fell, and Francisco Manuel da Silva presented his own composition. The date on which he wrote the music is disputed: some historians place it in 1822, others in early 1823, and others hold that it was written in 1831. The music is a patriotic march reminiscent of Gioachino Rossini. The date of its first public performance, 13 April 1831, is now the Day of the Brazilian National Anthem.

The music was first given words by the appeals judge Ovídio Saraiva de Carvalho e Silva, as a hymn commemorating Pedro I's abdication, known as the April 7 Hymn. Those words were thought poor and offensive to the Portuguese and fell out of use, but by 1837 the melody was played without words at all public ceremonies. A new text of 1841 was also abandoned, and Pedro II ordered that the music be played without lyrics whenever he appeared in public.

After the Proclamation of the Republic in 1889 a contest chose a new anthem by Leopoldo Miguez, but after protests Deodoro da Fonseca confirmed Francisco Manuel da Silva's music as the national anthem by a decree of 20 January 1890.

For three decades of the republic the anthem had no official words, and several texts were adopted in different states. The lyrics of Joaquim Osório Duque Estrada, first proposed in 1909, were adapted and made official by a decree of President Epitácio Pessoa on 6 September 1922, during the centennial of independence. The government bought the rights to the text. The lyrics have been described as Parnassian in style and Romantic in content.
brazzaville: Brazzaville lies on the north bank of the Congo River just below Pool Malebo, about 506 km inland from the Atlantic Ocean and at an altitude of 317 m. Directly across the river stands Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and this is the only place in the world where two national capitals developed on opposite banks of a river within sight of each other. Downriver the Congo has numerous rapids, called Livingstone Falls, which prevent navigation from the Atlantic to the city. The name honours the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza, born in Italy, who became a French citizen in 1874.

Before colonial rule the site held two trading centres, Mfwa and Mpila, which belonged to the Tio Kingdom. Brazza officially founded the settlement on 10 September 1880, on the existing Bateke settlement of Ncuna. The Tio king Iloo I signed a treaty of protection that placed his lands under French authority, and from October 1880 until May 1882 a small force led by Sergeant Malamine Camara occupied the site to keep it out of Belgian hands. The Berlin Conference of 1884 confirmed French control. The city became the capital of the French Congo in 1904 and remained capital when French Equatorial Africa was formed in 1910 as a federation that included Gabon, the Central African Republic and Chad.

The Congo-Ocean Railway, opened in 1934, linked Brazzaville with the Atlantic port of Pointe-Noire and bypassed the rapids; its construction cost the lives of more than 17,000 Africans. During World War II the city served as the capital of Free France. In 1944 it hosted a meeting of French resistance leaders and representatives of France's African colonies, whose Brazzaville Declaration tried to redefine the relationship between France and its colonies.

Brazzaville is the capital and largest city of the Republic of the Congo, with a population of about 2.15 million at the 2023 census. It is both a department and a commune, divided into nine arrondissements. Its port receives raw materials such as rubber, wood and agricultural products, which are sent on to Pointe-Noire for export, and the World Health Organization has its regional office for Africa there. The Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza Mausoleum and the Poto-Poto School of Painting are among its landmarks, and UNESCO named it a City of Music in 2013.
breda: Breda lies in the southern Netherlands, equidistant from Rotterdam and Antwerp. The name derives from brede Aa, the wide Aa, and refers to the confluence of the rivers Mark and Aa. As a fortified city it was of strategic military and political significance. Although a direct fiefdom of the Holy Roman Emperor, the city obtained a municipal charter, and its acquisition through marriage by the House of Nassau placed it at the centre of political and social life in the Low Countries.

In the 11th century Breda was a direct fief of the Holy Roman Emperor, and its earliest known lord was Henry of Brunesheim, who held it from 1080 to 1125. The first mention of Breda in the historical record dates from 1125, when Engelbertus van Breda witnessed a document. The city obtained a municipal charter in 1252, which gave it the right to build fortifications, and it built brick walls and Roman-style gates.

Its acquisition by the House of Orange-Nassau made it a residence city, and the presence of the family attracted other nobles, who built palaces in the old quarters. The most impressive, built by the Italian architect Thomas Vincidor de Bologna for the first Dutch prince, was the first Renaissance-style palace north of the Alps. In the 15th century a great church in Brabantine Gothic style was built, with a tower 97 metres high, called the Grote Kerk or the Church of Our Lady. In 1534 Henry III of Nassau-Breda rebuilt the modest medieval fortifications in impressive style.

During the Cromwellian Commonwealth and Protectorate the exiled Charles II of England stayed in Breda for a little over a month, thanks to the nearness of his sister Mary, Princess Royal and Princess of Orange. His Declaration of Breda of 1660 announced his conditions for accepting the crown of England. The Treaty of Breda, signed on 31 July 1667, ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War. Between 1746 and 1748 Breda hosted the Congress of Breda, talks between Britain and France that led to the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.

Breda is a city and municipality in the province of North Brabant, the tenth largest in the Netherlands. Historically its economy was mainly industrial and it was a centre of the food and drink industry, with companies such as Hero, Van Melle, De Faam and Kwatta. It also housed the largest brewery in the Netherlands, Oranjeboom. Since 1970 it has become a city of education and students.
bregenz: Bregenz lies on the east and southeast shores of Lake Constance, the third-largest freshwater lake in Central Europe, between Switzerland to the west and Germany to the northwest, with the large forests of the Bregenzerwald to the east. It stands on a plateau falling in a series of terraces to the lake at the foot of the Pfänder mountain. It is a junction of the arterial roads from the Rhine valley to the German Alpine foothills, and cruise ships run on the lake. Vorarlberg, of which it is the capital, is the westernmost state of Austria.

The first settlements date from about 1500 BCE. Strabo mentions the Brigantii as a Celtic sub-tribe of this region of the Alps, and in the 5th century BCE the Celts settled at Brigantion, one of their most heavily fortified places. After a series of battles in 15 BCE the Romans conquered it and it became a Roman camp, and around 50 CE it was made a municipality, Brigantium. It was the seat of the Roman admiralty for Lake Constance and had a theatre. The Alemanni destroyed it in 259/60 and settled the area around 450. Saint Columbanus and Saint Gall worked there as missionaries from 610 to 612.

From 917 the castle was the residence of the Udalrichinger, the ruling dynasty of Vorarlberg, who called themselves Counts of Bregenz; the house died out around 1150. Around 1170 Hugo of Tübingen, called Montfort, founded a town settlement, first documented in 1249. The city was sold to the Habsburgs in 1451 and again in 1523 and stayed under Austrian rule, apart from a brief occupation by Swedish forces under Carl Gustaf Wrangel in the 30 Years' War, until the 19th century. The Swedes destroyed the fortress of Hohenbregenz on the Gebhardsberg in 1647. Bregenz was under Bavarian rule from 1805 to 1814, and since 1726 it has been the main seat of Austrian administration in Vorarlberg.

The harbour on Lake Constance was built from 1842 to 1850, Austrian ship service began in 1884, and railway services have existed since 1872. The Allies bombed the town in 1945, destroying 72 houses, and French troops set up the military government in April and May of that year. The Bregenz Festival, with the Vienna Symphony Orchestra, began in 1946 and is held every summer, with a stage floating on the lake. The upper town keeps remains of its walls, the old town hall of 1662 and Martin's Tower, originally built by the Romans, whose Baroque steeple is the largest bulb-shaped one in Central Europe. The Kunsthaus Bregenz, a modern art museum, was built from 1991 to 1997.
bremen: Bremen is the largest city on the River Weser, about 60 kilometres upstream from its mouth into the North Sea at Bremerhaven, and is completely surrounded by the state of Lower Saxony. The oldest part of the Altstadt, the Old Town, is an oval bounded by the Weser and by the Wallgraben, the former moats of the medieval city walls. It begins at the Marktplatz and ends at the Schnoor quarter.

The city traces its origins to a settlement of the early Middle Ages and became the seat of a bishopric in 787. In the High Middle Ages it grew into a trading centre and joined the Hanseatic League in the 13th century. For most of its 1,200-year history Bremen was an independent city within the Holy Roman Empire, governed by merchants and guilds.

To confirm its independence it had to contend, until the Reformation, with the temporal power of the Church, and after the Thirty Years' War with Sweden, which ruled the surrounding Duchy of Bremen-Verden. George I Louis, Elector of Hannover and from 1714 King of Great Britain and Ireland, acquired Bremen-Verden in 1715 and recognised Bremen as a free city in 1720. The city was captured in 1806, annexed by France in 1810 and regained independence in 1815.

In the late 19th century Prussia drew Bremen into the German Empire. With its new anchorage and wharves at Bremerhaven it became the principal port of embarkation for German and central European emigrants to the Americas. The Norddeutscher Lloyd, founded there in 1857, became one of the world's leading shipping companies. After the First World War Bremen was briefly a Soviet republic, and it lost its autonomy under the Hitler regime. Almost two thirds of the city's fabric was destroyed in the Second World War. Its autonomy was restored, and it became one of the founding states of the Federal Republic of Germany.

Bremen is the capital and most populous city of the state of the Free Hanseatic City of Bremen, which consists of the city and Bremerhaven, with about 586,000 inhabitants. Its Town Hall, built between 1405 and 1410 in Gothic style with a Renaissance façade of 1609–12, and the Bremen Roland, a statue of 1404, form a UNESCO World Heritage Site, listed in July 2004. St Peter's Cathedral dates from the 13th century and the Liebfrauenkirche, the oldest church in the town, from the 11th. The city is also known for the Brothers Grimm fairy tale of the Town Musicians of Bremen.
bremerhaven: Bremerhaven lies on the east bank of the Weser estuary in northern Germany, and the River Geeste flows through it before reaching the Weser. Neighbouring villages such as Lehe existed by the 12th century, and Geestendorf is mentioned in documents of the ninth century, on small islands in a swampy estuary. In 1381 Bremen established de facto rule over the lower Weser, including Lehe, later called Bremerlehe. Swedish troops of Bremen-Verden captured it in 1653, and Bremen ceded it in the peace of November 1654 that followed the First Bremian War. In 1672 colonists tried unsuccessfully to build a castle there, Carlsburg, to control shipping bound for Bremen.

In 1827 Bremen, under Bürgermeister Johann Smidt, bought the territory at the Weser's mouth from the Kingdom of Hanover. Bremen sought it to keep its share of overseas trade, which silting of the river threatened. Bremerhaven was founded as a second harbour 50 km downstream, and trade with North America and emigration made it grow quickly. In 1848 it became the home port of the German Confederation's navy under Karl Rudolf Brommy. Hanover founded a rival town, Geestemünde, in 1845. In 1924 Geestemünde and Lehe united as Wesermünde, and in 1939 Bremerhaven, apart from its overseas port, was joined to it.

As a North Sea base of the Kriegsmarine, the city lost 79% of its buildings in Allied bombing, and the raid of 18 September 1944 left the inner city largely destroyed. Key parts of the port were deliberately spared. After the war Wesermünde was an enclave run by the United States within the British zone. In 1947 it became part of the Free Hanseatic City of Bremen and took the name Bremerhaven.

Bremerhaven is a city in its own right and also part of the two-city state of Bremen. It remains one of the busiest ports in Germany, with a large container terminal and Europe's largest car transshipment centre. Its centre was largely rebuilt after the war. The German Emigration Center and the German Maritime Museum, designed by Hans Scharoun, record its seafaring past, and the Alfred Wegener Institute, a national research institute for maritime and climate science, is based there.
brest-belarus: Brest lies at the border with Poland, opposite the Polish town of Terespol, where the Bug and Mukhavets rivers meet. It is one of the oldest cities in Belarus. Its traditional name Berestiy appears in the Primary Chronicle; the name may come from the Slavic root berest, elm, or from the Lithuanian brasta, ford. It was called Brest-Litovsk from the 1600s to 1923 and Brest-on-the-Bug from 1923 to 1939. Its Yiddish name is Brisk, from which comes the term Brisker for followers of the Soloveitchik family of rabbis.

The town was first mentioned in the Primary Chronicle in 1019, when Kievan Rus took the stronghold from the Poles. It was hotly contested between Polish rulers and the princes of Rus, recaptured by Poland in 1020 and unsuccessfully besieged by Yaroslav the Wise in 1022. In 1319 it became part of the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, and in 1390 it became the second city of the Grand Duchy after Vilnius, and the first in the lands of present-day Belarus, to receive Magdeburg rights. In 1440 a Sejm held there chose Casimir IV Jagiellon as Grand Duke of Lithuania, and in 1563 the Brest Bible, the second complete Bible translation into Polish, was published in the city.

In 1594 and 1596 councils of Catholic and Orthodox bishops met there, and the 1596 council established the Uniate Church. On 13 January 1660 Russian forces took Brest Castle in a surprise attack and massacred the 1,700 defenders and their families, according to an Austrian observer. Brest was annexed by Russia with the Third Partition of Poland in 1795, and the Brest Fortress was built in the 19th century, for which the Russians demolished the Royal Castle and most of the Old Town. In March 1918 the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk was signed in the fortress.

Brest was a Polish city between the wars, and Jews formed 41.3 percent of its population in 1936. After the German attack of 22 June 1941 the fortress held out for six days, and nearly all its Soviet defenders died. The Germans established the Brześć Ghetto in December 1941, and its remaining Jews, about 20,000, were murdered in October 1942; only seven survived. The Red Army retook the city on 28 July 1944, and it was annexed from Poland the following year. Brest is now the administrative centre of Brest Region, and the fortress was recognized by the Soviet Union as a Hero Fortress for its defence in June 1941.
brihatkatha: The date of the work is uncertain. Gunadhya may have flourished under a Satavahana king of Pratishthana, the modern Paithan in Maharashtra; according to D. C. Sircar he probably lived between the 1st century BCE and the 3rd century CE. Another account, in the Nepala Mahatmya of the Skanda Purana, makes him a native of Mathura and court poet of King Madana of Ujjain, a tradition Sircar calls less authentic. Paishachi, the language he used, is a little-known Prakrit, described as the speech of the common people of the border regions of northwest India.

The earliest surviving reference seems to be that of Subandhu in his Vasavadatta, and Banabhatta refers to the work in the Harshacharita and the Kadambari. Dandin, in the Kavyadarsha, calls it marvellous and says it was composed in the vernacular of the bhutas, though his information appears to be second-hand. A Cambodian inscription of about 875 names Gunadhya, and the Kannada Kavirajamarga of about 850 mentions a Sanskrit version, now lost, by Durvinita. A romantic work by Gunadhya can safely be assumed to have existed before 600 CE.

The adaptations differ too much for the original to be reconstructed whole, but what they share allows strong inferences. The life of Udayana of Kaushambi served as a prelude: his upbringing in a hermitage after a monstrous bird carried off his pregnant mother, his captivity under Pradyota, king of Ujjayini, his elopement with Pradyota's daughter Vasavadatta, and his second marriage to Padmavati, arranged by ministers who made him believe Vasavadatta dead. The central story was that of their son Naravahanadatta, born as a boon of Kubera and fated to become emperor of the Vidyadharas. Kshemendra's version is in eighteen books called lambakas, as the original is thought to have been.

Besides the two Kashmiri versions, the story is known from the Sanskrit Brihatkathashlokasamgraha of Budhasvamin, of which the complete text has not been found, and from the Perunkatai and the Vasudevahimdi in vernacular languages. Dandin states that the original was in prose, not in the verse of the Kashmiri recensions. Scholars compare Gunadhya with Vyasa and Valmiki, and the disappearance of his text is counted a very great loss to Indian literature.
brindisi: Brindisi lies on a natural harbour that penetrates deeply into the Adriatic coast of Apulia. The name comes from the Latin Brundisium, which came through the Greek Brentesion from the Messapic Brention, meaning head of a stag, probably a reference to the shape of the harbour, which resembles a head or antlers. Within the arms of the outer harbour lie the Pedagne islands, a tiny archipelago. The surrounding municipality belongs to the Brindisi Plain, a flat and heavily farmed country of limestone and marine sand, and the climate is Mediterranean, with hot dry summers and mild winters.

Several traditions concern the city's founders. One claims that the hero Diomedes founded it, and the geographer Strabo says it was colonized from Knossos in Crete. It became a Roman colony in 244 BCE and expanded greatly; according to Pliny the Elder it was one of the most important Italian cities.
