The Ostrogoths conquered it and the Byzantine Empire reconquered it in the 6th century, by which time Procopius describes a small city without defensive walls. In 674 the Lombards under Romuald I of Benevento destroyed it, though so fine a harbour meant that it was soon rebuilt, and pirates stormed a Saracen settlement near the city in 836.

The port was abandoned for several centuries and the town shrank to a smaller area around the temple of San Leucio. Revival came under Byzantine domination in the 11th century and above all under the Normans and the Swabians in the 12th and 13th centuries, when Brindisi became a prime port for the Crusades. Emperor Frederick II built the Castello Svevo, to which the Crown of Aragon later added four towers. Joachim Murat turned the castle into a prison in 1813. The reopening of the Pigott channel in 1775 and the opening of the Suez Canal at the end of the 19th century renewed traffic with the East. From September 1943 to February 1944 Brindisi was the provisional government seat of the Kingdom of Italy.

Brindisi is the capital of its province and remains a major port for trade with the Balkan Peninsula, Greece and the Middle East, as well as a ferry port. Its industries include chemical works, aerospace, agriculture and the generation of electricity. It is the seat of the Archdiocese of Brindisi-Ostuni; the diocese was erected in the 4th century and its first bishop was St. Leucio of Alexandria. In the 20th century many people emigrated, first to the Americas around the First World War and then to northern Europe and northern Italy after the Second.
brisbane: Brisbane lies in the south-east corner of Queensland, centred on the Brisbane River, whose mouth is about 15 km from the central business district at Moreton Bay. The city spreads across the hilly floodplain of the river valley between the Pacific Ocean and the Taylor and D'Aguilar ranges. It takes its name from the river, which was named for Sir Thomas Brisbane, governor of New South Wales from 1821 to 1825. The climate is humid subtropical, with hot, wet summers and mild, drier winters. Most central streets are named after members of the House of Hanover, and Queen Street, named for Queen Victoria, is the traditional main street.

The Brisbane region has been inhabited for more than 22,000 years by the Yagara (Yuggera), Turrbal and Quandamooka peoples. The river, known as Maiwar, formed the heart of cultural, economic and ceremonial life, and the central city peninsula was traditionally known as Meeanjin. Matthew Flinders charted parts of Moreton Bay in 1799, and John Oxley found the river in 1823 with the help of castaways and recommended the area for a penal settlement. The penal station, first set up at Redcliffe, moved to North Quay in May 1825. Under Captain Patrick Logan it gained a reputation as one of the harshest in New South Wales, and it saw recurrent conflict with neighbouring Indigenous peoples. It was closed in 1842, opening the district to free colonisation.

German Lutherans founded the first free settlement, Zion Hill at Nundah, in 1838, and in 1859 Brisbane was chosen as capital when Queensland separated from New South Wales. In the early 20th century it saw labour unrest, including the 1912 Brisbane general strike. The creation of the City of Brisbane in 1925, by merging twenty smaller local government areas, formed Australia's largest municipal authority. During the Second World War the Allied command in the South West Pacific was based in the city, together with the headquarters of General Douglas MacArthur.

Brisbane is the capital of Queensland and the third most populous city in Australia, with about 2.8 million people in the metropolitan area. Its surviving early buildings include the Commissariat Store on William Street, built by convict labour in 1828, and the Old Windmill in Wickham Park, the oldest surviving building in the city. City Hall opened in 1930 and the Story Bridge in 1940. The city hosted the 1982 Commonwealth Games and World Expo 88, and has been chosen to host the 2032 Summer Olympics. Its surrounding region includes Moreton Bay and the Gondwana Rainforests, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
british-columbia: British Columbia lies between the Pacific Ocean and the Rocky Mountains and has a varied geography of rocky coasts, forests, lakes, mountains, inland deserts and grassy plains. It borders Alberta to the east, Yukon and the Northwest Territories to the north, the US states of Washington, Idaho and Montana to the south, and Alaska to the northwest. Its southern border was established by the Oregon Treaty of 1846. The coastline runs for more than 27,000 km and includes deep fjords and about 6,000 islands.

The first known people settled in the area at least 10,000 years ago, among them the Coast Salish, Tsilhqotʼin and Haida peoples. There are more than 200 First Nations in the province. Smallpox killed at least 30 per cent of the First Nations of the Pacific Northwest in the 1770s, and the epidemic of 1862 killed about half to two thirds of the native population of what became British Columbia.

Fort Victoria, founded in 1843, was one of the earliest British settlements, and it gave rise to the city of Victoria, capital of the Colony of Vancouver Island. The name British Columbia was chosen by Queen Victoria in 1858 and refers to the Columbia District, the British term for the region drained by the Columbia River, which the Hudson's Bay Company had administered; British was added to distinguish it from the American territory to the south. In 1858 an influx of Americans during the Fraser Canyon Gold Rush led the Colonial Office to designate the mainland as the Colony of British Columbia. Richard Clement Moody founded the colony and chose New Westminster as its capital.

Further gold rushes followed, the largest being the Cariboo Gold Rush of 1862, which pushed the colonial government deeper into debt. The Vancouver Island colony had financial crises of its own, and the two colonies were merged in 1866, with Victoria as capital. Once the Canadian government agreed to extend the Canadian Pacific Railway to the province and assume the colony's debt, British Columbia became the sixth province to join Confederation on 20 July 1871.

British Columbia is the westernmost province of Canada. Its capital is Victoria and its largest city is Vancouver, whose port is the largest in Canada. Forestry, mining and tourism are among the main sectors of its economy. English is the common language of the province, and the Franco-Columbian community is an officially recognised linguistic minority.
british-empire: The empire began with the overseas possessions and trading posts that England established in the late 16th and early 17th centuries, and with Scottish colonisation attempts in the 17th century. Motivated by the wealth of the Portuguese and Spanish empires, England, France and the Netherlands founded colonies and trade networks in the Americas and Asia. The first permanent English settlement in the Americas was Jamestown, founded in 1607, and the English East India Company, chartered in 1600, challenged the Portuguese monopoly of trade with Asia.

Wars of the 17th and 18th centuries with the Netherlands and France left Britain the dominant colonial power in North America, and the East India Company's conquest of Mughal Bengal at the Battle of Plassey in 1757 made it a major power in India. Britain lost the Thirteen Colonies after the American Revolution, and independence was acknowledged at the Peace of Paris in 1783. Colonial expansion then turned to Asia, Africa and the Pacific. The first convicts arrived in Australia in 1788, and colonisation brought disease, violence and dispossession to Indigenous Australians.

Parliament abolished the slave trade in the empire in 1807, and the Slavery Abolition Act ended slavery there from 1 August 1834, with an apprenticeship system that lasted until 1838 and compensation paid to slave-owners. After the defeat of Napoleon in 1815 Britain had no serious rival at sea, and between 1815 and 1914 around 26 million km2 and roughly 400 million people were added. The Maratha Empire was defeated in 1818, rivalry with Russia in Central Asia became the Great Game, and the Scramble for Africa followed.

The white settler colonies gained self-government step by step, from Canada's confederation in 1867 to the Australian federation in 1901, and the term dominion status was introduced in 1907. The empire reached its largest extent after the First World War, covering 24 per cent of the Earth's land in 1920. India gained independence on 15 August 1947 with the partition that cost hundreds of thousands of lives. Harold Macmillan spoke of the wind of change in Cape Town in 1960, and nearly thirty colonies became independent in that decade.

Most former colonies joined the Commonwealth of Nations, a voluntary association of equal members. Hong Kong was handed to China on 1 July 1997, an event that symbolised the end of the empire for many. Britain keeps sovereignty over fourteen overseas territories. Historians' approaches to the empire are diverse and still changing, and post-colonial studies have led to a critical re-evaluation of the history of imperialism.
british-museum: The British Museum was founded as a universal museum on the will of Sir Hans Sloane (1660–1753), an Anglo-Irish physician and naturalist who lived in London. He gathered a large collection of curiosities and, not wishing it to be broken up, bequeathed it to King George II for the nation, with Parliament to pay his heirs £20,000, far less than its estimated value. On 7 June 1753 the king gave royal assent to the act establishing the museum, which added the Cottonian and Harleian libraries to the Sloane collection. The Old Royal Library joined them in 1757. The trustees bought Montagu House, and the museum opened to the public in 1759.

From 1778 objects from the South Seas, brought back from the voyages of Captain James Cook, drew visitors. After the French defeat at the Battle of the Nile in 1801 the museum acquired more Egyptian sculpture, and in 1802 King George III presented the Rosetta Stone. Thomas Bruce, 7th Earl of Elgin, ambassador to the Ottoman Empire from 1799 to 1803, removed marble sculptures from the Parthenon, and they were acquired under an act of 1816. Assyrian and Babylonian antiquities bought from Mary Mackintosh Rich in 1825 began the Ancient Near Eastern collection.

Sir Robert Smirke's neoclassical building replaced Montagu House from 1823, and Sydney Smirke's Round Reading Room opened in 1857. The natural history collections were removed to South Kensington by 1887. The library department was separated in 1973 under the British Library Act 1972, and once the British Library left in 1998 the Queen Elizabeth II Great Court, the largest covered square in Europe, opened in 2000.

The original 1753 collection has grown to over 13 million objects at the museum. Its Middle Eastern collection of some 330,000 works is the largest collection of Mesopotamian antiquities outside Iraq, with rooms panelled in alabaster Assyrian palace reliefs from Nimrud, Nineveh and Khorsabad. Some of its best-known acquisitions, among them the Elgin Marbles and the Rosetta Stone, are subject to long-term disputes and repatriation claims. Like all national museums in the United Kingdom, it charges no admission fee except for loan exhibitions.
british-overseas-territories: The British Overseas Territories are the remnants of the former British Empire that stayed under British sovereignty after decolonisation, with varying constitutional statuses. Early English colonies were generally called plantations, and the first, unofficial, colony was Newfoundland, where English fishermen set up seasonal camps in the 16th century. Gibraltar was captured from Spain in 1704 by a force under Admiral Sir George Rooke, acting for the Grand Alliance, and was ceded to Great Britain by the Treaty of Utrecht in 1713. The Colonial Office once oversaw all British colonies. Today the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office does so, except for the Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia in Cyprus, which come under the Ministry of Defence.

The fourteen territories lie outside the British Islands and are not part of the United Kingdom itself. They recognise the British monarch as head of state, and in territories with a permanent population a governor is appointed on the advice of the British government. Each has its own legal system, generally based on English common law, and the highest court for all of them is the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London. The United Kingdom keeps authority over defence, foreign relations and internal security. Three territories, the British Antarctic Territory, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands and the British Indian Ocean Territory, have no permanent civilian population.

From 1949 to 1983 residents of the territories shared the status of Citizen of the United Kingdom and Colonies with residents of the United Kingdom. In 1983 the British Nationality Act 1981 replaced their status with British Dependent Territories citizenship. Falkland Islanders were automatically granted full British citizenship because of the Falklands War. Of the eleven territories with permanent populations, all except the Sovereign Base Areas are on the United Nations list of non-self-governing territories. Many of the territories are used as military bases.
british-raj: The name comes from the Hindustani rāj, meaning reign, rule or government. The system was instituted on 28 June 1858, when, after the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the rule of the East India Company passed to the Crown in the person of Queen Victoria, who was proclaimed Empress of India in 1876. The Rebellion had shaken the British enterprise without derailing it, but the British became more circumspect and drew lessons about communication between British and Indians. The Raj extended over almost all of present-day India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Myanmar, except small holdings such as Goa, held by Portugal, and Pondicherry, held by France.

Two kinds of territory made up the Raj. British India was governed directly through the Governor-General and the provinces, while the princely states, 565 of them in 1947, were ruled by indigenous princes under British paramountcy. In the princely states, external affairs, defence and most communications were under British control. The Government of India Act 1858 changed governance in London, in the central government in Calcutta and in the provinces.

Railways, roads, canals, bridges and telegraph links were built rapidly, tying the economies of India and Britain together. By 1890 some 60,000 Indians had matriculated at the universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, producing an educated professional bureaucracy, though almost all of the top civil service posts were held by Britons. The population reached 255 million in the first census of 1881. India also saw major famines. Estimates of deaths in the Great Famine of 1876 to 1878 run from 6.1 million to 10.39 million, and historians continue to debate whether British rule accelerated or distorted the country's economic development.

A new middle class grew after 1880, and Indians took encouragement from Queen Victoria's proclamation of 1858. Lord Curzon's partition of Bengal in 1905 drew a largely Hindu protest, and in 1906 Muslim leaders asked the new viceroy, Lord Minto, for separate electorates, which led to the founding of the All-India Muslim League in Dacca. About 1.4 million Indian and British soldiers of the British Indian Army served in the First World War. On 13 April 1919 troops commanded by Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer fired on an unarmed gathering at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar; the government reported 379 dead and 1,100 wounded, and the Indian National Congress estimated three times as many dead.

In 1939 the viceroy, Lord Linlithgow, declared war on India's behalf without consulting Indian leaders, and the Congress provincial ministries resigned in protest, while the Muslim League supported the war effort and grew rapidly. In 1946 mutinies in the armed services, notably in the Royal Indian Navy, prompted the Labour government to send the Cabinet Mission. In 1947 the Raj was partitioned into two dominions, the Union of India and the Dominion of Pakistan.
brixen: Brixen, in Italian Bressanone, lies about 40 kilometres north of Bolzano at the confluence of the Eisack and Rienz rivers, 45 kilometres south of the Brenner Pass. To the east rises the Plose mountain massif, and to the west the Sarntal Alps. The town is more than 70 percent German-speaking and officially bilingual in German and Italian. Finds at Stufels suggest a Rhaetian culture here before the Romans.

The area has been settled since the Stone Age, and in 15 BCE the Romans conquered it, with their main settlement at nearby Säben (Sabiona). They held it until about 590, when Bavarians occupied it. The first mention of Brixen, as Prihsna, is in a document of 901 by King Louis III the Child, which gave a farm to Bishop Zacharias of Säben. The bishops moved here from Säben in 992, after the cathedral was finished.

In 1048 Poppo, Bishop of Brixen, was made pope by the emperor Henry III as Damasus II and died after 23 days. On 15 June 1080 the synod of Brixen condemned Pope Gregory VII in the Investiture Controversy. A first ring of walls was finished in 1115, and fires devastated the town in 1174, 1234 and 1445. After the German mediatisation, Brixen was awarded to Austria in 1802, ceded to Bavaria in 1805 after Austerlitz and returned to Austria by the Congress of Vienna in 1814.

Under the Treaty of London of 1915 Italy was promised South Tyrol, and in 1919 the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye awarded Brixen to Italy. After the Second World War Austria considered the settlement unsatisfactory, raising the South Tyrolean Question, and in 1972 South Tyrol was granted autonomy within Trentino-Alto Adige.

Brixen is the third-largest city and the oldest town in South Tyrol. The cathedral, dedicated to the Assumption of Mary, dates from the 10th century, was rebuilt in the 13th century and again in 1745–54 in Baroque style, and has a ceiling fresco by Paul Troger. The Hofburg, a Renaissance bishop's palace begun in the 13th century, houses the Diocesan Museum. The White Tower of 1591 holds a carillon of 43 bells.
bucharest: Bucharest stands on the banks of the Dâmbovița River, which flows into the Argeș, a tributary of the Danube. Several lakes, the largest being Herăstrău, Floreasca, Tei and Colentina, lie across the northern parts of the city along the Colentina River. In the centre a small artificial lake is surrounded by the Cișmigiu Gardens, opened in 1847 to plans by the German architect Carl F. W. Meyer and long frequented by poets and writers.

The origin of the name București is unverified. Tradition links the founding with a man named Bucur, variously a prince, an outlaw, a fisherman, a shepherd or a hunter, and connects the name with the Romanian word bucurie, 'joy'. The Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi claimed it came from a certain Abu-Kariș, and an early 19th-century book derived it from a beech forest, Bukovie.

Bucharest was first mentioned in 1459 as the 'Citadel of București', when it was the residence of the ruler of Wallachia, Vlad the Impaler. The Old Princely Court was built by Mircea Ciobanul in the mid-16th century, and the city became the summer residence of the court. It competed with Târgoviște for the status of capital, as the Ottoman Empire, the suzerain power, increased the importance of southern Muntenia. After 1698, beginning with the reign of Constantin Brâncoveanu, it was the permanent seat of the Wallachian court. Natural disasters partly destroyed it several times in the following two centuries.

From the 18th century the Ottomans appointed Greek Christian administrators, the Phanariotes, to run the town, and their rule ended after the Wallachian uprising of 1821 led by Tudor Vladimirescu. Bucharest became the capital of the Romanian United Principalities in 1862 and boomed after the founding of the Romanian Kingdom in 1881, when it became known for cosmopolitan life and eclectic architecture and was nicknamed the Paris of the East. It was severely damaged in the Second World War. Its population grew rapidly from the late 19th century until the war, and again under Nicolae Ceaușescu from 1965 to 1989, when a massive urbanization campaign drew migrants from rural areas; it first reached one million in the 1940s.

Bucharest is the capital and largest city of Romania. It has a unique administrative status, being the only municipal area that is not part of a county, though its population of 1,716,961 at the 2021 census is larger than that of any county. Among its landmarks is the Palace of the Parliament, built in the 1980s under Ceaușescu and the largest parliament building in the world.
budapest: Budapest stands on the River Danube, at the centre of the Pannonian Basin, on an ancient route linking the hills of Transdanubia with the Great Plain. The names Buda and Pest are of obscure origin. Buda was probably the name of the first constable of the fortress built on Castle Hill in the 11th century, or derives from a personal name of Turkic origin, Bod or Bud, meaning 'twig'. Before the unification of 1873 the towns together were sometimes called Pest-Buda. In colloquial Hungarian, Buda means the districts west of the Danube, including the former Óbuda, and Pest those to the east. The city is now divided into 23 districts.

The first settlement on the territory of Budapest was built by Celts before 1 CE and was later occupied by the Romans. The Roman settlement of Aquincum became the main city of Pannonia Inferior in 106 CE. It began as a military settlement, around which a city gradually rose, and its site corresponds to the Óbuda district. The Romans built roads, amphitheatres, baths and houses with heated floors. The area east of the Danube was outside the Roman Empire and remained Germanic and Sarmatian in character.

After the foundation of Hungary in the late 9th century the area was pillaged by the Mongols in 1241. It became the royal seat in 1361, and under Matthias Corvinus Buda was by the 15th century one of the European centres of Renaissance culture. The siege of Buda in 1541 was followed by nearly 150 years of Ottoman rule, and after the reconquest of Buda in 1686 the region entered an age of prosperity. The city was the focal point of the Hungarian Revolution of 1848, the Battle of Budapest in 1945 and the Hungarian Revolution of 1956. In 1896 it opened the first underground transit line on the European continent, now the M1 Millennium Underground.

Budapest is the seat of the Hungarian national government, and the National Assembly sits in the neo-Gothic Hungarian Parliament, the largest building in the country. The historic centre along the Danube, with Buda Castle and the 13th-century Matthias Church, is a World Heritage Site, as are the Castle Hill, the Danube embankments and Andrássy út. Other landmarks include the State Opera House, St Stephen's Basilica, which displays the Holy Right Hand of Hungary's first king, and the Roman remains of the Aquincum Museum. The city has been a spa destination since Roman times, with more than 100 medicinal geothermal springs.
buddhas-of-bamiyan: Bamiyan lies on the Silk Road in the Hindu Kush, about 130 kilometres north-west of Kabul at an elevation of 2,500 metres. Since the 2nd century CE it had been a Buddhist religious site under the Kushans, a thriving centre of religion, philosophy and art. Monks lived as hermits in small caves cut into the cliffs, many decorating them with statues and frescoes in the culture of Gandhara. The two Buddhas were carved possibly around the 6th century, when the Hephthalites ruled the region as principalities.

The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited the site on 30 April 630. He described Bamyan as a flourishing Buddhist centre with more than ten monasteries and more than a thousand monks, and noted that both figures were decorated with gold and fine jewels.

The Buddhas were technically reliefs, since each merged at the back into the cliff wall. The smaller, 38 metres tall, was called Shah Mama, Queen Mother, and the larger, 55 metres tall, Salsal. The main bodies were hewn from the sandstone cliff, and the details were modelled in mud mixed with straw and coated with stucco, which was painted to enhance the faces, hands and folds of the robes. The larger statue was painted carmine red and the smaller in several colours. The sculptures show a later stage of the blended Greco-Buddhist style of Gandhara.

Numerous caves around the Buddhas were decorated with wall paintings. The ceiling above the smaller Buddha showed a solar deity in a golden chariot drawn by four horses, derived from the Iranian god Mithra as revered in Sogdia. The paintings combine Buddhist art, Gupta art from India, and influences from the Sasanian and Byzantine empires.

Bamiyan passed to Muslim rule in 770 and finally, in 977, under Turkic Ghaznavid rule. In 1221 Genghis Khan invaded the valley, wiping out most of its population, but left the Buddhas undamaged. In the 17th century the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb briefly ordered artillery used against the carvings, which survived without major harm. In July 1999 Mullah Omar decreed that the statues be preserved.

On 26 February 2001 Omar ordered the destruction of all statues in Afghanistan, and in March 2001 the Taliban destroyed both Buddhas, a decision justified by the Taliban as being in accordance with Islamic law. International and local opinion condemned it. The site was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003 as an outstanding expression of Gandharan Buddhism. The outlines of the Buddhas remain recognisable in their niches.
buddhism: Buddhism is based on teachings attributed to the Buddha, a wandering ascetic and religious teacher who lived in South Asia in the 6th or 5th century BCE, the 5th century being the best estimate. The accounts of his life in the early texts are inconsistent. They give his family name as Gautama and place his birth at Lumbini, in present-day Nepal. Legends make his father a king named Suddhodana, but scholars such as Richard Gombrich doubt this, since the evidence suggests he came from the Shakya community, governed by a small oligarchy or council.

The roots of the religion lie in the intellectual ferment of Iron Age India around the middle of the first millennium BCE, the period of the Upanishads and the rise of the Śramaṇa movements, which included Buddhism and Jainism.

According to tradition, the Buddha taught a path that leads to release from dukkha, suffering or unsatisfactoriness, by reaching nirvana, the extinguishing of the passions. He regarded it as a Middle Way between extreme asceticism and sensory indulgence. The Four Noble Truths hold that everything is impermanent, yet people crave and cling to impermanent things, which is dukkha, and that the Noble Eightfold Path leads out of the cycle of rebirth. Taking the Three Refuges, in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, is the traditional first step in most schools.

The Buddha's words were first passed on orally, and the first canonical texts were probably written down in Sri Lanka about 400 years after his death. Scholars generally recognise two surviving branches, Theravāda and Mahāyāna. Theravada holds the Pali Canon as its only authority, and Mahayana, with roots in the 1st century BCE, also honours later literature and stresses the Bodhisattva ideal of working for the liberation of all beings. Vajrayāna, which includes esoteric tantric techniques, may be seen as a separate branch or part of Mahayana.

Buddhism spread gradually through much of Asia along the Silk Road and reached the West in the 19th century. Until the early second millennium it was widely practised in the Indian subcontinent before declining there. Learning centres such as Nalanda and Vikramashila preserved classical Indian disciplines, including grammar, astronomy and medicine, and taught foreign students from across Asia. The religion influenced the cultures of Asia deeply, in philosophy, art, architecture and festivals, and shaped the development of Hinduism, Taoism and Confucianism.
buenos-aires: Buenos Aires lies on the southwest shore of the Río de la Plata, which is called the world's widest river, in the pampa region. Several districts, among them Puerto Madero and the main port, were built on land reclaimed along the river. The area was once crossed by streams and lagoons. As floods damaged the city's infrastructure in 1908, many streams were channelled, and from 1919 most were enclosed. The Maldonado was tubed in 1954 and now runs below Juan B. Justo Avenue. The city is laid out on a rectangular grid of square blocks, 110 metres long, called manzanas.

The name comes from Santa Maria de los Buenos Aires, Holy Mary of the Good Winds. Spanish sailors, especially Andalusians, invoked the Virgin of the Buen Ayre, named after Our Lady of Bonaria in Cagliari, Sardinia. Juan Díaz de Solís was the first European to reach the Río de la Plata, in 1516, and was killed in an attack by the Charrúa. Pedro de Mendoza founded the city on 2 February 1536, in what is now the San Telmo district.

Attacks by indigenous people forced the settlers away, and the site was abandoned in 1541 or 1542. A second and permanent settlement was established on 11 June 1580 by Juan de Garay, who came down the Paraná River from Asunción. He named it Santísima Trinidad, and its port became the Puerto de Santa María de los Buenos Aires. Later rule is grouped as Habsburg Spain to 1700, Bourbon Spain to 1808, the United Provinces of the Río de la Plata from 1810 and the Argentine Confederation from 1831. The State of Buenos Aires existed from 1852 to 1861.

In 1880, after the Argentine Civil War, the city was federalised and split from Buenos Aires Province, and its limits grew to include Belgrano and Flores. Since the 19th century the city and country have received millions of immigrants from many parts of the world. The Parque Tres de Febrero was inaugurated on 11 November 1875, and the Botanical Gardens on 7 September 1898, both later work of the French Argentine urbanist Carlos Thays.

Buenos Aires is the capital and largest city of Argentina. A constitutional amendment of 1994 gave it autonomy, hence its formal name, the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires, and its citizens elected their first chief of government in 1996. The city proper had 2,891,082 residents at the 2010 census, with 13,147,638 in Greater Buenos Aires. It is home to the Teatro Colón, an opera house, and to the Avenida 9 de Julio, 140 metres wide. The city joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network in 2005 as a City of Design.
bulawayo: Bulawayo is the largest city of Zimbabwe's Matabeleland region. It covers 546 square kilometres in the west of the country along the Matsheumhlope River, and most of its people belong to the Ndebele, with minorities of Shona and others. The city lies close to Matobo National Park and the Khami World Heritage Site.

The settlement began as a kraal of the Ndebele king Mzilikazi, who led his people north from Kwazulu. His son Lobengula succeeded him in the 1860s and ruled from Bulawayo until 1893. The name comes from the Ndebele word bulala and is translated as the one to be killed. Many European powers coveted the town, and Britain used Cecil Rhodes and the Chartered Company to avoid alarming its rivals. Lobengula once described Britain as a chameleon and himself as the fly.

In the First Matabele War of 1893, troops of the British South Africa Company invaded and forced Lobengula to leave, after he had blown up munitions and set the town on fire. On 4 November 1893 Leander Starr Jameson declared Bulawayo a settlement under company rule, and Rhodes ordered it founded on the ruins of the royal kraal, where State House now stands. During the Second Matabele War the town was besieged from March 1896. Settlers sheltered in a laager, and more than 10,000 Ndebele warriors gathered but never mounted a significant attack. Relief forces arrived in late May 1896.

Bulawayo became a municipality in 1897 and a city in 1943. By the late 1930s it was no longer the country's largest city, as activity shifted east towards Salisbury, but after the Second World War it grew again as an industrial centre.

Bulawayo is Zimbabwe's second largest city, and a hub of the national rail network and headquarters of the National Railways of Zimbabwe. Its wide central streets were designed so that ox-drawn carts could turn in them. The National University of Science and Technology and the Natural History Museum of Zimbabwe are in the city, which is nicknamed the City of Kings.
bulgaria: Bulgaria covers 110,994 square kilometres in the east of the Balkans, south of the Danube and west of the Black Sea, with a coastline of 354 kilometres. Its main topographical features are the Danubian Plain, the Balkan Mountains, the Upper Thracian Plain and the Rila-Rhodope massif. The Balkan Mountains run from west to east through the middle of the country, and Musala, at 2,925 metres, is the highest point in both Bulgaria and the Balkans. Plains occupy about a third of the territory and plateaux and hills 41%. The climate is varied and changeable because the country lies at the meeting point of Mediterranean, Oceanic and Continental air masses.

Neanderthal remains of around 150,000 years ago are among the earliest traces of human activity, and the Karanovo culture arose c. 6,500 BCE. The Varna culture is credited with the invention of goldworking and produced the oldest golden jewellery in the world, over 6,000 years old. The Thracians appeared on the Balkan Peninsula before the 12th century BCE, and after the defeat of the second Persian invasion in 479 BCE most of the tribes united under king Teres to form the Odrysian kingdom.
Philip II of Macedon vassalised it in 341 BCE, and it became a Roman province in 45 CE. In the 6th century the Slavs entered the Balkans and assimilated the Thracians.

The Bulgars, led by Asparuh, permanently invaded the Balkans in the late 7th century and established the First Bulgarian Empire, recognised by the Byzantine Empire in 681. It dominated most of the Balkans and influenced Slavic cultures through the Cyrillic script, which the Preslav Literary School developed. It lasted until the early 11th century, when the Byzantine emperor Basil II conquered and dismantled it.

A revolt in 1185 established the Second Bulgarian Empire, which reached its apex under Ivan Asen II (1218–1241), and in 1396 the empire, weakened by wars and feudal strife, fell under Ottoman rule for nearly five centuries.

The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78 resulted in the third and current Bulgarian state, which declared independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1908. Many ethnic Bulgarians were left outside its borders, which stoked irredentist sentiment, conflicts with neighbours and alliances with Germany in both world wars.

In 1946 Bulgaria came under the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc as a socialist state, and the Communist Party gave up its monopoly on power after the revolutions of 1989. It has been a parliamentary republic of 28 provinces since the constitution of 1991, and a member of the European Union and NATO.
bulgarians: Bulgarians derive their name from the Bulgars. The name is not fully understood and is difficult to trace back before the 4th century CE; it may come from a Proto-Turkic word meaning to mix or stir. Among the main elements that formed the Bulgarians are the Thracians, a native ancient Balkan people, and the early Slavs, who migrated into the Balkans in the 6th and 7th centuries CE and imposed their language and culture on the local Thracian, Roman and Greek communities.

The question of ethnogenesis has been contested since the 19th century. Suggested proportions of Thracian, Bulgar and Slavic ancestry have shifted with the political situation: the Communist government encouraged the study of the Thracians in the 1970s, while some nationalist writers have reinterpreted the Danubian Bulgars as a numerous people rather than a limited group of Turkic horsemen.

Bulgaria was founded in 681 as a Slav-Bulgar state. A symbiosis took place between the numerically weak Bulgars and the numerous Slavic tribes who accepted the common name Bulgarians. After the adoption of Orthodox Christianity in 864 it became one of the cultural centres of Slavic Europe, and its position was consolidated by the invention of the Cyrillic script in its capital Preslav at the eve of the 10th century.

The development of Old Church Slavonic literacy in the 10th century prevented the assimilation of the South Slavs into neighbouring cultures and stimulated a Bulgarian national identity. Ottoman rule lasted from 1396 to 1878. During the Russo-Turkish Wars of 1806–1812 and 1828–1829 Bulgarian emigrants formed the Bulgarian Countrymen's Army and joined the Russian army, hoping for liberation. Under the Ottoman Empire a struggle began for schools and liturgy in Bulgarian and for an independent church organisation, which flared up in several dioceses in the 1820s.

Most Bulgarians live in Bulgaria, and there are historical communities in North Macedonia, Ukraine, Moldova, Serbia, Albania, Romania, Hungary and Greece. Bulgarians speak a South Slavic language mutually intelligible with Macedonian. It shares some developments with Romanian, Albanian and Greek, and was influenced by Greek and Turkish.

Most Bulgarians are at least nominally members of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church, founded in 870 and autocephalous since 927. It was abolished during Ottoman rule, revived in 1873 as the Bulgarian Exarchate and soon raised again to a patriarchate.
burgos: Burgos lies in the north of the Iberian Peninsula, near the confluence of the Arlanzón and the Vena rivers and at the edge of the central plateau, at an elevation of 865 metres. Early humans occupied sites around Burgos as early as 800,000 years ago, and the nearby site of Atapuerca, 20 kilometres to the east, has yielded fossils and stone tools of the earliest known hominids in western Europe. When the Romans took possession the site had been a Celtic city. The name Burgos probably reflects the Visigothic word for walled villages, from the Gothic baurgs.

After the Visigoths drove back the Suebi in the 5th century and the Berbers briefly held Castile in the 8th, Alfonso III of Asturias conquered the area about the middle of the 9th century and built castles, from which Castile took its name, the land of castles. Diego Rodríguez Porcelos gathered the inhabitants of the surrounding country into one fortified village in 884, and the city began to be called Caput Castellae, Head of Castile. In the 11th century it became an archdiocesan see and capital of the Kingdom of Castile. It was a major stop for pilgrims on the French Way to Santiago de Compostela and a centre of trade, attracting a large foreign merchant population that joined the city oligarchy.

In the 13th and 14th centuries Burgos was a favourite seat of the kings of León and Castile and a favoured burial site. Royal charters of 1255 and 1266 relieved from taxes those citizens who owned horses and could arm themselves. In 1285 Sancho IV added a body called the jurado to the town council, and on 9 June 1345 Alfonso XI established direct royal rule through the Regimiento of sixteen appointed men. In 1574 Pope Gregory XIII made the bishopric a metropolitan archbishopric at the request of Philip II. During the Peninsular War Wellington withdrew from the siege of Burgos, and the castle was destroyed by the French in 1813.

Burgos is the capital of its province in Castile and León and its second most populated city. Construction of its Gothic cathedral began in 1221 and spanned mainly the 13th to 15th centuries; it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and holds the remains of El Cid and his wife Doña Jimena. The city also has the monastery of Las Huelgas, founded in 1180 by Alfonso VIII, and the Carthusian monastery of Miraflores, with the tombs of Juan II and Queen Isabella of Portugal. The Museum of Human Evolution, opened in 2010, draws on the Atapuerca site. The University of Burgos was established in 1994.
burkina-faso: Burkina Faso covers 274,223 square kilometres. Most of the country is a peneplain, a gently undulating landscape with a few isolated hills that are the last vestiges of a Precambrian massif. The southwest is a sandstone massif, bordered by cliffs up to 150 metres high, where the highest peak, Ténakourou, rises to 749 metres. The country owed its former name, Upper Volta, to three rivers, the Black Volta (Mouhoun), the White Volta (Nakambé) and the Red Volta (Nazinon). Only the Black Volta and the Komoé flow year-round, and water shortages are often a problem in the north.

The northwest was populated by hunter-gatherers from about 14,000 BCE to 5,000 BCE, and agricultural settlements were established between 3600 and 2600 BCE. The oldest evidence of iron smelting in Burkina Faso dates from 800 to 700 BCE and forms part of the Ancient Ferrous Metallurgy World Heritage Site. The Bura culture existed in the southeast from the 3rd to the 13th century CE.

From medieval times until the end of the 19th century the central region was ruled by the Mossi, descendants of Dagomba warriors from present-day Ghana who mixed with Mandé and other local peoples in the 11th century. They established separate kingdoms, among them Tenkodogo, Yatenga, Zandoma and Ouagadougou, and defended their territory, beliefs and social structure against attempts at conquest and conversion from Muslims to the northwest.

The Tarikh al-Sudan reports that a Mossi ruler took control of Timbuktu between 1328 and 1338, during the reign of Mansa Musa, and the Tarikh al-fattash describes conflicts between the 15th-century Mossi king Komdao and the Songhay ruler Sonni Ali. The Mossi were defeated at the Battle of Kobi in 1483. The French colonised the area in 1896 as part of French West Africa, and it became fully independent in 1960 as the Republic of Upper Volta. On 4 August 1984 President Thomas Sankara renamed it Burkina Faso.

Ouagadougou is the capital and largest city. The name joins Burkina, from Mooré, meaning upright, with Faso, from Dyula, meaning fatherland. The country is a semi-presidential republic and a member of the United Nations. About half the population is Mossi, whose kingdom is led by the Mogho Naba, whose court is in Ouagadougou. There are more than 60 indigenous languages, and Mooré is spoken by more than half the population. Most people are Muslim, with Christian and animist minorities. Literature rests on oral tradition, and Ouagadougou hosts the International Art and Craft Fair, one of the most important African handicraft fairs.
byblos: Byblos lies on the coast of Lebanon about 42 kilometres north of Beirut. It is believed to have been first settled between 8800 and 7000 BCE and continuously inhabited since 5000 BCE. Urbanisation is thought to have begun in the third millennium BCE, making it one of the oldest cities in the world. The name appears as kbnj in Egyptian records going back to the pharaoh Sneferu and as Gebal in Phoenician inscriptions, and it seems to mean Well of the God. Because the city imported papyrus from Egypt, byblos came to mean papyrus in Greek, and the English word Bible ultimately derives from it.

In the Early Bronze Age Byblos developed from a fishermen's village around a shrine at a natural spring into a town with a temple compound. It was a wealthy ally of Egypt for many centuries. About 1350 BCE the Amarna letters include 60 letters from Rib-Hadda and his successor Ili-Rapih, rulers of Byblos, mostly Rib-Hadda's pleas to Akhenaten for military help. When the New Kingdom collapsed in the 11th century BCE, Byblos became the foremost city of Phoenicia. Five royal inscriptions of about 1150–950 BCE, among them the Ahiram sarcophagus, show a Phoenician alphabet of twenty-two characters.

Sibittibaal of Byblos became tributary to Tiglath-Pileser III in 738 BCE, and under the Achaemenid Empire Byblos was one of four Phoenician vassal kingdoms. Alexander the Great brought Hellenistic rule in 332 BCE. In the Greco-Roman period it was a centre of the cult of Adonis, and a theatre was built in the 3rd century. Prosperity returned with the First Crusade in 1098.

As Gibelet the city belonged to the Crusader County of Tripoli, and the Genoese Embriaco family held it as a hereditary lordship. Saladin took the town in 1187 and Baibars conquered it in 1266, but the Embriacos kept it until around 1300. The Ottoman Empire ruled it from 1516 until 1918, and it was under the French Mandate from 1920 until 1943.

Byblos is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its archaeological site includes the L-shaped temple of about 2700 BCE, the Temple of the Obelisks, the royal necropolis with the tomb of King Ahiram, the Roman theatre and the Crusader castle of the 12th century. A medieval wall surrounds the old town.
byelorussian-ssr: Before the First World War the lands of modern Belarus belonged to the Russian Empire, which had gained them in the Partitions of Poland. After the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk of March 1918 the Belarusian Democratic Republic was proclaimed under German occupation. As German troops left, the Bolsheviks advanced west, took Minsk on 10 December 1918, and set up the Socialist Soviet Republic of Byelorussia. It was merged with the Lithuanian Soviet Socialist Republic, a union that ceased to exist in the Polish–Soviet War.

The Red Army broke the Polish front in 1920 and retook Minsk on 11 July, and the republic was re-founded on 31 July 1920. The Treaty of Riga of February 1921 divided the country: almost half, Western Belarus, went to Poland, and the rest was the Soviet republic, with 52,400 square kilometres and 1.544 million people. It became one of the four founding members of the Soviet Union in December 1922.

The 1930s marked the peak of Soviet repressions in Belarus. By incomplete calculations about 600,000 people fell victim to them between 1917 and 1953, and over 250,000 Belarusians were deported as kulaks or their families. In September 1939, after the Molotov–Ribbentrop Pact, the Soviet Union incorporated the territories known as West Belarus into the republic.

Nazi Germany occupied Belarus in the summer of 1941. It deported some 380,000 people for forced labour and killed hundreds of thousands of civilians. About 800,000 Belarusian Jews, about 90 percent of the Jewish population, were killed in the Holocaust, and more than 600 villages such as Khatyn were totally annihilated. Over 2,000,000 people, almost a quarter of the population, died during the three years of occupation.

After the war the republic became a founding member of the United Nations, with its own seat beside the Soviet Union and the Ukrainian SSR. Its Supreme Soviet declared sovereignty on 27 July 1990 and independence on 25 August 1991, and on 19 September the republic was renamed the Republic of Belarus.

Until 1990 the republic was a one-party state governed by the Communist Party of Byelorussia, a branch of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union. Minsk was its capital and largest city, and the official languages were Belarusian and Russian. Most of its 10 million people in 1989 were Belarusians, with significant minorities of Russians, Poles, Ukrainians and Jews. It was one of the more developed Soviet republics, with advanced manufacturing and agriculture.
bytom: Bytom lies in Upper Silesia, 7 km northwest of Katowice. Its bedrock holds coal and iron ore from the Carboniferous period, and in the Bytom basin triassic rocks carry ore, zinc and lead reserves. The city's coat of arms shows a miner mining coal on one half and a yellow eagle on a blue field, the symbol of Upper Silesia, on the other.

The town is first recorded as Bitom in 1136, when it was part of the medieval Kingdom of Poland. Excavations show a fortified settlement, probably founded by Bolesław I the Brave in the early 11th century. It profited from its place on trade routes linking Kraków with Silesia and Hungary with Moravia and Greater Poland. The first church of the Virgin Mary was built in 1231, and the Mongols raided the town in 1259. The duchy lay under the overlordship of the Kingdom of Bohemia from 1289 and lasted until 1498, when it was reunited with the Duchy of Opole.

The town came under the Habsburg monarchy in 1526, and in 1742 it became part of the Kingdom of Prussia during the Silesian Wars. In 1683 King John III Sobieski visited on his way to the Battle of Vienna. After 1871, in the German Empire, the city grew and industrialised rapidly. According to the Prussian census of 1905 it had 60,273 inhabitants, of whom 59% spoke German, 38% Polish and 3% both.

Bytom was a main centre of Polish organisation in Upper Silesia. The newspaper Dziennik Górnośląski appeared from 1848, and Polish societies were harassed by the Prussian authorities. In the plebiscite of 1921, 74.7% of the votes in the city were for Germany and 25.3% for Poland. The synagogue was burned on 9 and 10 November 1938, and the Red Army captured the city in January 1945.

Bytom is a city in the Silesian Voivodeship of southern Poland. It is the home of the Silesian Opera and the Upper Silesian Museum, and it holds part of the Tarnowskie Góry Lead-Silver-Zinc Mine and its Underground Water Management System, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
byzantion: The origin of the name is unknown. It has been suggested to be Thracian, perhaps from the personal name Byzas, which means he-goat. Greek legend names Byzas as the leader of the Megarian colonists and founder of the city. The city was mainly a trading city because it stood at the only entrance to the Black Sea, and it later conquered Chalcedon across the Bosphorus. Its position, surrounded by water on almost all sides, made it highly defensible.

Tradition says Byzas of Megara founded the city after sailing northeast across the Aegean. The date is usually given as 667 BCE on the authority of Herodotus. Constantine the Great favoured that dating and marked the city's 1,000th anniversary between 333 and 334. The Persian Empire took the city at the time of Darius I's Scythian campaign in 513 BCE. In the Peloponnesian War Sparta took it in 411 BCE to cut off grain supplies to Athens, and the Athenians retook it in 408 BCE.

After the city sided with Pescennius Niger against Septimius Severus, Roman forces besieged it and badly damaged it in 196 CE. Severus rebuilt it, and it soon regained its prosperity. In 330 CE Constantine I refounded it as an imperial residence modelled on Rome, known as Nova Roma and later as Constantinople. For centuries it was the capital of the Byzantine Empire. The Ottoman Turks conquered it on 29 May 1453.

The name Byzantium was used for the Eastern Roman Empire as a whole only from 1555, when the historian Hieronymus Wolf introduced it. Its inhabitants continued to call their state the empire of the Romans. From the 9th century the names Byzantius and Byzantinus were applied to the empire's gold coinage, which gave the English words besant, byzant and bezant.
